videos.w: Recommended as the standard companion to any Adam Curtis film, since it lampoons the style and gives reasons to take his claims with skepticism.
videos.q: You should always acompany this documentary with a watch of this short little video.

videos.t: LISA11 - Fork Yeah! The Rise and Development of illumos
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill's LISA11 talk on how illumos arose after Oracle closed OpenSolaris. It covers the history of Sun, ZFS, DTrace and Zones, and the diaspora of kernel engineers, with a famous rant about Oracle and Larry Ellison.
videos.w: HN points to it as the definitive, entertaining account of Sun's fate under Oracle, and quotes its Ellison lawnmower advice whenever Oracle behaves badly.
videos.q: If you're interested how it came to be check out this epic talk by Bryan Cantrill

videos.t: Tech Talk: Linus Torvalds on git
videos.s: Linus Torvalds gives a Google tech talk on git, the source control system he created two years earlier. He argues for distributed version control over centralized systems such as CVS and Subversion.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the iconic explanation of why git is designed as it is and why distributed VCS beats centralized ones.
videos.q: This talk by Linus is iconic, if you haven't watched it you should.

videos.t: Why American Cities Are Broke - The Growth Ponzi Scheme [ST03]
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains the Strong Towns argument that car-dependent American suburbs cost more to maintain than they generate in taxes. It describes the growth Ponzi scheme that props up municipal finances.
videos.w: HN keeps pointing to it as the clearest explanation of how low-density infrastructure is financed and why it is unsustainable.
videos.q: I can't recommend this video [1] by Not Just Bikes enough.

videos.t: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
videos.s: Andrej Karpathy's three-hour-plus general-audience deep dive into how ChatGPT-style LLMs are built, covering the full training stack from pretraining to post-training. It also gives mental models for their quirks, like hallucination, and how to use them well.
videos.w: HN's most frequent recommendation for a clear, approachable foundation in how LLMs work without heavy math.
videos.q: I highly recommend Andrej Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT

videos.t: The Coming Collapse of the Middle Class with Elizabeth Warren
videos.s: Elizabeth Warren's 2007 Berkeley lecture, when she was a Harvard law professor, on why middle-class families are under growing financial strain. She draws on bankruptcy research to examine rising costs of housing, health care and education.
videos.w: HN cites it often in debates on inequality, cost disease and stagnant middle-class income, praising its data-driven approach.
videos.q: it's gripping stuff, because she develops insights based on research and hard-nosed science.

videos.t: Alan Kay's tribute to Ted Nelson at "Intertwingled" Festival
videos.s: Alan Kay's tribute to Ted Nelson at the Intertwingled festival, presented using a revived Smalltalk-78 system running on emulated 1970s Xerox PARC hardware. It shows live, user-programmable software from that era.
videos.w: HN returns to it again and again as a demonstration of how programmable and composable 1970s systems were compared with today's.
videos.q: a great example of what's not-even-close to possible on today's systems

videos.t: The Century of the Self - Part 1: "Happiness Machines"
videos.s: The first part of Adam Curtis' documentary series on Sigmund Freud and his nephew Edward Bernays, who invented public relations. It shows how Bernays used Freud's ideas to link mass-produced goods to unconscious desires and create modern consumer persuasion.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it constantly in threads about advertising, propaganda and manipulation as the origin story of the consumer society.
videos.q: There's a great four-part documentary by Adam Curtis about Edward Bernays

videos.t: "Turning the database inside out with Apache Samza" by Martin Kleppmann
videos.s: Martin Kleppmann argues that databases are global shared mutable state and proposes treating them as an ever-growing log of immutable facts. Derived data such as caches, indexes and views is then built by stream processors like Apache Samza. The talk draws on Kafka and LinkedIn's experience with commit logs.
videos.w: Commenters repeatedly cite it as the talk that reframed how they think about caching, derived data and event sourcing.
videos.q: This talk on Apache Samza completely changed how I think about caching and derived data in general

videos.t: Jonathan Blow - How to program independent games -  CSUA Speech
videos.s: Jonathan Blow speaks at UC Berkeley's CSUA about how to program independent games. He argues for keeping code simple, avoiding unnecessary work, and shipping.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a talk whose advice on simplicity and avoiding unnecessary work applies well beyond games.
videos.q: It's about much more than games. To me, it's about identifying and not doing unnecessary work.

videos.t: The Problem With Facebook
videos.s: Veritasium's Derek Muller argues that Facebook's business model works against pages and creators, because it charges them to reach the audiences they built. He explains how filtering and paid promotion undermine the value of likes.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it, with its follow-up, as an exposé of fake likes and bot activity, and as a warning before spending on Facebook ads.
videos.q: before you waste any money, watch these two videos

videos.t: "How NOT to Measure Latency" by Gil Tene
videos.s: Gil Tene of Azul Systems explains common pitfalls in measuring latency and response time, including why averages mislead and the problem of coordinated omission. He introduces open source tools like HdrHistogram for better measurement and reporting.
videos.w: The canonical recommendation whenever percentiles, tail latency, load testing or averages come up, described by some as life changing.
videos.q: This a life changing video by Gil Tene on this topic.

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #1035 - Paul Stamets
videos.s: A two-hour Joe Rogan Experience conversation with mycologist Paul Stamets about fungi, mycelium, bioremediation and medicinal mushrooms. It touches on Lion's Mane, psilocybin and the many uses of fungi.
videos.w: Commenters offer it as a fascinating, accessible introduction to the world of fungi whenever mushrooms or mycelium come up.
videos.q: made a nice introduction to the world of funghi- absolutely fascinating

videos.t: The Engoodening of No Man's Sky
videos.s: Internet Historian tells the story of No Man's Sky, from its over-hyped and badly received launch to years of updates by Hello Games that redeemed the game. It is a long, comedic mini-documentary.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as an entertaining account of a failed launch and recovery, especially in threads about Star Citizen and over-promising.
videos.q: surprisingly a well told, heart-warming (albeit quite long) video telling the story of No Man's Sky

videos.t: Tim Ewald - Clojure: Programming with Hand Tools
videos.s: Tim Ewald's Clojure/conj talk uses furniture making with hand tools versus machine tools as an allegory for software. It explores how automation changes what we make and how we think about our work, and why Clojure's small set of simple tools matters.
videos.w: HN repeatedly names it among the best programming talks, loved for its craftsmanship message that complex tooling can hide simpler solutions.
videos.p: craftsmanship and simple tools in software
videos.q: I loved this talk on how as your tooling becomes more complex and automated, you start to lose sight of simpler solutions to problems.

videos.t: RSA ANIMATE: Drive: The surprising truth about what motivates us
videos.s: An RSA Animate whiteboard adaptation of Dan Pink's talk on what motivates people at work. It argues that beyond simple tasks, autonomy, mastery and purpose drive performance more than money.
videos.w: HN uses it in discussions of pay, management, and motivation as the standard short explanation of autonomy, mastery and purpose.
videos.q: the "Drive: The surprising truth about what motivates us" video is a great rebuttal of this idea.

videos.t: Computer program that learns to play classic NES games
videos.s: Tom7 explains and demos software that learns to play NES games by finding score patterns in memory and then searching for inputs that raise it. It is the video companion to his SIGBOVIK paper.
videos.w: Loved on HN as a hilarious, brilliant example of hacker-academic work and cited whenever game-playing AI or fuzzing comes up.
videos.q: Watch the whole thing, it's delightful.

videos.t: Ruby Conf 12 - Boundaries by Gary Bernhardt
videos.s: Gary Bernhardt's RubyConf 2012 talk on testing in isolation without mocking everything. It goes through behavior versus data, mutation versus immutability, and how a functional core with an imperative shell yields natural isolation and parallelism.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the canonical presentation of 'functional core, imperative shell' and a practical answer to unit versus integration testing.
videos.q: I highly recommend this video for a more philosophical take on how to do "impure FP" without OO

videos.t: CppCon 2016: Jason Turner “Rich Code for Tiny Computers: A Simple Commodore 64 Game in C++17”
videos.s: Jason Turner's CppCon 2016 talk builds a simple Commodore 64 game using C++17, showing how constexpr and const let a modern compiler produce tight 6502 code. He walks through assembly output to show abstractions being optimized away.
videos.w: A perennial favorite, recommended as proof that expressive modern C++ can compile to efficient code even on tiny retro hardware.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: there is a wonderful talk by Jason Turner about writing a simple Pong clone for the Commodore 64 in modern C++

videos.t: Brian Beckman: Don't fear the Monad
videos.s: Microsoft's Brian Beckman gives an hour-long, whiteboard-style walk through monads, building from function composition and monoids using school-level math. It is aimed at practicing programmers rather than category theorists.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the clearest and most correct beginner explanation of monads, with several commenters saying it finally made them click.
videos.q: This video is all you, as a practicing programmer, need to know about monads and it's just 1 hour long.

videos.t: USENIX ATC '21/OSDI '21 Joint Keynote Address-It's Time for Operating Systems to Rediscover Hardware
videos.s: Timothy Roscoe of ETH Zurich delivers the joint USENIX ATC/OSDI 2021 keynote arguing that operating systems must reckon with modern hardware, which is a heterogeneous collection of processors, firmware and coprocessors rather than a simple machine. It shows how much runs below and beside Linux.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended as a revelatory talk on how little control the main OS has over modern SoCs and PCs.
videos.q: There's this great USENIX talk by Timothy Roscoe [1]

videos.t: Why Being Delusional is a Superpower
videos.s: Veritasium examines the role of luck in success, with simulations and examples showing how small advantages and chance can compound. It argues that top outcomes are disproportionately luck-driven while still crediting effort.
videos.w: Linked in threads about meritocracy, careers and startups as a reminder that luck shapes who ends up on top.
videos.q: if you attribute just 5% of outcomes to luck, then the people who have the best outcomes are among the luckiest people

videos.t: The Only Unbreakable Law
videos.s: Casey Muratori's lecture, originally given at the Technical University of Madrid, arguing that Conway's Law is the only viable candidate for a true law of software architecture. He explains how software mimics the organization over time, using examples like Windows' multiple volume controls.
videos.w: HN treats it as the definitive explanation of Conway's Law and links it in almost any thread about org structure shaping software.
videos.q: Casey Muratori has an excellent lecture on this same topic

videos.t: Dr. Michael Greger | How Not To Die | Talks at Google
videos.s: Dr. Michael Greger presents his book How Not to Die at Google NYC, arguing that diet and lifestyle changes can prevent or reverse many of the top causes of death. He walks through evidence on whole-food plant-based eating.
videos.w: Frequently recommended in threads on nutrition, cancer and veganism as a science-focused case for plant-based diets, with at least one commenter saying it made them go vegan.
videos.q: If you're interested in the science, here's a long (but good) talk by Dr. Michael Greger

videos.t: Personal Growth Series: Dr. William Dement on Healthy Sleep and Optimal Perfo...
videos.s: A Google Tech Talk by sleep researcher Dr. William Dement on healthy sleep and performance. He argues sleep debt must be repaid and describes the three characteristics of healthy sleep.
videos.w: HN has recommended it for years as the most useful and entertaining talk on sleep, often to people struggling with tiredness or productivity.
videos.q: The source of information about this that I have found most useful is an hour long talk given by Dr. William Dement

videos.t: Using Python to Code by Voice
videos.s: Tavis Rudd describes how RSI forced him to program by voice, and shows the Python and Emacs Lisp system he built with voice recognition. A live demo creates and deploys a small system without touching the keyboard.
videos.w: Recurs in threads about RSI, accessibility and voice coding as the go-to demo of a custom spoken command language.
videos.q: Travis Rudd's incredible demo of voice coding [1]

videos.t: Clasp: Common Lisp using LLVM and C++ for Molecular Metaprogramming
videos.s: Christian Schafmeister's Google Tech Talk on designing spiroligomer molecules and building Clasp, a Common Lisp on LLVM that interoperates with C++, to program molecular design. It covers the chemistry, automatic differentiation for force fields, and how the compiler is built.
videos.w: HN repeatedly cites it as a striking example of Common Lisp used to push the frontier of science, and as one of the most inspiring tech talks.
videos.q: I challenge anyone to watch this lecture from Christian Schafmeister and say they are not impressed

videos.t: The Wrong Way to Set Speed Limits [ST06]
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains how North American speed limits are set and why posted limits matter far less than street design. It argues that drivers follow the road's cues, so safe speeds have to be built into the street.
videos.w: Recommended again and again in traffic-safety threads as an eye-opener on road design versus posted limits and driver behavior.
videos.q: it really opened my eyes on the relationship between rules and actual behavior.

videos.t: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Most Ingenious Algorithm Ever?
videos.s: Reducible's visual walkthrough of the Fast Fourier Transform, motivated by polynomial multiplication. It shows how the FFT's key ideas can be discovered by asking the right questions.
videos.w: HN repeatedly calls it a fantastic explanation that made FFT click, with some rewatching it periodically.
videos.q: It derives the FFT algorithm from polynomial multiplication and it’s fantastic . I rewatch it every 6 months or so.

videos.t: Marty Lobdell - Study Less Study Smart
videos.s: Psychology professor Marty Lobdell gives a one-hour lecture on how to study effectively, covering short focused sessions with breaks, study environment, note-taking and memory techniques. It was aimed at students who cram without improving.
videos.w: HN recommends it for productivity, focus and working-from-home threads, since its advice on breaks and mental modes applies beyond studying.
videos.q: Marty Lobdell did a fantastic talk a while back [1] that changed the way I used to study

videos.t: Dick Proenneke in Alone in the Wilderness
videos.s: A condensed film of Dick Proenneke's footage of building a cabin and living alone in the Alaskan wilderness, using hand tools and local materials. It draws on the 8mm films he shot himself.
videos.w: HN recommends it often and warmly, as an inspiring and peaceful view of self-reliance and handcraft, in threads on cabins, solitude and woodworking.
videos.q: I think HN would really appreciate the story of Dick Proenneke

videos.t: Mike Monteiro: F*ck You, Pay Me
videos.s: Mike Monteiro's CreativeMornings talk on getting paid for creative and freelance work, covering contracts, working with lawyers, and refusing to work for free. It is delivered with blunt humor.
videos.w: HN regulars send freelancers and consultants to it whenever clients don't pay or contracts come up.
videos.q: I watched this video from Mike Monteiro and I always refer to it since.

videos.t: "Simple Made Easy" - Rich Hickey (2011)
videos.s: Rich Hickey's Strange Loop 2011 keynote separates 'simple' (not intertwined) from 'easy' (familiar or near at hand) and argues that software complexity comes from complecting things. It offers a vocabulary for judging designs and abstractions.
videos.w: It is one of HN's most frequently recommended programming talks, cited whenever people debate complexity, simplicity and abstraction, and valued well beyond Clojure.
videos.q: I highly recommend Rich Hickey's "Simple Made Easy" talk as a way to think about software complexity.

videos.t: We the People, and the Republic we must reclaim | Lawrence Lessig
videos.s: In this TED talk, Lawrence Lessig argues that American politics is corrupted by Congress's dependence on funding from a tiny fraction of citizens. He uses rapid-fire visuals and calls for a bipartisan push to reclaim the Republic.
videos.w: HN cites it repeatedly as the root-cause argument that money in politics must be fixed before other issues, and as background for his Mayday PAC.
videos.q: This TED lecture[0] is only 18 minutes long and it offers rather a chilling perspective on any sensible reform.

videos.t: You Need a Theme, Not a Goal
videos.s: CGP Grey argues for picking a theme for the year or season instead of setting goals or new year's resolutions. He explains how a theme gives direction without a pass/fail target.
videos.w: A staple recommendation in new year and goal-setting threads, with many commenters adopting yearly themes.
videos.q: CGP Grey has an excellent video on this exact kind of goal setting

videos.t: Transforming Code into Beautiful, Idiomatic Python
videos.s: Raymond Hettinger's PyCon 2013 talk on transforming code into idiomatic Python through a series of before-and-after refactorings. It shows how to use iterators, dictionaries, named tuples and other language features well.
videos.w: HN treats it as a must-watch classic for writing Pythonic code, though somewhat dated for modern Python.
videos.q: the excellent talk "Transforming Code into Beautiful, Idiomatic Python".

videos.t: Spec-ulation Keynote - Rich Hickey
videos.s: Rich Hickey's keynote on software versioning, arguing that breaking changes are the real problem and that libraries should only grow by providing more and requiring less. It critiques semantic versioning and ties into Clojure spec.
videos.w: HN returns to it in every versioning and API stability debate as a challenging, contrarian talk worth watching.
videos.q: Whenever an idea about API versioning springs into mind it is always worthwhile to watch Rich Hickey's Spec-ulation talk

videos.t: Modern Dictionaries by Raymond Hettinger
videos.s: Python core developer Raymond Hettinger explains how Python's dictionary implementation evolved into the compact, ordered dict in Python 3.6. He uses pictures and small bits of pure Python, and covers key-sharing, compaction and versioning.
videos.w: HN treats it as the definitive, engaging talk on hash table internals and Python dict ordering, and recommends it in tech-talk lists.
videos.q: one of the most insightful videos I've seen in a long time.

videos.t: Refterm Lecture Part 1 - Philosophies of Optimization
videos.s: Casey Muratori's first refterm lecture lays out philosophies of optimization, distinguishing optimization from non-pessimization, which means avoiding needless work. It uses his fast terminal renderer project to show how fast computers really are.
videos.w: HN returns to it constantly in software performance debates as the primer on non-pessimization and why modern software is slow.
videos.q: The video on Philosophies of Optimisation is a good primer on the tenets of the course.

videos.t: "Money doesn't interest me" - Ton Roosendaal 2017 Interview
videos.s: A long interview by Blender Guru with Ton Roosendaal, creator of Blender. They cover Blender's origins, the move to open source, why Ton is not driven by money, Autodesk, and what sets Blender apart from other open source projects.
videos.w: Recommended as the best account of Blender's history and its user-focused approach as a free software success story.
videos.q: I highly encourage to watch the whole interview

videos.t: CppCon 2014: Mike Acton "Data-Oriented Design and C++"
videos.s: Mike Acton of Insomniac Games argues that a program's purpose is transforming data, and shows how common C++ approaches work against that in performance-critical game development. He covers cache behavior, data layout and the limits of compilers.
videos.w: It is the go-to talk HN points to for data-oriented design and hardware-aware performance thinking, despite Acton's blunt style.
videos.q: one of the most digestible ways to start thinking about performance in high throughput systems

videos.t: Why Your Vote Doesn't Count
videos.s: CGP Grey explains first-past-the-post voting and why it pushes elections toward two dominant parties. It is the first in his series on electoral systems.
videos.w: HN's go-to explainer for why FPTP leads to a two-party system, linked in countless voting-reform and US politics threads.
videos.q: this CGP Grey video explains how a first-past-the-post voting system all-but-guarantees a two party system to emerge over time

videos.t: Shenzhen: The Silicon Valley of Hardware (Full Documentary) | Future Cities | WIRED
videos.s: A WIRED Future Cities documentary on Shenzhen, covering its hardware-prototyping culture and shanzhai copycat manufacturing. It looks at how the city's ecosystem evolved and what the rest of the world can learn.
videos.w: Strongly recommended in Shenzhen and hardware threads for its view of fast cycles, loose IP and the maker ecosystem.
videos.q: There's an excellent documentary on the hardware/hacking ecosystem in Shenzhen on YouTube

videos.t: Ideas about a new programming language for games.
videos.s: Jonathan Blow's first talk on designing a new programming language for games, which became Jai. He explains the problems with C++ and why Go, Rust and D do not fit game development.
videos.w: HN programmers recommend it, and the Jai series that followed, for the game-industry view on replacing C++ and for watching a language being invented.
videos.q: I also found watching his process for inventing the language extremely instructive, just as a programmer.

videos.t: Siggraph2019 Geometric Algebra
videos.s: A SIGGRAPH 2019 course on geometric algebra. Charles Gunn gives an intro, then Steven De Keninck gives a programmer-focused course with live examples in ganja.js.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly point people to it as the most accessible, developer-friendly introduction to geometric algebra and its use in graphics and physics.
videos.q: just watch this mind blowing video

videos.t: The essence of calculus
videos.s: The first video of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Calculus series, which builds toward integrals, derivatives, and the fundamental theorem of calculus from a simple geometry question. It aims to make viewers feel they could have invented calculus themselves.
videos.w: A staple recommendation for anyone learning math, praised for visual intuition that makes memorized formulas make sense.
videos.q: When I discovered that video, all the formulas they tried to make me memorize started making a LOT more sense.

videos.t: How to Do 90% of What Plugins Do (With Just Vim)
videos.s: A thoughtbot meetup talk by Max Cantor on getting most of what popular plugins provide using only built-in Vim features. It covers autocomplete, file jumping, filesystem navigation, build integration and snippets, with slides and a vimrc available.
videos.w: HN treats it as the canonical talk for the case that vanilla Vim goes a long way and plugin dependencies are a burden.
videos.q: Max Cantor has a great talk about that on YouTube

videos.t: The Mother of All Demos, presented by Douglas Engelbart (1968)
videos.s: The full recording of Douglas Engelbart's 1968 demonstration, which introduced the mouse, hypertext, video conferencing, word processing, and real-time collaborative editing. It runs about 100 minutes.
videos.w: HN treats it as an essential piece of computing history that shows how many modern interface ideas were already solved in 1968.
videos.q: If you haven't seen it, it's well worth the hour and forty minutes.

videos.t: RSA ANIMATE: Changing Education Paradigms
videos.s: An RSA Animate drawn from a Sir Ken Robinson talk arguing that current education systems are modeled on the industrial age. It discusses divergent thinking, standardization, and how schools disengage kids.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible, widely shared critique of schooling, and cites it in threads on ADHD, creativity and education reform.
videos.q: One of my favorite videos on reforming education

videos.t: This is how you treat ADHD based off science, Dr Russell Barkley part of 2012 Burnett Lecture
videos.s: A short excerpt from Dr Russell Barkley's 2012 Burnett Lecture on ADHD, focused on treatment. He argues ADHD is a disorder of executive function and self-regulation, and that environments should be designed to compensate.
videos.w: HN people with ADHD or ADHD-affected relatives share it as an authoritative, practical talk that helped some seek diagnosis.
videos.q: It's a talk by Dr. Russell Barkley on ADHD and it's what made me finally schedule a full analysis

videos.t: RL Course by David Silver - Lecture 1: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
videos.s: The first lecture of David Silver's reinforcement learning course, introducing the field and its basic concepts. The course follows the Sutton and Barto textbook.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as an excellent, clear introductory RL course from the lead of AlphaGo, pairing well with Sutton and Barto.
videos.q: Really clear explanations that went hand in hand when I was reading Sutton and Barto's introductory book.

videos.t: Lecture 6: Version Control (git) (2020)
videos.s: A lecture from MIT's Missing Semester course covering version control with git. It builds up git from its data model rather than from commands.
videos.w: HN frequently calls it the best single video on git because it teaches the underlying data structures.
videos.q: I think that this video should be considered mandatory viewing if you're a developer using Git

videos.t: 28c3: The Science of Insecurity
videos.s: Meredith Patterson and Sergey Bratus argue that networked software stays insecure because protocols and inputs are too complex to recognize safely. They propose using formal language theory and grammars to build secure, verifiable input handling.
videos.w: HN commenters call it one of the best security talks and the standard introduction to LANGSEC, which they use to argue for simpler, well-specified input formats.
videos.q: The best talk on computer security I have seen is Meredith Patterson's Science of Insecurity at 28c3

videos.t: Mindfulness with Jon Kabat-Zinn
videos.s: Jon Kabat-Zinn leads an hour-long Google tech talk on mindfulness, introducing the basic ideas and including a guided meditation. It is aimed at newcomers.
videos.w: For over a decade HN has pointed people asking about stress, focus or meditation to this as a restful and approachable introduction to mindfulness.
videos.q: Its almost embarrassing how much that video changed my perception of my decisionmaking.

videos.t: Is Most Published Research Wrong?
videos.s: Veritasium explains why a large share of published research findings may be false, covering p-values, p-hacking, publication bias and low replication rates. It draws on John Ioannidis's well-known paper and describes reforms such as preregistration.
videos.w: HN commenters link it whenever a shaky study or the p<0.05 threshold comes up, as a short primer on false positives in science.
videos.q: This video is a good primer

videos.t: How I program C
videos.s: Eskil Steenberg's two-hour talk on his personal approach to writing C, covering code style, structure, naming, pointers and large-project organization. He warns it contains a fair bit of programming religion.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the one long programming video worth watching, a provocative and influential take on C.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: the only 2 hour YouTube video I'll ever recommend

videos.t: The Extreme Engineering of ASML’s EUV Light Source
videos.s: Asianometry explains the EUV light source inside ASML's lithography machines, where lasers hit falling tin droplets twice to produce 13.5 nm light. It walks through the engineering of the droplet generator, the pre-pulse and main laser, and the plasma that results.
videos.w: Commenters repeatedly point to it whenever EUV, ASML or chip manufacturing comes up, as a clear and astonishing explanation of one of the hardest engineering problems in chipmaking.
videos.q: This video from Asianometry on EUV light sources is well worth the watch. It's pretty incredible.

videos.t: Agile is Dead • Pragmatic Dave Thomas • GOTO 2015
videos.s: Dave Thomas, a co-author of the Agile Manifesto, argues at GOTO Amsterdam 2015 that Agile as a branded industry has lost its meaning. He says agile is an adjective, not a noun, and urges developers to reclaim agility.
videos.w: Offered in nearly every Agile or Scrum complaint thread as the authoritative take on what agile was meant to be versus what it became.
videos.q: I highly recommend this video of a Dave Thomas talk about what agile was supposed to be vs what it has become.

videos.t: 30 Essential Ideas you should know about ADHD, 1A Intro, Chronic Developmental Disability
videos.s: The first clip from Russell Barkley's 30 Essential Ideas about ADHD series, introducing ADHD as a chronic developmental disability. It is part of a lecture series on the disorder by a leading ADHD researcher.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend Barkley's lectures as the best introduction to understanding ADHD.
videos.q: Probably the best introduction to ADHD is a 1.5 lecture by Dr. Russell Barkley, a top researcher in this area.

videos.t: Cities Aren't Loud: Cars Are Loud
videos.s: Not Just Bikes argues that urban noise comes mostly from motor vehicles, drawing on the book Curbing Traffic and a visit to Delft, a city that takes noise seriously.
videos.w: HN cites it constantly in threads on noise, EVs and car-free cities as the source that cars, not cities, are loud.
videos.q: Fantastic video with that very name exploring just how true this is

videos.t: 8. The Sumerians - Fall of the First Cities
videos.s: Episode 8 of the Fall of Civilizations podcast, a roughly two and a half hour history of the Sumerians. It covers their mysterious origins, invention of writing and mathematics, great early cities and eventual collapse, with myths, proverbs and recreated music.
videos.w: HN commenters strongly recommend it as an audiobook-length, deeply informative introduction to Sumer and early Mesopotamian civilization.
videos.q: I highly recommend the _Fall of Civilizations Podcast_ episode 8.

videos.t: Music Software & Bad Interface Design: Avid’s Sibelius
videos.s: Tantacrul dissects the UX and UI of Avid's Sibelius music notation software, going through a long list of bad design choices. The review is both a comic rant and a practical lesson in interface design.
videos.w: Recommended as the most entertaining serious critique of a software interface, and a crash course in UX mistakes.
videos.q: might be the most entertaining serious critique of a software user interface ever posted to YouTube.

videos.t: Google I/O 2012 - Go Concurrency Patterns
videos.s: Rob Pike's Google I/O 2012 talk shows how goroutines and channels solve tricky concurrency problems with simple Go code. It features a playful goroutine demo with gophers passing messages and a search engine example.
videos.w: The canonical recommendation for learning Go concurrency, praised as entertaining and clarifying when to use channels versus mutexes.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Great talk by Rob Pike

videos.t: The Secret War
videos.s: A compilation of the 1977 BBC series The Secret War, a documentary on British scientific and technical efforts in WWII, including radar, German navigation beams and V-weapons. It features interviews with people who were there, including Albert Speer.
videos.w: HN readers recommend it as a detailed, intelligent documentary about wartime technology that assumes viewers aren't stupid.
videos.q: It's very long, very detailed but well presented - in a style that assumes you aren't stupid.

videos.t: Václav Smil at Driva Climate Investment Meeting 2019
videos.s: Vaclav Smil's talk on historic energy transitions and what they imply for climate investment. He argues that transitions are slow, technology improves gradually, and only absolute cuts in energy use would truly work.
videos.w: Frequently linked as a sobering, data-grounded counterpoint to techno-optimism about decarbonization and green growth.
videos.q: Here's a fascinating talk by Václav Smil at the Driva Climate Investment Meeting in 2019

videos.t: Origins of Precision
videos.s: Machine Thinking traces where mechanical precision comes from, from flat surface plates and the three-plate method up through lathes and early measuring tools. It is the first in a series on recreating the first micrometer.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as a half-hour mini-documentary on how precision is bootstrapped from scratch, relevant to machining and chip manufacturing threads.
videos.q: The Origins of Precision" is a half hour well spent

videos.t: Category Theory 1.1: Motivation and Philosophy
videos.s: The first lecture in Bartosz Milewski's category theory series for programmers. It covers the motivation and philosophy behind category theory and why composition matters for handling complexity.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly name it as the friendliest entry point to category theory for working programmers.
videos.q: I think they are a very nice place to start learning these things.

videos.t: "Propositions as Types" by Philip Wadler
videos.s: Philip Wadler's Strange Loop talk on Propositions as Types, the link between logic and computation (the Curry-Howard correspondence). He traces its history through Church, Godel and Turing and shows how it shaped theorem provers and programming languages.
videos.w: HN regards it as an entertaining and eye-opening introduction to why logic and functional programming are connected, and it is a frequent pick in favorite-tech-talk threads.
videos.q: best ~40 minutes I've ever spent.

videos.t: This Is What Winning Looks Like (Full Length)
videos.s: Ben Anderson's VICE documentary shows embedded reporting on Afghan security forces and US Marines in Helmand during the troop drawdown, exposing incompetence, drug abuse and corruption.
videos.w: Recommended during Afghanistan withdrawal threads as a sobering look at why the transition to local forces was failing.
videos.q: I highly recommend the 2013 documentary

videos.t: Why Some Diseases Only Traveled One Direction
videos.s: CGP Grey explains why European diseases devastated the Americas while few deadly diseases traveled the other way. He ties it to livestock domestication, dense cities, and the ideas of Guns, Germs and Steel.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a clear, short explanation of one-directional disease spread and the core argument of Guns, Germs, and Steel.
videos.q: I think CGP Grey does a great job at communicating the actual meat of Guns, Germs, and Steel here

videos.t: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
videos.s: Andrej Karpathy builds a GPT from scratch in code, following Attention Is All You Need and GPT-2/3, in about two hours using PyTorch. He connects it to ChatGPT and assumes familiarity with his earlier makemore videos.
videos.w: It is the go-to recommendation for learning how transformers and LLMs actually work, praised for its clarity and Karpathy's teaching.
videos.q: the best video I have seen on the topic

videos.t: Richard Feynman Fire
videos.s: A short clip from a Richard Feynman interview in which he explains fire, describing how burning wood releases sunlight stored by the tree, which built itself mostly from air. It showcases his curiosity and plain-spoken explanations.
videos.w: HN repeatedly cites it as an elegant, eye-opening explanation of fire and photosynthesis and as an example of Feynman's infectious love of knowledge.
videos.q: it's impossible to stay in any kind of negative mood if you watch Feynman

videos.t: Jim Keller: Moore's Law, Microprocessors, and First Principles | Lex Fridman Podcast #70
videos.s: Lex Fridman interviews legendary chip architect Jim Keller about Moore's Law, microprocessor design, and first-principles thinking. Keller draws on his work at AMD, Apple, Tesla and Intel, discussing instruction sets, transistor budgets, and self-driving.
videos.w: HN cites it whenever chip architecture, Moore's Law or CPU design comes up, as an unusually deep and accessible view from a top designer.
videos.q: I was stunned by Jim's total command of Computer Architecture, and his deep insights about the subject.

videos.t: The Spider's Web: Britain's Second Empire | The Secret World of Finance
videos.s: A feature-length documentary on how the City of London and Britain's overseas territories built a global web of offshore secrecy jurisdictions after the empire declined. It traces how this network captured and hid wealth from around the world.
videos.w: Commenters repeatedly recommend it in tax haven and offshore finance threads as an excellent, low-budget overview of British offshore finance.
videos.q: The guy who behind it not only did an excellent job

videos.t: Stop Writing Classes
videos.s: Jack Diederich's PyCon 2012 talk argues that classes are overused in Python and walks through real code, refactoring away unnecessary classes, exceptions and modules. It popularized the heuristic that a class with two methods, one being __init__, should be a function.
videos.w: HN returns to it repeatedly as the canonical argument for simplicity and against premature abstraction, and several commenters say it changed how they write code.
videos.q: Jack Diederich has a great video called Stop Writing Classes: It's about Python, but the observation can apply to several languages.

videos.t: Alan Kay: Doing with Images Makes Symbols (Full Version)
videos.s: A full upload of Alan Kay's 1987 talk, with demos of several Smalltalk-era software systems and ideas about visual, kinesthetic and symbolic reasoning. It includes a Smalltalk program written by a 12-year-old and footage of the Rand tablet.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a favourite tech talk full of good ideas from forgotten 1980s software, worth watching in full.
videos.q: The whole talk is well worth watching

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #1109 - Matthew Walker
videos.s: Joe Rogan interviews Matthew Walker, Berkeley neuroscience professor and author of Why We Sleep. They discuss what sleep does for the brain and body, the effects of sleep deprivation, and sleep myths.
videos.w: HN readers recommend it as an accessible, motivating summary of Why We Sleep for people who will not read the book.
videos.q: His interview on Joe Rogan is a good summary

videos.t: Object-Oriented Programming is Bad
videos.s: Brian Will makes the case for procedural programming over object-oriented programming, arguing that OOP's promised encapsulation and decoupling are largely illusory. He analyzes real code examples and the problems of tying data to behavior in classes.
videos.w: HN returns to it as the go-to critique of OOP, recommended for explaining the costs of abstraction better than most written arguments.
videos.q: I highly recommend this video by Brian Will who does a much better job explaining this problem than I could.

videos.t: The UK Is a Country Made of Countries
videos.s: CGP Grey's quick, witty explainer on the differences between the United Kingdom, Great Britain and England, and the countries that make up the UK.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the standard short answer whenever someone confuses Britain, the UK and England.
videos.q: The best thing to do is to watch this great, quick and witty primer on the whole thing Britain/UK/England thing

videos.t: The Language of the System - Rich Hickey
videos.s: Rich Hickey's 2013 talk applies language-design thinking to whole systems, covering names, queues, data, failure, and the interfaces between programs. It ends with a call to action for building systems holistically.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a key Hickey talk on system design that changes how people think about distributed state and interfaces.
videos.q: it has really changed the way I look at distributed persistent storage.

videos.t: Your Brain Thinks Your Whole Home Is One Room
videos.s: CGP Grey argues that your brain treats a whole home as one room during lockdown, blurring work, rest and leisure. He recommends creating separate spaces and routines for different activities to stay balanced.
videos.w: HN recommends it constantly in work-from-home, burnout and procrastination threads as practical advice for separating work from life at home.
videos.q: i watch it once a week to keep things in perspective.

videos.t: Why Canadians Can't Bike in the Winter (but Finnish people can)
videos.s: Not Just Bikes argues that winter is not what stops Canadians cycling, using Oulu, Finland as proof that safe, well-maintained cycling infrastructure enables year-round biking despite harsh weather.
videos.w: HN links it whenever someone claims cold or snow rules out cycling, as the concise rebuttal that infrastructure and maintenance decide it.
videos.q: winter cycling has nothing to do with the weather, and everything to do with safe cycling infrastructure.

videos.t: This Video Is Sponsored By ███ VPN
videos.s: Tom Scott writes a more honest VPN ad, with the sponsor's name redacted, and explains why the typical claims in VPN advertising are misleading. He notes the sponsor was not happy about it.
videos.w: The standard link when VPN marketing comes up, as a clear debunking of the scare tactics behind VPN ads.
videos.q: It's well worth the seven and a half minutes to watch it, IMO.

videos.t: Pete Hunt: React: Rethinking best practices -- JSConf EU
videos.s: Pete Hunt of Facebook and Instagram introduces React at JSConf EU 2013 and explains its design principles. He argues that separating templates from logic only separates technologies, not concerns, and makes the case for components.
videos.w: HN calls it the famous talk for understanding why React rejected separation of concerns by technology and for newcomers puzzled by JSX.
videos.q: See Pete Hunt's famous talk

videos.t: How the Dutch got their cycle paths
videos.s: A short BicycleDutch video on how the Netherlands got its cycling infrastructure, including the 1970s protests and the shift away from car-centric planning. The channel later published an updated version.
videos.w: HN uses it as the standard short answer to whether car-dominated cities can become bike-friendly, since the Dutch had to fight for it.
videos.q: There is a great video about the protest movement and the transformation of dutch infrastructure here

videos.t: Quantum Entanglement & Spooky Action at a Distance
videos.s: Veritasium explains quantum entanglement and spooky action at a distance, walking through Bell's inequality and the experiments that rule out hidden variables, in under ten minutes.
videos.w: HN recommends it as one of the clearest layman explanations of Bell's theorem.
videos.q: It's my favorite video for explaining how we know that the state is not determined until it has been measured.

videos.t: The man with 1,000 Klein Bottles UNDER his house - Numberphile
videos.s: Numberphile visits Cliff Stoll, the man behind ACME Klein Bottles, and sees how he stores a thousand glass Klein bottles in a crawlspace under his house. A remote-controlled forklift fetches them.
videos.w: HN commenters love Cliff Stoll's earnest, playful personality and point to this as a delightful look at his unusual warehouse.
videos.q: Cliff is an amazing person. Just a joy!

videos.t: David Heinemeier Hansson at Startup School 08
videos.s: David Heinemeier Hansson's talk at Startup School 2008 on building a profitable startup. He argues for bootstrapping and small, well-run companies instead of chasing investment and exits.
videos.w: For over a decade HN has pointed bootstrappers and skeptics of hyper-scale startup culture to it as a motivating, influential talk.
videos.q: The 2008 DHH boostrapping talk during Startup School is still one of the most influential videos on my career as a founder.

videos.t: I bought 1000 meters of wire to settle a physics debate
videos.s: AlphaPhoenix builds a scaled-down version of the Veritasium electricity thought experiment using about a kilometer of wire and an oscilloscope. He measures how the signal actually propagates and explains the result.
videos.w: HN considers it the best experimental rebuttal and clarification of the Veritasium wire debate, with real measurements.
videos.q: Yeah I really liked the AlphaPheonix video[0] where he actually built the thing in a field and explained the entire effect properly.

videos.t: Building a realistic artificial sun (for dark winter days)
videos.s: DIY Perks builds a realistic artificial sun for dark winters, using a powerful water-cooled LED, a satellite dish reflector for near-parallel rays, and a scattering layer to mimic the blue sky. The video explains the optics behind why most lamps do not look like sunlight and shows the build and its results.
videos.w: Whenever HN discusses seasonal affective disorder, myopia, or bright home lighting, people point to this as the most convincing buildable example of sunlight-like illumination.
videos.q: The result is quite stunning. I've never seen anything like it.

videos.t: 1. How Buildings Learn - Stewart Brand - 1 of 6 - “Flow”
videos.s: The first episode of Stewart Brand's 1997 BBC series based on his book How Buildings Learn, covering how buildings change after they are built. Brand presents and the series has music by Brian Eno.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a view of buildings as dynamic systems, with lessons for software architecture and long-term maintenance.
videos.q: It changed my view of a building from a static thing to a dynamic system, changing over time.

videos.t: Contrepreneurs: The Mikkelsen Twins
videos.s: Dan Olson of Folding Ideas investigates the Mikkelsen Twins and the ghostwritten-audiobook passive-income course industry, even playing along with the scheme. It is a long video essay on get-rich-quick publishing grifts.
videos.w: HN links it whenever threads cover book spam, AI-written ebooks or passive-income hustle culture.
videos.q: Folding Ideas on youtube has an excellent explanation of the business model behind the rise of EBook Spam.

videos.t: Invited Talk - Guy Steele
videos.s: Guy Steele's invited talk at Clojure/conj on the informal metanotation computer scientists use in papers to describe languages. He traces how this notation developed and why it is often unspecified and arcane.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it whenever someone asks how to read type-system or CS notation in papers.
videos.q: Excellent talk by Guy Steele explaining the history of maths/comp notations

videos.t: Literate Devops with Emacs
videos.s: Howard Abrams demonstrates, in an EmacsConf 2015 talk, how he uses org-mode's Babel and Tramp to configure and operate remote servers from a single document. Code blocks, their results and the explanatory text all live together.
videos.w: HN people point to it as the best demonstration of literate devops, showing documentation and execution woven together in Emacs.
videos.q: His video on literate programming for DevOps via Emacs' Org-mode was very impressive and inspiring to me. It's my favorite.

videos.t: America Keeps Rejecting an ID Card It Already Has
videos.s: CGP Grey explains the history of the US Social Security card and number, and why they became a de facto national ID despite never being meant for it. He also covers why America resists a proper identity card.
videos.w: HN reaches for it in every identity theft and data breach thread as the clearest, most enjoyable short explainer of why SSNs make bad identifiers.
videos.q: this is the most enjoyable explanation for it I've seen, by CGP Grey

videos.t: May 1, 1969: Fred Rogers testifies before the Senate Subcommittee on Communications
videos.s: Seven-minute footage of Fred Rogers testifying before a US Senate subcommittee in 1969 to defend federal funding for the new Corporation for Public Broadcasting. A skeptical Senator Pastore starts out abrasive and is won over during Rogers' brief, calm testimony.
videos.w: HN commenters hold it up as a model of persuasive public speaking and as the go-to reminder of why public broadcasting deserves funding.
videos.q: Fred Rogers' 1969 testimony before the Senate in defense of PBS funding is very moving.

videos.t: SNES Code Injection -- Flappy Bird in SMW
videos.s: SethBling uses Super Mario World glitches to inject and run Flappy Bird code on an unmodified SNES, entering it purely with controller inputs. It was the first time a human completed this kind of exploit by hand.
videos.w: Constantly cited as the canonical example of arbitrary code execution through gameplay and of deep system knowledge among speedrunners.
videos.q: By hand. No savestates. It took forever and the run through is really and truly fascinating

videos.t: DEF CON 25 - John Sotos - Genetic Diseases to Guide Digital Hacks of the Human Genome
videos.s: John Sotos, a physician and former Intel chief medical officer, argues at DEF CON 25 that genetic diseases are exploitable vulnerabilities in the genome. He warns that CRISPR and related tools will make malicious genome hacks and targeted bioweapons feasible.
videos.w: Recommended whenever DNA testing, CRISPR or bioweapons come up, often as the talk that made commenters decide to keep their DNA out of databases.
videos.q: The talk is absolutely amazing, probably the most captivating talk I have ever watched

videos.t: A Hackers' Guide to Language Models
videos.s: Jeremy Howard's 90-minute practical tour of language models. It covers how they work, GPT-4's capabilities and limits, using the OpenAI API, code writing, data analysis and fine-tuning.
videos.w: Repeatedly named the best practical tutorial for using LLMs, with a well-liked fine-tuning section.
videos.q: highly recommend "Hackers Guide to language models" by Jeremy Howard. 1.5h video packed with practical information

videos.t: Tiedustelueverstin arvio Venäjästä | 3.12.2018
videos.s: A 2018 lecture, with subtitles available, by former Finnish intelligence colonel Martti J. Kari on Russian strategic culture. He walks through the historical layers of Russia and explains why the country behaves as it does.
videos.w: After the 2022 invasion, commenters spread it widely as an eye-opening explanation of Russian mindset, corruption and propaganda, though a few doubt the presenter's rigor.
videos.q: is fantastic since its from 2018 but still 100% valid

videos.t: Essence of linear algebra preview
videos.s: A five-minute preview of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, which uses animation to build geometric intuition for topics from a standard linear algebra course.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends the series as the best intuition-first, visual introduction to linear algebra and a benchmark for clear math explanation.
videos.q: 3Blue1Brown's youtube series I cannot recommend highly enough.

videos.t: Why Heat Pumps are Immensely Important Right Now
videos.s: Technology Connections explains why heat pumps matter right now, covering their efficiency, how they hold up in cold weather and the energy savings over burning fuel. It follows his earlier explainer on how they work.
videos.w: HN's default link for anyone asking whether heat pumps work and why they're efficient, thanks to the presenter's clear and enthusiastic delivery.
videos.q: If you want an (entertaining) deep dive into heat pumps, I can recommend Technology Connection's

videos.t: Analogy as the Core of Cognition
videos.s: Douglas Hofstadter's Stanford Presidential Lecture argues that analogy is the core of cognition, illustrating how concepts, categorization and thought arise from analogy-making.
videos.w: HN regulars treat it as an essential, fun Hofstadter talk for any discussion of concepts, analogy and metaphor.
videos.q: No discussion about concepts, analogy and metaphor is complete with a mention of

videos.t: Failing to Fail: The Spiderweb Software Way
videos.s: Jeff Vogel of Spiderweb Software gives a GDC 2018 retrospective on surviving as an indie game maker since 1994, from shareware days through Steam. It covers business realities, costs and sustaining a comfortable living without chasing riches.
videos.w: HN keeps recommending it as an inspirational, funny talk on running a long-lived indie studio and what Steam provides for its 30% cut.
videos.q: this talk is legendary and inspirational to aspiring game devs

videos.t: AT&T Archives: The UNIX Operating System
videos.s: A 1982 Bell Labs film hosted by Victor Vyssotsky on the origins and design philosophy of the UNIX operating system, with appearances by Kernighan, Thompson and Ritchie. It shows pipes, filters and a shell one-liner spell checker being built.
videos.w: HN points people to it as the clearest primary-source explanation of Unix pipes and the small-tools philosophy, straight from the creators.
videos.q: The pipelines explanation was incredibly clear.

videos.t: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford Commencement Address
videos.s: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford commencement address, told through three stories: connecting the dots, love and loss, and death. It includes the calligraphy class and the 'stay hungry, stay foolish' close.
videos.w: HN returns to it for motivation and perspective, and quotes it constantly, especially the connect-the-dots and remembering-death passages.
videos.q: Great speech, very worth watching for those who haven’t seen it.

videos.t: How to green the world's deserts and reverse climate change | Allan Savory
videos.s: Allan Savory's TED talk arguing that desertification of grasslands can be reversed with holistic managed grazing, which he says would also help reverse climate change. TED notes that other scientists have challenged his claims.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up in climate and food threads as a hopeful, if contested, idea about grazing and soil carbon.
videos.q: This is the idea behind this fantastic TED talk

videos.t: Dan Abramov - Live React: Hot Reloading with Time Travel at react-europe 2015
videos.s: Dan Abramov live-codes hot reloading with time-travel debugging at React Europe 2015, debuting Redux and its devtools. The slides themselves are driven by application state.
videos.w: Seen as the canonical Redux introduction and a model live-coding talk about better developer tools.
videos.q: One of my favourites I watched recently was Dan Abramov introducing React hot loading, Redux and Redux Dev Tools in the same 30 minute talk

videos.t: 34C3 -  The Ultimate Apollo Guidance Computer Talk
videos.s: Michael Steil and Christian Hessmann's 34C3 talk explaining the Apollo Guidance Computer end to end: hardware design, operating system, and mission software.
videos.w: Repeatedly called the best and most comprehensive AGC talk, with commenters rewatching it and treating it as foundational computer architecture learning.
videos.q: This is the best description of AGC I have seen so far, from hardware design to mission software, layer by layer

videos.t: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
videos.s: A short explainer on the history and mechanics of public key cryptography and the Diffie-Hellman key exchange. It uses a mixing-paint-colors analogy to show how two parties can agree on a shared secret in public.
videos.w: It is the go-to beginner explanation of Diffie-Hellman, recommended because the paint analogy makes the idea click without prior cryptography knowledge.
videos.q: I found this video, Public key cryptography - Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange (full version), to be completely enlightening

videos.t: Can YOU Fix Climate Change?
videos.s: Kurzgesagt examines what individuals can do about climate change, covering lesser-known carbon sources and why systemic and political change matter more than personal footprints.
videos.w: Cited in climate threads to argue that individual action is not enough and that political pressure is needed.
videos.q: It's a Kurzgesagt video about why individual action is far from enough, and why we need systemic action.

videos.t: Jackie Chan - How to Do Action Comedy
videos.s: Every Frame a Painting analyzes how Jackie Chan stages action comedy, with nine principles such as starting from a disadvantage, using the environment, clear shots, and keeping action and reaction in the same frame.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the clearest explanation of why Chan's fight scenes beat fast-cut Hollywood action.
videos.q: does an excellent job of explaining why Jackie Chan's way of doing action is awesome

videos.t: Bay Area Vision Meeting: Unsupervised Feature Learning and Deep Learning
videos.s: Andrew Ng presents unsupervised feature learning and deep learning, showing how algorithms can learn representations from unlabeled data instead of hand-designed features. He gives examples in vision and audio, including visualizations of features learned by successive layers.
videos.w: HN commenters recommended it for years as a simple, exciting overview of the deep learning wave.
videos.q: he explains very simply how all this works for images and some examples about the audio case.

videos.t: Elevator Hacking: From the Pit to the Penthouse
videos.s: Deviant Ollam's two-hour conference talk explains how elevators work, from the pit and buffers to the car top, controller logic and access-control features. It shows how this knowledge can be used for optimization and for bypassing building security.
videos.w: HN commenters call it an absorbing, entertaining deep dive on elevator security and the go-to link whenever elevators come up.
videos.q: it was so interesting to me that I ended up watching the entire 2 hours in one sitting.

videos.t: Powers of Ten™ (1977)
videos.s: The Eames Office's 1977 film Powers of Ten starts at a picnic in Chicago and zooms out by a factor of ten every ten seconds to the edge of the universe. It then zooms inward to a proton in a carbon atom.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the classic visualization for building intuition about scale, and it comes up whenever a thread concerns scale or size comparisons.
videos.q: a classic video that demonstrates the scale of the Universe from the micro to the macro perspectives

videos.t: [Linux.conf.au 2013] - Git For Ages 4 And Up
videos.s: A Linux.conf.au 2013 talk that explains git's internal model using a playful, toy-based approach. It presents git operations as operations on a graph of commits, aimed at people who find git confusing.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the talk that finally makes git's data model click for beginners, despite its odd title.
videos.q: it's the one video that allowed me to fully grasp everything

videos.t: Sunlight: Optimize Health and Immunity (Light Therapy and Melatonin)
videos.s: Dr. Roger Seheult of MedCram reviews the benefits of sunlight beyond vitamin D, covering the solar spectrum, circadian rhythm, melatonin and infrared light. The lecture runs nearly two hours with timestamps.
videos.w: HN cites it as an accessible physician-led review supporting claims about infrared light, mitochondria and morning sun.
videos.q: MedCram has some easily digestible reviews on the topic

videos.t: A Swift Introduction to Geometric Algebra
videos.s: An animated introduction to geometric algebra, presented as a language that can describe most of physics. It was made with manim and covers multivectors and how they generalize familiar tools like cross products and quaternions.
videos.w: HN calls it the best video on geometric algebra, one that makes the subject click in about 40 minutes.
videos.q: If you want an inspiring (imho) overview of the power of geometric algebra, I thoroughly enjoyed the video

videos.t: Seattle is Dying | A KOMO News Documentary
videos.s: A one-hour 2019 KOMO News documentary hosted by Eric Johnson on Seattle's homelessness and drug crisis, with interviews and looks at proposed solutions including a drug court program in Rhode Island. It argues addiction and mental illness are at the core of the problem.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it in homelessness threads about San Francisco and Seattle as an eye-opening, widely viewed argument for treatment-first policy, though some see it as pro-law-enforcement framing.
videos.q: Seattle Is Dying” is a great investigative report about the problems and potential solutions to homelessness.

videos.t: Debt: The First 5,000 Years | David Graeber | Talks at Google
videos.s: David Graeber's Talks at Google presentation on his book Debt: The First 5,000 Years, covering the history of debt, the myth of barter and the Jubilee tradition.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an 80-minute way to get the gist of the book and a different view of what money is.
videos.q: this excellent talk by the late David Graeber about the history of debt

videos.t: Julia: to Lisp or not to Lisp?
videos.s: Stefan Karpinski's European Lisp Symposium 2016 talk asks whether Julia is a Lisp. He covers the features it borrows from Lisp, such as macros and closures, and where it departs, including syntax and its type system, with generated machine code shown.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a brilliant talk on Julia's design and how it is or isn't a Lisp.
videos.q: the recent brilliant talk about design of Julia

videos.t: Life in Syntropy
videos.s: A short film from Agenda Gotsch introducing syntropic agriculture and Ernst Gotsch's agroforestry methods, made for COP21. It shows degraded land regenerated into productive forest farms.
videos.w: HN users repeatedly offer it as the best introduction to agroforestry as a climate and food solution.
videos.q: Ever since watching the video on syntropic agriculture which I bumped into by reading a comment here in HN

videos.t: The Egg - A Short Story
videos.s: Kurzgesagt animates Andy Weir's short story The Egg, in which a person learns that they are every human who has ever lived. It adds music and narration to the original text.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a beloved story and link the animation when threads touch on consciousness, empathy or identity.
videos.q: The Egg is one of my life long favorite histories.

videos.t: 7 minutes of Pharo Smalltalk for Rubyists
videos.s: Ruby developer Avdi Grimm gives a seven-minute tour of Pharo Smalltalk's development environment, focusing on tools like search-by-example and the integrated, live coding experience.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a quick, compelling look at what Smalltalk tooling feels like, especially for Ruby programmers.
videos.q: As a Ruby developer this video about Pharo smalltalk made me a smalltalk believer

videos.t: Compiling C to printable x86, to make an executable research paper
videos.s: Tom7 explains how he built a SIGBOVIK 2017 paper made only of printable ASCII bytes that is also a valid DOS executable. He writes a C compiler targeting printable x86 without self-modifying code and solves the puzzles the constraint creates.
videos.w: HN fans call it a favorite engineering video and a showcase of Tom7's masterpiece-level, playful hacking.
videos.q: His video about the printable x86[1] is my favorite engineering video of all time.

videos.t: How close is nuclear fusion power?
videos.s: Sabine Hossenfelder explains how close nuclear fusion really is to break-even, and why headlines about ITER and lab milestones are misleading. She distinguishes plasma gain (Q plasma) from whole-system gain (Q total) and shows the latter is still far below one.
videos.w: HN commenters post it under nearly every fusion breakthrough story as the standard reality check on Q-factor hype.
videos.q: Mandatory video by Sabine Hossenfelder

videos.t: "The Mess We're In" by Joe Armstrong
videos.s: Joe Armstrong, co-inventor of Erlang, gives a funny and opinionated Strange Loop talk on the tangled state of software: build tools, package managers, entropy and the physical limits of computation. He argues for ideas like naming things by content hash and throwing away your first version.
videos.w: HN returns to it constantly as a witty, still-accurate diagnosis of why software is bloated and messy, and as a go-to recommendation in any thread on modules, package managers or software quality.
videos.q: one of those talks which were incredibly funny and informative at the same time

videos.t: I messed up. You're using too much detergent.
videos.s: Technology Connections explains dishwasher detergent use, arguing people use too much and that powder beats pods and gels. It follows an earlier dishwasher video and covers enzymes, bleach, rinse aids and when salt is needed.
videos.w: HN regards the dishwasher videos as must-watch practical explainers, linked whenever dishwashers, detergents or pods come up.
videos.q: the two Technology Connection videos on dishwashers are must watch

videos.t: Once you understand game theory, you understand the world.
videos.s: Veritasium explores the Prisoner's Dilemma and Axelrod's tournaments, showing why tit-for-tat and forgiving strategies win in repeated games. It extends the ideas to cooperation in evolution and conflict.
videos.w: HN commenters reach for it constantly as an approachable explanation of why cooperation and reciprocity are rational strategies.
videos.q: Veratasium just made an approachable video on this subject recently, I definitely recommend.

videos.t: The Speed of Light is NOT About Light
videos.s: PBS Space Time argues that the speed of light is better understood as the speed of causality, the universal limit on how fast cause and effect propagate. Light travels at that speed because it is massless, but the limit itself is a property of spacetime.
videos.w: HN commenters send people to it whenever a thread confuses the speed of light with a light-specific limit, and several say it deepened their understanding of relativity.
videos.q: The video about “the speed of causality” is the one that caused me to level up

videos.t: Master Your Sleep & Be More Alert When Awake
videos.s: Andrew Huberman's podcast episode on what makes us sleepy, helps us sleep soundly and keeps us alert. It lays out the science and a set of behavioral tools such as light timing.
videos.w: HN users repeatedly credit it with fixing their sleep, especially its advice on morning light and dimming lights in the evening.
videos.q: I highly recommend it. The key is light.

videos.t: Jim Keller: Moore’s Law is Not Dead
videos.s: Jim Keller gives a UC Berkeley EECS colloquium arguing that Moore's Law is not dead. He surveys upcoming technologies and the multiple innovation curves that can keep transistor density and performance scaling.
videos.w: The go-to citation in Moore's Law threads, a convincing counterargument from a top CPU designer.
videos.q: It is worth watching Jim Keller's lecture at UC Berkeley literally titled "Moore's law is not dead".

videos.t: The hardest problem on the hardest test
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown walks through a very hard Putnam competition problem and its elegant solution, emphasizing the visual intuition and the thought process behind solving it.
videos.w: HN fans list it among their favorite 3Blue1Brown videos for showing how mathematical problem solving actually unfolds.
videos.q: these videos give a sense of how someone might actually go about thinking through and solving these kinds of problems

videos.t: Jonathan Blow - Preventing the Collapse of Civilization (English only)
videos.s: Jonathan Blow's DevGAMM 2019 talk argues that software knowledge is being lost between generations and that growing layers of abstraction could lead to a decline in technological civilization.
videos.w: A perennial HN reference for arguments that software is getting worse and that hard-won knowledge is disappearing.
videos.q: Very much worth watching in its entirety and thinking about

videos.t: VidMe or Why Platforms Aren't Your Friends
videos.s: Folding Ideas uses the rise and fall of the YouTube competitor VidMe to examine why platforms are not friends to creators. It argues that alternatives to big platforms tend to attract the users banned from the original and lack a core vision.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever a thread asks why clones of or alternatives to YouTube, Reddit or Twitter fail or turn toxic.
videos.q: Folding Ideas (on YouTube) had a solid video about VidMe, which is a case study in how NOT to do this

videos.t: Break Me00 The MoVfuscator Turning mov into a soul crushing RE nightmare Christopher Domas
videos.s: Christopher Domas's Derbycon 2015 talk on the M/o/Vfuscator, a compiler that emits only x86 mov instructions, showing mov is Turing complete. It explains how a full machine is built from mov and why the output is a nightmare to reverse engineer.
videos.w: HN calls it a legendary, clearly explained hacker talk whenever mov-only computing or anti-decompilation comes up.
videos.q: Christopher Domas's conference talk on the movfuscator is legendary

videos.t: Trackers: The Sound of 16-Bit
videos.s: Ahoy's documentary traces tracker music from early Amiga software like SoundMonitor and Soundtracker through the demoscene, Protracker, and PC trackers such as Screamtracker and FastTracker. It covers the sound, culture and history of 16-bit module music.
videos.w: It is the go-to chronological, in-depth overview of tracker music, recommended whenever trackers, the Amiga or the demoscene come up.
videos.q: is an incredible, in-depth overview of trackers, their sound and history

videos.t: 27C3: Adventures in analyzing Stuxnet (Bruce Dang from Microsoft)
videos.s: Bruce Dang of Microsoft gives a 27C3 talk on how the Stuxnet vulnerabilities were found and analyzed. He walks through the techniques used to triage them and the details of each zero-day exploit, down to the opcode level.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the definitive technical deep dive into Stuxnet's zero-days from someone who analyzed it first-hand.
videos.q: For an amazing technical deep dive into each 0-day Stuxnet vulnerability watch this talk with Bruce Dang from Microsoft[1].

videos.t: Eating less Meat won't save the Planet. Here's Why
videos.s: Joseph Everett, with Dr. Frank Mitloehner, argues that eating less meat will not do much for the climate. He covers beef's water footprint, land and feed use, and methane.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a counterpoint to claims about beef's environmental cost, though some critique its methane argument.
videos.q: I was much more concerned about my beef consumption before watching this WIL video. It put things in perspective for me.

videos.t: Imaginary Numbers Are Real [Part 1: Introduction]
videos.s: The first part of Welch Labs' series on imaginary numbers, presenting them as the natural extension of the number line into two dimensions. It covers the history and the math with strong visuals.
videos.w: HN commenters rate the series as some of the best visual teaching on complex numbers and recommend it for building intuition.
videos.q: The greatest audiovisual content on the topic I have ever seen

videos.t: Bottom Up vs  Top Down Design in Clojure - Mark Bastian
videos.s: Mark Bastian contrasts top-down object-oriented design with bottom-up, data-oriented design in Clojure. He models a board game as plain data plus small composable functions and compares it with a roughly 22-class OOP version.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the talk that made data-oriented, REPL-driven bottom-up design click.
videos.q: is the talk that really made it clear to me how to design programs this way.

videos.t: Dr. Jason Fung - 'Therapeutic Fasting - Solving the Two-Compartment Problem'
videos.s: Dr. Jason Fung, a nephrologist, explains therapeutic fasting as a treatment for obesity and type 2 diabetes. He frames it around the two-compartment problem of fat storage and insulin resistance.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as a free, evidence-citing overview of fasting that counters worries about muscle loss and safety.
videos.q: I always recommend people watch this by Dr. Jason Fung

videos.t: TempleOS | Down the Rabbit Hole
videos.s: Fredrik Knudsen's 86-minute documentary on Terry A. Davis, creator of TempleOS, tracing his work, his schizophrenia and his decline. It is a chronological video essay built on his public posts and videos.
videos.w: Regarded as the definitive, if heartbreaking, account of Terry Davis and TempleOS.
videos.q: This video is the definitive rundown on his life and illness

videos.t: Frank Abagnale | Catch Me If You Can | Talks at Google
videos.s: Frank Abagnale, the real subject of Catch Me If You Can, speaks at Google about his life as a con man turned FBI fraud and cybersecurity expert, including advice on fraud, breaches and credit cards.
videos.w: Praised as a charismatic, engaging talk with practical security lessons, like why credit cards protect you better than debit cards.
videos.q: One of the best google talks I have seen.

videos.t: Falcon Heavy Test Flight
videos.s: SpaceX's livestream of the Falcon Heavy test flight, including the launch, side booster landings and Tesla Roadster payload. It was the first launch of the most powerful operational rocket at the time.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as a landmark launch broadcast, and also dissect details like the duplicated booster landing feeds.
videos.q: You should watch the launch, its probably one of the most interesting engineering projects of the last few years.

videos.t: Why Japan Looks the Way it Does: Zoning
videos.s: A video explaining why Japanese cities look the way they do, through Japan's national tiered zoning system that permits mixed use and flexible development. It compares this approach with more restrictive zoning elsewhere.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the go-to explanation of Japanese zoning in housing and urbanism debates.
videos.q: The best videos on this (in my opinion)

videos.t: Brown; color is weird
videos.s: Technology Connections explains why brown is not a spectral color but a context-dependent perception, essentially dark orange seen against brighter surroundings.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as a surprisingly magical explainer on color perception, often cited in color-space discussions.
videos.q: made me watch a 20 minutes videos on the color brown and makes it feel like magic

videos.t: Plover: Thought to Text at 240 WPM
videos.s: Mirabai Knight's PyCon 2013 talk on Plover, a free cross-platform stenography engine that lets people write at up to 240 WPM on ordinary hardware, including a demo of coding by steno.
videos.w: HN's standard reference when typing speed, ergonomics, or alternative input comes up, for its live demo and the open-source steno ecosystem.
videos.q: Mirabai Knight's talk about this is one of my all time faves

videos.t: "The Economics of Programming Languages" by Evan Czaplicki (Strange Loop 2023)
videos.s: Evan Czaplicki, creator of Elm, examines how programming languages are funded. He looks at where compiler engineers' salaries come from, why Go has about 5 engineers while Dart has about 30, and how this limits language design.
videos.w: Recommended repeatedly as a funny, informative talk on the economics behind programming languages and open source.
videos.q: Very highly recommend this funny, informative talk to understand aspects of creating a programming language other than the theoretical ones.

videos.t: Conflict Resolution for Eventual Consistency • Martin Kleppmann • GOTO 2016
videos.s: Martin Kleppmann's GOTO Berlin 2016 talk on how collaborative editors, offline apps, and multi-datacenter databases handle concurrent updates. It covers conflict resolution approaches including operational transformation and CRDTs, with a worked look at text CRDTs.
videos.w: Treated as the go-to approachable yet deep primer on CRDTs and collaborative editing, recommended repeatedly in threads on Automerge, local-first software and OT versus CRDT.
videos.q: Rest of the talk is also highly recommended for anyone interested in an approachable primer on CRDTs.

videos.t: BlackHat USA 2011: SSL And The Future Of Authenticity
videos.s: Moxie Marlinspike's BlackHat 2011 talk examines weaknesses of SSL and the certificate authority system and proposes Convergence, a decentralized notary approach with trust agility.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the best explanation of why the CA system is broken and what alternatives exist.
videos.q: best talk I know of this subject

videos.t: DOUGLAS ADAMS: Parrots, the Universe and Everything
videos.s: Douglas Adams gives a talk at UCSB, recorded shortly before his death, about the odd lives of animals and what they suggest about humanity's future. It draws on his Last Chance to See work and is funny and wide-ranging.
videos.w: Adams fans repeatedly call it one of his best talks, a funny and moving look at extinction and the environment.
videos.p: douglas adams on nature and extinction
videos.q: Watch the whole thing. You will thank me later.

videos.t: "Programming a 144-computer chip to minimize power" - Chuck Moore (2013)
videos.s: Chuck Moore, inventor of Forth, presents GreenArrays' 144-core asynchronous chip at Strange Loop 2013. He explains how idle cores draw almost no power and how tight code minimizes energy use.
videos.w: It is the favorite recommendation for understanding Moore's minimalist, low-power multi-core designs and stack machines.
videos.q: This talk by Chuck Moore at Strange Loop was amazing

videos.t: Blockchains Are a Bad Idea (James Mickens)
videos.s: James Mickens of Harvard gives a funny lecture at HBS's Future Assembly arguing that blockchains are a very bad idea. He covers their trust, legal and practical shortcomings for real-world problems.
videos.w: A staple HN recommendation in crypto and Web3 threads as an entertaining, compelling case against blockchain.
videos.q: James Mickens' "Blockchains are a bad idea" talk [1] is a great explanation that discusses exactly that.

videos.t: DebConf 14: QA with Linus Torvalds
videos.s: A 72-minute Q&A with Linus Torvalds at DebConf 14. Topics include the pain of distributing Linux binaries, distro fragmentation, kernel backwards compatibility, GPLv2 versus GPLv3 and conduct.
