videos.w: HN returns to it as Linus's own explanation of why shipping software on Linux is hard and why he dislikes GPLv3.
videos.q: Highly recommend watching Linus's answer ~6 minutes in

videos.t: This is Financial Advice
videos.s: Dan Olson's long Folding Ideas video on the GameStop meme stock phenomenon, its online community and the conspiracy thinking around it. It runs over two hours.
videos.w: Recommended as a thorough, sober critique of meme-stock culture and a good starting point whenever GameStop news appears.
videos.q: I would highly recommend "This is Financial Advice" by Dan Olson to anyone not already familiar with the community.

videos.t: NaN Gates and Flip FLOPS
videos.s: Tom Murphy (suckerpinch) presents a deliberately trollish computer architecture built on IEEE-754 floating point, using NaN and infinity to define logic gates. He builds working hardware around the idea.
videos.w: HN fans hold it up as a favorite among his videos and an example of gloriously bonkers technical art, and cite it in floating-point discussions.
videos.q: Suckerpinch barely ever releases a video, but when he does they are great.

videos.t: Why Are You So Angry? Part 1: A Short History of Anita Sarkeesian
videos.s: The first part of Innuendo Studios' six-part video essay series on the online hostility around Anita Sarkeesian and GamerGate. It lays out the history and the motivations of the people involved.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as a nuanced analysis of online harassment, defensiveness, and gaming culture conflict.
videos.q: This video series does a pretty amazing job in describing those two groups and their motivations

videos.t: DNA animation (2002-2014) by Drew Berry and Etsuko Uno wehi.tv #ScienceArt
videos.s: A compilation of molecular animations of DNA replication and gene transcription by Drew Berry and Etsuko Uno at WEHI, made with no narration. It shows molecular machinery at work inside cells.
videos.w: Recommended whenever people want to see the mechanical, jostling reality of molecular biology, which many find awe-inspiring.
videos.q: Seeing the mechanical nature of gene transciption and chemical signaling blew my mind.

videos.t: "Stop Writing Dead Programs" by Jack Rusher (Strange Loop 2022)
videos.s: Jack Rusher's Strange Loop 2022 talk argues that most programming languages are still designed around punchcard-era assumptions. He makes the case for live, interactive programming environments, drawing on Lisp, Smalltalk and REPL-driven development.
videos.w: HN returns to it constantly as the talk on live programming and what modern tooling is missing, though a few found it too much.
videos.q: One of my favorite talks is

videos.t: Principles of Technology Leadership | Bryan Cantrill | Monktoberfest 2017
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill's Monktoberfest 2017 talk on leadership and organizational principles, ranging from the Gettysburg Address to Uber and Amazon. He argues for the difference between principles and values and criticizes vague corporate principles.
videos.w: HN treats it as a classic, must-watch talk for any discussion of company values, and especially for its takedown of Amazon's leadership principles.
videos.q: No discussion of company values would be complete without a link to Bryan Cantrill’s classic talk,

videos.t: #HITB2012KUL D1T3 - The Grugq - OPSEC: Because Jail is for wuftpd
videos.c: Hack In The Box Security Conference
videos.s: The Grugq's Hack In The Box 2012 talk on operational security for hackers, drawing on hacker indictments and counter-intelligence research. It reviews OPSEC goals and methods for avoiding detection and arrest, with case studies of how hackers got caught.
videos.w: HN treats it as the go-to talk on OPSEC and pseudonymity, recommended in threads about Tor, Silk Road and staying anonymous online.
videos.q: It's a great watch if you're interested in how various (in)famous hackers thought they were secure and got busted anyway.

videos.t: Feynman on Scientific Method.
videos.s: A short clip of Richard Feynman explaining the scientific method: guess, compute consequences, compare to experiment, and why vague theories like astrology cannot be proven wrong.
videos.w: Widely recommended as one of the clearest, funniest short explanations of what makes something science.
videos.q: it remains one of the best explanations of the scientific method around because it is clear, funny and short

videos.t: Incels | ContraPoints
videos.s: ContraPoints' 35-minute video essay on incels, examining the community, its worldview and how people get radicalized. It is delivered with theatrical style and an empathetic tone.
videos.w: Recommended as an empathetic, non-judgmental analysis of incel radicalization and how to counter it.
videos.q: Natalie Wynn's video^0 on incels always struck me as uniquely useful

videos.t: "Unison: a new distributed programming language" by Paul Chiusano
videos.s: Paul Chiusano's Strange Loop 2019 talk introduces Unison, an open-source functional language for distributed, elastic systems. It covers content-addressed code identified by hashes of the syntax tree, a codebase manager, and algebraic effects called abilities.
videos.w: HN treats it as the best introduction to Unison, with commenters finding hash-addressed immutable code mind-blowing.
videos.q: this talk might be a better introduction than just skimming at the landing page.

videos.t: Sinclair Broadcast Group: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on Sinclair Broadcast Group, the largest owner of US local TV stations, and how it injects political content and scripted must-run segments into local news.
videos.w: HN repeatedly points to it as the eye-opening explanation of media consolidation and scripted local news.
videos.q: Highly recommend.

videos.t: Lecture: 2017 Maps of Meaning 01: Context and Background
videos.s: The first lecture of Jordan Peterson's 2017 Maps of Meaning course, setting out the Cold War context for his theory of belief and culture. He introduces the narrative structure of culture and archetypal characters for the individual, the known and the unknown.
videos.w: Several HN commenters credit the lecture series with helping them through depression or personal collapse and recommend it as long-form learning.
videos.q: this series genuinely helped me put myself back together after my ego was shattered

videos.t: The 7 Habits of Highly Miserable People
videos.s: CGP Grey's sarcastic animated video adapted from the book How to Be Miserable, listing habits that reliably make people unhappy. By inverting the advice, it shows what to avoid and prompts reflection on goals and routines.
videos.w: HN recommends it widely in advice threads on depression, habits, and goal setting as a funny, memorable way to see what to do by seeing what not to do.
videos.q: Here's a great video going over the same concepts but in a humorous way.

videos.t: Hey Underscore, You're Doing It Wrong!
videos.s: Brian Lonsdorf explains why Underscore.js falls short as a functional programming library, then introduces currying, composition and point-free style in JavaScript. He argues for data-last argument ordering.
videos.w: A repeatedly recommended introduction to functional JavaScript that explains currying and why data should come last.
videos.q: this video gives a pretty good explanation in ~30 minutes

videos.t: Everything is a Remix (Original Series)
videos.s: Kirby Ferguson's video essay series arguing that creativity is built on copying, transforming and combining existing work. It covers music, film and technology, then turns to copyright and patents.
videos.w: HN invokes it constantly in debates over originality, copyright and AI training, and calls it the best explanation of creativity as remixing.
videos.q: The best explanation of creativity that I have found is a video series by Kirby Ferguson called Everything Is a Remix

videos.t: I Was SCARED To Say This To NASA... (But I said it anyway) - Smarter Every Day 293
videos.s: Destin Sandlin of Smarter Every Day gives a talk to an aerospace audience, comparing how Apollo was engineered and managed with NASA's Artemis program. He raises concerns about unresolved details, the number of launches and in-orbit fuel transfer needed to reach the Moon, and the loss of institutional knowledge.
videos.w: Commenters point to it whenever Artemis, SLS or Starship refueling comes up, as a candid and critical engineering assessment delivered directly to NASA.
videos.q: one of the bravest talks I’ve seen in a while about the lessons of the Apollo program for Artemis

videos.t: Exploring the Tech and Design of Noita
videos.s: In this 2019 GDC session, Petri Purho of Nolla Games explains the technical side of Noita's physics engine, including scaling a falling-sand simulation to large continuous worlds and adding destructible rigid bodies. It also shows how the emergent physics drives the gameplay.
videos.w: It is the go-to talk for anyone building falling-sand or pixel-physics simulations, and several commenters say they modeled their own engines on it.
videos.q: Highly recommended if you want to dive deeper into the topic.

videos.t: Why No One Has Measured The Speed Of Light
videos.s: Veritasium explains why the one-way speed of light has never been measured, only the round-trip speed, since measuring it requires synchronized clocks that assume the answer. It explores the implications for relativity.
videos.w: Used as the standard reference in threads about light speed, clock synchronization and untestable assumptions in physics.
videos.q: I found the video very compelling even as a thought experiment.

videos.t: Wealth Inequality in America
videos.s: A short infographic video on the distribution of wealth in America, contrasting what people believe, what they consider ideal, and the actual numbers. It highlights how top-heavy US wealth is.
videos.w: HN commenters drop it whenever wealth inequality comes up, as a quick visual of the gap between perceived and actual distribution.
videos.q: This short info-graphic video makes is pretty clear how dramatically top heavy wealth distribution in the U.S. is

videos.t: A Talk Near the Future of Python (a.k.a., Dave live-codes a WebAssembly Interpreter)
videos.s: David Beazley's PyCon India closing keynote, in which he live-codes a stack machine and grows it into an interpreter that runs WebAssembly, then uses it to play a Rust-written game. It requires no prior WebAssembly knowledge.
videos.w: Regarded as a brilliant live-coding talk that teaches WASM and interpreter writing, with several calling it among the best conference talks they have seen.
videos.q: it's quite possible the best conference talk I've ever seen.

videos.t: Keynote: Paul Graham, YCombinator
videos.s: Paul Graham's keynote at PyCon 2012, in which he talks about startup ideas and what kinds of companies are likely to matter in the future. He discusses ideas such as a better email client and a search engine for hackers, and argues for looking back at the present from the future.
videos.w: HN commenters return to it as a worldview-shaping talk whose predictions about technology and startup ideas turned out to be prescient.
videos.q: It was the talk that brought about the biggest change in the way I think about the world, my ambitions.

videos.t: Rails Conf 2012 Keynote: Simplicity Matters by Rich Hickey
videos.s: Rich Hickey's keynote at RailsConf 2012, a close sibling of his 'Simple Made Easy' talk. He distinguishes simple (not intertwined) from easy (familiar), and argues that software complexity comes from complecting things, with Rails-specific examples including large gem collections.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an alternative or companion to 'Simple Made Easy', and quotes its ideas about simplicity, complexity and 'hairballs' in discussions of frameworks, JSON and data design.
videos.q: maybe watch this version instead, since it's almost the same talk but for a Rails Conference, with a few references

videos.t: Roblox Pressured Us to Delete Our Video. So We Dug Deeper.
videos.s: A People Make Games follow-up investigation into Roblox, built on stories from players and creators after the channel's first video. It covers the platform's treatment of young developers and its moderation.
videos.w: Cited heavily in Roblox threads as a damning investigation into child labor, exploitation, and weak moderation, and suggested viewing for parents.
videos.q: Watch both People Make Games video about Roblox and try to argue that the company should not deserve all the public controversy it is getting.

videos.t: Mastering the Vim Language
videos.s: Chris Toomey of thoughtbot explains Vim as a language of commands, motions and text objects that combine into precise edits. He shows how to master the built-in pieces and extend them.
videos.w: Repeatedly called the best video introduction to Vim's underlying model.
videos.q: In video form, the best introduction I have seen is Chris Toomey’s

videos.t: Casey Muratori – The Big OOPs: Anatomy of a Thirty-five-year Mistake – BSC 2025
videos.s: Casey Muratori's two-hour talk tracing the history of object-oriented programming back to the 1960s and examining how its ideas, and later entity component systems, came about. It is followed by a Q&A.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for its source-based history of OOP, though some dispute its account of Alan Kay.
videos.q: which really is hunting back and back for the cosmogenesis of objects, and covers so much terrain.

videos.t: CppCon 2015: Kate Gregory “Stop Teaching C"
videos.s: Kate Gregory argues at CppCon 2015 that C++ should be taught without starting from C: no char* strings, printf or raw arrays at first, with references before pointers.
videos.w: HN people cite it constantly in C versus C++ debates as the case for teaching modern C++ idioms rather than C first.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Not only is she a great presenter, but she makes amazing points about what is fundamentally wrong with how C++ is taught in classrooms around the globe.

videos.t: Zig: A programming language designed for robustness, optimality, and clarity –  Andrew Kelley
videos.s: Andrew Kelley, creator of Zig, introduces the language at the Recurse Center's Localhost series in 2018. He covers its goals of robustness, optimality and clarity, C interop, cross-compilation and explicit allocators.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the definitive introduction to Zig straight from its author, and links to it whenever Zig's design choices come up.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: here's a great talk on zig from the recurse center

videos.t: Michael Moore Presents: Planet of the Humans | A Film by Jeff Gibbs | Full Documentary
videos.s: Planet of the Humans, a full documentary by Jeff Gibbs presented by Michael Moore, arguing that the green movement has been co-opted by corporate and wealthy interests and that techno-fixes are not enough.
videos.w: HN uses it as a contrarian critique of renewables and green tech, often recommended with caveats about bias and flawed conclusions.
videos.q: Strongly recommended.

videos.t: What Really Happened During the Texas Power Grid Outage?
videos.s: Practical Engineering's explanation of the February 2021 Texas winter storm and the resulting power grid outage. It lays out the facts about ERCOT, the grid's isolation, and how generation across fuel types failed in the cold.
videos.w: Whenever Texas grid failures come up, HN people link it as the calm, technically informed account that cuts through political blame.
videos.q: The best low-emotion, technically informed analysis of "Snowpocalypse" is probably this one from "Practical Engineering

videos.t: The Voting System That Should Replace Every Election
videos.s: A short CGP Grey explainer on the alternative vote (instant runoff voting) versus first past the post, made around the 2011 UK referendum. It shows how ranked ballots are tallied and why they avoid spoiler effects.
videos.w: HN's go-to link whenever ranked-choice voting or voting reform comes up, because it explains the mechanics quickly and entertainingly.
videos.q: I've been a huge fan of this system ever since CGP Grey made an excellent video on how it works and why it's great.

videos.t: The Art of Code - Dylan Beattie
videos.s: Dylan Beattie's NDC London talk on code written for art, fun and curiosity rather than utility. It includes quines, live music programming with Sonic Pi, and a memorable closing.
videos.w: HN regularly names it among the best programming talks ever, praising the storytelling, the demos and the ending.
videos.q: one of the most captivating tech talks I've ever seen.

videos.t: Clean Code - Uncle Bob / Lesson 1
videos.s: The first lesson of Uncle Bob (Robert C. Martin)'s "Coding Better World Together" series. It makes the case for clean code and for treating software craftsmanship as an ethical and professional responsibility. It runs about 109 minutes.
videos.w: HN commenters call it better than the Clean Code book, a must-watch for engineers that changes how they read and write code.
videos.q: Clean Code is a great book, but the presentation is so much better

videos.t: 'A Universe From Nothing' by Lawrence Krauss, AAI 2009
videos.c: Richard Dawkins Foundation for Reason & Science
videos.s: Lawrence Krauss's 2009 talk on the current picture of the universe, how it will end and how it could have come from nothing. It covers the expanding universe, cosmic background radiation and the cosmological constant.
videos.w: HN regards it as a famous, mesmerizing talk, especially for the point that distant galaxies will become unobservable.
videos.q: There is also one of my favorite talks tangentially related by Lawrence Krauss.

videos.t: Why It Was Almost Impossible to Make the Blue LED
videos.s: Veritasium tells the story of how Shuji Nakamura and others made the blue LED, long thought nearly impossible. It covers the materials challenge of gallium nitride and the persistence it took.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a gripping story of single-minded persistence against the herd, and as the back story behind modern LED lighting.
videos.q: is goes into great detail on what it took to make the blue LED. It's quite fascinating.

videos.t: The EU Has Orbits, and the UK Fell Out of All of Them
videos.s: CGP Grey's six-minute explainer of the relationships the UK could have with the EU, based on Barnier's slide, shown as orbits of different closeness. It explains why the UK's red lines ruled out the closer options.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the quickest clear overview of the Brexit options, though later commenters note it predates the final outcome.
videos.q: taking from the amazing short overview here

videos.t: Intro to Synthesis Part 1 - The Building Blocks of Sound & Synthesis
videos.s: Dean Friedman's near-hour-long introduction to synthesis, covering the building blocks of sound and the controls on a synthesizer. He slowly adjusts knobs so viewers hear what each parameter does.
videos.w: Repeatedly called the best beginner course on audio synthesis, since the concepts have not changed since it was made.
videos.q: It's the best educational video I've seen on YT

videos.t: The Best Country in the World for Drivers
videos.s: Not Just Bikes argues that the Netherlands, famed for cycling, is also the best country for drivers. It explains how prioritizing walking, cycling and transit makes driving faster and more pleasant.
videos.w: Recommended as the argument that better alternatives to driving also improve things for drivers, and as an introduction to Dutch urban planning.
videos.q: One of the many excellent videos on the Not Just Bikes YouTube channel [1] shows how the Netherlands has done it.

videos.t: Richard Feynman Computer Science Lecture - Hardware, Software and Heuristics
videos.s: A lecture by Richard Feynman on how computers work, using the analogy of a filing clerk that becomes progressively dumber and faster. It also covers heuristics and how computers handle data and solve problems in finite time.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as the clearest plain-language explanation of what a computer fundamentally is, with at least one commenter saying it changed how they think about programming.
videos.q: This actually changed the way I think about it after years of programming.

videos.t: CppCon 2014: Chandler Carruth "Efficiency with Algorithms, Performance with Data Structures"
videos.s: Chandler Carruth's CppCon 2014 talk on writing fast C++, explaining why data structure choice and memory layout matter more than clever algorithms. It covers why standard containers like unordered_map perform poorly on modern CPUs.
videos.w: A perennial recommendation for anyone learning performance optimization, cited whenever hash tables, cache behavior or STL containers come up.
videos.q: I'm also a big fan of "Efficiency with Algorithms, Performance with Data Structures" by Chandler Carruth at CppCon 2014.

videos.t: Joe Ades , Greatest Salesman in New York City History !!! #KONYH !!
videos.s: A short street-level clip of Joe Ades, the New York pitchman who sold vegetable peelers to crowds on the sidewalk. It shows his patter, showmanship and crowd handling in action.
videos.w: HN treats him as a master class in salesmanship and live presentation, where how you sell matters more than what you sell.
videos.q: I urge you, I implore you, I beg you, stop what you're doing and watch Joe in action

videos.t: It’s Time To Break Up With Our Gas Stoves | Climate Town
videos.s: Climate Town argues for moving away from gas stoves. It covers the gas industry's decades of marketing and lobbying, health effects of gas cooking, methane leaks, and the case for induction.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it in gas stove and induction threads for exposing how the idea that gas is better for cooking was a marketing ploy.
videos.q: Here's a great video on the topic by Climate Town, an awesome educator on climate change

videos.t: [EPILEPSY WARNING] How fast should an unoptimized terminal run?
videos.s: Casey Muratori shows how fast a terminal renderer can run, building a simple reference renderer that handles Unicode and colored text far quicker than Windows Terminal. He argues that common excuses for slow terminals do not hold up.
videos.w: It is the canonical reference for the claim that modern software wastes hardware, and the proof-of-concept behind the Windows Terminal performance debate.
videos.q: Casey spent <1 week making RefTerm, a skeleton proto-terminal with the same constraints Microsoft people had

videos.t: The determinant | Chapter 6, Essence of linear algebra
videos.s: A 10-minute 3Blue1Brown chapter explaining the determinant as the factor by which a linear transformation scales area or volume. It builds the idea geometrically with animations before any formulas.
videos.w: HN repeatedly points people to it as the clearest visual intuition for determinants, often saying it finally made the concept click.
videos.q: I have warmed up to determinants ever since I saw 3Blue1Brown give a fairly intuitive explanation for them

videos.t: I Genetically Engineered *MYSELF* to Fix Lactose Intolerance
videos.s: The Thought Emporium's host describes making and taking a DIY gene therapy to treat his own lactose intolerance. It uses an AAV virus to deliver DNA coding for the lactose-digesting enzyme, made with biohacker Gabriel Licina's help.
videos.w: HN keeps citing it as the standard example of accessible DIY gene engineering and self-experimentation, in threads on gene therapy, CRISPR and biohacking.
videos.q: The rest of the channel is pure biohacking gold.

videos.t: Richard Feynman  - The.Character of Physical Law - Part 1 The Law of Gravitation (full version)
videos.s: The first of Richard Feynman's 1964 Cornell Messenger Lectures, The Character of Physical Law, focusing on the law of gravitation. Feynman builds up from planetary motion to the nature of physical laws.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as a masterclass in explaining physics clearly without condescension, accessible without formal training.
videos.q: Feynman is so good at explaining these concepts that you don't even need any formal training to understand them.

videos.t: The Machinery Of Freedom: Illustrated summary
videos.s: An illustrated 23-minute summary of David Friedman's talk based on The Machinery of Freedom. It describes how law, police and courts could work as market services in a stateless society, covering private law, polycentric law and objections.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as a short introduction to anarcho-capitalist ideas about private law and how disputes could be resolved without a state.
videos.q: it's an illustrated talk by David D. Friedman, explaining how police, courts and other things would exist and work in a world without government

videos.t: Minding your mitochondria | Dr. Terry Wahls | TEDxIowaCity
videos.s: Dr. Terry Wahls tells how she used diet to manage her multiple sclerosis and get out of a wheelchair, drawing on mitochondrial biology. TED flagged the talk as health advice based on personal narrative.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a moving personal story that motivated dietary changes, though it is also cited as anecdotal evidence.
videos.q: I highly recommend the talk, it is both very informative and very moving.

videos.t: Breaking the x86 Instruction Set
videos.s: Christopher Domas presents at Black Hat 2017 how page fault analysis and processor fuzzing can exhaustively search the x86 instruction set. The talk uncovers undocumented instructions and hardware bugs and shows limits of disassemblers.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clever, entertaining and easy-to-follow talk on finding hidden x86 instructions with the Sandsifter tool.
videos.q: I found it easy to follow and pretty entertaining.

videos.t: Why Grocery Shopping is Better in Amsterdam
videos.s: A four-minute Not Just Bikes comparison of grocery shopping in Amsterdam versus car-centric North America, arguing that frequent small fresh-food trips beat bulk shopping. It ties this to land use and reduced food waste.
videos.w: Linked in urbanism and car-dependence threads as a concise case for walkable fresh-food shopping.
videos.q: had me pretty convinced land use was the key to breaking through a bad food waste vs shelf-stable food trade-off.

videos.t: What can Seattle learn from Dutch street design?
videos.s: Seattle landscape architect Fred Young gives an hour-long visual tour of Dutch cycling infrastructure, covering design details, continuous networks and how cycling fits daily life in the Netherlands.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an in-depth tech talk for urban planning, full of small design touches that make cycling safer.
videos.q: It's a great in depth look for anyone interested in this stuff, basically a tech talk for urban planning.

videos.t: The world's worst video card?
videos.s: Ben Eater explains how VGA signals work and builds a breadboard circuit that produces correct sync timing so a monitor recognizes the signal. He then builds toward displaying an image from simple logic chips.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear, from-scratch look at how video hardware works, understandable with just basic logic knowledge.
videos.q: Anyone with a basic understanding of logic circuits has enough background to understand it. Worth a watch.

videos.t: NVC Marshall Rosenberg - San Francisco Workshop - FULL ENGLISH SUBTITLES TRANSCRIPTION
videos.s: A roughly three-hour San Francisco workshop by Marshall Rosenberg on Nonviolent Communication, with full English subtitles added by a fan. He teaches the model with his jackal and giraffe language examples.
videos.w: HN commenters send people to it as the primary source for NVC, recommended for relationships, compassion and difficult conversations.
videos.q: I recommend going directly to the source

videos.t: Functional Composition - Chris Ford
videos.s: Chris Ford builds up from a single sine wave through layered abstractions to a Bach canon, using Clojure and the Overtone audio environment. The talk shows music theory as a natural fit for functional programming.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as a delightful talk that makes music theory click and introduces Clojure and Overtone.
videos.q: Recommend this talk that made Music 'click' for me.

videos.t: Alan Kay, 2015: Power of Simplicity
videos.s: Alan Kay's 2015 talk on the power of simplicity, arguing that systems become simpler by building on more sophisticated fundamental building blocks and that big research horizons drove invention at Xerox PARC. It ranges across computing, tools and scaling software.
videos.w: HN repeatedly cites it as a thought-provoking talk on reducing software complexity and on the state of computing research.
videos.q: Easily over of the most thought provoking presentations I have seen recently.

videos.t: Cybersecurity as Realpolitik by Dan Geer presented at Black Hat USA 2014
videos.s: Dan Geer's Black Hat 2014 keynote argues that cybersecurity is a matter of power and policy rather than wishful thinking. He covers surveillance, the vulnerability market, software liability and privacy as the capacity to misrepresent yourself.
videos.w: Cited over and over as an important talk, with commenters borrowing its ideas on cheap surveillance, offense-favoring security and liability.
videos.q: Dan Geer, in his incredible talk last year[1]

videos.t: 01 - Course Introduction & Relational Model (CMU Databases Systems / Fall 2019)
videos.s: The first lecture of Andy Pavlo's CMU 15-445 Intro to Database Systems (Fall 2019), covering course introduction and the relational model.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as the best free university course on database internals, praised for depth and Pavlo's presentation.
videos.q: Highly recommended both for the depth and how Andy Pavlo presents the topic.

videos.t: The Psychology of Human Misjudgement - Charlie Munger Full Speech
videos.s: Audio of Charlie Munger's 1995 Harvard speech on the psychology of human misjudgment, laying out a framework of cognitive biases and mental models for decision making. It covers factors like incentives, social proof and denial.
videos.w: HN regards it as a classic to revisit every few years for improving decisions and self-awareness.
videos.q: Develop an intuitive understanding of the key mental models mentioned by Charlie Munger in his classic speech

videos.t: What your Differential Pairs Wish You Knew with Rick Hartley - AltiumLive Keynote
videos.s: Rick Hartley's AltiumLive keynote on differential pairs in PC boards. He argues the rules from cables and twisted pairs do not carry over, and covers which pair geometry gives the best impedance control, the right spacing, routing practice and how much skew is acceptable.
videos.w: HN engineers cite Hartley as the intuitive, field-based alternative to cargo-cult PCB advice, especially on differential pair routing, reference planes and EMI.
videos.q: this is absolutely worth your time if you design PCBs.

videos.t: DEF CON 26 - Svea, Suggy, Till - Inside the Fake Science Factory
videos.s: A DEF CON 26 talk by investigative journalists and hackers on the fake science industry, with bogus conferences and predatory journals that give studies false credibility. It draws on a large investigation into the money behind them.
videos.w: Recommended as a funny but depressing investigation, and the usual link in threads on predatory publishing and fake citations.
videos.q: It's a funny talk, if depressing. A great investigation.

videos.t: FIXING the ENTIRE SM64 Source Code (INSANE N64 performance)
videos.s: Kaze Emanuar explains how he rewrote and optimized the Super Mario 64 source code so it runs far faster on real N64 hardware. He covers performance bottlenecks and fixes in detail for his ROM hacks.
videos.w: HN loves the deep, hands-on look at N64 hardware quirks such as bus contention and the surprisingly large wins from low-hanging optimizations.
videos.q: amazing video about refactoring Mario 64 to reach 30 FPS and render 6x faster on N64

videos.t: Starbase Tour with Elon Musk [PART 1 // Summer 2021]
videos.s: Tim Dodd of Everyday Astronaut tours SpaceX's Starbase with Elon Musk as guide. They cover the high bay, grid fins, Raptor V2, the HLS lander and stage separation, and Musk explains his engineering management process.
videos.w: HN cites it as evidence of Musk's hands-on engineering depth and for his advice to question requirements and not optimize things that should not exist.
videos.q: Watch this walk around Starbase with Elon and Tim Dodd, and you'll get a pretty good sense that he has an engineering brain

videos.t: mRNA Translation (Advanced)
videos.s: A short animation from the DNA Learning Center showing how mRNA carries a gene's message to the ribosome, where tRNA and codons are used to assemble amino acids into a protein.
videos.w: Frequently linked as a mind-blowing visualization of how RNA is translated into protein, especially in threads on mRNA vaccines and cell biology.
videos.q: viewing these visualizations blew my mind

videos.t: Brainwash: The Gender Equality Paradox
videos.s: An episode of the Norwegian documentary series Brainwash, in which a comedian interviews academics from different sides about gender differences and gender equality. It looks at why more equal societies can still show unequal career choices.
videos.w: Recommended in HN threads on gender gaps in tech as a well-researched look at how gender differences and professional choices may arise.
videos.q: the whole series is brilliant

videos.t: Guided Wim Hof Method Breathing
videos.s: An 11-minute guided Wim Hof breathing session built around an expanding and contracting bubble to pace the breath. Wim breathes along with the viewer over ambient sound.
videos.w: HN commenters share it as an easy-to-follow guided exercise for anxiety, stress, and recovery, with many reporting daily use.
videos.q: It's been very valuable to me.

videos.t: Miguel de Icaza: Swift Godot: Fixing the Multi-million dollar mistake  #GodotCon2023
videos.s: Miguel de Icaza's GodotCon 2023 talk on Swift bindings for Godot. He argues that garbage-collector pauses in C# are a persistent problem and that Swift's reference counting avoids them.
videos.w: Frequently recommended for an experienced game-engine builder's view on why GC pauses are inevitable and why Swift's approach is appealing.
videos.q: Miguel De Icaza’s talk on the topic is highly recommended

videos.t: Guarding Against Physical Attacks: The Xbox One Story — Tony Chen, Microsoft
videos.s: Microsoft's Tony Chen explains how the Xbox One was designed to resist physical attacks, including secure boot, encrypted memory, a security processor and a hypervisor. The goal was to make any hardware attack cost more than the price of many games.
videos.w: HN points to it constantly in console, DRM and hardware-security threads as the authoritative account of Xbox One's threat model.
videos.q: This is a very interesting talk from Microsoft about how they made Xbox immune to physical attacks

videos.t: Google Self-Driving Car Project | SXSW Interactive 2016
videos.s: Chris Urmson's SXSW 2016 talk on Google's self-driving car project, covering 1.3 million self-driven miles and the gap between hype and reality. It shows sensor visualizations and playbacks of hard situations the cars met, and discusses failures such as the low-speed bus collision.
videos.w: HN returns to it repeatedly as one of the best candid talks on how a real self-driving system sees the road and where it struggles.
videos.q: It's one of the best talks on the subject.

videos.t: Domain Modeling Made Functional - Scott Wlaschin
videos.s: Scott Wlaschin's NDC talk on using statically typed functional programming, F# in particular, to model a business domain. Types are used to represent the domain precisely and to encode business rules so that illegal states cannot be built, with the compiler acting as an instant unit test.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as an eye-opening talk whose domain-modeling ideas carry over to other languages and make a strong compiler feel like a coding partner.
videos.q: If anyone is looking for a really eye-opening video take a look at that this.

videos.t: 'Diablo':  A Classic Game Postmortem
videos.s: David Brevik's GDC 2016 postmortem of Diablo covers how it went from a turn-based claymation DOS concept to a real-time action RPG, plus the story of Blizzard North and development anecdotes.
videos.w: Frequently recommended whenever Diablo or its origins come up, for its candid account of the human side of game development.
videos.q: heartily recommended if you want to know about the human aspect behind game dev

videos.t: Animations of unseeable biology | Drew Berry | TED
videos.s: Drew Berry shows scientifically accurate animations of molecular processes inside cells, such as DNA replication, at TEDxSydney.
videos.w: HN recommends it for mind-blowing visuals that make cell biology tangible.
videos.q: I had a much greater appreciation for how our bodies are made up of trillions of tiny protein machines.

videos.t: QuakeCon 2012 - John Carmack Keynote
videos.s: John Carmack's long QuakeCon 2012 keynote, a free-ranging talk covering software engineering, game platforms, game streaming, and his early head-mounted display and VR work.
videos.w: HN rates his QuakeCon keynotes among the best technical talks, and cites this one for the VR segment and for his views on Linux gaming.
videos.q: John Carmack did a pretty fascinating segment about his work on something to this effect

videos.t: Ira Glass on Storytelling 3
videos.s: A five-minute clip of Ira Glass on the gap between good taste and early creative work. He says beginners know their work falls short and must keep producing to close the gap.
videos.w: HN commenters return to it as motivation for creators who feel their work is not good enough yet.
videos.q: Ira Glass's take on this is so good and I go back to it often

videos.t: Michael Levin: The electrical blueprints that orchestrate life | TED
videos.s: Biologist Michael Levin explains the bioelectric layer that coordinates cells to build organs and bodies, showing footage of two-headed worms and introducing xenobots. He discusses implications for medicine and the nature of life.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as the accessible 20-minute entry point to Levin's bioelectricity research whenever regeneration or cell signaling comes up.
videos.q: If you have 20 minutes to watch this ted talk interview I highly recommend it.

videos.t: The Truth about American Cities - Part 1 - Strong Towns [ST01]
videos.s: The first video in Not Just Bikes' Strong Towns series explains the financial instability of North American cities, based on Strong Towns research. It argues that low-density suburban growth costs more to maintain than it brings in.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as the best introduction to why sprawl and car dependence are fiscally unsustainable, often pointing to the whole series.
videos.q: A good introduction on that part is the strong towns playlist by the youtube channel Not Just Bikes

videos.t: MountainWest RubyConf 2013 Devs and Depression by Greg  Baugues
videos.s: Greg Baugues tells his story of living with bipolar II and ADHD as a developer at a Ruby conference. He urges openness about mental illness and explains how to get help and support colleagues.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended in mental health threads for its honest storytelling that resonates with developers.
videos.q: I recommend this talk about depression and software developers: There are newer versions of this talk, but I think this one has the most powerful storytelling.

videos.t: Line Goes Up – The Problem With NFTs
videos.s: Dan Olson's roughly two-hour video essay critiques NFTs, cryptocurrency, and Web3, covering their technical, economic, and ideological flaws. It is heavily sourced and ends with the advice to ask whether a project needs crypto to work.
videos.w: It is the go-to long-form critique of crypto that HN commenters recommend whenever skeptics ask for a thorough, well-researched takedown.
videos.q: probably the most detailed and incisive critique of cryptocurrency and NFTs that I've seen

videos.t: Most Cities Got More Democratic. This One Didn't.
videos.s: CGP Grey explains the City of London's unusual governance, including the Lord Mayor, guilds, and how it differs from the rest of London.
videos.w: A favorite entry point to the weird history and privileges of the City of London.
videos.q: My favorite gateway drugs to learning more about the city of London are probably CGP Grey's videos

videos.t: BOLTR: Juicero, Cold Press Juicer for Rich Weirdos
videos.s: AvE tears down the Juicero cold-press juicer, examining its heavily machined parts, electronics and the pricey juice packs. He pokes fun at the product and venture-funded culture along the way.
videos.w: HN treats it as the classic teardown and the go-to example of over-engineered hardware built without real-world constraints.
videos.q: A beautiful technical / engineering take on why Juicero failed

videos.t: Elevated by RGBA and TBC
videos.s: Elevated is a 4 kilobyte PC demo by RGBA and TBC from Breakpoint 2009. It fly-throughs a realistic procedurally generated landscape with synthesized music and post-processing, all from a tiny executable.
videos.w: HN repeatedly holds it up as the benchmark for what procedural generation and size-coding can achieve in 4K.
videos.q: you'll have a hard time believing it if you haven't seen it yet

videos.t: I promise this story about microwaves is interesting.
videos.s: Tom Scott investigates the claim that the microwave was invented to heat hamsters, and interviews James Lovelock about freezing and microwave-thawing hamsters in the 1950s. It traces early magnetron uses beyond radar.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a well-told chase of a weird fact that lands a rare interview with Lovelock at age 101.
videos.q: The whole story is worth a watch since Tom Scott does an admirable job of explaining

videos.t: Unix and Google
videos.s: A short animated simulation comparing how Multics and Unix were developed, showing why Unix's small composable programs and pipes gave it a efficiency advantage. It frames Unix as a moonshot achievable by a small team.
videos.w: Cited constantly in threads on microservices, composability and the Unix philosophy as a compact explanation of why small interoperable pieces win.
videos.q: A guy on YT [1] simulates in 7 minutes how the two biggest operating systems were built in the sixties

videos.t: Ep. 1 - Awakening from the Meaning Crisis - Introduction
videos.s: The first episode of John Vervaeke's lecture series on the modern meaning crisis, tracing its history through philosophy, cognitive science, religion and psychology. It introduces the series and its themes.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as a thorough, non-dogmatic look at meaning, spirituality and escaping nihilism.
videos.q: this series has it all.

videos.t: "NO CGI" is really just INVISIBLE CGI - 1
videos.s: VFX supervisor Jonas Ussing examines what studios mean by "no CGI", showing how much invisible CGI hides behind practical-effects marketing. It is the first part of a multi-part series that includes analysis of doctored behind-the-scenes footage.
videos.w: Strongly recommended whenever HN discusses CGI, practical effects, or trusting behind-the-scenes footage.
videos.q: I highly recommend this 5-part essay series

videos.t: Chris McCord - Keynote: Phoenix LiveView - Interactive Apps without Javascript - ElixirConf EU 2019
videos.s: Chris McCord's ElixirConf EU 2019 keynote introducing Phoenix LiveView, which builds interactive server-rendered apps without writing JavaScript. It explains how only changed dynamic parts are sent over a websocket.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the primary source for understanding LiveView's advantages and its middle ground between multipage apps and SPAs.
videos.q: Great talk about it from the developer here

videos.t: A New Way to look at Networking
videos.s: Van Jacobson's 2006 Google Tech Talk argues that networking should be rethought around named data rather than host-to-host conversations. He contrasts the circuit and datagram views of the internet and sketches content-centric networking as a replacement for the location-centric TCP/IP model.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a clear explanation of why data-centric networking fits how the internet is actually used, and as a core talk on content addressing.
videos.q: This video explains very clearly how this is the case

videos.t: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (in plain English)
videos.s: Okta developer advocate Nate Barbettini explains OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect in a roughly hour-long talk. It starts from the problems the protocols solve and walks through the flows. The description notes the implicit flow material is now out of date.
videos.w: HN repeatedly points people to it as the clearest way to finally understand OAuth, to the point that one team made it required viewing for new hires.
videos.q: it was a requirement for new joiners to watch this in their first week

videos.t: The House I Live In Official Trailer #1 (2012) Drugs Documentary Movie HD
videos.s: Official trailer for Eugene Jarecki's 2012 documentary The House I Live In, an investigative look at America's war on drugs and its effect on the criminal justice system. It won the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend the film itself as an eye-opening account of how drug laws drove mass incarceration and militarized policing.
videos.q: a fantastic documentary about the US drug war/justice system. Go watch it now.

videos.t: LEADERSHIP LAB: Writing Beyond the Academy 1.23.15
videos.s: Larry McEnerney of the University of Chicago Writing Program argues that good writing is defined by what readers value, not by rules or the writer's own ideas. He explains why academic habits fail outside academia and how to write so readers find the work valuable.
videos.w: HN treats it as the definitive writing lecture and recommends it repeatedly, with several commenters saying it changed how they write.
videos.q: good writing is not about rules, it's about the function of the text, the readers, and what they value.

videos.t: Jonathan Blow: Game design: the medium is the message
videos.s: Jonathan Blow's CreativeMornings talk arguing that business models shape game design, drawing an analogy between 1970s TV and HBO and between free-to-play and premium games. He calls for games that inspire awe rather than chase constraints.
videos.w: HN cites it repeatedly in debates about in-app purchases and monetization corrupting games.
videos.q: how the business model deeply corrupts the game through the metaphor of bad 70's TV shows vs HBO

videos.t: I painted a Landscape with Mathematics
videos.s: Inigo Quilez live-paints a mountain landscape using only math in a shader, building up from a basic polynomial noise surface through fractal terrain, lighting and atmosphere. The code runs in real time on Shadertoy so viewers can edit it as they follow along.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as the best demonstration of procedural graphics from a master, accessible to beginners yet deep enough for advanced viewers.
videos.q: My favorite video of his is Painting a Landscape with Maths.

videos.t: The Economics of Airline Class
videos.s: Wendover Productions explains how airlines make money from different cabin classes and why premium seats matter so much to profits. It also touches on how this shaped decisions such as the decline of supersonic travel.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an in-depth, accessible look at airline class economics and revisit it in many discussions about airlines.
videos.q: Would highly recommend the YouTube video below [0] from Wendover

videos.t: James Powell: So you want to be a Python expert? | PyData Seattle 2017
videos.s: James Powell's nearly two-hour PyData talk builds up Python's data model, decorators, generators and context managers, coding live in Vim. It aims to take intermediate programmers toward real Python expertise.
videos.w: HN calls it one of the best technical talks and the clearest explanation of decorators, generators and context managers.
videos.q: It's legitimately the best technical talk I think I've seen and I can't recommend it highly enough.

videos.t: Emacs Rocks! Episode 14: Paredit
videos.s: A three-minute Emacs Rocks screencast by Magnar Sveen demonstrating paredit, which edits Lisp code structurally as a tree of s-expressions rather than characters.
videos.w: Repeatedly offered as the quickest, most convincing demo of structured editing and why Lisp programmers love paredit.
videos.q: it's well worth the 3:40.

videos.t: What Alcohol Does to Your Body, Brain & Health
videos.s: A two-hour Huberman Lab podcast episode on the physiological effects of alcohol on the brain and body at different levels of consumption. It covers genetic predisposition to alcoholism, alcohol metabolism, and how it causes cellular stress and changes thinking and behavior.
videos.w: HN commenters say it convinced them to quit or cut down on drinking, and point to it as a more comprehensive treatment than most articles.
videos.q: Andrew Huberman's 2-hour blog post on the negative effects of alcohol[1] convinced me to stop drinking.

videos.t: Manufactured Discontent and Fortnite
videos.s: Dan Olson of Folding Ideas critiques Fortnite's monetization, arguing it uses manufactured discontent, such as shop design and skins, to push spending. The video dissects the psychological techniques behind the game's business model.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as the definitive critique of Fortnite's monetization and of manipulative free-to-play design.
videos.q: There's a great video[1] that goes into detail on the psychological manipulation used in Fortnite's monetization model.

videos.t: Net Neutrality: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver's 13-minute Last Week Tonight segment explains the 2014 net neutrality fight over cable companies creating unequal internet speeds. It uses comedy to make a dull regulatory topic engaging and tells viewers how to comment to the FCC.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as the go-to funny, accessible explanation of net neutrality and credit it with driving public comments to the FCC.
videos.q: John Oliver did a much better job (and funnier, btw)

videos.t: Fractals are typically not self-similar
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown explains fractal dimension and shows why many fractals are not strictly self-similar. Self-similarity turns out to be a special case of the broader idea of fractional dimension.
videos.w: It is the standard pointer for a clear, visual explanation of what fractals are, and for correcting the idea that fractal means self-similar.
videos.q: Here is are two very clear explanations of fractal dimension by the man himself, Grant from 3b1b.

videos.t: Simple Code, High Performance
videos.s: Casey Muratori's University of Twente guest lecture is a case study in how straightforward code can cut thousands of lines and tens of seconds of runtime down to a few dozen lines running in under a second. It uses concrete examples to show why software is often an order of magnitude slower than it should be.
videos.w: HN people recommend it to anyone wanting a practical sense of what CPUs can really do and why abstraction layers cost so much performance.
videos.q: I highly recommend watching it.

videos.t: The LED Traffic Light and the Danger of "But Sometimes!"
videos.s: Technology Connections explains how LED traffic lights, which do not melt snow, drew complaints and were blamed for accidents. He uses it to illustrate the 'but sometimes' fallacy against new technology.
videos.w: Cited constantly as the name and example of the 'but sometimes' argument, where edge cases are used to resist better technology such as EVs and solar.
videos.p: led traffic lights and technology criticism
videos.q: I love Technology Connections' take on this line of argument [0]

videos.t: The Road to Zig 1.0 - Andrew Kelley
videos.s: Zig creator Andrew Kelley justifies why Zig exists and tours its distinctive features, including C interoperability and comptime, along with what people had built and what 1.0 would bring. It was given at Philly ETE 2019.
videos.w: HN treats it as the standard introduction to Zig by its creator, with some calling it among the best talks they have seen.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Andrew Kelley's intro[0] is probably the best talk I've ever seen

videos.t: Math's Fundamental Flaw
videos.s: Veritasium's explainer on Godel's incompleteness theorems and the limits of mathematical proof, tracing set theory, Hilbert's program and the road to Turing and modern computing.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a clear, accessible introduction to incompleteness and the self-referential proof idea.
videos.q: I found Veritaseum's video about it really clear and instructive

videos.t: Andrej Karpathy - AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla
videos.s: Andrej Karpathy, then Tesla's head of AI, presents at ScaledML 2020 on how Tesla builds full self-driving using vision-based neural nets and fleet data collection. He covers training custom detectors and neural nets gradually replacing traditional code.
videos.w: HN repeatedly points to it as the best public technical overview of Tesla's FSD approach, used both to defend and to critique Tesla's progress.
videos.q: I highly recommend watching head of AI at Tesla Andrej Karpathy's talk on their self driving architecture.

videos.t: Stephen Fry Kinetic Typography - Language
videos.s: A kinetic typography animation set to Stephen Fry's spoken essay on language. Fry argues against grammar pedantry and for the way language evolves, including the verbing of nouns.
videos.w: HN uses it as the go-to short piece against pedantry and for language change, recommended whenever grammar disputes come up.
videos.q: I highly encourage this 6 minute take by Stephen Fry on Language

videos.t: Darius Kazemi, Tiny Subversions - XOXO Festival (2014)
videos.s: Darius Kazemi's XOXO 2014 talk on releasing 72 weird internet side projects in a year. Framed as 'How I Won the Lottery,' it argues that success needs both luck and buying many tickets.
videos.w: HN uses it as the favorite antidote to survivorship-bias success stories, arguing that trying many cheap things raises your odds.
videos.q: Darius Kazemi's iconic 2014[1] talk

videos.t: The Voting System That's Actually Too Good for Politicians to Allow
videos.s: CGP Grey explains the Single Transferable Vote, a proportional ranked-ballot system, and why politicians have little incentive to adopt it. It is a short animated explainer of how multi-winner ranked voting works.
videos.w: HN's default link for explaining STV in any thread on voting reform, ranked choice or gerrymandering.
videos.q: CGP Grey did a great video on STV

videos.t: Immigration, World Poverty and Gumballs
videos.s: Roy Beck's short gumball presentation using World Bank and Census data to argue that letting people immigrate to the US cannot solve world poverty because the numbers are so large. It is made by NumbersUSA, an immigration-restriction advocacy group.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a quick visualization of the scale of global poverty versus immigration capacity, though it is advocacy with a specific viewpoint.
videos.q: Please, please watch this 6 minute TED-style talk on immigration numbers

videos.t: Gwynne Dyer -- Geopolitics in a Hotter World
videos.s: Historian and journalist Gwynne Dyer gives a long UBC talk on how climate change will reshape international politics. He covers food, borders, refugees and the possibility of unilateral geoengineering by affected nations.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a sobering, still-relevant look at the geopolitical consequences of warming, including why official reports lag the data.
videos.q: This is a great dissertation on how the GeoPolitics will play this little game out

videos.t: Peter Thiel on "The Portal", Episode #001: "An Era of Stagnation & Universal Institutional Failure."
videos.s: Peter Thiel is the first guest on Eric Weinstein's The Portal, in a nearly three-hour conversation about technological stagnation, institutional failure and the link between growth and violence. They discuss universities, the economy and the search for a more ambitious future.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as a thought-provoking, wide-ranging case for the stagnation thesis, worth hearing even if you disagree with Thiel.
videos.q: I recommend that people listen to that episode even if it's not interesting to you.

videos.t: HD Feynman: FUN TO IMAGINE complete (with optional Chinese subtitles)
videos.s: A restored HD upload of the 1983 BBC series Fun to Imagine, in which Richard Feynman talks informally about everyday science. Topics include jiggling atoms, fire, rubber bands, magnets, electricity, mirrors, seeing, big numbers and ways of thinking.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as an equation-free, charming way to hear Feynman explain physics to laypeople, including his famous refusal to explain magnetism with simple analogies.
videos.q: It's an hour of fun science, and especially accessible for anyone who is curious about physics but doesn't enjoy all the equations.

videos.t: Toward Rational, Authentic Food Choices | Melanie Joy | TEDxMünchen
videos.s: Psychologist Melanie Joy's TEDxMunchen talk introduces carnism, the invisible belief system that conditions people to eat some animals but not others, and how it shapes reactions to food choices.
videos.w: Recommended in vegetarian and animal-welfare threads as an introduction to the psychology behind how we treat animals differently.
videos.q: This TED talk from Dr. Melanie Joy is a good introduction to Carnism

videos.t: Nina Teicholz - 'Vegetable Oils: The Unknown Story'
videos.s: Nina Teicholz, author of The Big Fat Surprise, speaks at Low Carb Gold Coast 2017 about the history and health implications of vegetable and seed oils. She covers the political and institutional forces behind dietary fat advice.
videos.w: Several HN commenters say it was memorable or life-changing and use it to argue against seed oils.
videos.q: This lecture on vegetable oils is one of the most memorable lectures I've ever watched

videos.t: CppCon 2019: Chandler Carruth “There Are No Zero-cost Abstractions”
videos.s: Chandler Carruth argues in a CppCon 2019 talk that C++ has no truly zero-cost abstractions. Using examples like unique_ptr, ABI constraints and compile-time costs, he shows that abstractions cost runtime, compile time or human effort.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever zero-cost abstraction claims come up, especially for why unique_ptr is not free on some ABIs.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Chandler presents his point clearly and goes deep enough into the subject.

videos.t: Erlang The Movie II: The Sequel
videos.s: A humorous 10-minute parody sequel to Erlang: The Movie, in which Erlang's creators discuss the aging language and meet a surprise helper. It plays on the Outlaw Techno Psychobitch joke for OTP.
videos.w: HN loves it as a funny, shorter sequel and even uses it to introduce Erlang in university classes.
videos.q: I use Erlang the Movie and its Sequel whenever I teach my classes at Oxford Uni.

videos.t: The Banach–Tarski Paradox
videos.s: Vsauce's roughly 24 minute explainer on the Banach-Tarski paradox, building from infinity and set theory to the decomposition of a sphere into pieces that form two spheres.
videos.w: Recommended as an accurate, entertaining on-ramp to set theory and infinity, worth pausing and rewatching.
videos.q: This vsauce video is actually a really accurate (and entertaining!) introduction to set theory

videos.t: How not to be ignorant about the world | Hans and Ola Rosling
videos.s: Hans Rosling and his son Ola run an audience quiz with global population, health and income data to show how wrong most people are about the world. Ola then gives four ways to get less ignorant.
videos.w: Recommended as evidence that the world is improving despite negative news, and for how people misjudge global trends.
videos.q: I promise it is not a waste of your time.

videos.t: CppCon 2017: Juan Pedro Bolivar Puente “Postmodern immutable data structures”
videos.s: Juan Pedro Bolivar Puente explains immutable and persistent data structures in C++ and how they support value semantics. He presents the Immer library, rrb-trees, and a prototype text editor that opens a huge file instantly.
videos.w: HN people point to it for rrb-trees, text editor data structures and bringing Clojure-style persistent structures to C++.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Immer [0][1] seems like a really serious attempt at bringing high-quality persistent data structures to C++.

videos.t: The Simple Path to Wealth | JL Collins | Talks at Google
videos.s: Author JL Collins discusses his book The Simple Path to Wealth at Google, covering avoiding debt, simple index fund investing, and retirement accounts like 401(k)s and IRAs. It is an hour-long interview in plain language.
videos.w: HN points people to it as the clearest single video on simple, long-term index fund investing.
videos.q: This video is probably the most clear resource I can think of that has all the information in one place.

videos.t: On The Turing Completeness of PowerPoint (SIGBOVIK)
videos.s: A short SIGBOVIK 2017 presentation by Tom Wildenhain showing that PowerPoint animations are Turing complete, with a working Turing machine built in slides. The talk is delivered deadpan as a serious research result.
videos.w: HN repeatedly names it as one of the funniest and best talks, a favorite example of absurd computation.
videos.q: Nerding out should always be hilarious like that!

videos.t: Why Electronic Voting is a BAD Idea - Computerphile
videos.s: Tom Scott explains for Computerphile why electronic voting is a bad idea, arguing that paper ballots are transparent, auditable and hard to tamper with at scale. He covers why moving voting to phones, tablets or computers undermines trust and verifiability.
videos.w: It is the go-to short explainer HN commenters link whenever e-voting, voting machines or online voting come up.
videos.q: I love [this video]( ) from Tom Scott in which he explains quite well why e-voting is inherently bad.

videos.t: You Actually Share Your Brain With a Silent Stranger
videos.s: CGP Grey explains split-brain patients, where severing the corpus callosum lets the two hemispheres act independently. He uses this to explore the idea of two minds in one head.
videos.w: HN returns to it constantly in consciousness and decision-making threads as a clear, entertaining explanation of split-brain.
videos.q: I recommend watching this video by GPGrey, one of the best educational channels on YouTube

videos.t: A new way to visualize General Relativity
videos.s: ScienceClic explains why the rubber sheet analogy for general relativity is misleading and offers a new visualization that includes the curvature of time and shows gravity as motion through curved spacetime.
videos.w: Called the best visualization of general relativity by many commenters, who say it cleared up long-held misunderstandings of gravity.
videos.q: hands down the best visualization of general relativity I've seen.

videos.t: Carl Sagan - Pale Blue Dot
videos.s: Carl Sagan's narration of the Pale Blue Dot passage, reflecting on the Voyager photograph of Earth as a tiny speck in space. It is a short meditation on humanity's smallness and shared home.
videos.w: HN commenters return to it for perspective, comfort and Sagan's soothing voice, and suggest watching it periodically.
videos.q: Puts everything in perspective, and makes everything feel insignificant

videos.t: The Art of Making a Nixie Tube
videos.s: Dalibor Farny documents the hand manufacture of a nixie tube, from glassblowing to evacuation, with text notes rather than narration. He revived the lost craft of nixie tube making.
videos.w: HN commenters call it mesmerizing and a great look at how things are actually made by a dedicated craftsman.
videos.q: The video in the article is just amazing. You don't normally get to see the exact details of how things get made.

videos.t: Casey Muratori | Smart-Pointers, RAII, ZII? Becoming an N+2 programmer
videos.s: Casey Muratori argues against smart pointers and RAII, advocating grouped-element thinking, zero-is-initialization and stubs as better ways to structure memory and handle errors.
videos.w: HN commenters in memory management and language design threads cite it as the best explanation of group lifetimes versus per-object ownership.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: The best video on this might be from Casey Muratori

videos.t: "Voice Driven Development: Who needs a keyboard anyway?" by Emily Shea
videos.s: Emily Shea explains how repetitive strain injury pushed her to program by voice using speech recognition (Talon), and gives a live coding demo. She argues voice-driven development can be pain-free, efficient and enjoyable.
videos.w: It is the go-to recommendation whenever someone asks about voice coding or RSI-friendly programming setups.
videos.q: There's a great strangeloop talk[2] demonstrating talon and the actual state of voice coding

videos.t: Chicken chicken chicken
videos.s: Doug Zongker's deadpan conference presentation of his famously chicken-filled paper, given at the 2007 AAAS humor session. It satirizes academic talks while showing the pitfalls of bad presentation.
videos.w: Beloved as a humor masterpiece and often cited as required viewing on what not to do in an academic talk.
videos.q: The presentation is truly a humor masterpiece.

videos.t: Longer-lasting light bulbs: it was complicated
videos.s: Technology Connections examines why light bulbs have the lifespans they do, including the real history of the Phoebus cartel. He shows that bulb life trades off against brightness and efficiency rather than being simple planned obsolescence.
videos.w: HN's go-to link for correcting the lightbulb conspiracy myth, giving an engineer's view of the lifespan versus efficiency tradeoff.
videos.q: highly recommended if you want an engineers perspective, with no 'great conspiracy' hype.

videos.t: Theory and Practice of Cryptography
videos.s: A Google Tech Talk by Steve Weis that introduces modern cryptography and its use in practice and at Google. It covers proofs of security and security definitions and a special topic. HN commenters treat it as a talk on verifiable electronic voting.
videos.w: HN keeps pointing to it as a long, fascinating talk on cryptographic, verifiable voting whenever e-voting security comes up.
videos.q: Here's a long but fascinating tech talk on a real solution

videos.t: Why Would AI Want to do Bad Things? Instrumental Convergence
videos.s: Robert Miles explains instrumental convergence: why an AGI with almost any goal would tend to pursue sub-goals like self-preservation and resource acquisition. It builds on Omohundro's basic AI drives and his orthogonality thesis video.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the clearest introduction to why smart AI might behave badly by default.
videos.q: Robert Miles' videos are among the best presented arguments about specific points in this list

videos.t: [1hr Talk] Intro to Large Language Models
videos.s: Andrej Karpathy gives a one-hour general-audience introduction to large language models, covering what they are, how they are trained, comparisons to operating systems, and security challenges such as jailbreaks.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the dense, approachable starting point for understanding LLMs and often cites it for specific claims about scaling and training.
videos.q: Start with his short intro to LLMs, only 1 hour long but is dense with valuable stuff

videos.t: Quantum Fields: The Real Building Blocks of the Universe - with David Tong
videos.s: David Tong, a Cambridge theoretical physicist, explains at the Royal Institution that the fundamental building blocks of nature are quantum fields rather than particles. He covers what we know about these fields and how they fit into the Standard Model.
videos.w: Called a favorite and a masterpiece by commenters as the clearest accessible explanation that there are only waves in fields, and what physics still doesn't know.
videos.q: is a masterpiece. Some very interesting facts, mostly about what we don't know.

videos.t: Thinking outside the 10-dimensional box
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown visualizes high-dimensional spheres to explain a surprising puzzle about how a sphere fits in a box as dimensions grow. It builds geometric intuition for counterintuitive properties of high-dimensional space.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the go-to intuitive visualization of high-dimensional geometry, relevant to machine learning, optimization and sphere packing.
videos.q: There's a great 3blue1brown video that demonstrates this unintuitive result in a relatively intuitive way

videos.t: The Physics and Philosophy of Time - with Carlo Rovelli
videos.s: Physicist Carlo Rovelli gives a public lecture at the Royal Institution on how our understanding of time has changed, from Boltzmann and Einstein to quantum theory and loop quantum gravity. He blends physics, philosophy and art to argue that time is stranger than everyday intuition suggests.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a lucid, general-audience lecture that shows how wrong common conceptions of time are, often in threads on entropy and the arrow of time.
videos.q: There is a great lecture »The Physics and Philosophy of Time« by Carlo Rovelli [1] aimed at the general public

videos.t: HyperNormalisation 2016
videos.s: Adam Curtis's 2016 BBC documentary HyperNormalisation, about 160 minutes long. It cuts together roughly forty years of politics, finance and technology to argue that people have retreated into a simplified fake world.
videos.w: Strongly and repeatedly recommended as a visually distinctive documentary and a guide to postmodern ideas on politics, truth and technology.
videos.q: he's essentially cross cut the last 40 years into a 3 hour cliff notes guide to some of the darker corners of postmodern philosophy.

videos.t: Millennials Don't Exist! Adam Conover at Deep Shift
videos.s: Adam Conover's talk at a millennial marketing conference argues that generations are an unscientific, condescending idea and that millennials do not exist as a real category. The description notes that researcher Jean Twenge later said he misrepresented some of her work.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it when arguing that generational labels are marketing inventions used to belittle groups.
videos.q: Adam (from Adam Ruins Everything) does a really good talk at a marketing conference on why Millennials don't exist.

videos.t: Veritasium: What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning – Derek Muller Explains
videos.s: Veritasium's Derek Muller gives a Perimeter Institute livestream on how AI might change teaching and learning. He draws on past technology shifts and cognitive science to argue that learning requires effortful repetition.
videos.w: Recommended as a balanced take on AI and education, with the point that learning takes work that no technology can do for you.
videos.q: I think the best take on that I've seen so far was from Derek (Veritasium) in this recent talk

videos.t: How Special Relativity Makes Magnets Work
videos.s: Veritasium explains magnetism as a consequence of special relativity. Length contraction of moving charges makes a current in a wire attract or repel a nearby moving charge.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a short, clear explanation of why moving charges create magnetic fields.
videos.q: if you are curious why a moving charge creates a magnetic field watch this Veritasium video

videos.t: Apollo Guidance Computer Part 1: Restoring the computer that put man on the Moon
videos.s: The first episode of CuriousMarc's series restoring a real Apollo Guidance Computer, led by AGC expert Mike Stewart. They set up a makeshift lab in a Houston hotel room to open up a rare machine owned by a private collector.
videos.w: HN people recommend the whole AGC restoration series as a deeply nerdy look at real Apollo-era hardware, including core rope memory.
videos.q: My new favorite YouTuber, CuriousMarc, has a whole series of videos about restoring the Apollo Guidance Computer (AGC).

videos.t: Civil Forfeiture: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on civil asset forfeiture, the process by which police can seize property they suspect is tied to crime. It explains how the property itself is put on trial and how departments profit.
videos.w: HN treats it as the standard accessible explainer on civil forfeiture, linked in nearly every thread about police seizures.
videos.q: John Oliver did a great job of explaining Civil Forfeiture a few years back

videos.t: Debate Noam Chomsky & Michel Foucault - On human nature [Subtitled]
videos.s: The full 1971 Dutch television debate between Noam Chomsky and Michel Foucault on human nature, with subtitles. They discuss creativity, knowledge, power and politics.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a famous, revealing clash between two thinkers, though some note they largely talk past each other.
videos.q: For anyone who hasn't watched the actual, full video of the debate, you should do so.

videos.t: Monktoberfest 2016: Bryan Cantrill - Oral Tradition in Software Engineering
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill's Monktoberfest 2016 talk on how software engineers pass knowledge down through oral tradition, from folk rhymes to programmer lore and stories like why C lacks a logical XOR. He argues for writing software with future generations in mind.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining, well-delivered talk full of stories that shows the value of historical context and long comments in code.
videos.q: really helped me appreciate that long comments in code can be a treasured part of a software space

videos.t: Dani DaOrtiz at Fool US 2022 (the act that Penn and Teller didn’t even try to figure out.)
videos.s: A ten-minute card-magic act by Dani DaOrtiz performed on Penn & Teller: Fool Us in 2022. It is built on timing, misdirection and psychology, and the method defeated the show's hosts.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly call it among the best magic performances ever, valuing it as acting and craft that stays impressive even once you know the method.
videos.q: This is one of the greatest performances of all time

videos.t: Tobacco: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: A Last Week Tonight segment on how tobacco companies sustain profits by pushing sales overseas. It covers suits against countries like Australia over plain packaging through trade-deal arbitration.
videos.w: HN uses it in TPP and trade-deal threads as a clear example of ISDS being used by corporations against governments.
videos.q: I really encourage you to check it out. It's about 18min long, but well worth it

videos.t: I don't like notebooks.- Joel Grus (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
videos.s: Joel Grus's JupyterCon talk explaining why he dislikes Jupyter notebooks. He covers hidden state, trouble with reproducibility and testing, and how notebooks frustrate teaching. He shows his preferred workflow and what Jupyter could change.
videos.w: It is the go-to funny, irreverent critique of notebooks, linked whenever HN debates notebooks versus testable code.
videos.q: The parent article links this great talk that goes into more detail than the parent post and is much easier to understand

videos.t: The Marvel Symphonic Universe
videos.s: An Every Frame a Painting video essay asking why Marvel films lack memorable musical themes. It blames temp tracks and directors scoring to filler music.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an insightful explanation of why modern film scores sound alike, with lessons beyond Marvel.
videos.q: You don't have to have seen any Marvel movies, the insights are universal.

videos.t: Ground Source / Geothermal Heat Pumps and Other Info
videos.s: A Technology Connections video on how ground-source (geothermal) heat pumps work and why they hold efficiency in winter. It also covers related heat pump information, and the description notes air-source heat pumps have since improved.
videos.w: Recommended as part of an excellent, approachable series explaining residential heat pumps.
videos.q: He made several excellent videos explaining residential heat pumps

videos.t: Vladimir Pozner: How the United States Created Vladimir Putin
videos.s: Russian-American journalist Vladimir Pozner lectures at Yale on how US foreign policy toward Russia after the Soviet collapse shaped Putin, then takes audience questions on election interference, the Skripal poisoning and media independence.
videos.w: During the 2022 Ukraine war threads, HN commenters recommended it as a non-Western perspective on Russia-West relations and Putin's motives.
videos.q: I strongly recommend to watch this talk

videos.t: C++ and Beyond 2012: Herb Sutter - atomic Weapons 1 of 2
videos.s: Herb Sutter's deep C++ and Beyond 2012 talk on atomics and the C++ memory model, covering why programmers chasing top performance need to understand hardware ordering. This is part one of two.
videos.w: HN treats it as the classic go-to for learning atomics and memory ordering, recommended over books.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: which are extremely good

videos.t: David Fravor: UFOs, Aliens, Fighter Jets, and Aerospace Engineering | Lex Fridman Podcast #122
videos.s: Lex Fridman interviews Navy pilot David Fravor, a primary witness of the 2004 Tic Tac UFO encounter, about the sighting, military aviation and aerospace engineering. The conversation runs close to four hours.
videos.w: HN commenters send people here for a detailed first-hand account from the pilot, and some say it changed their view on the sightings.
videos.q: this is a great interview interesting in its own right, even without the UFO part

videos.t: What People Get Wrong About Dense Urban Living
videos.s: Oh The Urbanity! argues that most city dwellers live in dense residential neighbourhoods outside downtown, which can be calm and peaceful. It draws on older, denser parts of Toronto and Montreal.
videos.w: HN users repeatedly post it to rebut the idea that urban living means Manhattan or Hong Kong apartment blocks.
videos.q: Fifteen minutes pedalling in one direction is downtown Amsterdam, fifteen minutes in the other is farm land.

videos.t: The Biggest Misconception About Electricity
videos.s: Veritasium argues that electric energy is carried by fields around the wires rather than by electrons moving through them, using a thought experiment with a large circuit.
videos.w: Often recommended as an eye-opening field-based explanation of electricity, though it was also controversial and criticized as pedantic.
videos.q: It’s an eye opening alternative explanation

videos.t: CppCon 2017: Matt Godbolt “What Has My Compiler Done for Me Lately? Unbolting the Compiler's Lid”
videos.s: Matt Godbolt's CppCon 2017 talk shows what modern compilers do with your C++ code, using Compiler Explorer to inspect generated assembly. It covers surprising optimizations and how the tool works.
