videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining, mind-blowing look at compiler cleverness from a great speaker.
videos.q: Both are great presentations going into details on some of the crazy optimizations compilers will do.

videos.t: Jake Archibald on the web browser event loop, setTimeout, micro tasks, requestAnimationFrame, ...
videos.s: Jake Archibald's JSConf.Asia 2018 talk "In the Loop" explains the browser event loop, covering tasks, microtasks, requestAnimationFrame, and how rendering interleaves with JavaScript. It uses visual walkthroughs to show why code runs in surprising orders and why setTimeout fixes are unreliable.
videos.w: HN treats it as the best primer on the event loop, praising its entertaining, easy-to-grasp visual explanations.
videos.q: actually making it both entertaining and easily grokable!

videos.t: RiftSketch: Live coding in VR with the Oculus Rift, Firefox WebVR, JavaScript and Three.js
videos.s: Brian Peiris demonstrates RiftSketch, a web app where you write JavaScript with Three.js while wearing an Oculus Rift and watch the world around you change live. It runs on Firefox builds with WebVR.
videos.w: Repeatedly cited as an inspiring demo of what programming in VR could look like, which led some commenters to buy headsets.
videos.q: this was an impressive demo of someone coding their environment in the Rift.

videos.t: The Future of Mathematics?
videos.s: Mathematician Kevin Buzzard explains why he believes the Lean theorem prover will shape the future of mathematics, and describes digitizing his university curriculum in Lean with undergraduates, plus the cultural challenges.
videos.w: Recommended as the clearest mathematician's perspective on formal proof assistants and why mathematics should be formalized.
videos.q: For a perspective of a mathematician that came to evangelize theorem provers, I recommend Kevin Buzzard's MS 2019-09 presentation [0] about LEAN.

videos.t: Dr Shashi Tharoor MP - Britain Does Owe Reparations
videos.s: Shashi Tharoor's Oxford Union speech arguing that Britain owes reparations to its former colonies, focused on the effects of British rule in India. It lists economic and political damage done by colonialism.
videos.w: HN commenters link it repeatedly in colonial history threads as an eloquent, fact-dense short speech.
videos.q: This talk has many facts not even commonly known to Indians.

videos.t: All-In Summit: Bill Gurley presents 2,851 Miles
videos.s: Bill Gurley's talk at the All-In Summit 2023, titled 2,851 Miles after the distance between Washington and San Francisco. He describes how incumbents use lobbying and regulation to entrench themselves, followed by a conversation with the hosts.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as the clearest explanation of regulatory capture, and cite it in threads on AI regulation, GDPR and telecom.
videos.q: I strongly encourage watching Bill Gurley's talk from the All-In Summit

videos.t: Joe Armstrong & Alan Kay - Joe Armstrong interviews Alan Kay
videos.s: Joe Armstrong, creator of Erlang, interviews Alan Kay at Code Mesh. They discuss the meaning of object orientation, message passing, the META II paper, and the state of computer science.
videos.w: HN uses it in debates about what OOP originally meant, since Kay's message-passing view lines up with Erlang's processes.
videos.q: To get some perspective on both of their perspectives, here's "Joe Armstrong interviews Alan Kay"

videos.t: Sorting Algorithms: Speed Is Found In The Minds of People - Andrei Alexandrescu - CppCon 2019
videos.s: Andrei Alexandrescu's CppCon 2019 talk revisits sorting, showing how branchless tricks, hybrid strategies and a cost metric can speed up std::sort-style algorithms on modern hardware.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining talk that starts simple and goes deep on practical performance optimization.
videos.q: At first he is just showing simple stuff, but stay with it, he goes deep.

videos.t: "Production Prolog" by Michael Hendricks
videos.s: Michael Hendricks of PriceCharting shares tricks and pain points from running Prolog in production for 18 months at Strange Loop. It argues Prolog is a productive modern language beyond logic puzzles, and includes a demo of changing code mid-execution.
videos.w: It is the go-to answer to whether Prolog is used for real-world work, praised as a survey of its uses, advantages and drawbacks.
videos.q: gives an excellent high-level survey of the uses, advantages, and drawbacks of Prolog

videos.t: !!Con 2016 - How I Code and Use a Computer at 1,000 WPM!! By Sina Bahram
videos.s: A short !!Con 2016 talk by blind developer Sina Bahram on how he uses a computer and writes code with a screen reader at about 1,000 words per minute. He plays how common interfaces sound and challenges the audience to go a day using only the keyboard.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly share it because it is an eye-opening look at screen-reader use, and because at about 6:30 it addresses how inaccessible Hacker News itself is.
videos.q: There's an amazing 10min !!Con 2016 talk by Sina Bahram

videos.t: Co-dfns Live Stream: Compiler Design and Architecture
videos.s: A two-hour live stream in which Aaron Hsu explains the architecture, design history and aesthetic of Co-dfns, his parallel APL compiler. He walks through the code and the reasoning behind its dense style.
videos.w: HN readers say it changed their view of APL and array languages, with a clear walkthrough of how a compiler can be written in this style.
videos.q: Nothing has ever convinced me about the potential for array languages in practice quite like watching Aaron Hsu

videos.t: Kurt Vonnegut, Shape of Stories (subtitulos castellano)
videos.s: Kurt Vonnegut's 2004 Case College lecture, with Spanish subtitles, in which he sketches the shapes of stories on a blackboard. He plots story arcs as good and bad fortune against time.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as a delightful, influential way to think about story structure.
videos.q: Vonnegut is really special. I always like coming back to his Shape of Stories talks

videos.t: Intelligence and Stupidity: The Orthogonality Thesis
videos.s: Robert Miles explains the orthogonality thesis: how an agent can be highly intelligent while pursuing goals that seem stupid or alien to humans. He separates intelligence from goals and touches on the stamp-collector example.
videos.w: HN people use it as the standard short explanation for why AI can understand human ethics without sharing them, and often recommend the whole channel.
videos.q: this video to me states the problem in a nutshell (that whole channel is gold)

videos.t: Bryan Cantrill on Jails and Solaris Zones
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill's Papers We Love talk on FreeBSD Jails and Solaris Zones, tracing how OS-level virtualization grew out of chroot and the limits of the traditional UNIX security model.
videos.w: Recommended repeatedly as the best account of container history and how Zones built on and went beyond Jails.
videos.q: I highly recommend this talk, talking about Jails and Zones.

videos.t: The Biggest Ideas in the Universe: Introduction
videos.s: Sean Carroll introduces his video series on the biggest ideas in physics, such as symmetry, space and matter, as informal discussions with follow-up Q&A videos. This is the short opening video of the series.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend the series as engaging, substantial physics with just enough math for non-specialists.
videos.q: Just enough math to be interesting but nothing requiring a math degree.

videos.t: Creating a Doom-style 3D engine in C
videos.s: Bisqwit builds a Doom or Duke Nukem 3D style software-rendered 3D engine in C from scratch, supporting non-Euclidean geometry. It covers vector rotation and portal rendering with sped-up, tool-assisted coding.
videos.w: A favorite on Ask HN lists of programming YouTube channels, praised for mind-blowing systems and graphics programming and a watchable coding style.
videos.q: My favourite programming YouTuber by a long stretch.

videos.t: 28c3: The coming war on general computation
videos.s: Cory Doctorow's 28c3 keynote argues that the copyright wars were just a skirmish and that the real fight will be a war on the general-purpose computer. He explains why locked-down devices, DRM and surveillance tools all depend on removing general computation.
videos.w: HN returns to it constantly as a prescient talk, cited whenever threads cover DRM, locked-down devices, app verification or restrictions on running your own software.
videos.q: which I very strongly recommend that everybody watch

videos.t: The best stats you've ever seen | Hans Rosling
videos.s: Hans Rosling uses the Gapminder animated-data tool to debunk myths about world development, with sportscaster-like energy. It shows trends in health, income and child survival across countries.
videos.w: HN invokes it as the classic evidence that the world has improved and that people misjudge it, and as an example of great data presentation.
videos.q: the original 2007 Gapminder talk[1] still surprised and educates people today

videos.t: How to Invent the Future I - Stanford CS183F: Startup School
videos.s: Alan Kay's Stanford Startup School lecture covers his career at Xerox PARC and how to think about inventing the future. He goes through what came out of PARC and why companies fail to capitalize on such ideas.
videos.w: It is HN's standard answer to questions on creativity, finding problems and PARC history, valued for Kay's thinking about thinking.
videos.q: Alan Kay gave a couple lectures at Stanford on "How to Invent the Future" and went over all the stuff that came out of there.

videos.t: Moleman 2 - Demoscene - The Art of the Algorithms (2012)
videos.s: Moleman 2 is a feature-length documentary about the demoscene, tracing its rise from 1980s Commodore 64 culture to modern real-time art. It explains the algorithms and creative process behind demos and intros.
videos.w: Recommended whenever the demoscene comes up as a well-made, accessible history and tour of the art form.
videos.q: Both are expertly crafted and fun documentaries

videos.t: DEF CON 22 - Zoz - Don't Fuck It Up!
videos.s: Zoz's DEF CON 22 talk on operational security in the age of pervasive surveillance. He shows how hard it is to avoid mistakes even for people who should know better.
videos.w: It is the usual cite for why good OPSEC is so hard, including entry and exit point correlation and digital exhaust.
videos.q: According to Zoz in his excellent DEFCON 22 talk

videos.t: Dr. Robert Zubrin with a brilliant answer to "Why Should We Go To Mars?"
videos.s: A short clip of Dr. Robert Zubrin, author of The Case for Mars, answering why humanity should go to Mars. He argues that societies grow by challenging themselves and that exploration inspires young people.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly link it as the best concise answer to the question of why go to Mars when problems remain on Earth.
videos.q: Robert Zubrin has what I consider a great, comprehensive answer to why we should go to Mars.

videos.t: Paxos lecture (Raft user study)
videos.s: John Ousterhout's slides-and-voiceover lecture on Paxos, made for the Raft user study comparing how students learn Raft and Paxos. It is a full introduction to the Paxos consensus algorithm.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear, lucid way to learn Paxos and Multi-Paxos, ideally alongside the companion Raft video.
videos.q: The 2 videos do an excellent job of explaining both the Paxos and Raft algorithms and the key differences between them.

videos.t: Demystifying the Higgs Boson with Leonard Susskind
videos.s: Stanford physicist Leonard Susskind explains what the Higgs mechanism is and what it means to give mass to particles. He also covers what is at stake for physics and cosmology.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as an approachable, math-light route to understanding mass and the Higgs field.
videos.q: I highly highly recommend this talk by Leonard Susskind

videos.t: Steve Jobs Secrets of Life
videos.s: A short excerpt from a 1994 interview of Steve Jobs in which he says everything around us was made up by people no smarter than you, and that you can change and shape the world.
videos.w: Quoted in threads on motivation, agency and regret as an encouraging reminder that the world can be changed.
videos.q: the world is something you can change, not merely participate in.

videos.t: OOPSLA Conference: Growing a Language
videos.s: Guy Steele's classic 1998 OOPSLA keynote on how a programming language must grow with its user community. He delivers it in a playful style, starting with only monosyllabic words and defining new terms as he goes.
videos.w: Treated as a must-watch for language designers, and cited whenever extensibility and language size are debated.
videos.q: In case anyone hasn't seen this most excellent talk on this topic, I highly recommend

videos.t: Why We Get Fat: And What to Do About It | Gary Taubes | Talks at Google
videos.s: Gary Taubes presents the argument of his book Why We Get Fat to Googlers in 2011. He claims the type of calories matters more than the count, challenges calories-in-calories-out thinking and criticizes the low-fat dietary consensus.
videos.w: Recommended in diet and weight-loss threads as the accessible case for the carbohydrate-insulin view of obesity.
videos.q: Highly recommend you watch this amazing lecture by Garry Taubes at Google

videos.t: Optimistic Nihilism
videos.s: Kurzgesagt's short animated take on optimistic nihilism. It argues the universe has no inherent meaning, so we are free to create our own and enjoy life.
videos.w: HN users recommend it as a comforting, clear introduction to nihilism for anxiety, mid-life doubts and feeling behind in life.
videos.q: I highly recommend it, as they explain these concepts very well in a short 6min video.

videos.t: George Carlin Talks About "Stuff"
videos.s: George Carlin's classic stand-up routine about 'stuff' and how much of life is spent accumulating and storing it, from Comic Relief 1986. It satirizes American consumerism and possessions.
videos.w: HN keeps linking it in threads on clutter, storage units, real estate and consumerism as a perfectly apt comic take.
videos.q: George Carlin put it quite eloquently

videos.t: VisiData Lightning Demo at PyCascades 2018
videos.s: A five-minute lightning demo of VisiData, a terminal tool for exploring and manipulating data. It uses two months of NYC 311 complaint data to drill down, plot points on a virtual map and save selected rows.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the fastest way to understand what VisiData can do, since seeing it work is clearer than reading about it.
videos.q: visdata is pretty mind-blowing...at least, that's how i felt when i saw the demo the first time

videos.t: (1/4) Intro/History: Introducing a 100-year-old mechanical computer
videos.s: The first of four short videos from Bill Hammack (engineerguy) introducing and giving the history of a 100-year-old mechanical computer, Michelson's harmonic analyzer. The series goes on to explain Fourier synthesis, analysis and operation of the machine.
videos.w: Commenters recommend the series whenever Fourier analysis or analog computing comes up, praising Hammack's clear explanations and the short episodes.
videos.q: There is a series of four fantastic videos

videos.t: "The Hard Parts of Open Source" by Evan Czaplicki
videos.s: Evan Czaplicki, creator of Elm, discusses the hard parts of running an open source project: online community conflict, why its patterns arise, and a cultural history of open source. He offers ideas for more civil, productive communication.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an insightful look at the people side of open source maintenance, especially in Elm and maintainer-burnout threads.
videos.q: Regardless of whether you agree with his approach to developing a programming language, it is a talk worth listening to. Very insightful.

videos.t: The Fastest Way to Board a Plane Feels Like the Slowest
videos.s: CGP Grey compares airplane boarding methods, based on an arXiv paper, and shows why the intuitive back-to-front approach is slow while random or outside-in boarding does better.
videos.w: It is the default link in any thread about boarding or deplaning order, praised as an excellent, clear treatment.
videos.q: Highly recommend this video of plane boarding methods by CGP Grey

videos.t: DEF CON 22 - Deviant Ollam & Howard Payne - Elevator Hacking - From the Pit to the Penthouse
videos.s: Deviant Ollam and Howard Payne give an in-depth DEF CON 22 explanation of how elevators work, from the pit to the penthouse. It covers their control modes and how pen testers use elevators to bypass building security.
videos.w: HN brings it up in any thread about elevators or physical security as a fascinating, entertaining deep dive.
videos.q: If you liked the original post, you will probably LOVE this DEFCON talk about elevator hacking

videos.t: Why We Won't Raise Our Kids in Suburbia
videos.s: Not Just Bikes argues that car-dependent suburbs rob children of independence, contrasting North American suburbia with Dutch cities where kids walk and bike on their own. It is the creator's remake of an earlier video on the topic.
videos.w: The standard link in threads about child autonomy, helicopter parenting and car-centric planning.
videos.q: Not Just Bikes has a really good video on why suburbia (usually single family housing) is often worse for children than denser environments.

videos.t: Gtk to Qt - a strange journey [linux.conf.au 2014]
videos.s: Dirk Hohndel explains why the Subsurface dive log project migrated from Gtk to Qt, the obstacles encountered, and advice for other applications frustrated with Gtk. It is a linux.conf.au 2014 talk.
videos.w: Go-to reference in GTK versus Qt debates, valued for a candid account from experienced developers who tried both toolkits.
videos.q: One of the best discussions on the subject, made by old hackers, but new guys to GUI programming, who tried both

videos.t: Joscha Bach: Artificial Consciousness and the Nature of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #101
videos.s: Lex Fridman has a three-hour conversation with Joscha Bach about artificial consciousness, the workings of the mind, intelligence and the possibly simulated nature of reality.
videos.w: Praised as a long but rewarding conversation, with commenters especially liking Bach's emphasis on modelling as a skill and his bridge between mind and computation.
videos.q: If watching this isn't worth anyone's time, I'm not sure what would be.

videos.t: 7 Habits For Effective Text Editing 2.0
videos.s: Vim creator Bram Moolenaar's 2007 Google Tech Talk on habits for efficient text editing. He explains how to spot repetition and inefficiency, then use editor features to fix it.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a lasting philosophy for improving your editing process incrementally, and it was widely remembered after Moolenaar's death.
videos.q: There is a wonderful presentation called '7 Habits For Effective Text Editing 2.0' [1] explaining this philosophy.

videos.t: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown's chapter on eigenvectors and eigenvalues in the Essence of Linear Algebra series. It builds a visual intuition for what they mean, why an eigenbasis is useful, and ends with a puzzle.
videos.w: HN repeatedly names it the best, most intuitive explanation of eigenvalues, and a gateway to the whole linear algebra series.
videos.q: By far the best explanation of eigenvalues is found on 3blue1brown

videos.t: Introduction to NoSQL • Martin Fowler • GOTO 2012
videos.s: Martin Fowler's GOTO 2012 introduction to NoSQL databases: where they came from, their data models, how consistency thinking differs, and when to use them. He argues they won't make relational databases obsolete and introduces polyglot persistence.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as a balanced, beginner-friendly overview of SQL versus NoSQL, and some teachers assign it to students.
videos.q: one of the rare videos I've required students in my database classes to watch.

videos.t: dotGo 2015 - Rob Pike - Simplicity is Complicated
videos.s: Rob Pike's dotGo 2015 talk argues that Go only seems simple, and that its simplicity hides real complexity that is part of the design. He explains the thinking behind Go's restraint in features.
videos.w: HN returns to it to explain why Go deliberately resists syntactic sugar and new features.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: It's an active choice of the language to not allow many syntactic sugars that make the code have a much higher learning curve.

videos.t: The Hyperloop: BUSTED!
videos.s: Thunderf00t, a physicist, critically assesses the Hyperloop concept, covering the vacuum, pressure, safety, and cost problems of high-speed tube travel. He argues the media accepted the claims uncritically.
videos.w: HN repeatedly cites it as the best skeptical engineering analysis of why Hyperloop is impractical.
videos.q: His videos on the hyperloop are pretty comprehensive and succinct about their reasoning.

videos.t: [HOPE X] Elevator Hacking: From the Pit to the Penthouse
videos.s: A HOPE X talk giving an in-depth explanation of how elevators work, from their history in hacker culture to using their control systems to bypass building security. It covers features and abilities of elevators that most people never see.
videos.w: HN commenters call it one of the most entertaining and informative con talks, and a good window into elevators from a hacker's view.
videos.q: This version is the best, with all details, no secrets withheld.

videos.t: Fasting For Survival Lecture by Dr Pradip Jamnadas
videos.s: Cardiologist Dr. Pradip Jamnadas lectures on the rationale for dietary restriction and fasting, covering insulin resistance, glucose intolerance, and low-carb eating over about 81 minutes.
videos.w: Several HN commenters call it one of the best explanations of fasting and insulin and recommend it in diet and weight loss threads.
videos.q: This is the best video I have found to explain the incredible changes and benefits of multi-da

videos.t: The Patent Scam Intro
videos.s: Austin Meyer, developer of the X-Plane flight simulator, explains how he was sued by a patent troll over a trivial claim about an app's license server. He walks through how the shell-company litigation works and why ignoring the suit makes things worse.
videos.w: HN commenters pass it around as an eye-opening first-hand account of patent trolling and the Texas courts that favor it.
videos.q: This video from Austin Meyer (creator of X-Plane) is pretty eye-opening

videos.t: Jonathan Blow: Video Games and the Human Condition
videos.s: Jonathan Blow's 2010 Rice University talk argues that game designers refine their techniques in ways that can manipulate players, as with A/B-tested social games. He discusses the ethical responsibility of designers and what games can offer beyond addiction.
videos.w: Recommended as a thoughtful critique of addictive game design and the designer's role in building ethical games.
videos.q: Jonathan Blow has a great presentation on the mechanisms of video game addiction and the role of the game designer in building ethically responsible games [0]. I highly recommend it

videos.t: CppCon 2017: Titus Winters “C++ as a "Live at Head" Language”
videos.s: Titus Winters' CppCon 2017 talk argues for C++ and Google's Abseil to be maintained as a live at head language, relying on testing and automated tooling rather than never changing or promising no compatibility. It covers Hyrum's law and the limits of semantic versioning.
videos.w: Recommended whenever versioning, semver, monorepos and backward compatibility are debated, for its nuanced treatment of dependencies.
videos.q: a much more nuanced look at dependencies & versioning

videos.t: Start with why -- how great leaders inspire action | Simon Sinek | TEDxPugetSound
videos.s: Simon Sinek's TEDx talk arguing that great leaders and companies inspire action by communicating why they do something before how or what. He uses Apple as his main example.
videos.w: Recommended as a quick way to get the core of 'Start with Why' for pitches and communication, though some note small companies are not Apple.
videos.q: A much faster way to understand the central message of "Start with Why" would be to watch the TEDx talk

videos.t: Why Is It So Hard to Do Something That Should Be Easy? (Wall of Awful pt. 1)
videos.s: A short How to ADHD explainer, featuring Brendan Mahan, on why simple tasks can feel impossible for people with ADHD. It introduces the 'wall of awful', a pile of past failures, shame and anxiety that builds up in front of a task and blocks starting it.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as the go-to name and explanation for task paralysis and procrastination, and say it helped them see why they avoid tasks.
videos.q: It totally changed how I approached my procrastination by simply asking myself "why" I was avoiding a task.

videos.t: Functional architecture - The pits of success - Mark Seemann
videos.s: Mark Seemann argues that functional programming naturally yields many of the best practices object-oriented developers learn painfully. He shows how functional architecture leads to a pit of success, with a pure core and impure shell.
videos.w: Recommended as a practical demonstration of how functional thinking improves design without going off the deep end.
videos.q: Here is a great talk demonstrating that by following a simple functional approach, your code can naturally fall into a “pit of success

videos.t: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD by Martin Görner
videos.s: Martin Gorner's Devoxx talk introduces deep learning with TensorFlow, walking through neural networks for MNIST, how to choose an architecture and how to diagnose networks that fail to train.
videos.w: Repeatedly called an excellent, practical introduction that covers a lot in two hours and explains issues academic textbooks skip.
videos.q: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD" is really good, and covers a lot of material in a single 2hr talk.

videos.t: How does a USB keyboard work?
videos.s: Ben Eater explains how a USB keyboard communicates, covering the electrical interface, bit and packet encoding, packet contents, and a comparison with PS/2.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a clear, comprehensive explanation of USB signaling and keyboard polling.
videos.q: Fantastic breakdown if you have 30 minutes

videos.t: Data Brokers: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment explains how data brokers collect and sell personal information, including a stunt in which his team bought data to identify members of Congress.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible overview of the data broker industry in privacy discussions.
videos.q: I strongly recommend this episode of Last Week Tonight

videos.t: Life in life
videos.s: A two-minute video of Conway's Game of Life running inside Conway's Game of Life, built from OTCA metapixels and Golly. It zooms smoothly between scales.
videos.w: The canonical visual for nested simulation, Turing completeness and self-reference; HN readers call it mind-blowing and reach for it constantly.
videos.q: here's a famous and really clear sub-2 minutes representation of the scales involved

videos.t: What Languages Sound Like To Foreigners
videos.s: Finnish YouTuber Saara improvises gibberish that mimics how various languages sound to people who do not speak them. The sentences are mostly made up, and the clip went viral.
videos.w: HN points to it as a favorite example of astonishing accent mimicry and fake-language gibberish that sounds real.
videos.q: Internet personality Saara turned speaking fake languages into a career with this amazing little clip

videos.t: Democracy at Work: Curing Capitalism | Richard Wolff | Talks at Google
videos.s: Economist Richard Wolff's Talks at Google lecture on his book Democracy at Work. He critiques capitalism and argues for worker-run cooperatives as a path to a more democratic economy.
videos.w: HN commenters share it as an accessible case for worker cooperatives and workplace democracy as a model for a modern left.
videos.q: I recently came across an interesting talk by Richard Wolff at Google [1]

videos.t: The Epidemic of Fake Disease
videos.s: A Medlife Crisis video by cardiologist Rohin Francis on overdiagnosis and over-screening. It explains how detecting more disease does not necessarily mean saving more lives, and covers harms such as unnecessary treatment.
videos.w: Pointed to in threads about cancer screening, PSA tests, full-body MRIs and consumer diagnostics as an explanation of why more testing can hurt.
videos.q: This video does a good job also of covering the topic of over-testing/over-treating potential cancer

videos.t: James Burke Connections, Ep. 4 "Faith in Numbers"
videos.s: Episode 4 of James Burke's Connections series, tracing how commercialism, climate change and the Black Death shaped the move to the Renaissance. It follows threads through waterpower, the printing press, the Jacquard loom and the Hollerith punch card toward modern computing.
videos.w: HN commenters strongly recommend it for its account of how the Jacquard loom and punch cards led to computers.
videos.q: Every computer engineer, computer scientist and software developer should learn about the Jacquard loom

videos.t: Secret History of Silicon Valley
videos.s: Steve Blank's Computer History Museum lecture argues that Silicon Valley's roots lie in WWII radar and electronic warfare work, Stanford's Fred Terman and Cold War military funding rather than the semiconductor alone.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a favorite introduction to Valley history and cite it whenever government and military funding of tech comes up.
videos.q: my favorite introduction to the valleys history was Steve Blanks The Secret History of Silicon Valley. It's well worth the hour

videos.t: How we fit an NES game into 40 Kilobytes
videos.s: Morphcat Games explains how they fit Micro Mages, a full-featured NES game, into 40 kilobytes. It covers compression of sprites and level layouts and other space-saving tricks.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever discussion turns to how old games were so small, as a clear tour of 8-bit optimization and creative work under hardware limits.
videos.q: Here is my favorite video about 8-bit era optimisations. Makes you appreciate games from this era even more.

videos.t: Adriano Celentano - Prisencolinensinainciusol
videos.s: A 1972 song by Adriano Celentano whose lyrics are nonsense syllables designed to sound like American English to non-English speakers. It is a rock and rap-flavored novelty track with a video.
videos.w: It comes up whenever threads touch on fake languages, accents, or gibberish that sounds plausible, and commenters like sharing it with people who haven't heard it.
videos.q: For anyone who hasn't seen it before, here's a song by an Italian composer made to sound like American English

videos.t: Google I/O 2009 - The Myth of the Genius Programmer
videos.s: Brian Fitzpatrick and Ben Collins-Sussman argue that the 'genius programmer' ideal harms collaboration. They advocate trading ego for growth, sharing work early, and understanding how tools shape social behavior.
videos.w: HN regulars recommend it as a career-shaping talk on code review, humility and collaborative development.
videos.q: One of the best talks about code reviews and similiar things

videos.t: Emacs + org-mode + python in reproducible research; SciPy 2013 Presentation
videos.s: John Kitchin shows how Emacs org-mode with Python lets researchers combine narrative, math, figures and executable code in one document. It exports to LaTeX, HTML and PDF, and he used it for papers and e-books.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended as the canonical demo of org-mode for literate programming and reproducible research.
videos.q: on Emacs + org-mode + python in reproducible research is worth a watch

videos.t: FarewellEtaoinShrdlu
videos.s: A documentary on the last day the New York Times was printed with linotype machines in 1978, following the process from the newsroom to the press. It marks the move to computerized typesetting.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as an absorbing look at hot-metal typesetting and the end of the linotype era.
videos.q: the final day the New York Times was printed using their linotype machines.

videos.t: Captain Disillusion: World's Greatest Blenderer - Live at the Blender Conference 2018
videos.s: Captain Disillusion's comedic talk at the 2018 Blender Conference recounts how he uses Blender as a production tool for his VFX-debunking web series. It is part case study and part love letter to the Blender community.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining and inspiring Blender talk, and often links it in threads about learning Blender.
videos.q: this is a must watch for inspiration and laughs

videos.t: Watch electricity hit a fork in the road at half a billion frames per second
videos.s: AlphaPhoenix uses a custom high-speed measurement setup to watch voltage waves travel down wires and split at a fork. It answers how electricity knows where to go and how quickly that process happens.
videos.w: Praised as the clearest visual explanation of transmission lines, impedance and signal propagation, with several commenters saying it made it all click.
videos.q: by far the best explanations of electricity that I've encountered in any format

videos.t: Competition is for Losers with Peter Thiel (How to Start a Startup 2014: 5)
videos.s: Peter Thiel's lecture from the How to Start a Startup course on business strategy and monopoly theory, arguing that competition destroys profits and that startups should aim to build monopolies. It covers the ideas of Zero to One.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a serious, influential talk on market size and monopoly, though some commenters criticize its philosophy as endorsing anti-competitive goals.
videos.q: this talk from YC's Startup School 2014 covering the ideas from Zero to One is excellent

videos.t: Lambda Calculus - Fundamentals of Lambda Calculus & Functional Programming in JavaScript
videos.s: Gabriel Lebec's Fullstack Academy talk introduces lambda calculus syntax, the history of mathematical logic, and the essence of functional programming using JavaScript. It also covers combinators, currying and Church encodings.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended as one of the most approachable introductions to lambda calculus and combinators.
videos.q: they are the most approachable videos on the topic I have ever seen.

videos.t: I Tried To Make Something In America (The Smarter Scrubber Experiment) - Smarter Every Day 308
videos.s: Destin Sandlin of Smarter Every Day tries to manufacture a grill scrubber entirely in the United States. Along the way he runs into missing supply chains, tooling and institutional manufacturing knowledge.
videos.w: HN cites it constantly in US manufacturing debates as a vivid demonstration of how much domestic industrial capability has been lost.
videos.q: Here's a great video by Smarter Every Day that came out a few months ago

videos.t: 4 2 1 Christopher Domas   The future of RE Dynamic Binary Visualization
videos.s: Christopher Domas presents his Cantor Dust tool at Derbycon 2012, a 3D visual approach to reverse engineering binaries by visualizing their structure dynamically.
videos.w: Regarded as one of the coolest talks ever, with a futuristic binary visualization demo that has inspired later tools.
videos.q: really blew my mind when I saw it.

videos.t: The REAL Possibility of Mapping Alien Planets!
videos.s: PBS Space Time explains the proposal to use the Sun's gravity as a giant lens, sending a train of small light-sail spacecraft to the focal point roughly 550 AU out. It covers how such a telescope could image exoplanets in surprising detail and the engineering challenges involved.
videos.w: It is the go-to explanation whenever a thread touches on imaging exoplanets or solar gravitational lens telescopes.
videos.q: Pretty good explanation of the technique and challenges involved

videos.t: The Great Global Warming Swindle Full Movie
videos.s: A 2007 Channel 4 documentary by Martin Durkin arguing that human-caused global warming is overstated or a scam. It features contrarian scientists such as Richard Lindzen and promotes sunspot and cosmic-ray explanations for temperature change. Its claims are rejected by mainstream climate science.
videos.w: Climate-skeptic commenters link it as evidence against the CO2 consensus, while others cite it as an example of climate-change denial.

videos.t: The Expert Myth
videos.s: Veritasium examines which experts have real expertise, drawing on chess research and work by Klein and Kahneman. It explains that expertise comes from pattern recognition built through deliberate practice in valid, feedback-rich environments.
videos.w: Frequently recommended in threads on learning, the 10,000 hours rule and deliberate practice as a clearer account of how expertise develops.
videos.q: Veritasium has a really good video on the subject [0], with a much more compelling explanation for what it takes to develop expertise.

videos.t: All the Numbers - Numberphile
videos.s: Matt Parker talks Numberphile through the different kinds of numbers: algebraic, transcendental, computable, normal, and beyond. It shows how few numbers we can actually name or describe.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible explanation of number categories and why almost all numbers are unknowable.
videos.q: here's a video that explains from the basics what kinds of numbers exist

videos.t: "Transducers" by Rich Hickey
videos.s: Rich Hickey introduces transducers in Clojure, a way to make map, filter and similar algorithms composable independent of the data source. This avoids duplicated implementations and intermediate collections across sequences, channels and streams.
videos.w: HN treats it as the original and definitive explanation of transducers, recommended whenever the concept comes up.
videos.q: If you want a really good intro, watch Rich Hickey's talk about transducers

videos.t: Hewitt, Meijer and Szyperski: The Actor Model (everything you wanted to know...)
videos.s: A standing whiteboard conversation at Lang.NEXT 2012 among Carl Hewitt, Erik Meijer and Clemens Szyperski about the actor model. Hewitt, who originated the model, explains its foundations.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the best video introduction to the actor model, straight from its inventor, and revisited it after Hewitt's death.
videos.q: It's truly a masterclass.

videos.t: David Kriesel: Traue keinem Scan, den du nicht selbst gefälscht hast
videos.s: David Kriesel's 31C3 talk, in German, on the discovery that Xerox scanner-copiers silently replace digits and letters in scanned documents. He explains how the bug stayed unnoticed in the wild for years.
videos.w: Called a classic CCC talk, and the Xerox bug is cited as a cautionary tale about trusting scans and digitized archives.
videos.q: If you speak german and haven’t seen this yet, watch it, this is a classic.

videos.t: The Intense 8 Hour Hunt | Attenborough Life of Mammals | BBC Earth
videos.s: A clip from Attenborough's Life of Mammals following a San tribesman in the Kalahari on an eight-hour persistence hunt, running down a kudu through harsh heat. It shows tracking, endurance running and the hunter's reaction after the kill.
videos.w: HN returns to it as the canonical footage of persistence hunting in threads about human endurance running and evolution.
videos.q: It's a beautiful video, and the way the hunter reacts after the kill is very moving.

videos.t: Containers From Scratch • Liz Rice • GOTO 2018
videos.s: Liz Rice live-codes a minimal container runtime in a few lines of Go at GOTO Amsterdam 2018. She explains namespaces, control groups and what a host knows about its containers.
videos.w: HN considers it one of the best talks for understanding how containers work from the ground up.
videos.q: Probably one of the most enlightening presentations I've seen in recent years, full-stop.

videos.t: How to sound smart in your TEDx Talk | Will Stephen | TEDxNewYork
videos.s: Will Stephen's humorous six-minute TEDx talk shows presentation techniques that make you sound brilliant while saying essentially nothing.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a funny deconstruction of TED talk style, and as a favorite example of the appearance of meaning without content.
videos.q: spent 6 minutes talking about nothing

videos.t: I Like Notebooks
videos.s: Jeremy Howard defends Jupyter notebooks as a serious development environment, especially when paired with nbdev. He responds directly to Joel Grus's talk about why he dislikes notebooks, and contrasts REPL-style and notebook-style work.
videos.w: Whenever notebooks get criticized, HN commenters point to it as the standard rebuttal from a prominent practitioner.
videos.q: I strongly recommend Jeremy Howard's (founder of fast.ai) recent talk

videos.t: Gabe Brown: Keys To Building a Healthy Soil
videos.s: Farmer Gabe Brown talks about how he rebuilt the soil on his ranch using no-till farming, cover crops, and grazing animals. The talk was recorded at a sustainable agriculture symposium in Idaho in 2014.
videos.w: HN readers share it as a persuasive, first-hand account of regenerative agriculture, citing its claims about soil organic matter, yields and reduced fertilizer use.
videos.q: This talk introduced me to the no-till, soil health farming paradigm

videos.t: Bret Victor - The Humane Representation of Thought
videos.s: Bret Victor's closing keynote at UIST and SPLASH 2014 argues that our tools for thinking ignore most of human sensory and motor capability. He sketches representations that engage more modalities beyond screens and keyboards.
videos.w: HN treats it as a foundational Bret Victor talk that reshaped how people think about software and interfaces, often cited alongside Dynamicland.
videos.q: have had a huge impact on the way I think about software

videos.t: Rich Hickey rants about HttpServletRequest in 1080p: Death By Specificity from Clojure Made Simple
videos.s: A five-minute excerpt of Rich Hickey's Clojure Made Simple talk, with new slides, ranting about HttpServletRequest and specificity. He argues for using generic maps instead of many specific classes and getters.
videos.w: Cited as the classic rant on maps versus objects in discussions of data modeling and OOP.
videos.q: A classic rant by Rich Hickey

videos.t: The Battle of Midway 1942: Told from the Japanese Perspective (1/3)
videos.s: Part one of Montemayor's animated-map documentary on the Battle of Midway, told using only the information available to the Japanese side. It focuses on Nagumo's dilemma.
videos.w: HN recommends it for its information-dense maps and voice-over and for showing how commanders decide with limited information.
videos.q: This youtube series telling the Battle of Midway from Japanese perspective

videos.t: Timothy Snyder: The Making of Modern Ukraine. Class 1: Ukrainian Questions Posed by Russian Invasion
videos.s: The first class of Timothy Snyder's Yale course on the making of modern Ukraine. It introduces the course and asks what it means for a nation to exist in light of the Russian invasion.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as an accessible, well-taught history of Ukraine and a counter to propaganda narratives.
videos.q: gives you invaluable understanding about much more than just Ukraine.

videos.t: How Much Do Rockets Pollute? Are They Bad For Our Air?
videos.s: Everyday Astronaut's Tim Dodd runs an hour-long, data-driven analysis of what rockets actually emit and how that compares with airliners and other industries. It breaks down exhaust by propellant type, per-passenger and total emissions, and ways launches could be cleaner.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever rocket launch pollution comes up as a rebuttal to alarm, since it shows launches are small next to other sources.
videos.q: I highly recommend to everyone who is concerned about this.

videos.t: Visualizing the 4d numbers Quaternions
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown builds visual intuition for quaternions, showing how to think about this four-dimensional number system using stereographic projection and rotations in 3D space. It is part one of a two-part series with an interactive companion site.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the best visual explanation of quaternions and a good way to visualize higher dimensions.
videos.q: He does a great job of explaining quaternions though visual intuition.

videos.t: A CONSERVATIVE solution to global warming (Part 1)
videos.s: Potholer54 presents the climate science case and a market-oriented, conservative-friendly approach to addressing global warming, with sources listed. It is part one of a two-part series.
videos.w: HN users recommend it as a model of communicating climate science to conservative and libertarian audiences without alienating them.
videos.q: I've been recommending this video as a quick intro for people who don't feel at home with left wing solutions to climate change

videos.t: "Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers: Stress and Health" by Dr. Robert Sapolsky
videos.s: Robert Sapolsky's lecture on how the body's stress response, evolved for short-term physical emergencies, harms long-term health when triggered by psychological stressors. It was given as the inaugural Fenton-Rhodes Lecture.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an entertaining and informative explanation of how stress affects health.
videos.q: It's a little under 90 minutes and is enormously entertaining as well as being informative.

videos.t: The Clean Architecture in Python
videos.s: Brandon Rhodes' PyOhio 2014 talk on applying the Clean Architecture in Python. He shows how this high-level design pattern fits Python's features and addresses maintainability problems in large applications.
videos.w: HN points to it as a practical way to separate business logic from I/O, which reduces mocking and underlies the functional core, imperative shell idea.
videos.q: I'd really recommend this video.

videos.t: Brains, Sex, and Machine Learning
videos.s: Geoffrey Hinton's Google Tech Talk linking machine learning to biology, explaining dropout as a form of model averaging and why sexual reproduction and stochastic spiking neurons may prevent overfitting.
videos.w: Recommended as a simple, elegant explanation of dropout and its connection to how the brain works.
videos.q: If you want a great overview of the dropout technique, watch this tech talk by Hinton

videos.t: 30 Weird Chess Algorithms: Elo World
videos.s: Tom Scott-style absurdist tour by Tom7 of SIGBOVIK chess projects: a tournament of 30 weird chess algorithms used to rate a color- and piece-blind chess program. Topics include mirrors, arithmetic encoding, perverted game tree search and a diluted Stockfish.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a must-watch for its deadpan, absurdly elaborate engineering and cite it for ideas like diluting strong engines with random moves.
videos.q: if you like this kind of thing, you'll love Elo World.

videos.t: Pythagoras' theorem (a) | Math History | NJ Wildberger
videos.s: The first lecture of N J Wildberger's History of Mathematics course, starting with Pythagoras' theorem and following Stillwell's text. It emphasizes the flow of ideas over proofs.
videos.w: Recommended as an easy-to-follow math history course that gives perspective on the subject.
videos.q: Highly recommend his History of Mathematics lectures on YouTube

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #1258 - Jack Dorsey, Vijaya Gadde & Tim Pool
videos.s: A three-hour-plus Joe Rogan podcast with Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey, policy lead Vijaya Gadde and journalist Tim Pool. They discuss Twitter's moderation, bans and rule enforcement, with Pool challenging Dorsey and Gadde with examples.
videos.w: HN people cite it as insight into how Twitter thought about moderation, and as a source for Tim Pool's arguments about uneven enforcement.
videos.q: provided a lot of insight into how Twitter thought about moderation. It was a lot more nuanced than I expected.

videos.t: The Future is a Dead Mall - Decentraland and the Metaverse
videos.s: Dan Olson of Folding Ideas spends months in the virtual world Decentraland and delivers a long critique of the metaverse, NFTs and DAOs, and why virtual worlds fail as places.
videos.w: Regarded as the definitive takedown of the metaverse hype and the Decentraland ecosystem.
videos.q: For me, the definitive analysis here is Dan Olson's[1]

videos.t: How Valve is Profiting from Steam's Back-Door Casinos
videos.s: People Make Games investigates the unregulated CS:GO skin gambling economy and Valve's role in it. It includes interviews with people who lost large sums and examines why Valve does not intervene.
videos.w: HN recommends it as well-researched reporting on skin gambling, especially its effect on minors, in threads about gambling and Valve.
videos.q: More people need to see interviews such as those in the People Make Games video

videos.t: Notation Must Die: The Battle For How We Read Music
videos.s: Tantacrul's 76-minute deep dive into the history of western music notation and the many proposed replacements, such as piano rolls, colored notes and the jubilate. He explains why none have displaced the current system.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended as the definitive, well-made explanation of why attempts to reinvent music notation fail and what tradeoffs the current system makes.
videos.q: excellent deep-ish dive into music notation by the inimitable Tantacrul

videos.t: Do Chairs Exist?
videos.s: A Vsauce video exploring whether chairs exist, through metaphysics, mereology and the philosophy of categorizing objects. It runs about 38 minutes and cites academic work on ontology.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining tour of how we define and categorize things, and it is cited when concept boundaries come up.
videos.q: it's basically an entertaining, whirlwind tour of the philosophy of categorizing and labeling things

videos.t: Civil War General-Purpose Computing | Cory Doctorow | Talks at Google
videos.s: Cory Doctorow's Talks at Google lecture on the coming civil war over general-purpose computing. He argues that locked-down devices, DRM, and surveillance threaten user control of computers.
videos.w: It is HN's go-to reference whenever device lockdown, DRM, or restrictions on installing software come up, with commenters noting how prescient it was.
videos.q: I highly recommend reading up on what Cory has to say on DRM and the war on general purpose computing. It may change your mind.

videos.t: How Big is Graham's Number? (feat Ron Graham)
videos.s: Numberphile talks with mathematician Ron Graham about the magnitude of Graham's number, building up from arrow notation to show how impossibly large it is. It is part of a series of videos on this number.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for hearing Graham himself and for its clear introduction to up-arrow notation and enormous numbers.
videos.q: And here is the man himself describing it

videos.t: Dr. Gabor Maté — Trauma, Addiction, Ayahuasca, and More
videos.s: A long Tim Ferriss podcast interview with physician Gabor Mate on trauma, addiction, depression, ADHD and ayahuasca. Mate explains how childhood stress and emotional pain underlie many addictions and illnesses.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a thoughtful, honest look at the causes of addiction and depression, and as a deeper Mate interview than most.
videos.q: I recommend Tim Ferris’ interview with Gabor Mate for a great honest look into the causes and mechanisms of addiction.

videos.t: Robust-first computing: Demon Horde Sort (full version)
videos.s: Dave Ackley demonstrates the Demon Horde Sort, an inherently robust sorting machine running in his Movable Feast Machine simulator. This is the uncut version with all details and side thoughts.
videos.w: HN readers recommend it as the best introduction to robust-first computing, where randomness and fault tolerance are built into the architecture.
videos.q: it's certainly esoteric, but has some extremely important properties.

videos.t: Why can't you multiply vectors?
videos.s: Freya Holmer's Dutch Game Day 2023 talk asking why vectors can't be multiplied, building from complex numbers to a single axiom and arriving at geometric algebra, quaternions and multivectors.
videos.w: HN treats it as the best entry point to geometric algebra and an intuitive route to understanding quaternions.
videos.q: The absolute first video to watch should be the (ironically titled) Why can't you multiply vectors?

videos.t: DjangoCon 2008 Keynote: Cal Henderson
videos.s: Cal Henderson's DjangoCon 2008 keynote, "Why I Hate Django", is a funny critique of Django from a Flickr architect. It touches on scaling topics such as database replication.
videos.w: Recommended as a brilliant, hilarious talk, though not the most educational.
videos.q: a brilliant (and hilarious) talk

videos.t: Copying Is Not Theft - Official Version
videos.s: Nina Paley's one-minute animated free culture anthem with vocals by Connie Champagne, arguing that copying is not theft.
videos.w: Linked constantly in copyright and piracy debates as a short explainer of the difference between copying and physical theft.
videos.q: A one minute ELI5 explanation about the difference between physical and intellectual property.

videos.t: The IOU Machine: How Currency Is Created | Hidden Secrets of Money Ep. 4
videos.s: Episode 4 of Mike Maloney's Hidden Secrets of Money, explaining how currency is created through a chain of IOUs among the Treasury, banks and the Federal Reserve. It covers bonds, Fed checks, debt, taxes and fractional reserve lending, from a gold-and-silver advocate's viewpoint.
videos.w: Recommended, often in Bitcoin and monetary threads, as a clear introduction to how the US money system works, though it comes with a strong goldbug slant.
videos.q: This is the best explanation I've ever seen of how the Fed and US Dollar money printing actually works

videos.t: We're building a dystopia just to make people click on ads | Zeynep Tufekci
videos.s: Technosociologist Zeynep Tufekci argues that the machine-learning systems used to serve ads also decide what political and social information people see. She explains how opaque algorithms can nudge, segment and manipulate users, and warns that the real danger is powerful people using AI to control populations.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever engagement-optimizing feeds, micro-targeting or ad infrastructure come up, as an accessible warning about algorithmic amplification.
videos.q: This TED talk[0] on persuasion architectures brings up some interesting moral arguments against this idea.

videos.t: The Man Who Accidentally Killed The Most People In History
videos.s: Veritasium tells the story of Thomas Midgley Jr., who introduced leaded gasoline and CFCs, and covers the science behind lead exposure and ozone damage. It also touches on isotope geochemistry used to uncover the history.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it whenever leaded fuel, toxic chemicals or corporate profit motives come up, praising its storytelling and accessible science.
videos.q: here's an excellent one by Veritasium on how it happened.

videos.t: George Hotz: Comma.ai, OpenPilot, and Autonomous Vehicles | Lex Fridman Podcast #31
videos.s: Lex Fridman's two-hour podcast with George Hotz, founder of Comma.ai, covering openpilot, autonomous driving and Hotz's views on AI and technology.
videos.w: HN recommends it for Hotz's reasoning on cameras versus lidar and for an opinionated, original thinker's overview of comma and openpilot.
videos.q: I strongly recommend Lex Firdman’s recent interview with George Hotz

videos.t: Ramanujan: Making sense of 1+2+3+... = -1/12 and Co.
videos.s: Mathologer examines how identities like 1+2+3+... = -1/12 arise in Ramanujan's work, starting from his 1913 letter to Hardy. The video explains the rules for summing infinite series and why such results are meaningful but not naive sums.
videos.w: Recommended as a careful, honest treatment of the -1/12 claim, often preferred over flashier videos.
videos.q: If you have half an hour to spare, I highly recommend to watch

videos.t: Zipline - How Rwanda Built A Drone Delivery Service
videos.s: Real Engineering explains how Zipline built a drone delivery network for medical supplies in Rwanda. It covers the fixed-wing drones, catapult launch, parachute drop and the logistics behind the service.
videos.w: HN points to it as the best explanation of how Zipline's whole system works and as an example of drones doing real, useful work.
videos.q: this video by Real Engineering that does a great job of explaining how the whole thing works

videos.t: These Stupid Trucks are Literally Killing Us
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains how SUVs and light trucks have grown in size and share of US sales, and why that is dangerous for pedestrians, cyclists and city life. He covers the regulatory loopholes, such as fuel economy rules and the chicken tax, that favored them.
videos.w: It is HN's default link whenever vehicle size comes up, with commenters recommending it for the history of the light-truck loophole and the safety effects of tall bumpers.
videos.q: a very relevant video about the very real problems that SUVs and modern trucks have on urban environments.

videos.t: Evil Mode: Or, How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love Emacs
videos.s: Aaron Bieber, a longtime Vim user, describes his experience trying Emacs with evil mode. He covers what he found, what he missed from Vim, and what Vim could borrow from Emacs.
videos.w: HN recommends it to Vim users considering Emacs, and several say it persuaded them or their coworkers to switch.
videos.q: Aaron gave a great talk about his switch here

videos.t: How Differential Gear works (BEST Tutorial)
videos.s: A 1930s Chevrolet training film explaining the principles and development of the differential gear. It builds the idea step by step from first principles to the finished mechanism.
videos.w: HN loves it as an example of old-school instructional film that makes how a differential works fully understandable in clear, simple language.
videos.q: after watching this ancient Chevrolet training video from the 1930's I feel like I completely understand how diffs work

videos.t: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Multiple Dispatch | Stefan Karpinski | JuliaCon 2019
videos.s: Julia co-creator Stefan Karpinski explains why multiple dispatch makes Julia code and types reusable across packages with so little friction. He covers sharing basic types and sharing generic algorithms.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the definitive explanation, from a language designer, of why multiple dispatch makes Julia's composability work.
videos.q: a talk by a core developer at JuliaCon 2019 titled 'The unreasonable effectiveness of multiple dispatch'

videos.t: Robocalypse Now: Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive
videos.s: Valve's John McDonald presents at GDC 2018 on how Valve uses deep learning (VACnet) to detect cheaters in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. He covers training on human-reviewed replays and how model output is confirmed by manual review.
videos.w: The go-to link in any anti-cheat thread for a concrete, well-delivered account of machine-learning cheat detection in production.
videos.q: The presenter delivered the problem and solution approach so well I'd still like to work on something like this some time.

videos.t: You are being misled about renewable energy technology.
videos.s: A long Technology Connections video arguing that public understanding of renewable energy is distorted. It covers solar economics, land use compared with ethanol corn, and battery myths such as cobalt.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as an up-to-date, fact-focused case for solar and batteries that readers can cite on land use and costs.
videos.q: Alec Watson’s recent, and excellent, Technology Connections YouTube piece on renewable energy.

videos.t: User-level threads....... with threads. - Paul Turner - Google
videos.s: Paul Turner of Google presents kernel interfaces for user-level scheduling of real threads, aiming at a uniform synchronous programming model across C++, Java, Go and Python. It introduces the switchto-style system calls behind Google's fibers.
videos.w: HN cites it as the key explanation of cooperative, user-scheduled kernel threads and the prior art behind later async and coroutine debates.
videos.q: Paul Turner explained this really well at this year's Linux Plumbers Conference. The whole talk is fantastic

videos.t: Interactive programming Flappy Bird in ClojureScript
videos.s: Bruce Hauman live-codes Flappy Bird in ClojureScript in about six minutes, using figwheel to hot-reload changes into the running game. The demo shows game behavior being changed interactively without restarting.
videos.w: It is the canonical demo HN people cite for live interactive development and hot reloading, as proof the workflow is real and not smoke and mirrors.
videos.q: I still marvel at Bruce Hauman's demo

videos.t: Stevey's Tech Talk E39 -- A guided tour of Emacs
videos.s: Steve Yegge records himself working in Emacs and shows off about a dozen features in a roughly 45-minute screen capture. It is an informal, enthusiastic tour rather than a structured tutorial.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as an excellent, convincing overview of Emacs for newcomers and skeptics, shown by someone who clearly loves it.
videos.q: Two videos by Steve Yegge should be enough to convince the most dyed-in-the-wool anti-Emacser to consider re-evaluating their position.

videos.t: Orbital Rings
videos.s: Isaac Arthur explains the orbital ring, a megastructure launch-assist system that could move bulk cargo cheaply to orbit and beyond. He compares it with space elevators and discusses power transmission.
videos.w: HN commenters offer it as the likely future of cheap access to space, feasible without exotic materials.
videos.q: we can build an orbital ring around Earth with today's technology, and it'd be much better than space elevators.

videos.t: The more general uncertainty principle, regarding Fourier transforms
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown shows how the uncertainty principle arises from Fourier transforms. A wave packet cannot be narrow in both position and frequency, so the principle is a property of waves rather than of measurement.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the clearest visual explanation that uncertainty is intrinsic to waves, separate from measurement disturbance.
videos.q: The clearest, most intuitive explanation of the Fourier Uncertainty Principle that I have come across is by Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown.

videos.t: Building The World's First Computer - Greeks, Clocks and Rockets - Antikythera Mechanism Episode 1
videos.s: The first episode of Clickspring's series on reproducing the Antikythera Mechanism by hand, laying out the plan and the history. The series follows a machinist building the ancient Greek device with traditional tools and methods.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends the series for its extraordinary craftsmanship and its credible demonstration of how the mechanism could have been made.
videos.q: Highly recommend for anyone who is fascinated by the care that goes into handmade mechanical devices.

videos.t: Build a real-time Twitter clone in 15 minutes with LiveView and Phoenix 1.5
videos.s: Phoenix creator Chris McCord builds a real-time Twitter-style app live with Phoenix LiveView 1.5 in about 15 minutes. It shows interactive, real-time updates without writing JavaScript.
videos.w: HN points people to it as the demo that shows why LiveView and Elixir are worth a look.
videos.q: the demo completely blew my mind

videos.t: 38C3 - From Silicon to Sovereignty: How Advanced Chips are Redefining Global Dominance
videos.s: A 38C3 talk on how advanced chips are made, centered on EUV lithography and the global supply chain behind it. It covers technical challenges from raw materials to finished chips and the geopolitical weight of semiconductors.
videos.w: HN users recommend it as an excellent, accessible overview of how modern chips are produced and why EUV matters.
videos.q: I can highly recommend this to everybody who is "somehow in tech or IT

videos.t: CGA Graphics - Not as bad as you thought!
videos.s: The 8-Bit Guy covers IBM's 1981 CGA graphics system, including how composite output and artifacting produced extra colors beyond the nominal palette. He argues CGA looked better in period than it does on RGB monitors.
videos.w: HN recommends it for showing how old developers exploited the smeary nature of composite signals and what CGA really looked like on period hardware.
videos.q: The 8-Bit guy did a great piece on CGA that goes into detail about how old developers abused the fuzzy smeary nature of composite signals

videos.t: 2016 - On The Shoulders Of Giants - Damian Conway
videos.c: The Perl and Raku Conference - Greenville, SC 2026
videos.s: Damian Conway's hour-long keynote at the Perl conference, On the Shoulders of Giants, showing off Perl 6 (Raku) features with history, algorithms and a quantum math operator built with grammars. It is delivered with comic flair.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining, technically masterful showcase of what Perl 6 can do.
videos.q: the whole thing is like watching a great movie

videos.t: Evan Czaplicki - Let's be mainstream! User focused design in Elm - Curry On
videos.s: Evan Czaplicki, creator of Elm, talks at Curry On 2015 about user-focused language design. He explains the principles behind Elm and how to make a functional, typed language as approachable as JavaScript.
videos.w: Recommended as the clearest explanation of Elm's design thinking and of making functional languages mainstream, plus a popular monad explanation clip.
videos.q: He makes a strong case for Elm not as a language-to-rule-them-all, but as a tool for the average programmer

videos.t: Visualization of Quantum Physics (Quantum Mechanics)
videos.s: An animated visualization of basic quantum mechanics using a free particle, with simulations based on the actual equations. It covers waves, particles, and how measurement collapses the wavefunction.
videos.w: HN commenters call it one of the best visual explanations of the wave, particle and measurement relationship, free of silly metaphors.
videos.q: Highly recommended for anyone trying to grok the relationship between a wave, a particle, and an observation.

videos.t: Amiga Hardware Programming 1 - Use the Assembler and wait for left click
videos.s: The first video in Photon of Scoopex's Amiga hardware programming series. It shows how to set up an assembler and write a minimal 68000 program that waits for a left mouse click.
videos.w: Recommended as an approachable start to Amiga demo and 68000 assembly programming.
videos.q: you should fasten your seatbelts and check out this video tutorials by Photon of Scoopex

videos.t: CppCon 2015: Greg Law " Give me 15 minutes & I'll change your view of GDB"
videos.s: Greg Law's 15-minute CppCon 2015 lightning talk shows what GDB can do beyond basic use, including its text user interface and reverse debugging.
videos.w: Recommended as a fast, brilliant introduction to GDB's TUI mode and lesser-known features, useful for anyone who has only used IDE debuggers.
videos.q: this brilliant short talk (15min) about gdb's TUI.

videos.t: Jack Szostak (Harvard/HHMI) Part 1: The Origin of Cellular Life on Earth
videos.s: Jack Szostak's lecture covers how cellular life could have arisen from chemistry on the early Earth, starting from the odds of life elsewhere in the galaxy. It is part of a series on protocells and the RNA world.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear, authoritative lecture series on plausible origin-of-life theories.
videos.q: Jack Szostak does a pretty good job of outlining how life might have arisen.

videos.t: Feynman: Magnets (and Why?)  FUN TO IMAGINE  4/ higher quality version!
videos.s: A 1983 BBC interview in which Richard Feynman is asked how magnets work and explains why 'why' questions are hard to answer in everyday terms. He reflects on what counts as an explanation and the limits of analogy.
videos.w: HN returns to it as a model of intellectual honesty and good explanation, often linking it in discussions of why-questions and science communication.
videos.q: his riff for 8 minutes on this is just a joy to watch.

videos.t: JPEG DCT, Discrete Cosine Transform (JPEG Pt2)- Computerphile
videos.s: Mike Pound explains the discrete cosine transform and how it underpins JPEG compression. It is part two of Computerphile's JPEG series.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an easy, clear intro to the DCT that finally made it click for several commenters.
videos.q: I finally understood DCT after watching

videos.t: Pulling Power from the Sky: The Story of Makani [Feature Film]
videos.s: A feature-length film by the Makani team chronicling their thirteen-year effort to build energy kites that harvest wind power, with footage from test sites in Hawaii, California and Norway. It shows the engineering, the team and the eventual shutdown.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a technically rich, beautifully made documentary on ambitious hardware engineering and failure.
videos.q: There's a beautiful feature film about the story of Makani. It's a great watch with plenty of technical details

videos.t: Can You Watch This Without Getting Angry?
videos.s: CGP Grey explains how ideas spread like germs, and why content that triggers outrage spreads fastest, using a study on what makes online content viral. He argues that opposing outrage-driven memes feed each other.
videos.w: HN links it constantly in threads on social media, polarization and outrage as the canonical explanation of why angry content wins.
videos.q: Great TED talk on the original twitter kerfuffle referenced in the article

videos.t: The Biggest Myth In Education
videos.s: Veritasium debunks the idea of learning styles, such as being a visual learner, with an interview with Daniel Willingham and a memory experiment. It argues that a multimodal approach helps everyone.
videos.w: The standard link whenever someone claims to be a visual learner or learning styles come up, with sources listed in the description.
videos.q: Veritasium covered this in much greater detail but still approachable by the laymen

videos.t: BlueHat IL 2019 - Andrew "bunnie" Huang - Supply Chain Security: "If I were a Nation State...”
videos.s: Andrew "bunnie" Huang examines how realistic hardware supply chain attacks are, from rogue insiders to nation states, in the wake of the Bloomberg Businessweek report. He explains how undocumented components could be hidden on boards and how hard they are to spot.
videos.w: HN people point to it as the sober, technically grounded picture of hardware supply chain security, and an eye-opening one.
videos.q: This is an eye opening talk in the subject

videos.t: Old-fashioned rice cookers are extremely clever
videos.s: Technology Connections explains how old-fashioned non-electronic rice cookers work, using a magnet and spring switch tripped by the Curie point. It shows the thermodynamics and magnetism behind a simple appliance.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a delightful breakdown of the cleverness in dumb appliances and an entry point to the channel.
videos.q: I had no idea they were so clever, combining thermodynamics and the physics of magnetism.

videos.t: Irving Finkel | The Ark Before Noah: A Great Adventure
videos.c: The Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures
videos.s: Irving Finkel of the British Museum tells how a 4,000-year-old cuneiform tablet came to him for examination. It revealed the oldest known account of Noah's Ark and led to a book and a documentary.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a funny, fascinating talk on cuneiform tablets and the ancient world by an engaging curator.
videos.q: equal parts fascinating and hilarious

videos.t: golden balls. the weirdest split or steal ever!
videos.s: A Golden Balls episode in which one contestant announces he will steal, leading to an unexpected outcome in the split-or-steal prisoner's dilemma.
videos.w: The canonical real-world example in game theory discussions of manipulating a prisoner's dilemma.
videos.q: This is a classic IMO.

videos.t: DOOM: Behind the Music
videos.s: Mick Gordon's GDC 2017 session on composing the Doom (2016) soundtrack. He details his compositional process, production techniques and the experimental instrument and synth design behind the music.
videos.w: HN raves about it as one of the best conference talks, showing a master's creative process and sound design.
videos.q: One of my favorite conference talks ever

videos.t: Alex Evans at Umbra Ignite 2015: Learning From Failure
videos.s: Media Molecule's Alex Evans recounts the journey, including the failures, of finding the Dreams engine, based on his Siggraph 2015 talk. It covers the signed-distance-field and splat-based rendering approach and the artistic goals behind it.
videos.w: HN calls it an inspirational must-see on SDF rendering and a favorite tech talk for graphics programmers.
videos.q: the Dreams presentation which is an inspirational must see

videos.t: Old pinball machines are amazingly complex
videos.s: Technology Connections takes a long, detailed look at how a 1970s electromechanical pinball machine works, from relays to stepper motors and mechanical logic. It is the first part of a series.
videos.w: HN points people to it as a deep dive showing how complex logic was built without computers.
videos.q: I shared it with everyone I know, and now I'm sharing it with you

videos.t: Great Earthquakes of the Pacific Northwest
videos.s: Geologist Nick Zentner of Central Washington University gives an hour-long public lecture on the great earthquakes of the Pacific Northwest, including the Cascadia subduction zone and the evidence for past megaquakes. It is part of his Downtown Geology Lecture Series, recorded in Ellensburg in 2016.
videos.w: HN commenters offer it as a dry but fascinating, hype-free introduction to Cascadia earthquake risk and the evidence for past events.
videos.q: It's better than most TV if you've got the time.

videos.t: Bryan Cranston's Advice to Aspiring Actors
videos.s: A one-minute clip of Bryan Cranston at an Academy new-member reception, advising actors to approach auditions without desperation and focus on solving the problem rather than landing the job.
videos.w: HN applies it to job interviews and confidence, recommending the mindset of not interviewing from a place of desperation.
videos.q: Nobody explains this better than Bryan Cranston (possibly one of the most successful TV actors of recent times)

videos.t: Threads (1984) ORIGINAL TRAILER [HD 1080p]
videos.s: The original trailer for Threads, the 1984 British TV film depicting the aftermath of a nuclear attack on Sheffield. The trailer hints at the film's bleak tone.
videos.w: HN commenters use it to point people to Threads, which they call the most harrowing depiction of nuclear war and say should be mandatory viewing.
videos.q: should be mandatory viewing for all people in positions of power

videos.t: In Search of Tomorrow
videos.s: Chris Granger, creator of Light Table and the Eve language, gives a Berkeley data science lecture on what computation and programming might look like in ten years. He covers the path that led to Eve and ends with demos.
videos.w: HN keeps pointing to it as a thoughtful vision of programming for non-programmers and as background on Eve's motivations.
videos.q: very good talk about the background of eve

videos.t: TigerStyle! (Or How To Design Safer Systems in Less Time) by Joran Dirk Greef
videos.s: Joran Dirk Greef's Systems Distributed '23 talk on TigerStyle, the engineering methodology behind TigerBeetle. It covers designing safer systems in less time through up-front design, assertions, and deterministic simulation.
videos.w: HN commenters, including TigerBeetle people, recommend it as the explanation of a methodology for building defect-free, high-assurance software.
videos.q: The TigerStyle video is well worth watching for anyone who wants to build defect-free software systems

videos.t: Jancovici : Can we save energy, jobs and growth at the same time ? 08/01/2018
videos.s: Jean-Marc Jancovici lectures at ENS Paris on whether energy use, jobs and growth can all be preserved. He argues for a physical approach to economics, since resource depletion and climate limits make perpetual GDP growth unrealistic.
videos.w: Recommended as a sober, physics-based account of how energy underlies the economy.
videos.q: this doc illustrates the enormous realities of energy challenges with sober clarity often exposed by Jancovici

videos.t: The Inner Life of the Cell Animation
videos.s: An award-winning 3D animation by XVIVO for Harvard's BioVisions showing the molecular machinery inside a cell as a white blood cell responds to a stimulus.
videos.w: Recommended as a jaw-dropping view of the complexity and machine-like nature of cells.
videos.q: For anyone who hasn't already seen it, I highly recommend The Inner Life of a Cell

videos.t: Coding Adventure: Ant and Slime Simulations
videos.s: Sebastian Lague explores an ant-inspired algorithm and simulates ant and slime mold behavior, using compute shaders. Source code for both simulations is available.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a beautiful example of what simple rules and compute shaders can produce, and many commenters were inspired by it.
videos.q: reminded how beautiful coding can be

videos.t: A New Car UI: How touch screen controls in cars should work
videos.s: Matthaeus Krenn presents a concept for car touchscreen UI where the screen controls only one thing at a time, designed to suit driving. A tablet prototype accompanies the short demo.
videos.w: Repeatedly cited in car touchscreen debates as an elegant, sensible alternative to distracting automotive UIs.
videos.q: I feel compelled to share a video, now 9 years old, that shows how touch screens could be accommodated with sensible design in cars.

videos.t: Fourier Optics used for Optical Pattern Recognition
videos.s: Huygens Optics explains the Fourier transform and shows how a lens performs one optically. A DLP projector is used as a Fourier filter to do simple pattern recognition on lithographic character patterns.
videos.w: Recommended as one of the best explanations of Fourier transforms and a clear demo of analog optical computing.
videos.q: The video happens to have one of the best explanations of Fourier transforms I've yet encountered.

videos.t: Eric Bier Demonstrates Cedar
videos.s: Eric Bier, a PARC research scientist, demonstrates the Cedar integrated programming environment and language, an evolution of Mesa from Xerox PARC. The demo shows the Tioga editor, garbage collection, and a full graphical workstation environment.
videos.w: HN keeps citing it as proof of how advanced a GC-based systems language and integrated workstation were decades ago, and as a model for what desktop OSes could be.
videos.q: Be prepared to be amazed with what Xerox PARC and others were doing

videos.t: Floyd Toole - Sound reproduction – art and science/opinions and facts
