videos.s: Floyd Toole's CIRMMT distinguished lecture on the science of sound reproduction, drawing on decades of blind listening research. It covers what listeners prefer in loudspeakers and why measured accuracy and anechoic response matter.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a crash course on audio reproduction science, especially the finding that listeners reliably prefer more accurate speakers in blind tests.
videos.q: In blind testing, the average listener reliably prefers the more accurate speaker.

videos.t: Building a Cathedral without Science or Mathematics: The Engineering Method Explained
videos.s: Bill Hammack of engineerguy explains how medieval engineers designed stone cathedrals using rules of thumb, with no science, mathematics or literacy. He uses it to define the engineering method.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as a thoughtful account of engineering as rule-of-thumb problem solving that predates formal science.
videos.q: I encourage everyone to watch this series of videos.

videos.t: How to Invent the Future II - Stanford CS183F: Startup School
videos.s: Part two of Alan Kay's Stanford Startup School lecture on inventing the future. He draws on his time at Xerox PARC and elsewhere to discuss how to think about new technology and what makes ideas useful.
videos.w: Frequently suggested in Ask HN threads on finding ideas, creativity and why incumbents like Xerox missed what they invented.
videos.q: I also recommend Alan Kay's video series on "How To Invent The Future".

videos.t: Using a 1930 Teletype as a Linux Terminal
videos.s: CuriousMarc connects a restored 1930 Model 15 Teletype to a Linux machine and uses it as a terminal, after commenters requested it. The video shows the challenges of linking a 5-bit mechanical device to a modern OS.
videos.w: HN commenters love it as a vivid demonstration of terminal history, explaining why tools like ed and the tty echo model work the way they do.
videos.q: It's one of the best things on the Internet, IMO.

videos.t: Over 200,000 Servers in One Place! Visiting Hetzner in Falkenstein (Germany)
videos.s: Overclocker der8auer tours Hetzner's Falkenstein data center in Germany, showing custom racks, own mainboards, passively cooled servers and ATX-style cases on shelves.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever Hetzner comes up, as the best look inside their unusual, semi-custom and low-cost data center setup.
videos.q: There's a great YouTube tour of one of their data centres here

videos.t: The first 20 hours -- how to learn anything | Josh Kaufman | TEDxCSU
videos.s: Josh Kaufman's TEDx talk argues that you can reach practical competence in almost any skill with about 20 hours of focused practice, rather than the 10,000 hours often quoted. He describes how becoming a parent led him to rethink how adults learn, and lays out a short method for rapid skill acquisition.
videos.w: HN uses it as the standard counterpoint to the 10,000-hour rule and as an encouraging recipe for starting new skills.
videos.q: the threshold for acquiring new skills for personal or professional use is somewhere around 20 hours.

videos.t: Java on a 1000 Cores - Tales of Hardware / Software CoDesign
videos.s: Cliff Click of Azul Systems gives a Google Tech Talk on running Java business applications on a machine with about a thousand cores. He covers hardware and software codesign, including garbage collection hardware and the JIT.
videos.w: HN treats Cliff Click's talks as an excellent source on JVMs, garbage collection and hardware-assisted Java.
videos.q: Anything from Cliff Click is quite good.

videos.t: Ivan Sutherland Sketchpad Demo 1963
videos.s: A TV show about Ivan Sutherland's 1963 MIT thesis software Sketchpad, which ran on the TX-2 computer. It shows a light pen drawing, constraints, snapping, scaling and object-style graphics, foundations of GUIs and CAD.
videos.w: HN returns to it as a striking demonstration that core GUI, CAD and constraint-programming ideas existed in the 1960s.
videos.q: It blows me away that this kind of UI was even conceived in the 1960s.

videos.t: Bryan Cantrill from Joyent on Manta: internet-facing object storage facility that features compute
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill of Joyent presents Manta, an internet-facing object store that lets you run compute directly on the data. The talk is peppered with ZFS history and Cantrill's trademark commentary on the industry.
videos.w: HN recommends Cantrill talks generally for their mix of industry history, technical depth and entertaining delivery, and this one is a favorite for storage and data integrity threads.
videos.q: I highly recommend any talk you can find of Bryan Cantrill. A wonderful mix of industry history and great delivery.

videos.t: DEF CON 23 - Chris Rock - I Will Kill You
videos.s: A DEF CON 23 talk showing how weak controls in electronic death registration systems let someone virtually kill a person and obtain a real death certificate, with consequences for their identity and life.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it whenever fake deaths, identity verification or records fraud come up, praising how easy the attack seemed.
videos.q: Really eye opening, and potentially devastating if it's done to you.

videos.t: The Lottery: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on state lotteries. It argues that the claim that lotteries fund education is misleading, because the money is fungible and often diverted to general funds.
videos.w: Go-to reference in lottery threads for the point that earmarked lottery revenue does not really add to school funding.
videos.q: this video is worth watching.

videos.t: Where in the world is it easiest to get rich? | Harald Eia | TEDxOslo
videos.s: Sociologist and comedian Harald Eia argues in a TEDxOslo talk that Nordic social democracies produce more rich people per capita than the US or UK. He credits high taxes, welfare and strong unions for creating a safety net that enables risk taking.
videos.w: HN uses it as a counterintuitive data point in debates on welfare states, social mobility and entrepreneurship.
videos.q: In these kinds of discussions I like to promote this interesting TEDx talk

videos.t: Jon Stewart on Crossfire
videos.s: Jon Stewart appears as a guest on CNN's Crossfire in 2004 and criticizes hosts Tucker Carlson and Paul Begala for turning political debate into partisan theater that hurts America.
videos.w: HN returns to it constantly as the definitive critique of adversarial TV punditry, still seen as relevant to polarized media and online discourse.
videos.q: It's so very worth watching again even if you've seen it multiple times.

videos.t: "Controlling Time and Space: understanding the many formulations of FRP" by Evan Czaplicki
videos.s: Evan Czaplicki's Strange Loop 2014 talk surveys the many formulations of functional reactive programming and how they relate historically and theoretically. It then shows how Elm's variant enables hot-swapping and its time-traveling debugger.
videos.w: HN people point to it as the clearest explanation of what FRP actually means and how its flavors differ.
videos.q: I highly recommend Evan's Strange Loop talk

videos.t: Classic Game Postmortem: Sid Meier's Civilization
videos.s: A 2017 GDC postmortem in which Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley tell how Civilization came together from board game design and sim game experience. They cover its development history and design decisions, including fairness and luck.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a great account of how Civilization was made and as a source on perceived fairness in game design.
videos.q: Check out this great GDC talk by Sid and Bruce on the history of the development of the game.

videos.t: I Found The Source of the Coronavirus
videos.s: A 2020 video by laowhy86 arguing that the coronavirus did not originate outside China, pointing to evidence about the Wuhan institute and a possible patient zero. It cites sources in the description.
videos.w: Frequently posted in early COVID origin and lab-leak threads as a compelling early case, though other commenters cite rebuttals and note it is speculative.
videos.q: I wish more people would watch this [0], might not be true but damn does it seem convincing.

videos.t: K Lars Lohn - Keynote - PyCon 2016
videos.s: K Lars Lohn's PyCon 2016 keynote weaves together music theory, programming, biking road trips and fractals. It is a personal, wide-ranging talk rather than a Python how-to.
videos.w: Commenters call it a mind-blowing, beautiful talk and cite it among their favorite tech talks.
videos.q: It's a beautiful talk about music, programming, biking, and life

videos.t: Stanford Lecture: Don Knuth—"A Conjecture That Had To Be True" (2017)
videos.s: Donald Knuth's 2017 Christmas Tree Lecture at Stanford about a combinatorial geometry problem whose computed numbers matched a striking formula. He tells the story of the conjecture and its sequel.
videos.w: HN fans love it for Knuth's humor and for how he makes open math problems feel approachable, and it is often cited for details like dancing links and counting rectangle subdivisions.
videos.q: it's always a pleasure for me to see Knuth's talks or read his work

videos.t: Taking Vector Transposes Seriously | Jiahao Chen | JuliaCon 2017
videos.s: Jiahao Chen's JuliaCon 2017 talk argues that vector transposes should be taken seriously in type systems and linear algebra libraries. It explains why treating vectors as matrices causes trouble in languages.
videos.w: Strongly recommended for anyone working with vectors for its clear take on how they should be treated in types.
videos.q: but seriously take the time to watch this, it's fantastic

videos.t: Mock Interview with Shawn McGrath
videos.s: A live mock programmer interview in which Casey Muratori interviews game developer Shawn McGrath using a less confrontational format devised by Chris Hecker. It gets deep into technical details while showing how the candidate actually thinks and works.
videos.w: HN cites it as the example of a better alternative to whiteboard and fizzbuzz-style interviews.
videos.q: please watch this alternative method of interviewing

videos.t: Simplicity Ain't Easy - Stuart Halloway
videos.s: Stuart Halloway argues that simplicity is objective, with a definition and etymology useful to programmers, rather than a subjective buzzword. He shows how this view informs Clojure's design and how to make programs simpler.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it, alongside Rich Hickey's talk, for its precise definition of simple versus easy and its implications for code design.
videos.q: He talks about his definition of "simple" (by digging into what the original English definition was) and what that means for code.

videos.t: Lecture 1: Introduction
videos.s: The opening lecture of MIT 6.824 Distributed Systems (Spring 2020), introducing the course and core challenges of distributed systems. It begins a playlist that goes on to cover Raft and other consensus papers in Go.
videos.w: Recommended as the standard free course for learning distributed systems from real papers.
videos.q: Martin Kleppmann (author of DDIA)

videos.t: Type 2 diabetes | Sarah Hallberg | TEDxPurdueU
videos.s: Dr. Sarah Hallberg argues in a TEDx talk that type 2 diabetes can be treated and potentially reversed through diet, especially by restricting carbohydrates. TED flagged the talk as outside its guidelines and warned against taking it as medical advice.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it as a clear explanation of carbs, insulin and hunger, and several say it led them to try low-carb eating.
videos.q: Dr. Sarah Hallberg provides compelling evidence that it can, and the solution is simpler than you might think.

videos.t: Clojure Concurrency - Rich Hickey
videos.s: Rich Hickey's long presentation on Clojure and concurrency covers locking and immutability, then goes in depth on refs, transactions and agents. It ends with a multithreaded ant colony simulation demo.
videos.w: Seen as the definitive explanation of why traditional concurrency is hard and how Clojure's model addresses it, with some commenters crediting it with changing their careers.
videos.q: one my favorite talks I ever went to.

videos.t: Pete Hunt: React - Rethinking Best Practices (updated) - JSConf.Asia 2013
videos.s: Pete Hunt of Facebook and Instagram presents React at JSConf.Asia 2013, explaining its design principles and why they seemed shocking at first. He argues that React separates concerns rather than technologies, and the talk also announces the React Chrome developer tools.
videos.w: HN commenters credit it with persuading them to adopt React, and cite it for the argument that HTML and JS cannot truly be separated.
videos.q: Pete Hunt did a great job then, explaining how the false separation of concerns between HTML and JS really is unavoidable.

videos.t: A Sudoku Solver in APL
videos.s: A Dyalog demonstration of developing a Sudoku solver in APL, using an algorithm by Arthur Whitney with performance work by John Scholes. The narration steps through the array-oriented solution.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a beautiful demonstration that APL can be read and reasoned about step by step.
videos.q: I've always liked this video, where one of the Dyalog developers effortlessly writes a Sudoku solver in APL

videos.t: Akira Kurosawa - Composing Movement
videos.s: An Every Frame a Painting video essay on how Akira Kurosawa used movement, weather and composition to tell stories. It draws on clips and interviews with other filmmakers.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a deeply researched example of film analysis and one of the most educational videos on YouTube.
videos.q: check out the wonderful commentary by 'Every Frame a Painting'

videos.t: Can C++ be 10x Simpler & Safer?  - Herb Sutter - CppCon 2022
videos.s: Herb Sutter's CppCon 2022 talk on whether C++ can become ten times simpler and safer. He introduces his experimental Cpp2 syntax and the cppfront transpiler, explaining the limits on incremental improvement.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the main introduction to Cpp2 and cppfront, and as a credible effort to evolve C++.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: One of those few talks that left me genuinely enthused about the topic.

videos.t: Factor: an extensible interactive language
videos.s: A 2008 Google Tech Talk in which Slava Pestov introduces Factor, a concatenative language influenced by Forth, Lisp and Smalltalk. It covers the interactive environment, metaprogramming, and the language's modern high-level features and libraries.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the best introduction to Factor and concatenative programming, with commenters saying it impressed them with the engineering.
videos.q: It absolutely blew my mind.

videos.t: Happy People | Spring (part 1) [Happy People Documentary | Spring in Siberia Part 1
videos.s: The first part of Dmitry Vasyukov's four-part Russian documentary series about trappers and villagers living in the Siberian taiga. This episode follows spring life along the Yenisei, with hunting, fishing and subsistence in harsh surroundings.
videos.w: Recommended as the authentic original that many prefer over Werner Herzog's shortened re-cut.
videos.q: I like the original much better, I think of it as the authentic view

videos.t: Zebras All the Way Down - Bryan Cantrill, Uptime 2017
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill's Uptime 2017 talk on the engineering challenges of the stateful data path, including storage, firmware and hardware bugs. It uses the 'zebras vs. horses' diagnostic heuristic to explain why rare failures keep appearing.
videos.w: A perennial HN favorite whenever firmware, disks, ECC or opaque hardware come up, valued as both entertaining and sobering.
videos.q: As with all his talks, you can expect it to be quite entertaining as well as informative

videos.t: "Two incompatible sacred values in American universities" Jon Haidt, Hayek Lecture Series
videos.c: Duke University Department of Political Science
videos.s: Jonathan Haidt's Hayek Lecture at Duke argues American universities pursue two potentially incompatible sacred values, truth and social justice. He discusses campus conflict, honor, dignity and victimhood cultures, and viewpoint diversity.
videos.w: HN cites it heavily in diversity and academia debates as an intellectual analysis of the truth versus social justice conflict.
videos.q: This is the best intellectual analysis of the situation I've come across so far

videos.t: Founder School Session: The Future Doesn't Have to Be Incremental
videos.s: Alan Kay speaks at the DEMO Founder School session on why real progress takes invention rather than incremental innovation. He argues for problem-oriented thinking and long-term research funding.
videos.w: HN commenters treat it as a thought-provoking talk on invention versus innovation, and cite it in discussions of software complexity and startups.
videos.q: probably the most insightful and though-provoking technology talk I have ever seen

videos.t: Simulating an epidemic
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown builds toy SIR models to simulate how an epidemic spreads and tests scenarios like social distancing, travel restrictions, central gathering places and quarantine. It was made during the early COVID-19 outbreak.
videos.w: HN pointed to it during 2020 as a digestible, well-made illustration of epidemic dynamics and interventions.
videos.q: 3blue1brown's video on the topic is super digestible and informative [1].

videos.t: The Secret History of Silicon Valley
videos.s: Steve Blank tells how World War II, Stanford's Frederick Terman and military and intelligence agencies shaped the rise of Silicon Valley. The talk centers on the Cold War electronic warfare and signals intelligence work that seeded the region's tech industry.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an eye-opening, once-secret history of where Silicon Valley came from, and cites it whenever the military roots of tech come up.
videos.q: This is an eye opening perspective on some history "hidden in plain sight" of the origins of Silicon Valley.

videos.t: Margin Call (2011) - Senior Partners Emergency Meeting [HD 1080p] (Re-Upload / Audio Fixed)
videos.s: A clip from the 2011 film Margin Call in which senior partners hold an emergency meeting and decide to sell off toxic assets immediately. It is set at the start of the 2008 financial crisis.
videos.w: HN cites the scene as a model of clear, decisive communication and of leaders acting fast to survive, and recommends the film as the best take on 2008.
videos.q: There is a very fine example of this in cinema

videos.t: Advanced Topics in Programming Languages: A Lock-Free Hash Table
videos.s: A 2007 Google Tech Talk in which Cliff Click of Azul Systems presents a lock-free concurrent hash table that scales to 768 CPUs. He explains why it is correct by reasoning in a different way than usual happens-before and memory-order arguments.
videos.w: HN regards it as one of the best technical talks, a deep and clear walkthrough of scalable lock-free hash tables built on compare-and-swap.
videos.q: I highly recommend this talk by Cliff Click about building highly scalable hash tables via Compare And Swap

videos.t: Youtube duet: Miles Davis improvising on LCD Soundsystem
videos.s: A mashup that plays a Miles Davis improvisation video alongside an LCD Soundsystem clip with no editing, so the two seem to perform together. It also became known for an affectionate mouse cursor moving along.
videos.w: Commenters repeatedly call it a favorite and a mind-blowing introduction to jazz.
videos.q: which served as one of my most memorable early introductions to jazz

videos.t: Interactive notebooks ~ Pluto.jl | Fons van der Plas | JuliaCon 2020
videos.s: Fons van der Plas introduces Pluto.jl, a reactive notebook for Julia that tracks references between cells and re-runs affected cells when code changes. The talk was given at JuliaCon 2020.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an enthusiastic demo of spreadsheet-like reactive notebooks, which commenters think new notebook projects should copy.
videos.q: I think every new notebook project should take ideas from Julia's Pluto

videos.t: Traffic Has a Perfect Solution. Humans Are the Problem.
videos.s: CGP Grey explains how traffic jams come from human driving behavior such as tailgating and reaction delays, and how leaving gaps and smoothing speed would reduce congestion. It also touches on self-driving cars.
videos.w: HN cites it as a concise, well-illustrated explanation of traffic flow, in threads on congestion, self-driving cars and driving habits.
videos.q: CGP Grey did a really nice, concise video on the topic of traffic

videos.t: Object-Oriented Programming is Embarrassing: 4 Short Examples
videos.s: Brian Will follows up his earlier anti-OOP video by walking through four short code examples, including Java code in the style of Uncle Bob, to show how object-oriented design complicates simple programs. It argues that OOP hides and scatters state and adds needless indirection.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a sharp, example-driven critique of OOP and Clean Code style, often alongside Brian Will's other anti-OO videos.
videos.q: I highly recommend "Object Oriented Programming is Bad" and "Object Oriented Programming is Embarrassing" on Youtube.

videos.t: Bret Weinstein on "The Portal" (w/ host Eric Weinstein), Ep. #019 - The Prediction and the DISC.
videos.s: A long Portal podcast episode in which Bret Weinstein tells Eric Weinstein the story of his lab mice telomere work, the prediction behind it, and what it means for science and aging.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the full account of the lab mice issue and evolutionary tradeoffs between cancer and longevity, despite its length.
videos.q: an evolutionary biologist goes into depth about telomeres, evolution and how cancer and longevity are two sides of the same coin

videos.t: Introduction to Node.js with Ryan Dahl
videos.s: Ryan Dahl, the creator of Node.js, introduces the event-driven I/O framework built on V8 with examples, and discusses the v0.4.0 release and its new APIs.
videos.w: Recommended as a short, fun talk on Node's philosophy and the reasons it was built that remains relevant.
videos.q: it's not really outdated. It's a short talk, but it talks a little about Node's philosophy and I highly recommend watching it.

videos.t: You Suck at Excel - Joel Spolsky (Reupload)
videos.s: A reupload of Joel Spolsky's talk teaching spreadsheet users the Excel features they are probably missing, such as keyboard navigation, named ranges, tables and lookups. The original disappeared and this copy comes from the Wayback Machine.
videos.w: HN commenters call it an internet classic that makes you a more proficient Excel user, and note it is still relevant despite predating newer functions like XLOOKUP.
videos.q: will turn you into a more proficient user of Excel.

videos.t: England: South Sea Bubble - The Sharp Mind of John Blunt - Extra History - Part 1
videos.s: The first part of Extra History's animated miniseries on the South Sea Bubble. It explains how England's government debt led Robert Harley to turn to financier John Blunt, whose schemes began inflating artificial demand for shares.
videos.w: Recommended as an accessible, easily digestible introduction to the South Sea Bubble whenever financial manias, ICOs or overvalued companies come up.
videos.q: For those who want an accessible introduction to the South Sea Bubble, Extra History has a video series

videos.t: Michael Stonebraker | Big Data is (at least) Four Different Problems
videos.s: Database pioneer Michael Stonebraker argues that 'big data' is really at least four different problems: big volumes with small analytics, big analytics, velocity, and variety. He comments on where each market is heading.
videos.w: HN points to it as a thoughtful, first-principles take from a Turing award winner that cuts through NoSQL and big data hype.
videos.q: a rather interesting talk by a very thoughtful Turing award winning engineer named Michael Stonebraker

videos.t: string theory lied to us and now science communication is hard
videos.s: Physicist Angela Collier's roughly hour-long video on how string theory was hyped to the public and what that did to science communication. She traces the history of the theory as a narrative and argues it is interesting but was oversold.
videos.w: Recommended as an engaging critique of string theory hype and its effect on public trust in physics, and often cited alongside Peter Woit's writing.
videos.q: while the video is nearly an hour long, it feels much shorter and is well worth watching

videos.t: Is olive oil safe at high heat? Does it taste bad?
videos.s: Adam Ragusea examines whether olive oil is unsafe for high-heat cooking and whether it tastes bad when heated. He cites studies showing it is among the most stable cooking oils and that smoke-point worries are overblown.
videos.w: HN points to it to debunk the stubborn olive-oil-at-high-heat myth, valued for its cited sources and food scientist interviews.
videos.q: Adam Ragusea did a great video on the topic, with cited sources. I highly recommend watching it

videos.t: Propaganda Games: Sesame Credit - The True Danger of Gamification - Extra Credits
videos.s: An Extra Credits episode on China's Sesame Credit, which gamifies obedient citizenship through a social score. It covers how the system rewards conformity and pressures people through their friends' behavior.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as a short, accessible primer on social credit and surveillance-driven gamification, linking it in many privacy and China threads.
videos.q: It's 7.5 minutes long, and well worth the watch

videos.t: Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned — Kenneth Stanley
videos.s: A long Machine Learning Street Talk interview with Kenneth Stanley, creator of NEAT and novelty search, about his book on why greatness cannot be planned. They discuss open-endedness, the tyranny of objectives, serendipity and the evolution of ideas.
videos.w: Recommended to people who find it inspiring or perspective-changing on pursuing goals, open-ended search and AI beyond optimization.
videos.q: It really changed my perspective on achieving my long term goals

videos.t: "Shen: A Sufficiently Advanced Lisp" by Aditya Siram
videos.s: Aditya Siram introduces Shen, a small hosted Lisp with macros, a built-in Prolog and an optional type system. The talk demos a full web app moving between functional, logic and imperative styles, including turning JSON into a type with macros.
videos.w: It is the standard recommended introduction to Shen, pointed to whenever Shen or its type system comes up.
videos.q: @deech's talks, though older now, are fantastic and relevant[1,2].

videos.t: We WILL Fix Climate Change!
videos.s: Kurzgesagt's animated take on climate change argues that, despite alarming headlines, there are real reasons for hope as technology, policy and public attitudes shift. It surveys trends and solutions while acknowledging the scale of the problem.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an articulate, uplifting counterweight to climate doomerism, though one critic calls it a form of denialism and another notes it omits nuclear.
videos.q: I highly recommend this video from the wonderful Kurzgesagt science video series

videos.t: Why Trains Suck in America
videos.s: Wendover Productions explains why US passenger rail lags behind other countries. It covers freight companies owning most of the track, geography and population density, and the economics of competing with flying.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a short, solid walkthrough of why American trains are slow and limited, most notably because freight gets priority.
videos.q: This is worth your 8 minutes of time.

videos.t: Lecture 01 - The Learning Problem
videos.s: The first lecture of Caltech's CS 156 Machine Learning course by Yaser Abu-Mostafa, introducing the learning problem and supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. It is one of 18 lectures in the Learning from Data course.
videos.w: Recommended repeatedly in 'where do I start with ML' threads as a clear, math-aware introduction.
videos.q: I have found the Caltech machine learning intro course to be the most elucidating of any resource so far

videos.t: Bitcoin 2012 London: Mike Hearn
videos.s: Mike Hearn's talk at the 2012 London Bitcoin Conference on the future of Bitcoin, new applications and rebuilding the banking system. He covers lesser-known protocol features such as contracts, escrow and scripting.
videos.w: Recommended as a great overview of what Bitcoin's protocol can do beyond simple payments, particularly contracts and smart property.
videos.q: Mike Hearn's talk at Bitcoin 2012 is a great overview of all that

videos.t: The Collapse of The American Dream Explained in Animation
videos.s: A 30-minute animated film explaining how money, banking and the Federal Reserve work and arguing that the American economy is heading for collapse. It is opinionated and has a strong point of view.
videos.w: Recommended as an accessible animated primer on banking and the Fed, usually with the caveat that it is biased and dated.
videos.q: There's this amazing animated movie from 2011 that explains how banking works and the history of banks

videos.t: The man who almost faked his way to a Nobel Prize
videos.s: BobbyBroccoli's first of three parts on Jan Hendrik Schon, the Bell Labs postdoc whose fabricated organic semiconductor results nearly won a Nobel Prize. It covers his rise and the context around Bell Labs.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends the series as a gripping account of scientific fraud, and cites it whenever research misconduct comes up.
videos.q: amazing piece of documentary

videos.t: CppCon 2017: Carl Cook “When a Microsecond Is an Eternity: High Performance Trading Systems in C++”
videos.s: Optiver's Carl Cook explains how to build high-frequency trading systems in C++, where the critical path runs rarely but must be extremely fast. He covers techniques for low and predictable latency, including avoiding main memory and cache misses.
videos.w: HN repeatedly points people to it as the best overview of low-latency trading engineering.
videos.q: Here are some talks that will give you a small overview into that world

videos.t: ElixirConf 2018 - Docker and OTP Friends or Foes - Daniel Azuma
videos.s: Daniel Azuma's ElixirConf 2018 talk on whether Docker and OTP conflict. He shows they can coexist and uses Horde and DeltaCrdt, with a live tank-game demo, to keep state alive across container kills.
videos.w: Recommended for its practical strategy for preserving state on ephemeral containers, and for the live demo.
videos.q: I would recommend watching Dan Azuma's fantastic video (stick around for the live demo)

videos.t: Arithmetic, Population and Energy -  a talk by Al Bartlett
videos.s: Physicist Al Bartlett's well-known lecture on the arithmetic of exponential growth, applied to population, energy consumption and resource depletion. He argues that steady percentage growth cannot be sustained on a finite planet and that most public discussion ignores this.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as a mind-changing introduction to exponential growth, though some note his peak oil predictions did not pan out.
videos.q: have totally changed the way I look at all political discourse

videos.t: Steve Jobs, "Computers are like  a bicycle for our minds." - Michael Lawrence Films
videos.s: A short clip of Steve Jobs describing the computer as a bicycle for the mind. He compares human efficiency of travel to what computers do for mental work.
videos.w: HN uses it as the source of the 'bicycle for the mind' quote, which commenters cite in discussions of computing, programming and LLMs.
videos.p: computers as tools for the mind
videos.q: Immediately made me think of Steve Jobs and this great clip

videos.t: James Baldwin Debates William F. Buckley (1965)
videos.s: The 1965 Cambridge Union debate between James Baldwin and William F. Buckley Jr. on whether the American Dream comes at the expense of the American Negro. It is a historic recording of the two speaking.
videos.w: Recommended for Baldwin's riveting delivery and as an example of serious debate between opposing worldviews.
videos.q: I was watching James Baldwin's speech at Cambridge University the other day and was riveted the entire time

videos.t: Canceling | ContraPoints
videos.s: A long video essay by Natalie Wynn of ContraPoints on cancel culture, drawing on her own experience of being pile-on targeted by other leftists. It is theatrical and discursive, mixing argument with performance.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a more thoughtful, balanced and personal take on cancel culture than usual discussion.
videos.q: I think that it’s useful to hear a balanced take on cancel culture

videos.t: Emacs Org-mode - a system for note-taking and project planning
videos.s: A 2008 Google Tech Talk by the creator of Org-mode, introducing the Emacs subsystem for plain-text note-taking and project planning. It covers outlines, TODO states, tags, dates and priorities, and later shows using Org-mode as a spreadsheet.
videos.w: HN regards it as the best introduction and advertisement for Org-mode, and many say it was enough to get them started with it.
videos.q: The best advertisement for org-mode I've seen is this long Google Tech Talk

videos.t: Alan Kay at OOPSLA 1997 - The computer revolution hasnt happened yet
videos.s: Alan Kay's 1997 OOPSLA keynote, preserved on YouTube after being lost from Google Video. He discusses what object orientation was meant to be, messaging, system design, and the state of computing practice.
videos.w: Treated as a foundational talk, cited constantly for Kay's views on object-oriented programming and for rethinking software practice.
videos.q: I encourage all developers to watch that talk and do some thinking about the current state of our practice

videos.t: Kurt Vonnegut on the Shapes of Stories
videos.s: A short lecture in which Kurt Vonnegut graphs the simple shapes of stories, such as Man in Hole and Boy Gets Girl. He sketches how fortune rises and falls over a narrative.
videos.w: HN cites it as a charming, funny way to see story structure and a source for the idea that plots have shapes.
videos.q: Vonnegut is really special. I always like coming back to his Shape of Stories talks

videos.t: Randy Pausch Lecture: Time Management
videos.s: Carnegie Mellon professor Randy Pausch gives a lecture on time management at the University of Virginia in 2007. He covers practical habits such as tackling important tasks first and distinguishing important from urgent work.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a practical, memorable guide to prioritization, and some rewatch it every year.
videos.q: So much so that I rewatch it about once a year

videos.t: Cracking Ancient Codes: Cuneiform Writing - with Irving Finkel
videos.s: Irving Finkel of the British Museum lectures at the Royal Institution on the invention and decipherment of cuneiform writing in Mesopotamia, and why it is so hard to translate.
videos.w: HN users recommend it as a delightful, well-told account of how cuneiform developed and was decoded.
videos.q: Highly recommend Prof Irving Fink's talk to Royal Institution on the 3,000 year development of cuneiform

videos.t: Pig Butchering Scams: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: A Last Week Tonight segment on pig butchering scams, in which long-con romance and investment fraud is run, often by trafficked workers. It explains how victims are groomed and interviews people who lost large sums.
videos.w: Offered as an accessible, well-made explainer to share in threads on scam texts, crypto fraud and scam compounds.
videos.q: John Oliver did an excellent explainer about how pig butchering works.

videos.t: The Evolution of Bacteria on a “Mega-Plate” Petri Dish (Kishony Lab)
videos.s: A two-minute time-lapse from the Kishony Lab showing bacteria spreading across a giant petri dish with increasing antibiotic doses, evolving resistance as they go.
videos.w: HN links it as a visually striking demonstration of evolution and antibiotic resistance happening in days.
videos.q: the mega-plate video is an unbelievably good demonstration of bacterial evolution

videos.t: GigCityElixir23 - Bryan Hunter
videos.s: Bryan Hunter's GigCityElixir 2023 talk on HCA Healthcare's Waterpark system, built on Elixir/Erlang. It describes how the architecture is distributed and fault-tolerant, with a multi-datacenter cluster and runtime code swapping.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a rare real-world look at a large fault-tolerant Erlang/Elixir system with no downtime in healthcare.
videos.q: an excellent presentation of design/architecture of a Real-World fault-tolerant and distributed System in Erlang/Elixir

videos.t: The 919 Tribute Tour: On-board record lap, Nordschleife.
videos.s: Onboard footage of Timo Bernhard driving the Porsche 919 Hybrid Evo to an all-time Nurburgring Nordschleife record lap of 5:19.
videos.w: HN cites it as the benchmark lap record and recommends it even to non-car fans for its sheer speed and precision.
videos.q: If anyone hasn't seen this, I highly recommend it, even if you're not a car fan.

videos.t: Patrick Stewart interview - Parkinson - BBC
videos.s: Patrick Stewart on the BBC's Parkinson talk show talks humorously about going bald, how it affected his career and relationships, and how he came to accept it.
videos.w: HN recommends it in hair-loss threads as a funny, inspiring example of accepting baldness.
videos.q: Patrick Stewart has this awesome interview about his baldness.

videos.t: Bret Weinstein and Yuri Deigin: Did Covid-19 leak From a Lab?
videos.s: Bret Weinstein and Yuri Deigin discuss the evidence for the hypothesis that SARS-CoV-2 leaked from a lab, including the furin cleavage site and gain-of-function research. The conversation draws on Deigin's Medium article.
videos.w: HN commenters shared it in 2020 and 2021 as an early, in-depth presentation of the lab-leak case, though it is a contested viewpoint.
videos.q: he had a very interesting conversation with a russian virologist who also thinks this is the case

videos.t: Explained: New Navy UFO Videos
videos.s: Mick West explains the three Navy UFO videos (FLIR, GIMBAL and GOFAST) released in 2020, giving mundane explanations such as a distant plane and camera artifacts. He notes the videos were not new and had been circulating since 2017.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a calm, evidence-based debunking whenever the Navy UFO videos come up.
videos.q: Mick West has some great videos on it

videos.t: Alexander Pope Wrote a 35-Page Takedown of a Historian
videos.s: CGP Grey tells the story of Alexander Pope's long takedown of a historian, Thomas Hearne, framed around the quirks of library books and archival research. It is a funny, digressive video essay about literary feuds and tracking down original sources.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a masterpiece of humorous archival detective work and a great watch about books and libraries.
videos.q: Linking the full video because it's a masterpiece

videos.t: "I See What You Mean" by Peter Alvaro
videos.s: Peter Alvaro's Strange Loop 2015 talk argues that query languages let you state what you mean, and applies that to distributed programming. It covers Datalog, Dedalus and the Bloom lineage for reasoning about distributed systems.
videos.w: Recommended as a fantastic introduction to declarative and Datalog-based distributed systems and failure modeling.
videos.q: I highly recommend watching Peter Alvaro’s Strangeloop talk about creating Dedalus

videos.t: ORCA Sequencer Intro (Experimental Livecoding!)
videos.s: Allieway Audio gives an informal introduction and live-coding demo of ORCA, a free esoteric programming environment for building procedural sequencers from Hundred Rabbits. It walks through the interface and how to make music with it.
videos.w: HN commenters call it the best video overview of Orca, the explanation that makes the unusual interface click.
videos.q: It is by far the best video overview of the system that I am aware of.

videos.t: But what is the Riemann zeta function? Visualizing analytic continuation
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown visualizes the Riemann zeta function and the analytic continuation that extends it beyond where its series converges, building toward the Riemann hypothesis.
videos.w: HN praises its visualizations, its handling of the -1/12 result, and its ending, and often prefers it to other explanations of the topic.
videos.q: I don't think it comes close to 3blue1brown's video on the same topic -

videos.t: The REAL Reason McDonalds Ice Cream Machines Are Always Broken
videos.s: Johnny Harris investigates why McDonald's ice cream machines are so often broken, covering the Taylor machines, the repair restrictions on franchisees and the Kytch workaround device.
videos.w: HN links it in right-to-repair and McFlurry-machine threads as the go-to in-depth explainer of the franchisee and Taylor arrangement.
videos.p: right to repair and mcdonalds ice cream machines
videos.q: This video did a good indepth investigation.

videos.t: The Spectacular Failure of the Star Wars Hotel
videos.s: Jenny Nicholson's roughly four-hour review of her two-night stay on Disney's Star Wars Galactic Starcruiser immersive hotel. She goes through the experience, its story and production, and why it failed.
videos.w: HN people strongly recommend it as the best overview of the Galactic Starcruiser and a case study in misaligned incentives and poor guest experience, engaging despite its length.
videos.q: here's as an incredible documentary covering the misaligned incentives and poor guest experience at the now-shuttered Disney Star Wars hotel.

videos.t: Netscape Mozilla Documentary 1998 - 2000 ProJect Code Rush  - creative common licence
videos.s: Code Rush is a 2000 PBS documentary following Netscape engineers during the year they open-sourced the browser as Mozilla. It shows the pressure and long hours of work in Silicon Valley at the height of the dot-com era.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a great tech documentary on Mozilla's open-sourcing and the hard work of Netscape engineers.
videos.q: Code Rush is a great SV tech documentary about the initial release of Mozilla

videos.t: Distributed Systems 1.1: Introduction
videos.s: The first lecture in Martin Kleppmann's 8-lecture distributed systems series from the University of Cambridge undergraduate course. It introduces the subject, and accompanying lecture notes are available.
videos.w: HN regularly recommends the series as a free, accessible, theory-oriented course on distributed computing that complements his book Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
videos.q: the distributed system audio course on youtube is extremely accessible

videos.t: Stanford Seminar - The Soul of a New Machine: Rethinking the Computer
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill of Oxide Computer Company gives a Stanford EE380 talk on rethinking the server. He argues that hyperscaler-style rack-scale machines with open firmware, RISC-V and Rust should be available to everyone, not just the giants.
videos.w: HN points to it as the founders' own explanation of what Oxide is building and why, a frequent link whenever Oxide comes up.
videos.q: The talk lays out a history of servers, describes the problems with the servers that you can buy from vendors today

videos.t: "Outperforming Imperative with Pure Functional Languages" by Richard Feldman
videos.s: Richard Feldman explains how pure functional languages can match or beat imperative ones on performance. Compilers can turn immutable code into in-place mutation, avoiding naive copying. The talk draws on his work on the Roc language.
videos.w: Recommended as the clearest explanation of why immutable data need not be slow, and as the introduction to Roc.
videos.q: As a starting point for those nitty grittys, this talk is probably as good as any

videos.t: World Building in Blender - Ian Hubert
videos.s: Ian Hubert's Blender Conference talk on world building in Blender, covering photogrammetry, camera projection and assembling complex environments from simple shapes at great speed.
videos.w: HN considers it a fantastic, mind-blowing talk that shows how a single skilled artist can build detailed VFX scenes quickly.

videos.t: The Caretaker - Everywhere At The End Of Time - Stages 1-6 (Complete)
videos.s: The complete six-stage album series Everywhere at the End of Time by The Caretaker, about 6.5 hours of music that depicts the progression of dementia through distorted, decaying old ballroom recordings.
videos.w: HN recommends it, often emotionally, as an auditory depiction of memory loss, in threads about dementia and aging.
videos.q: It's haunting and beautiful and quite memorable.

videos.t: Why Electric Bikes are More Dangerous than Motorcycles
videos.s: FortNine argues that e-bikes have injury rates and speeds closer to motorcycles than to pedal bikes. It argues riders should treat them with similar safety gear and caution.
videos.w: Cited repeatedly in e-bike threads as a well-argued safety counterpoint from someone who rides both.
videos.q: Fortnine made an excellent argument against the safety of ebikes, worth watching as a rebuttal to this article

videos.t: Tom Scott vs Irving Finkel: The Royal Game of Ur | PLAYTHROUGH | International Tabletop Day 2017
videos.s: Tom Scott plays the Royal Game of Ur against British Museum curator Irving Finkel, who deciphered its rules from a cuneiform tablet. Finkel teaches the game and explains its history as the oldest playable board game.
videos.w: Recommended in threads on ancient games and cuneiform as a charming match with an enthusiastic expert.
videos.q: he also did a fantastic video on with Tom Scott

videos.t: The Roots of Your Profits - Dr Elaine Ingham, Soil Microbiologist, Founder of Soil Foodweb Inc
videos.s: Soil microbiologist Elaine Ingham speaks at the Oxford Real Farming Conference on how soil organisms cycle nutrients, unlock minerals from rock and air, and why pesticides and fertilizers harm soil life. Slides are linked in the description.
videos.w: HN commenters cite her as the explanation for why soil biology, not added fertilizer, drives plant nutrition and farm results.
videos.q: Dr Elaine Ingham delivers a salient presentation.

videos.t: Government Surveillance: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver interviews Edward Snowden about NSA surveillance, including street interviews showing people have not thought about what the government can see. The segment famously frames the issue through private photos.
videos.w: HN points to it as the best way to explain to ordinary people why privacy and mass surveillance matter.
videos.q: I believe John Oliver provided the best example when he interviewed Edward Snowden.

videos.t: What does it feel like to invent math?
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown explores infinite sums from convergent to divergent, with an introduction to the 2-adic metric, themed on the cycle between discovering and inventing mathematics.
videos.w: Recommended as a favorite Grant Sanderson video and a visual introduction to p-adic numbers and sums like 1+2+4+...
videos.q: Great intro

videos.t: How Bankrupt American Cities Stay Alive - Debt [ST04]
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains how many American suburbs, built all at once rather than incrementally, cannot cover their infrastructure costs and survive on growing debt. It draws on Strong Towns' work on the growth Ponzi scheme.
videos.w: Recommended as an introduction to the finances of suburban sprawl and its long-term consequences.
videos.q: I highly recommend this video on the finances around urban sprawl and their long term consequences

videos.t: How I Designed a Free Music Font for 5 Million Musicians (MuseScore 3.6)
videos.s: Tantacrul explains how he and engraver Simon Smith designed the free music notation font for MuseScore 3.6. It draws on the history of the SCORE notation application by Leland Smith.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining look at how hard notation fonts are to make, and it comes up in threads on music engraving and open source.
videos.q: He does a good job at making the topic of music notation come to life

videos.t: Milton Friedman - The Negative Income Tax
videos.s: A 1968 Firing Line interview in which Milton Friedman explains the negative income tax, a proposal to replace welfare bureaucracy with direct payments.
videos.w: The go-to primary source in basic income threads for Friedman's negative income tax idea.
videos.q: here's a nice intro

videos.t: Evo-Devo (Despacito Biology Parody) | A Capella Science
videos.s: A Capella Science parody of Despacito that sings through evolutionary developmental biology, explaining how a single cell becomes a body, including body-axis genes and dormant snake leg DNA. It runs about four minutes.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining four-minute introduction to evo-devo that works even for people who dislike the original song.
videos.q: A TL;DR in four minutes by A Capella Science

videos.t: The Agricultural Revolution: Crash Course World History #1
videos.s: The first episode of Crash Course World History, in which John Green covers the shift from hunting and gathering to agriculture and how it shaped civilization. It is delivered fast and with jokes.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as a funny, coherent high-school-level overview of world history that teaches a lot in a few hours.
videos.q: This series taught me in a few hours what I didn't learn in school over years

videos.t: Mouse Cursor History (and why I made my own)
videos.s: Posy gives a short history of the computer mouse cursor, from early straight pointers to the tilted arrow, comparing Apple and Windows designs. He then explains why he designed his own cursor set and offers it as a free download.
videos.w: HN treats it as the definitive, short, well-made video on mouse cursors and pulls it out whenever cursor design, pixel perfection or the tilted arrow comes up.
videos.q: It is one of those amazing videos that make the internet worthwhile, is short

videos.t: RailsConf 09:  Robert Martin, "What Killed Smalltalk Could K
videos.s: Robert Martin's RailsConf 2009 talk looks at why Smalltalk lost out despite its technical strengths. He draws lessons about language communities and arrogance that he argues could hurt Ruby too.
videos.w: HN cites it in discussions of language evangelism, community dynamics and zealotry, as an accessible account of how a good language can die for non-technical reasons.
videos.q: I find this talk [0] very informative and useful while interacting with other languages and communities.

videos.t: P vs. NP and the Computational Complexity Zoo
videos.s: An 11-minute animated introduction to P vs. NP and the wider landscape of complexity classes, inspired by the Complexity Zoo wiki. It assumes no background in computer science.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the best short, funny introduction to P vs. NP and complexity classes for people with no background.
videos.q: This 10 minute video is a great introduction to the P = NP problem and computational complexity theory if you have no context.

videos.t: Why don't Americans use electric kettles?
videos.s: Technology Connections explains why electric kettles are uncommon in the US, centering on 120V circuits limiting power. He tests ways of boiling water on gas, electric ranges and kettles.
videos.w: HN cites it constantly in threads on voltage, gas stoves and boiling water as the definitive measured comparison, with the kettle coming out fastest and most efficient.
videos.q: Technology Connections on YouTube has a good video about how electric kettles are the superior way to boil water

videos.t: Leslie Lamport: Thinking Above the Code
videos.s: Leslie Lamport argues that programmers, like architects, should write rigorous specifications before coding, especially for concurrent and distributed systems. The talk introduces the case for writing specs (the TLA+ mindset) as a way of thinking above the code.
videos.w: HN points people to it as Lamport's own case for thinking and writing a spec before coding, and as an entry point to TLA+.
videos.q: He's just saying that you should think before you code and that most specifications should be just a few sentences stating what you intend to do.

videos.t: Feeding Bill Gates a Fake Burger (to save the world)
videos.s: Mark Rober makes a plant-based burger for Bill Gates and explains why meat production strains the environment. Gates also appears and discusses his worry about steel and cement.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as a short, accessible overview of the climate and water case for plant-based meat.
videos.q: This video from Mark Rober was eye opening for me.

videos.t: EPC2018 | Wave Function Collapse in Bad North | Oskar Stalberg
videos.s: Oskar Stalberg explains how Wave Function Collapse assembles island dioramas from handcrafted tilesets in Bad North. He covers the theory, implementation, tooling, and how he blends art and technology.
videos.w: The go-to talk whenever Wave Function Collapse, Townscaper or tile-based procedural generation comes up.
videos.q: has some great talks on YouTube about how the systems in Bad North and Townscaper work.

videos.t: Pure Functional Programming in Excel • Felienne Hermans • GOTO 2016
videos.s: Felienne Hermans argues that Excel is the world's most popular programming language and shows how spreadsheets work as a pure functional language. She implements a few mathematical problems in spreadsheet formulas to illustrate why they are so powerful and approachable.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it whenever Excel, spreadsheets or functional programming come up, as a fun and serious take on spreadsheets as real programming.
videos.q: Felienne has a great talk on functional programming in Excel

videos.t: Zach Tellman - Everything Will Flow
videos.s: Zach Tellman's Clojure West talk covers the basics of queueing theory and its practical use in systems, including backpressure, how queues break down under load, and pitfalls of naive core.async use.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a fascinating explanation of queues, flow control and overload that applies well beyond Clojure.
videos.q: He talks about queues and how they break down under load.

videos.t: Scale By The Bay 2018: Bryan Cantrill, Rust and Other Interesting Things
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill argues that programming languages and platforms reflect core values, and compares languages through that lens, with Rust as a main example. He draws on his experience with Solaris, DTrace and ZFS.
videos.w: Cited again and again as the framework for discussing languages in terms of values, and how organizational values shape software quality.
videos.q: Bryan Cantrill has an excellent talk on this

videos.t: Heat Pumps are Not Hard: Here's what it will take to start pumping
videos.s: Technology Connections' long closing video in his heat pump series, arguing that adopting heat pumps is well within reach. It explains how they work and what it takes to start using them.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as an enthusiastic, entertaining deep dive into residential heat pumps whenever heating or climate threads arise.
videos.q: If you want an (entertaining) deep dive into heat pumps, I can recommend Technology Connection's

videos.t: Opioids: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: A Last Week Tonight segment on the US opioid epidemic, tracing how prescription painkillers fed addiction and heroin use. It is the first of three episodes the show devoted to the crisis.
videos.w: HN points to it as an informative, fact-heavy overview of the opioid crisis and Purdue Pharma.
videos.q: he managed to compile an impressive amount of testimonials and facts.

videos.t: MyHouse.WAD - Inside Doom's Most Terrifying Mod
videos.s: A long video essay on MyHouse.wad, a Doom II mod uploaded by an anonymous user that hides unsettling secrets in its walls. It tells the story of the map, its mystery and its liminal horror.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a gripping story and art piece worth watching even if you do not care about games.
videos.q: Just click the link and watch. One of my favorite YouTube rides of all time.

videos.t: Mike Monteiro - "Fuck you pay me" (PT Br)
videos.s: Mike Monteiro's Creative Mornings talk "Fuck You, Pay Me" with his lawyer Keith Levine, on contracts, scope creep and making sure designers and freelancers get paid. This copy has Portuguese subtitles.
videos.w: Recommended to freelancers and consultants as practical advice on contracts and getting paid.
videos.q: 1 of my favorite videos on the internet about this is [1].

videos.t: Tomorrow Corporation Tech Demo
videos.s: Allan Blomquist demonstrates the internal programming and debugging tools Tomorrow Corporation uses to make games, including live modification of a running game and time-travel debugging.
videos.w: Held up in debugger and tooling threads as an amazing ideal of a tight feedback loop and what debugging could be.
videos.q: this demo has got to be the closest thing to the perfect debugger I've ever seen

videos.t: Connecting Solar to the Grid is Harder Than You Think
videos.s: Practical Engineering explains why connecting solar and other inverter-based generation to the grid is hard. It covers grid stability, load balancing and the behind-the-scenes engineering challenges of renewables.
videos.w: HN people link it as the go-to explainer for grid and inverter stability, especially in threads about blackouts and distributed solar.
videos.q: Just watch this Practical Engineering video [1], if you are not familiar with the topic.

videos.t: Do Nothing- a message of motivation from Self-help Singh- (un) motivational speaker and life coach
videos.s: A short satirical 'motivational' talk by the character Self-help Singh, a sham life coach who urges viewers to do nothing. It parodies self-help gurus and hustle culture.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as funny anti-motivational comedy that also touches on real truths about productivity and the rat race.
videos.q: While it's meant to be funny, it actually touches some deeper philosophical truths.

videos.t: The Web That Never Was - Dylan Beattie
videos.s: Dylan Beattie's entertaining NDC talk imagines an alternate history of the web, asking what if different decisions had been made on operating systems, browsers and standards. It blends real history with humor.
videos.w: HN commenters strongly recommend it as a fun alt-history of the web and bring it up whenever people muse about how the web could have been different.
videos.q: Edit 2: finished, it is definitely worth watching.

videos.t: How lucky is too lucky?: The Minecraft Speedrunning Dream Controversy Explained
videos.s: Matt Parker analyzes the Minecraft speedrunning controversy in which Dream was accused of cheating via improbably lucky drops. He walks through the probability and the statistical arguments in the original accusation and the reply.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an engaging lesson in probability and in how statistics can expose cheating.
videos.q: It not only exposes the cheater, it also gives some intuition into negligible probabilities.

videos.t: Christopher Alexander - Patterns in Architecture
videos.s: Christopher Alexander's keynote at OOPSLA 1996 on patterns in architecture, addressed to the software community. He moves beyond patterns toward deeper ideas of wholeness and living structure.
videos.w: HN cites it as the primary source for the claim that Alexander deprecated patterns, and as a prescient talk for programmers.
videos.q: Just finished watching a great 1996 lecture by Christopher Alexander

videos.t: Admiral Grace Hopper Explains the Nanosecond
videos.s: Admiral Grace Hopper holds up a length of wire to show how far light travels in a nanosecond, about 11.8 inches. She explains how she made the idea concrete to people who could not picture a billionth of a second.
videos.w: HN uses it to illustrate physical latency limits and why performance and distance matter in computing.
videos.p: latency and the speed of light
videos.q: Admiral Grace Hopper Explains the Nanosecond" is a good illustration of this (segment is only 2m)

videos.t: Disney's FastPass: A Complicated History
videos.s: A feature-length Defunctland documentary on the history of Disney's FastPass and FastPass+ expedited queue systems. It covers how the systems evolved and how they were designed, with simulation of their effects on park lines.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible, engrossing lesson in queueing theory and systems design, even for people with no interest in Disney.
videos.q: If you ever wanted a feature-length explanation of queueing theory and how ignoring it makes everything worse, well... here you go

videos.t: Jordan Peterson debate on the gender pay gap, campus protests and postmodernism
videos.s: Channel 4 News's full interview with Jordan Peterson, in which Cathy Newman presses him on the gender pay gap, patriarchy, campus protests and postmodernism. It was widely discussed for its confrontational style.
videos.w: HN cites it as the classic example of an interviewer misrepresenting a guest, though opinions on who came out better differ.
videos.q: A classic, even if you don't like the guy

videos.t: Who cares about topology?   (Old version)
videos.s: An older 3Blue1Brown video on why topology matters, built around the inscribed rectangle problem. It walks through how tori and Mobius strips appear in the solution. The channel later replaced it with an updated version.
videos.w: Fans name it as a favorite 3Blue1Brown video, praising its detective-story treatment of the inscribed square and rectangle problem.
videos.q: A particular favourite is the one on the Inscribed Square Problem

videos.t: Fasting vs. Eating Less: What's the Difference? (Science of Fasting)
videos.s: A short explainer on the physiological differences between fasting and simply eating less. It covers ketosis, ghrelin and hunger waves, and the hormonal effects of fasting.
videos.w: Shared as an accessible, convincing case for intermittent fasting and its physiology.
videos.q: provide some compelling arguments for switching to intermittent fasting for many major systemic health benefits

videos.t: Inside the Mind of a Master Procrastinator | Tim Urban | TED
videos.s: Tim Urban's TED talk on why people procrastinate, covering YouTube binges and Wikipedia rabbit holes. It ends with the life-calendar idea as a nudge to act before time runs out.
videos.w: Recommended as a funny, empathetic take on procrastination and the origin of the life calendar concept.
videos.q: absolutely legendary TedX talk that humanizes procrastination

videos.t: The Carbon Offset Problem
videos.s: Wendover Productions examines why carbon offsets so often fail to reduce emissions, covering specific examples and the perverse incentives in offset schemes.
videos.w: Recommended in greenwashing and offset threads as a well-sourced, detailed explanation of how offsets underdeliver.
videos.q: does a much better job than the article of both highlighting specific examples and laying out the perverse incentive structures

videos.t: AWS re:Invent 2016: Tuesday Night Live with James Hamilton
videos.s: James Hamilton's Tuesday Night Live keynote at AWS re:Invent 2016, touring AWS infrastructure at scale including networking, power and custom silicon. It also features NASA JPL's Tom Soderstrom.
videos.w: HN treats Hamilton's annual talks as the best window into how AWS regions and hardware are actually built.
videos.q: The keynote by James Hamilton[1] is absolutely awesome.

videos.t: How Trees Bend the Laws of Physics
videos.s: Veritasium explains how trees lift water from roots to the top of tall trunks, using transpiration pull and the negative pressure that liquid water can sustain. It explains why trees do not need pumps or valves.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as one of Veritasium's best videos and one that has aged well.
videos.q: I recommend watching, I think it's one of the best veritasium Dereck has ever produced.

videos.t: IBM Selectric Typewriter & its digital to analogue converter
videos.s: Bill Hammack of engineerguy uses slow motion video to show how the IBM Selectric typewriter works. He focuses on its fully mechanical digital-to-analog converter, which turns key presses into rotation of the type ball.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it whenever the Selectric comes up, as a short, excellent explanation of its internals.
videos.q: I highly recommend watching

videos.t: Special Topics - The Kalman Filter (1 of 55) What is a Kalman Filter?
videos.s: The first video in a 55-part series by Michel van Biezen that introduces the Kalman filter and builds from the rationale through algebraic examples to the full matrix treatment. The videos are short, blackboard-style lectures.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends this series as a clear, step-by-step way to really understand Kalman filtering.
videos.q: It's really worth watching even just the first couple videos to get a deeper understanding of this very useful technique.

videos.t: Fat Chance: Fructose 2.0
videos.s: Robert Lustig of UCSF updates his sugar talk, arguing that fructose and processed foods drive obesity and metabolic syndrome through their endocrine effects. It is a roughly 90-minute university lecture.
videos.w: Recommended as a follow-up to Lustig's original sugar talk for the metabolic details of fructose.
videos.q: I'd highly recommend these two talks by Robert Lustig on the subject.

videos.t: How to learn any language in six months | Chris Lonsdale | TEDxLingnanUniversity
videos.s: Chris Lonsdale presents a TEDx talk on how adults can learn a language in about six months, centering on immersion, comprehensible input and a practical learning methodology.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an efficient, practical approach to adult language learning, with one commenter saying it changed their life.
videos.q: this talk which actually changed my life

videos.t: Energy Investments Dialogue | Bill Gates | Global Energy Forum
videos.s: Bill Gates at Stanford's Global Energy Forum argues that cheaper solar, wind and storage are not nearly enough to stop climate change. He discusses natural gas, a carbon tax, nuclear, battery costs and the responsibilities of developing versus developed economies.
videos.w: Cited in energy threads for Gates's argument on why batteries and renewables alone fall short and nuclear is needed.
videos.q: which I highly recommend watching

videos.t: How Far Are The Nearest Stars?
videos.s: Cody's Lab builds a 200-billionth-scale model to show how far away the nearest stars are, using parallax and light speed. A short astronomy explainer on interstellar distances.
videos.w: Recommended whenever threads need an intuition for the vast distances between stars.
videos.q: maybe watch this video that illustrates the distance only to the closest star, let alone any further away

videos.t: Compost-Fueled Cars: Wouldn't That Be Great? - Onion Talks - Ep. 1
videos.s: An Onion Talks satire in which a young media professional pitches compost-powered cars, offering the idea itself and leaving all implementation to others.
videos.w: HN uses it as shorthand for vague, detail-free visionary pitches and as a satirical jab at TED-style techno-utopian talks.
videos.q: neatly summarizes so much of the breathless excitement of vague, detail-free scientific and entrepreneurial claims

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #1361 - Cmdr. David Fravor & Jeremy Corbell
videos.s: A Joe Rogan podcast with retired Navy commander David Fravor, who describes his 2004 Tic Tac UFO encounter, and filmmaker Jeremy Corbell. Fravor walks through the incident and the released videos.
videos.w: HN refers to it as the direct first-person account from the pilot in UFO and UAP threads, though some find it unconvincing.
videos.q: one of the most compelling eyewitness accounts I’ve seen

videos.t: Why do prime numbers make these spirals? | Dirichlet’s theorem and pi approximations
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown explains why plotting primes in polar coordinates produces spiral patterns, using modular arithmetic, Dirichlet's theorem and rational approximations of pi.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as the clearest explanation of prime spirals and the Ulam spiral.
videos.q: Here is one of the most enlightening explanations for these kinds of spirals I have seen by 3blue1brown

videos.t: Ted Nelson demonstrates Xanadu Space
videos.s: Ted Nelson demonstrates Xanadu Space, his software for representing hypertext in three-dimensional space with linked, referenced content fragments.
videos.w: Recommended as the shortest way to grasp Nelson's idea of referential content and how the web could have been different.
videos.q: Too many great talks to mention, but if I had to pick one it would be Ted Nelson's few minutes of demonstration of Xanadu.

videos.t: 2 1 1 Jason Scott   Rescuing The Prince of Persia from the sands of time
videos.s: Jason Scott's DerbyCon 2012 talk on rescuing the Prince of Persia source code from old floppy disks, working with the game's author Jordan Mechner. It is a story of digital archaeology and recovering data from ancient media.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended as a favorite tech talk and a great example of digital preservation work.
videos.q: My favourite example of digital archaeology from recent years

videos.t: NSA operation ORCHESTRA: Annual Status Report
videos.s: Poul-Henning Kamp's FOSDEM 2014 talk is a hypothetical account of how an intelligence agency such as the NSA would sabotage open source software, standards and online discussion. It covers Skype's history, OpenSSL and psyops against standards.
videos.w: HN returned to it repeatedly, especially after Heartbleed, as an eye-opening argument about subverting open source and standards.
videos.q: The entire talk is an eye opener.

videos.t: Collapse of Complex Societies by Dr. Joseph Tainter
videos.s: Joseph Tainter lectures at a 2010 sustainability conference on why complex societies such as Rome collapse. His thesis is that rising complexity brings diminishing returns until societies cannot afford to maintain it.
videos.w: Recommended as the best exposition of Tainter's theory, and used to explain slowing innovation, centralization and collapse risk.
videos.q: Spend some time watching Tainter's speech on complexity and collapse

videos.t: "How to teach programming (and other things)?" by Felienne Hermans
videos.s: Felienne Hermans's Strange Loop keynote on the history and pedagogy of teaching programming. She questions exploration-only approaches like Logo and discusses research supporting explicit instruction and rote practice.
videos.w: Cited in threads about teaching kids and beginners to code as research-based evidence that explicit instruction beats pure discovery.
videos.q: The talk is on YouTube and I gotta say, it's very insightful.

videos.t: Plain Text - Dylan Beattie - NDC Copenhagen 2022
videos.s: Dylan Beattie's conference talk explores the history and mess behind plain text: encodings, Unicode, line endings and the many ways text goes wrong. It argues that the tidy idea of plain text hides a lot of complexity underneath everyday software.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as an entertaining, surprisingly deep talk that comes up whenever encodings, mojibake or Unicode are discussed.
videos.q: you owe it to yourself to check out this super entertaining talk

videos.t: Particles, Fields and The Future of Physics - A Lecture by Sean Carroll
videos.s: Sean Carroll's 2013 Fermilab Users Meeting lecture on particles, fields and the future of particle physics. He explains that particles are vibrations in underlying quantum fields and touches on the Higgs, neutrinos and dark matter.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the clearest long-form explanation of the everything-is-fields view for non-physicists.
videos.q: Sean Carroll is a master of making quantum mechanics approachable to non-physicists.

videos.t: LibreSSL with Bob Beck
videos.s: Bob Beck of OpenBSD describes the first month of LibreSSL, the fork aimed at cleaning up OpenSSL, including oddities found in the code base and why it was cleaned rather than audited cryptographically.
videos.w: Frequently linked as an entertaining and alarming account of OpenSSL code quality and why the fork happened.
videos.q: The entire talk is amazing, even 7 years later.

videos.t: [JSConfUS 2013] Steven Wittens: Making WebGL Dance
videos.s: Steven Wittens' JSConf US 2013 talk on drawing with WebGL, using animated visuals to walk through vectors, matrices and the rendering pipeline. Despite the title, it works as a visual primer on the linear algebra behind 3D graphics.
videos.w: HN treats it as one of the best intros to the math of 3D graphics and a staple answer to how to learn graphics programming.
videos.q: It's a fantastic, FANTASTIC tour of 3D graphics fundamentals.

videos.t: Star Size Comparison 2
videos.s: A visual scale comparison of stars and cosmic objects, from planets up to some of the largest known stars, set to music. It is meant to convey the vastness of the universe.
videos.w: Shared as a go-to humbling look at cosmic scale, noted for its chilling audio and visuals pairing.
videos.q: The combination of audio and content of this video gives me chills.

videos.t: Constraints Liberate, Liberties Constrain — Runar Bjarnason
videos.s: Runar Bjarnason's Scala World talk argues that restraint and precision in components beat power and flexibility. Constraints on parts make them easier to compose into systems.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a talk that changes how you think about system design, and links it whenever constraints, abstraction or least power come up.
videos.q: It had a real impact on the way I think about the design of systems.

videos.t: Future Computers Will Be Radically Different (Analog Computing)
videos.s: Veritasium explains why analog computing may suit AI workloads, covering old analog computers, The Analog Thing and Mythic's analog chips that use flash memory for neural network inference. It argues digital hardware is hitting limits.
videos.w: Treated as the accessible reference on analog computing for neural nets, especially the Mythic AI segment.
videos.q: Veritasium explains it really well in general here (and demos the device)

videos.t: I Shot You First: Networking the Gameplay of Halo: Reach
videos.s: Bungie's David Aldridge explains the networking programming behind Halo: Reach in a 2011 GDC session. It covers how gameplay stays in sync online, including forecasting and state reconciliation.
videos.w: HN considers it one of the best game networking talks, with insights that carry over to distributed systems generally.
videos.q: This talk from the Halo: Reach team might be one of my favorite game networking talks I've ever seen

videos.t: Simon Sinek on Millennials in the Workplace
videos.s: An excerpt of Simon Sinek on Inside Quest discussing millennials in the workplace. He covers parenting, technology, social media dopamine and what that means for managers.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for its take on managing young employees and on how technology and approval-seeking affect behavior.
videos.q: Simon Sinek explains it perfectly

videos.t: Uppestcase and Lowestcase Letters  [advances in derp learning]
videos.s: Tom Scott-style absurdist research by tom7 for SIGBOVIK 2021, using machine learning to discover letterforms that are 'uppercaser' than uppercase A and lowercaser than lowercase. It is a comedic, technically inventive deep dive with fonts and a paper.
videos.w: Tom7 is an HN favorite, and this video is praised as hilarious, educational silly ML that keeps getting better.
videos.q: it just keeps getting better and better as the video progresses. I laughed so hard.

videos.t: College Lecture Series - Neil Postman - "The Surrender of Culture to Technology"
videos.s: Neil Postman's 1997 lecture at College of DuPage, based on his book, argues that Americans treat technology as a national religion and depend on it to solve larger human problems. It includes audience questions.
videos.w: HN recommends it to engineers as a skeptical counterweight to technology boosterism, especially for those building AI and consumer tech features.
videos.q: I suggest the people working on those features watch Neil Postman's "The Surrender of Culture to Technology"

videos.t: Cliff Click @ VMSS16: Bits of Advice For the VM Writer
videos.s: Cliff Click, author of HotSpot's JIT compiler, shares hard-won advice for people writing virtual machines at the VMSS16 workshop. Topics include interpreters, JITs and performance lessons.
videos.w: HN recommends it, and Cliff Click's talks in general, as practical wisdom from someone who built HotSpot and worked on Azul's VMs.
videos.q: I strongly recommend following and listening to videos by Cliff Click who wrote HotSpot and worked on Azul and other VMs.

videos.t: exercises for tendinitis (tendonitis) and carpal tunnel (cps)
videos.s: A short video of stretching and hand exercises for preventing and easing tendinitis and carpal tunnel syndrome, from a percussion teacher. The exercises were shown to him by a doctor.
videos.w: Frequently recommended in RSI and wrist pain threads by people who say the stretches relieved their own symptoms.
videos.q: This video saved me from debilitating hand and wrist pain.

videos.t: The Black Lotus - Eon - Amiga Demo (50 FPS)
videos.s: Eon is a demoscene production by The Black Lotus, released at Revision 2019 and designed for an Amiga with OCS chipset, 512 kB chip and 512 kB fast memory. This is the party version, which has some known glitches.
videos.w: HN holds it up as a showcase of what a stock Amiga 500 can do and as one of the best demos ever in technique and storytelling.
videos.q: I feel like this is one of the best demos of all time from both a technical point of view plus storytelling.

videos.t: The Most Powerful Computers You've Never Heard Of
videos.s: Veritasium traces analog computers from the Antikythera mechanism and Kelvin's tide-predicting machines to fire control and modern analog approaches. It explains how these machines computed continuously rather than digitally.
videos.w: Recommended in threads on analog computing, photonic chips, AI hardware and tide prediction as an engaging history of Kelvin's machines.
videos.q: His video before this one[1] goes into detail on that, and it was incredible.

videos.t: Traffic Waves
videos.s: A short video from the trafficwaves.org site showing how traffic jams and standing waves form, including the fight between cheaters and blockers at an exit-lane backup. It also touches on how individual driving behavior affects the flow.
videos.w: HN likes it as a fun, clear explainer of traffic waves and of the benefits of leaving gaps while driving.
videos.q: One of my favorite videos of all time on this topic: Traffic Waves

videos.t: Why Vertical Farming Won't Save the Planet
videos.s: Utah State plant scientist Bruce Bugbee presents his analysis of the energy and environmental costs of vertical and indoor farming. He argues artificial lighting cannot compete with sunlight in fields or greenhouses.
videos.w: HN uses it as the go-to rebuttal to vertical farming hype, since it gives hard numbers from a leading controlled-environment authority.
videos.q: he does give hard numbers to do the math that shows that vertical farming is not as good as its proponents have made it out to be

videos.t: Javascript in 2015
