videos.s: A short screencast tour of JSPM, SystemJS and ES6 features, building a small app with the then-new JavaScript module and package tooling. It shows how JSPM works as a package manager, bundler and loader.
videos.w: Commenters credit it with opening their eyes to JSPM and using it to choose build systems.
videos.q: This video really opened my eyes to what it could do

videos.t: The Great Wave - Part 1
videos.s: The first part of a long series documenting Dave Bull's Tokyo woodblock workshop as it produces a reproduction of Hokusai's The Great Wave. It follows the carving, proofing and printing of the reward print for Kickstarter backers.
videos.w: HN commenters hold it up as a top-tier long-form process video, recommended whenever the Great Wave or Hokusai comes up.
videos.q: The series is up there with Clickspring's skeleton clock in my pantheon of "greatest long-form process videos

videos.t: Your dishwasher is better than you think (tips, tricks, and how they work)
videos.s: Technology Connections explains how dishwashers work and how to use them well, including detergent use, the prewash cycle and why pre-rinsing hurts. It follows his earlier dishwasher videos.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as the definitive, thorough guide to getting dishwashers to clean properly and often send it to friends.
videos.q: I’ve sent dozens of people the Technology Connections video on this topic to rave reviews

videos.t: Spinning Levers - How A Transmission Works (1936)
videos.s: A 1936 Chevrolet-sponsored film that explains how a car transmission works by treating gears as spinning levers. It uses physical models to make the mechanism clear.
videos.w: It is held up as a model of clear, well-paced educational film and of the old-era instructional style.
videos.q: The editing, pacing, and style were better.

videos.t: Jeff Bezos - Regret Minimization Framework
videos.s: A three-minute clip of Jeff Bezos describing his Regret Minimization Framework: imagining yourself at 80 to decide whether to leave a Wall Street job to start Amazon.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever someone asks whether to quit a job or start a company, as a simple decision heuristic.
videos.q: Hearing Bezos's regret minimization framework was one of the things that helped to make an easier decision

videos.t: Dconf 2014 Day 2 Keynote: The Last Thing D Needs -- Scott Meyers
videos.s: Scott Meyers' keynote at DConf 2014, drawing on 25 years of C++ experience to offer the D language community a plea about what it should avoid. It centers on the accumulated complexity and pitfalls of C++ as a cautionary tale.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up whenever C++ complexity or the pitfalls of language design come up, as a witty and authoritative warning.
videos.q: everyone should watch Scott Meyers's awesome presentation at a D conference

videos.t: But why would light "slow down"? | Visualizing Feynman's lecture on the refractive index
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown visualizes Feynman's lecture on the refractive index, explaining why light appears to slow down in glass and why the effect depends on color. It builds the idea from waves produced by oscillating charges in the material.
videos.w: HN considers it among the clearest accessible explanations of what refractive index actually is and how light moves through transparent matter.
videos.q: probably the clearest reasonably accessible explanation of this topic anywhere to date

videos.t: MiniDisc - An Appreciation
videos.s: Techmoan's 45-minute retrospective on Sony's MiniDisc, covering the first and last machines, ATRAC, MD-LP, Net-MD and HiMD. It argues the format deserves more credit than its US failure narrative suggests.
videos.w: The standard recommendation for MiniDisc history, especially as a non-American counterpoint to the failed-format story.
videos.q: Wonderful video about the format

videos.t: Why You Should Put YOUR MASK On First (My Brain Without Oxygen) - Smarter Every Day 157
videos.s: Destin Sandlin of Smarter Every Day undergoes hypoxia training and experiences his own impaired thinking as oxygen is withdrawn. The video shows how quickly and unnoticeably oxygen deprivation degrades judgment, illustrating why you put your own mask on first.
videos.w: It is the go-to demonstration of how hypoxia silently disables decision making, cited in threads on altitude, flying, diving, CO2 and breathwork.
videos.q: has a wonderful video demonstrating this effect [0]. I’d recommend watching the whole thing

videos.t: Exponential Growth Arithmetic, Population and Energy, Dr. Albert A. Bartlett
videos.s: A recording of physicist Albert Bartlett's well-known lecture on the arithmetic of exponential growth, applied to population and energy use. He argues that steady percentage growth in a finite world cannot continue and sneaks up suddenly.
videos.w: Treated as the classic lecture on why people misjudge exponential growth, and pulled out in threads on compound growth, epidemics, crypto and resource limits.
videos.q: The point is well illustrated in the talk, I highly recommend it.

videos.t: Kim Nilsson - Cracking MtGox
videos.s: Kim Nilsson presents his investigation into how Mt. Gox was hacked and mismanaged, tracing the finances and the missing bitcoins. It was given at the 2017 Breaking Bitcoin meetup.
videos.w: HN commenters call it one of the best, most unbiased explanations of what actually happened to Mt. Gox and its missing coins.
videos.q: One of the best summaries of the Mt Gox incident, as well as the fallout and subsequent investigations that I've watched.

videos.t: Computer Color is Broken
videos.s: MinutePhysics explains that computers store brightness nonlinearly, so blurring and blending colors in raw RGB gives wrong, dark results. It shows why mixed colors, such as in gradients, look off.
videos.w: HN cites it as the accessible go-to explanation of gamma and color blending errors in image programs.
videos.q: I found minutephysics' treatment of this subject to be really pleasant and easy to grok.

videos.t: Classic Game Postmortem: Ultima Online
videos.s: A 2018 GDC panel where Raph Koster, Starr Long, Richard Garriott and Rich Vogel look back on what went right and wrong building and running Ultima Online. They share candid stories from the early days, including player behavior and server architecture.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a transparent MMO postmortem and as the source of the story that the term 'shard' originated with Ultima Online.
videos.q: This is a much watch if MMOs fascinate you. They're very transparent. Absolutely great video.

videos.t: Characters, Symbols and the Unicode Miracle - Computerphile
videos.s: Tom Scott explains for Computerphile how Unicode and UTF-8 grew out of messy older character encodings to become the web's standard. It covers why the design works and how it handles worldwide text.
videos.w: HN treats it as the go-to short explanation of UTF-8, praised for making the topic stick.
videos.q: a wonderful, terse, very informative video describing how utf-8 encoding works and why

videos.t: Cheng Lou - On the Spectrum of Abstraction at react-europe 2016
videos.s: Cheng Lou's react-europe 2016 talk lays out a mental framework for thinking about abstraction levels in JavaScript tooling, from Angular and Grunt to Webpack and React. It uses that framework to reason about the cost of abstractions and how to choose between competing solutions.
videos.w: HN points to it as thought-provoking material on the tradeoffs and costs of abstraction, especially in frontend tooling debates.
videos.q: This talk is incredible food for thought

videos.t: The Pervert's Guide to Computer Programming Languages - SXSW
videos.s: A SXSW talk by W Watson that uses Lacanian psychoanalysis, with nods to Zizek, to critique popular programming languages. It argues that people choose and defend languages for emotional and ideological reasons rather than rational ones.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining and eye-opening look at the irrational psychology behind language preferences, though some note it is not scientifically precise.
videos.q: one of the best and eye-opening talks I've ever heard

videos.t: Keep your goals to yourself | Derek Sivers
videos.s: A four-minute TED talk in which Derek Sivers argues that announcing your goals can make you less likely to achieve them. He cites psychology research going back to the 1920s.
videos.w: Commenters credit it with changing how they handle plans and recommend it as a short, sourced talk.
videos.q: I did not really put two and two together until I saw this talk[0] many years ago and it clicked.

videos.t: Big Plane vs Little Plane (The Economics of Long-Haul Flights)
videos.s: Wendover Productions explains why Boeing's efficient 787 beat Airbus's giant A380, contrasting hub-and-spoke with point-to-point routes. It covers the economics of long-haul flights.
videos.w: Recommended in threads on the 747 and A380 for explaining why big planes were phased out.
videos.q: This is a great video on the economics of the hub and spoke vs. direct model embodied by the A380 vs 787

videos.t: ZFS: The Last Word in File Systems Part 1
videos.s: Jeff Bonwick and Bill Moore, the creators of ZFS, present 'ZFS: The Last Word in File Systems' at the 2008 SNIA Software Developers' Conference. They explain the design, including copy-on-write, checksumming and avoiding the write hole.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the definitive explanation of ZFS design straight from its inventors, with war stories about data integrity.
videos.q: I would recommend anybody interested in filesystems to watch Jeff Bonwick (ZFS inventor) explain the design of ZFS

videos.t: Breakout Session Presented by Dan Robinson of Heap at PGConf Silicon Valley 2015
videos.s: Dan Robinson, then CTO of Heap, explains how Heap runs its product analytics backend on PostgreSQL and CitusDB. It covers conversion funnels, retention and cohort queries across tens of billions of events and 50 TB of data, plus Postgres and Kafka together and the indexing strategy.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a first-hand overview of Heap's Postgres/Citus architecture and its distinctive indexing approach.
videos.q: Dan from Heap Analytics has a great talk about how they use Postgres and Citus.

videos.t: Hacker Way: Rethinking Web App Development at Facebook
videos.s: Facebook engineers explain why they abandoned the traditional MVC paradigm for a more functional architecture, introducing Flux and React. They use the unread-message-count bug as a case study of the problems of bidirectional data flow at scale.
videos.w: HN points to it as the original talk that explains the motivation behind React, Flux and Redux, and that sold some commenters on React.
videos.q: these talks, they are the ones that sold me on React

videos.t: HOW ROCKETS ARE MADE (Rocket Factory Tour - United Launch Alliance) - Smarter Every Day 231
videos.s: Destin Sandlin tours United Launch Alliance's rocket factory with CEO Tory Bruno, showing friction stir welding, structural rocket skins and large milled parts.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a rare look inside a rocket factory and cites it for manufacturing details like welding methods.
videos.q: If you haven't watched Smarter Every Day's ULA factory tour I highly recommend it.

videos.t: Symbolics Lisp Machine demo Jan 2013
videos.s: Symbolics developer Kalman Reti gives a short introductory demo of a Symbolics Lisp Machine running Genera in an emulator. It shows the context-aware command line, typed on-screen objects, and the live-editable system, including swapping in a C-compiled JPEG decoder.
videos.w: The go-to demo whenever HN discusses what Lisp machines were like and what modern shells and editors lack.
videos.q: It makes working on VSCode today look like banging rocks together

videos.t: Why I, as a black man, attend KKK rallies. | Daryl Davis | TEDxNaperville
videos.s: Black musician Daryl Davis tells how a chance encounter led him to befriend Ku Klux Klan members and seek the source of racial hate. He argues that sitting down and talking with people can change them.
videos.w: Recommended in moderation and deplatforming debates as a case for engagement and compassion over exclusion.
videos.q: I'd recommend watching his TedTalk it really helped me understand how to better work with others, and how to bring about understanding.

videos.t: Parking Laws Are Strangling America | Climate Town
videos.s: Climate Town traces the history of American parking minimums, how they came from shaky research and ITE guides, and how they shape zoning, cities and housing costs. It is a long, comedic video essay.
videos.w: Recommended as a fun but well-researched explanation of why parking requirements are arbitrary and harmful.
videos.q: This is a good video about the history behind idiotic American zoning laws and parking minimums.

videos.t: This equation will change how you see the world (the logistic map)
videos.s: A Veritasium video on the logistic map, showing how a simple population equation leads to chaos and bifurcation. It connects the idea to convection, neuron firing and the Mandelbrot set, with interactive animations.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a favourite Veritasium video, praised for how a simple equation reveals surprisingly complex patterns.
videos.q: But this is the one I think people on HN need to watch most

videos.t: Larry Hastings - Removing Python's GIL: The Gilectomy - PyCon 2016
videos.s: Larry Hastings explains what Python's GIL is, what problems it solves and how it works, and presents his Gilectomy project to remove it, including the performance and C-extension obstacles.
videos.w: The default reference in Python performance threads for why removing the GIL is hard.
videos.q: I think Larry Hasting's first Gilectomy talk was extremely insightful

videos.t: How We've Scaled Dropbox
videos.s: Dropbox engineer Kevin Modzelewski gives a Stanford colloquium on Dropbox's history and the technical problems it faced scaling, including detailed database schema decisions.
videos.w: Recommended as a detailed, candid case study of scaling a real system from zero users to millions.
videos.q: I found the Dropbox lecture [1] at Stanford one of the most riveting things ever.

videos.t: Control Bootcamp: Overview
videos.s: The opening lecture of Steve Brunton's Control Bootcamp, covering the kinds of control and why closed-loop feedback matters. It starts a series that follows the control chapter of the Brunton and Kutz data-driven science book.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as an approachable but rigorous way to learn control theory, with good production quality.
videos.q: a sweet lecture series called the Control Bootcamp that dives deep into control fundamentals while still being approachable

videos.t: Our democracy no longer represents the people. Here's how we fix it | Larry Lessig | TEDxMidAtlantic
videos.s: Harvard law professor Lawrence Lessig argues that US democracy is corrupted by money, since a tiny fraction of the population effectively funds who gets elected. He says fixing this must come before addressing issues like climate change or student debt.
videos.w: It is HN's go-to link in threads on lobbying, campaign finance and political dysfunction, as a clear statement of Lessig's root-cause argument.
videos.q: Very good video explaining the core issue of American politics by Harvard Law professor and founder of creative commons Lawrence Lessig

videos.t: David Beazley - Lambda Calculus from the Ground Up - PyCon 2019
videos.s: David Beazley's PyCon 2019 tutorial derives the lambda calculus from the ground up in Python, using only single-argument functions. He builds booleans, numerals and more with no other language features.
videos.w: HN calls it a brilliant, mind-bending introduction to lambda calculus for programmers.
videos.q: David Beazley gives a brilliant introduction to lambda calculus here

videos.t: KGB Defector Yuri Bezmenov 1985 Interview. Explains KGB Manipulation of US Public Opinion
videos.s: A 1985 interview by G. Edward Griffin with former KGB operative Yuri Bezmenov. He describes long-running Soviet efforts at ideological subversion and manipulation of US public opinion.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up in threads on propaganda, influence operations and platforms like TikTok, saying it feels more relevant than ever.
videos.q: I feel like everyone should watch this 1985 interview of an ex-KGB agent[1]. It's more relevant today than ever before

videos.t: Intro to AI Safety, Remastered
videos.s: Robert Miles gives a remastered introduction to AI safety, adapted from a talk in London. It lays out why advanced AI could go wrong and answers common objections.
videos.w: The default link for newcomers wanting an approachable, entertaining introduction to AI risk and alignment.
videos.q: It's quite an approachable intro, often entertaining

videos.t: Sparks of AGI: early experiments with GPT-4
videos.s: Sebastien Bubeck presents the Sparks of AGI paper at MIT, showing early experiments with GPT-4 across many domains and asking whether artificial intelligence has arrived. It includes the TikZ unicorn example.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking talk from a researcher with early GPT-4 access, especially for the unicorn degrading under safety tuning.
videos.q: Highly highly highly recommend listen to this lecture by Sebastien Bubeck

videos.t: How Great Leaders Inspire Action | Simon Sinek | TED
videos.s: Simon Sinek's TED talk presents the 'golden circle' model: great leaders and companies inspire action by starting with why they do something, before how or what. He illustrates it with Apple, Martin Luther King, the Wright brothers and, as a counterexample, TiVo.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it to explain why customers buy into a company's beliefs rather than its specs, especially in threads about Apple, marketing and product messaging.
videos.q: I think this video by Simon Sinek explains very well why Apple is successful.

videos.t: Gimbal UFO - A New Analysis
videos.s: Mick West analyzes the Navy's Gimbal UFO video and gives four checkable observations suggesting it is an infrared glare that appears to rotate because the camera rotates while tracking. He argues the object is likely a hot craft hidden behind the glare.
videos.w: Pointed to as the clearest, evidence-based debunk of the Gimbal footage, and a model of how to analyze such claims.
videos.q: The summary video is concise and only 20 minutes long. I challenge you to watch all of it and respond specifically.

videos.t: OK Go - This Too Shall Pass - Rube Goldberg Machine - Official Video
videos.s: OK Go's music video for This Too Shall Pass, featuring a huge Rube Goldberg machine built in a warehouse in Los Angeles with Syyn Labs. The band interacts with the contraption in one continuous take.
videos.w: HN points to it as an example of ambitious, practical-effects creativity in music videos, made without CGI.
videos.q: The Rube Goldberg machine [0] one is particularily impressive.

videos.t: Simon Peyton-Jones: Escape from the ivory tower: the Haskell journey
videos.s: Simon Peyton Jones gives Churchill College's annual computer science lecture on Haskell's birth and evolution. He covers the most influential ideas, from laziness to monads and type system evolution, plus current developments and guesses about the future.
videos.w: Recommended as a funny, accessible history of Haskell that is valuable even for people interested in language design in general.
videos.q: It's a funny talk and it's worth watching in full

videos.t: Penn and Teller on Vaccinations
videos.s: A short clip of Penn and Teller arguing, in blunt and profane language, for vaccination and against anti-vaccine claims. It covers risk versus benefit and herd immunity.
videos.w: HN commenters share it in vaccine threads as a quick, entertaining explanation of vaccination in layman's terms.
videos.q: This really drives home the point of herd immunity ( in ~ 90 seconds ).

videos.t: I'll Let Myself In: Tactics of Physical Pen Testers
videos.s: Deviant Ollam, head of a physical penetration testing team, presents tactics for getting into buildings, from bypassing door levers with a wire to defeating bank doors. He argues that physical security is often surprisingly weak.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining overview of physical pen testing, and cites it when threads discuss how easily doors and locks are bypassed.
videos.q: Deviant Ollam's talks are always first class.

videos.t: The $100 Billion Dollar Ingredient making your Food Toxic
videos.s: A What I've Learned video arguing that industrial seed and vegetable oils have displaced saturated fats and harmed health. It covers the history of vegetable oils, the American Heart Association's role, and rising consumption.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an accessible summary of the case against seed oils, and some say it changed what fats they cook with.
videos.q: one of the most important ones imo being the one on seed oils

videos.t: The Boeing 787: Broken Dreams l Al Jazeera Investigations
videos.s: An Al Jazeera investigation into Boeing's 787 Dreamliner, featuring current and former engineers who voice safety concerns. It covers quality control problems at the South Carolina plant and the roots of the battery problems that grounded the plane.
videos.w: Boeing threads cite it as early evidence of deep cultural and quality problems at Boeing, years before the 737 MAX crashes.
videos.q: AlJazeera deserves respect for this excellent footage they got from inside the factory.

videos.t: A Selfish Argument for Making the World a Better Place – Egoistic Altruism
videos.s: Kurzgesagt makes a selfish case for improving the world, arguing that helping people far away raises prosperity and innovation for everyone, including yourself. The animated video frames this as egoistic altruism and positive-sum cooperation.
videos.w: HN commenters link it to argue for cooperation and engagement over isolation, and as an accessible statement of positive-sum thinking.
videos.q: There is a video [0] I love that explains an argument for this well.

videos.t: Why Louisiana Stays Poor
videos.s: Together Louisiana asks why Louisiana stays poor despite its natural resources and industry, focusing on industrial tax exemptions and corporate welfare.
videos.w: Linked in threads on corporate tax incentives and subsidies as a detailed example of how they can trap a state.
videos.q: I found this insightful: Why Louisiana Stays Poor

videos.t: Neuromancer (BBC radio play adaptation ) William Gibson
videos.s: The BBC radio play adaptation of William Gibson's cyberpunk novel Neuromancer, running about two hours. It features professional voice acting, sound effects and music.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a good, condensed way to experience Neuromancer when short on time.
videos.q: The BBC did a great adaptation of the book to a radio play, complete with professional voice acting, sound effects, even music

videos.t: Are We There Yet - Rich Hickey
videos.s: Rich Hickey's talk on time, state, identity and values, arguing that mutable object-oriented modeling fits the world poorly. It lays out the thinking behind Clojure's approach to data and change.
videos.w: Recommended as one of the best explanations of why Clojure and a functional, immutable approach to state exist.
videos.q: One of the best "why Clojure" talks that I've seen

videos.t: Drip Coffee Makers — super simple, super cheap
videos.s: Technology Connections explains how the simple American drip coffee maker works, including the bimetal valve and bubble-pump heating, and compares the original Mr. Coffee with modern machines.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear, enjoyable look at why simple designs are brilliant, and as a pointer to a channel with a hacker's-eye view of everyday technology.
videos.q: Anyone interested in how the traditional american coffee maker works should watch this.

videos.t: How To Count Past Infinity
videos.s: Vsauce's Michael Stevens takes viewers past infinity using transfinite numbers, ordinals and cardinals, with input from mathematician Hugh Woodin. It is a fast-paced, mind-bending tour of different sizes of infinity.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the most accessible introduction to what lies beyond infinity.
videos.q: The most accessible resource I found was this VSauce video

videos.t: How Facebook is Stealing Billions of Views
videos.s: Kurzgesagt argues that Facebook's claimed 8 billion daily video views are inflated by freebooting, meaning re-uploads of creators' videos. It describes how this harms independent creators.
videos.w: HN cites it to explain freebooting, Facebook's inflated view metrics and why Content ID matters for small creators.
videos.q: This video changed my opinion on Content ID when I saw it last year

videos.t: Dtrace Review
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill's 2007 Google Tech Talk on DTrace, showing how dynamic tracing improves debugging of both development and live production systems. It includes a vivid war story about tracking down a problem on a Sun Ray server.
videos.w: HN regards it as a gem of a technical talk that tackles a fundamental debugging problem and shows a new technology solving it.
videos.q: I'm partial to Bryan Cantrill's Dtrace talk since it tackles a fundamental problem in software engineering and shows how to solve it using a new technology.

videos.t: "Games as a service" is fraud.
videos.s: Ross Scott of Accursed Farms makes a 76-minute argument that selling video games as a service is a form of consumer fraud. He lays out legal arguments that games are goods, covers ownership and programmed obsolescence, and discusses game preservation.
videos.w: It is the go-to explanation of why games that die when servers shut down harm consumers, and it is repeatedly cited in Stop Killing Games and game-delisting threads.
videos.q: Just watch this video so that you get up to speed with what we are talking about

videos.t: Richard Feynman on Pseudoscience
videos.s: A two-minute clip of Richard Feynman explaining why he considers much of social science pseudoscience. He stresses how easy it is to fool yourself and how much care real knowledge takes.
videos.w: Commenters post it whenever a thread touches on soft sciences, replication problems, or what counts as real science.
videos.q: it's very hard to know something and you have to be really careful that you've done the work and aren't just deluding yourself

videos.t: Climbing the Rating Ladder: Up to 1000
videos.s: Chess player John Bartholomew plays opponents rated below 1000 on Chess.com and comments on optimal strategy and typical mistakes at that level. It is part of his Climbing the Rating Ladder series.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a way to improve at chess, since it explains the basics and common mistakes at each rating level.
videos.q: He explains the basics and mistakes players at each level makes and how to avoid them

videos.t: DAIRY IS SCARY!
videos.s: Vegan advocate Erin Janus explains the dairy industry in about five minutes, covering how milk is produced and the treatment of cows and calves. It is an advocacy piece and includes graphic material.
videos.w: HN commenters in veganism and food threads link it as a short, info-dense explanation that some say opened their eyes, though others dispute it.
videos.q: I know it opened my eyes

videos.t: Free to Play
videos.s: Valve's feature-length documentary following three professional gamers competing in the first Dota 2 International tournament for a million dollar prize. It shows the sacrifices and pressures of top-level esports.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an engaging look at the life of pro Dota players and the early rise of esports, though one commenter notes it is somewhat promotional.
videos.q: I've enjoyed this documentary a lot.

videos.t: clojure.core/typing - Matt Adereth
videos.s: Matt Adereth's Clojure/conj talk covers the history of keyboards and how he used Clojure generating OpenSCAD to design and build his custom Dactyl ergonomic keyboard, including 3D printing and laser-cut parts.
videos.w: Recommended as a fantastic talk on code-driven CAD and custom keyboard design, linked in threads on OpenSCAD and keyboards.
videos.q: it is a fantastic talk but the part related to this starts at 17:35

videos.t: A JVM Does That?
videos.s: Cliff Click of Azul Systems asks what a JVM is supposed to do, in a Google Tech Talk from 2011. He covers the services a JVM provides, such as garbage collection and compilation, and the messy reality beneath the abstractions.
videos.w: A repeated recommendation for anyone interested in VMs, with Click's talks regarded as unusually informative on JVMs, JITs and the user/kernel boundary.
videos.q: It's well worth watching if you are interested in vms at all.

videos.t: What Is A Black Start Of The Power Grid?
videos.s: Practical Engineering explains what a black start is: restarting a power grid after total collapse. It shows why most plants need outside power to start and why rebuilding a synchronized grid is delicate and high-stakes.
videos.w: Go-to reference whenever a major blackout happens, recommended as an excellent explanation of why black starts are hard.
videos.q: Practical Engineering did a really great video a few years ago on why black starts are hard

videos.t: Rails Conf 2013 The Magic Tricks of Testing by Sandi Metz
videos.s: Sandi Metz's RailsConf 2013 talk offers practical guidelines for deciding what to test and how, so tests stay cheap and stable. She argues for testing the public interface rather than implementation and using mocks appropriately.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an incredible talk whose testing principles apply beyond Ruby.
videos.q: watch Sandi Metz' incredible RailsConf talk

videos.t: Ruby Manor 3 - Programming with Nothing by Tom Stuart
videos.s: Tom Stuart's Ruby Manor 3 talk builds FizzBuzz using nothing but Ruby lambdas, working through Church encodings of numbers, booleans and data structures. It is a hands-on introduction to lambda calculus.
videos.w: Strongly recommended in lambda calculus and Y-combinator threads as a mind-expanding half hour that clarifies the ideas.
videos.q: An awesome video which changed my perspective towards lambda calculus and programming in general

videos.t: Avie Tevanian: CMU math whiz goes from Mach to NeXT to Apple Software Chief | Oral History Part 1
videos.s: A Computer History Museum oral history with Avie Tevanian covering his math talent, work on the Mach microkernel at CMU, joining NeXT, leading NEXTSTEP development and the 1996 Apple acquisition.
videos.w: Recommended as a long, rich first-hand account of Mach, NeXT and Apple history and of working for Steve Jobs.
videos.q: Must watch recollection of the history of Mach and NeXT and Apple by Avie Tevanian.

videos.t: GPUs to Mars: Full-Scale Simulation of SpaceX's Mars Rocket Engine
videos.s: SpaceX engineers present at NVIDIA's GPU Technology Conference on a multi-physics code that simulates the full-scale Raptor methane engine. It covers GPU-based turbulent combustion modeling with adaptive grids and wavelet compression.
videos.w: HN points to it as evidence of SpaceX's serious simulation capability and as a showcase of GPU compute for CFD.
videos.q: This talk was given at NVIDIA GTC 2015 and inspired me to go into manufacturing

videos.t: 6 ways mushrooms can save the world | Paul Stamets | TED
videos.s: Mycologist Paul Stamets presents six ways mycelium and fungi could help save the world, in an 18-minute TED talk. Topics include environmental cleanup and other applications of fungi.
videos.w: Recommended as an engaging, down-to-earth talk on the world-changing potential of fungi.
videos.q: He has a brilliant TED talk on the world-changing potential of fungi research [1].

videos.t: The Neuroscience of Consciousness – with Anil Seth
videos.s: Neuroscientist Anil Seth gives a Royal Institution lecture on the science of consciousness. He separates conscious level, content and self, and argues that experience arises from the brain's predictive inference.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a clear, in-depth lecture on consciousness as a process of prediction.
videos.q: And The Neuroscience of Consciousness – with Anil Seth is really great

videos.t: What Everyone Gets Wrong About Gravity
videos.s: Veritasium explains, with expert input, that in general relativity gravity is not a force and objects follow straight paths through curved spacetime, including why standing on the ground means you are accelerating.
videos.w: HN links it as a go-to intuitive explanation whenever gravity as spacetime curvature or free fall comes up.
videos.q: his videos on special [1] and general relativity [2] were real eye-openers for me

videos.t: UNIX: Making Computers Easier To Use -- AT&T Archives film from 1982, Bell Laboratories
videos.s: A 1982 AT&T Bell Labs film for students about the Unix system and how it can be used practically. It includes Lorinda Cherry building a talking calculator by piping together Unix commands, and a spell checker made from Unix utilities.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a demonstration of the Unix philosophy, with small tools composed through pipes.
videos.q: both are really excellent demonstrations and eludications of the Unix philosophy and mindset

videos.t: Run for your life! At a comfortable pace, and not too far: James O'Keefe at TEDxUMKC
videos.s: Cardiologist James O'Keefe argues in a TEDx talk that moderate running confers the best longevity benefits, while extreme endurance training can damage the heart. He draws on data and his own experience as a lifelong runner.
videos.w: HN cites it whenever people question whether more exercise is always better, especially extreme endurance running.
videos.q: I think about this TED Talk from 2012 a lot..

videos.t: I made a NES emulator in 15 minutes
videos.s: Bisqwit writes a NES emulator in C++ in about 15 minutes of tool-assisted, sped-up coding, narrated with captions. It shows an accurate emulator built with a compile-time generated 6502 instruction table. Part 2 covers compiling and running it.
videos.w: HN programmers admire it as a clean, clever demonstration of emulator design and as the standout of a favorite programming YouTuber.
videos.q: Here's a very clean and clever NES emulator in C++ by Bisqwit of TAS fame

videos.t: FULL INTERVIEW with Yuri Bezmenov: The Four Stages of Ideological Subversion (1984)
videos.s: The full 1984 interview with Yuri Bezmenov, a former KGB operative, in which he lays out four stages of ideological subversion. It is a long interview with G. Edward Griffin.
videos.w: Cited in propaganda and disinformation threads, though some commenters present it more as a prediction of current events than established analysis.
videos.q: It is worth watching the whole interview

videos.t: ADL's Never Is Now 2019 | ADL International Leadership Award Presented to Sacha Baron Cohen
videos.s: Sacha Baron Cohen's speech accepting the ADL International Leadership Award, in which he criticizes social media companies for amplifying hate and propaganda. He argues that freedom of speech is not freedom of reach.
videos.w: Quoted heavily in moderation and free speech debates, particularly the line about freedom of speech and reach.
videos.q: This is a thought-provoking speech. Do yourself a favor and watch it in its entirety

videos.t: Complete Apple WWDC | Steve Jobs talk and answer developers questions | 1997
videos.s: The full 1997 WWDC session in which Steve Jobs, newly back at Apple, takes developer questions for about an hour. He discusses OpenDoc, Microsoft, clones, Newton, advertising and Apple's strategy.
videos.w: HN readers recommend it as an unfiltered view of Jobs' strategic thinking and decisiveness, including the famous answer on why OpenDoc was killed.
videos.q: For those that haven't seen it the whole thing is worth it

videos.t: Alan Kay - Programming and Scaling
videos.s: An Alan Kay talk on programming and scaling, covering theoretical limits of code size, engineering versus tinkering, and biological cells as inspiration for object-oriented design.
videos.w: HN fans call it one of Kay's best talks and recommend it for rethinking why programming paradigms have barely changed.
videos.q: This talk is excellent and will cue you in on how to go about thinking about the fact

videos.t: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
videos.s: Andrej Karpathy builds the GPT tokenizer from scratch, implementing byte pair encoding along with encode and decode. He shows how many odd LLM behaviors trace back to tokenization, and covers Unicode byte encodings along the way.
videos.w: Recommended as the best deep dive on tokenizers, worth the two hours for anyone working with LLMs.
videos.q: Worth spending 2h for the deeper understanding if you deal with LLMs.

videos.t: Steve Reich, "Music for 18 Musicians" - FULL PERFORMANCE with eighth blackbird
videos.s: A full performance of Steve Reich's Music for 18 Musicians by eighth blackbird with Third Coast Percussion and others, recorded in Chicago in 2011. It is an hour-long minimalist piece built on phasing and repeating patterns.
videos.w: Recommended in coding-music threads as lyric-free, repetitive music that aids focus.

videos.t: Riding through Iran on a small motorcycle as British person.
videos.s: Ed March rides a Honda C90 through Iran on his journey from Malaysia to the UK, showing the country and its people. He argues Iran is far more welcoming than the press suggests.
videos.w: Recommended for its heartwarming picture of Iranian hospitality toward a foreign rider.
videos.q: I highly recommend watching this fairly recent documentary about a British guy riding a motorcycle through the country.

videos.t: Great Impractical Ideas in Computer Science: PowerPoint Programming
videos.s: Tom Wildenhain's guest lecture for CMU's Esoteric Programming Languages course shows that PowerPoint transitions and slides are Turing complete without macros, building up to a mind-bending fractal ending.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended in best-talks threads as a fun, mind-blowing demonstration of unexpected computation.
videos.q: Strong recommend!

videos.t: Investigation: How Roblox Is Exploiting Young Game Developers
videos.s: People Make Games investigates how Roblox relies on young, often child, developers to build its content while paying them very little. It covers Roblox's monetization model, the revenue split, and the harms to kids who make games on the platform.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as the go-to evidence that Roblox exploits child developers, and parents are pointed to it before letting kids build games there.
videos.q: has a couple of reports that I'd suggest parents consider watching first before going down that road

videos.t: "You Have the Right to Remain Innocent" (James Duane)
videos.s: Law professor James Duane explains why you should not talk to the police even if you are innocent, drawing on case histories of wrongful convictions. It is a short version of the argument in his book on the right to remain silent.
videos.w: HN commenters send it to anyone who thinks innocent people have nothing to fear from answering police questions.
videos.q: this is a very important video for everyone to watch

videos.t: Massive-scale online collaboration | Luis von Ahn
videos.s: Luis von Ahn, creator of CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA, explains how small contributions from many people online can digitize books. He then introduces Duolingo as a way to translate the web while people learn languages.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the clearest account of human computation and games with a purpose, straight from the inventor.
videos.q: I highly recommend watching the TED talk by Luis von Ahn, creater of CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA.

videos.t: I Watched Ancient Apocalypse So You Don't Have To (Part 1)
videos.s: Miniminuteman begins a long, humorous point-by-point debunking of Graham Hancock's Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse and its claims of a lost ice-age civilization. It is part one of a multi-part critique.
videos.w: HN points people to it as an entertaining, thorough takedown of Hancock's pseudoarchaeology whenever his claims come up.
videos.q: lengthy, point-by-point takedown of the Ancient Apocalypse thing both entertaining and informative

videos.t: Noether's Theorem and The Symmetries of Reality
videos.s: PBS Space Time explains Noether's theorem: conservation laws such as energy and momentum are consequences of deeper symmetries. It also covers why those laws hold only under certain conditions.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as an approachable explanation of how symmetries give rise to conservation laws, including the story of Emmy Noether.
videos.q: It's such an aha moment.

videos.t: Cities: Skylines | Power, Politics, & Planning: Episode 1: Parking
videos.s: The first episode of a Cities: Skylines series on urban politics and planning, focused on parking. It uses the game to show how parking minimums shape cities, drawing on Donald Shoup's book The High Cost of Free Parking.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear illustration of how parking requirements produce car-centered, unwalkable American urban design.
videos.q: this video (shared recently in another HN discussion) is a _fantastic_ illustration of the problems of parking minimums

videos.t: Learn Low Poly Modeling in Blender 2.9 / 2.8
videos.s: Imphenzia's 83-minute tutorial covers the low poly modeling techniques he learned over five years of Blender use, with timestamps from navigation and extrusion onward. It uses Blender 2.83 with default keys.
videos.w: It is the most-recommended beginner Blender tutorial on HN, with several people saying it made them comfortable in a couple of hours.
videos.q: until this tut by Imphenzia, which made me comfortable in under 2 hours

videos.t: John Carmack's keynote at Quakecon 2013 part 4
videos.s: Part 4 of John Carmack's QuakeCon 2013 keynote, covering OpenGL, functional programming, Haskell, Lisp and Scheme, typing, multithreading, events and garbage collection.
videos.w: Cited again and again as Carmack's key public statement on functional programming and purity in game development, plus his remarks on garbage collection.
videos.q: There's an old video [0] where he talks in-depth about his explorations of functional programming.

videos.t: Building a Better Web Browser - James Mickens - Harvard CS Colloquium 2015
videos.s: James Mickens's 2015 Harvard colloquium argues that browsers are bloated and insecure because feature races trump clean interface design. He presents a cleaner, more secure browser architecture (Atlantis) with a much smaller API surface.
videos.w: HN cites it whenever people discuss rebuilding the web platform or what a better browser architecture could look like.
videos.q: which I definitely think this still the most forward-looking browser architecture out there

videos.t: Who Destroyed Three Mile Island? - Nickolas Means | The Lead Developer Austin 2018
videos.s: Nickolas Means recounts the 1979 Three Mile Island accident minute by minute, from the control rod insertion to the operator's decision to switch off emergency cooling. He argues that finding systemic causes is more useful than blaming individuals.
videos.w: HN recommends it whenever a failure is blamed on human error, as a clear case study in looking for the systemic second story.
videos.q: There's an excellent talk from Nick Means (GitHub) called "Who Destroyed Three Mile Island?".

videos.t: Leonard Susskind on The World As Hologram | TVO Docs
videos.s: Stanford physicist Leonard Susskind gives a public lecture on the holographic principle, the indestructibility of information and the nature of black holes. It asks whether the world could be a hologram.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an accessible yet substantive introduction to the holographic principle and black hole information, often when related physics news comes up.
videos.q: IIRC these are very good videos to start with

videos.t: Paleo Diet & Strength Training Biochemistry | Doug McGuff M.D. | Full Length HD
videos.s: Doug McGuff presents the biochemistry behind high-intensity strength training and the paleo diet, including how the body stores and burns fat. It is a roughly hour-and-a-half full-length lecture.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the theory behind Body by Science, explaining metabolism and why brief intense training works.
videos.q: Doug McGuff covers med school biochemistry and metabolism in the last part of this presentation

videos.t: Nintendo - Putting Play First
videos.s: Game Maker's Toolkit examines Nintendo's design approach of starting from a core play mechanic, making it fun, and building around it. Examples include Mario's jump and Luigi's Mansion's vacuum.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a concise video essay on why Nintendo games feel good and how the company iterates.
videos.q: I highly recommend Mark Brown's video

videos.t: Richard Feynman. Why.
videos.s: A short clip of Richard Feynman answering an interviewer's question about why magnets repel, explaining that a 'why' question depends on a shared framework of understanding. It illustrates how hard it is to explain fundamentals to a layperson.
videos.w: Cited constantly as the classic answer to 'why' questions, on explanation, frames of reference and the limits of physics.
videos.q: I like to refer people to Feynman's answer to a question about why magnets repel each other[0].

videos.t: Man Spends 30 Years Turning Degraded Land into Massive Forest – Fools & Dreamers (Full Documentary)
videos.s: Fools & Dreamers is a 30-minute documentary about Hinewai Nature Reserve in New Zealand, where botanist Hugh Wilson let gorse grow as a nurse canopy to regenerate native forest. It shows the results after 30 years and the local skepticism he faced.
videos.w: Shared in climate and land-use threads as a vivid example of how letting land regrow can restore forest.
videos.q: This is a great short film that goes into detail about the project and the challenges faced in getting it off the ground

videos.t: On the Expressive Power of Programming Languages by Shriram Krishnamurthi [PWLConf 2019]
videos.s: Shriram Krishnamurthi's PWLConf 2019 talk on the formal notion of expressive power of programming languages, based on Felleisen's paper. It explains how to tell when a feature adds power by whether emulating it requires global rewriting.
videos.w: Recommended as the approachable way into a precise definition of language expressiveness for language-design arguments.
videos.q: Shriram Krishnamurthi's talk from two years ago on this paper might be more approachable.

videos.t: MC Frontalot - It Is Pitch Dark
videos.s: MC Frontalot's nerdcore rap about the text adventure Zork, made for Jason Scott's Get Lamp documentary and featuring a cameo by Steve Meretzky. It was filmed over an evening in a basement.
videos.w: HN shares it whenever Zork or text adventures come up, as a fun tribute for geeks.
videos.q: Now enjoy this immortal tribute

videos.t: A Brief History of Quantum Mechanics - with Sean Carroll
videos.s: Sean Carroll gives a Royal Institution talk tracing the history of quantum mechanics from Einstein and Bohr to today. He covers the Copenhagen interpretation and the many worlds interpretation.
videos.w: Recommended as an approachable entry point to quantum interpretations, and cited on many worlds questions.
videos.q: Sean Carroll is a master of making quantum mechanics approachable to non-physicists.

videos.t: Are Electric Cars Worse For The Environment? Myth Busted
videos.s: Engineering Explained works through whether electric cars are really worse for the environment than gasoline cars. It covers battery production emissions, the electricity mix used to charge, and how long an EV takes to break even on lifetime emissions.
videos.w: HN commenters link it repeatedly as a clear, number-based rebuttal to the claim that EVs are worse for the climate than gas cars.
videos.q: This video crunches the numbers pretty thoroughly

videos.t: How does Computer Memory Work? 💻🛠
videos.s: A 36-minute animated deep dive from Branch Education into how DRAM works. It shows how memory connects to the CPU and how billions of bits are stored in nanoscale capacitor cells. It also covers why DRAM sits between SSDs and the processor.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it as a clear, well-animated explanation of memory, especially for visual learners.
videos.q: It is both detailed enough and clear thanks to the simplified visuals.

videos.t: 8 Frames in 16ms: Rollback Networking in Mortal Kombat and Injustice 2
videos.s: A 2018 GDC talk by NetherRealm's Michael Stallone on the engine changes, optimizations and tooling needed to roll back and re-simulate up to 8 frames in 16 ms in Mortal Kombat and Injustice 2. It is a deep dive into deterministic rollback netcode.
videos.w: HN treats it as the definitive practical talk on rollback networking in a shipped AAA fighting game.
videos.q: For an in-depth explanation, see this excellent GDC talk on its implementation in Mortal Kombat and Injustice 2

videos.t: E-Ink for Productivity: An Introduction
videos.s: Technology Connections gives first impressions of using an Onyx Boox Max2 e-ink tablet for productivity, including using it as an external display. He shows what the device can and cannot do.
videos.w: HN recommends it, with its companion video, as an honest hands-on account of e-ink devices as monitors, including their slow software and limits.
videos.q: Technology Connections on youtube tried to use an eink display and thoroughly described his experiences.

videos.t: Suburbia is Subsidized: Here's the Math [ST07]
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains, using Urban3's property-tax analysis, why car-dependent suburbs generate less tax revenue than they cost to maintain, so dense urban cores effectively subsidize them. It is part of a Strong Towns series.
videos.w: The go-to link in urban planning threads for the claim that suburban infrastructure costs more per resident than it pays back.
videos.q: Good overview of the research on this

videos.t: Televangelists: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on televangelists and the 'seed faith' prosperity gospel. It looks at how US tax law lets preachers extract money from poor viewers, and how easy it is to start a church.
videos.w: HN cites it in threads on churches, tax exemption and religious fundraising, as the go-to explainer on seed faith televangelism.
videos.q: John Oliver did an excellent piece on a new crop of so-called "seed faith" televangelists

videos.t: The Unanswered Question 1973 1  Musical Phonology Bernstein Norton
videos.s: Leonard Bernstein's 1973 Norton Lectures at Harvard, starting with Musical Phonology. He draws analogies between music and linguistics, including references to Chomsky.
videos.w: HN recommends it for a deep theory of why music sounds the way it does.
videos.q: Check out the Norton Lectures especially, where Bernstein analyzes musical structure with references to Chomsky.

videos.t: Plagues & Pleasures on the Salton Sea | KQED Truly CA
videos.s: A KQED Truly CA documentary narrated by John Waters about the Salton Sea, a once-glamorous California vacation spot now home to an eccentric community. It covers the area's economic, political and environmental problems and features Salvation Mountain.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an engaging, funny and fascinating documentary, and cites it in threads on the Salton Sea's history and environmental decline.
videos.q: Definitely one of my top 10 documentaries

videos.t: Raymond Hettinger, Keynote on Concurrency, PyBay 2017
videos.s: Raymond Hettinger's PyBay 2017 keynote on concurrency in Python. It covers threads, processes, asyncio, locks and the GIL, with live shell-based examples.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear, charismatic starting point for understanding Python concurrency and the GIL.
videos.q: the best learning material for me on this was this lecture

videos.t: A Look Inside Apple's $130 USB-C Cable
videos.s: Adam Savage and engineer Zach Radding examine Lumafield CT scans of Apple's $130 Thunderbolt 4 cable alongside cheaper USB-C cables. They explain the internal components that distinguish Thunderbolt from ordinary USB-C.
videos.w: Linked whenever people ask why a Thunderbolt cable costs so much; the CT scans show the construction difference clearly.
videos.q: if you're interested in why the Thunderbolt cable costs more than charging cables, some folks put one through a CT scanner recently

videos.t: William Shatner - Common People
videos.s: William Shatner's spoken-word cover of Pulp's 'Common People', from his album Has Been.
videos.w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it as a surprisingly good cover that brings out the contempt in the lyrics.
videos.q: I really like William Shatner's cover. It brings out the contempt in the lyrics. And it rocks.

videos.t: Marcus Aurelius' Meditations: The Stoic Ideal
videos.s: Michael Sugrue's lecture on Marcus Aurelius' Meditations and the Stoic ideal, covering the text and its philosophy. It is one of his humanities lectures known for their clarity.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a classic, clear introduction to Aurelius, with some saying it helped through hard times.
videos.q: have watched this lecture multiple times (each time I was going through some bad things in my life) and it helped me tremendously.

videos.t: !!Con 2017: HDR Photography in Microsoft Excel?! by Kevin Chen
videos.s: A short conference talk from !!Con 2017 in which Kevin Chen explains the HDR imaging algorithm from a foundational paper, framing it as a system of linear equations, and implements it in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. No prior image processing knowledge is needed.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a fun, short talk that shows how HDR photography actually works through an absurdly playful implementation.
videos.q: It's short and fun, I recommend it to all HN readers.

videos.t: The Lively & Liveable Neighbourhoods that are Illegal in Most of North America
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains how small pockets of shops and restaurants inside residential Dutch neighbourhoods create liveliness and help reduce traffic. It argues this kind of mixed-use design has been illegal in most of the US and Canada for a century because of zoning, and should be brought back.
videos.w: HN commenters link it in zoning, housing and car-dependency threads as an accessible explanation of how single-use zoning and parking rules shape cities.
videos.q: Not Just Bikes talks about zoning in the US vs Dutch cities in this video

videos.t: 1177 BC: The Year Civilization Collapsed (Eric Cline, PhD)
videos.s: Archaeologist Eric Cline lectures on the Late Bronze Age collapse around 1177 BC, when interconnected Mediterranean empires fell in rapid succession. He discusses the Sea Peoples and the combined causes of the collapse.
videos.w: Recommended as an informative and funny hour that serves as a good substitute for his book.
videos.q: Excellent informative and hilarious talk about his (at-the-time) new scientific hypothesis

videos.t: JavaScript: Understanding the Weird Parts - The First 3.5 Hours
videos.s: The first 3.5 hours of Tony Alicea's Udemy course on JavaScript's inner workings, covering topics such as first-class functions, closures, prototypal inheritance and how the language behaves under the hood.
videos.w: HN commenters call it one of the best JavaScript courses: rigorous and deep but not boring, and freely available.
videos.q: they are the holy grails of online education for me. Rigorous -- but not boring or too long.

videos.t: Was YOUR vote counted? (feat. homomorphic encryption) - Numberphile
videos.s: Numberphile interviews cryptographer Ron Rivest about end-to-end verifiable voting. He explains how homomorphic encryption and receipts let a voter confirm their ballot was counted without being able to prove how they voted to anyone else.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it in election-security threads as an accessible explainer of how a vote can be verifiable but not sellable.
videos.q: Cryptographers are clever and have figured out a way to let you know your vote was counted without being able to prove it to a third party!

videos.t: 1959 Chevrolet Bel Air vs. 2009 Chevrolet Malibu IIHS crash test
videos.s: A one-minute IIHS demonstration crash test of a 1959 Chevrolet Bel Air against a 2009 Chevrolet Malibu, showing how much better the modern car protects its occupants.
videos.w: The go-to demonstration in car-safety debates that old cars were not better, showing crumple zones and a rigid passenger cell at work.
videos.q: I always liked this IIHS crash test: 1959 Chevrolet Bel Air vs. 2009 Chevrolet Malibu It really shows the progress.

videos.t: Don't Be the Last Person to Die
videos.s: CGP Grey argues that aging and death are a problem worth defeating, using a short animated essay. It is part of a pair with a follow-up from Kurzgesagt.
videos.w: HN longevity fans point to it as a concise, fun statement of the case for fighting aging, and some say it changed their minds.
videos.q: CGP gray's videos on YouTube are maybe the most concise and fun to watch materials I've seen on the subject.

videos.t: Economics of Nuclear Reactor
videos.s: A professor from Illinois compares the cost of building, fueling and operating a nuclear plant against a natural gas plant, using visual charts. It shows how construction time and interest rates dominate, when the investment pays off and when costs cross over.
videos.w: It is the go-to short primer HN commenters cite to explain why nuclear is expensive upfront but cheap to run once the construction debt is paid.
videos.q: His videos are great. Worth your time.

videos.t: Why I changed my mind about nuclear power | Michael Shellenberger | TEDxBerlin
videos.s: In this TEDxBerlin talk, environmental activist Michael Shellenberger explains why he changed from opposing nuclear power to advocating it, after looking at the evidence on Chernobyl, Fukushima and air pollution.
videos.w: Frequently linked in nuclear-power threads as an eye-opening pro-nuclear argument from a former anti-nuclear activist.
videos.q: This is a self-professed anti-nuclear hippy giving a talk about how rationally looking at chernobyl and fukushima made him a nuclear power advocate.

videos.t: Feynman: How to think 1 of 2  FUN TO IMAGINE 11
videos.s: An excerpt from the 1983 BBC series Fun to Imagine in which Richard Feynman describes how he and a mathematician friend counted in their heads in different ways, one verbally and one visually. It shows that people can reach the same goal through quite different mental methods.
videos.w: HN points to it constantly in threads on inner monologue, visual versus verbal thinking and communication as the classic, entertaining demonstration that minds work differently.
videos.q: He does a great job of communicating this, despite our interpretive differences.

videos.t: Hello World - Machine Learning Recipes #1
videos.s: The first episode of Google's Machine Learning Recipes series. It introduces machine learning and builds a first supervised-learning classifier in about six lines of Python using scikit-learn.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an approachable first step into machine learning for programmers, with an apples-vs-oranges classifier.
videos.q: Very approachable! The first lesson is a classifier to separate apples and oranges.

videos.t: Revolutionary Paint: How to Make Surfaces Stay Cool in the Sun
videos.s: Tech Ingredients shows how to make a homemade radiative cooling paint, with a custom liquid panel that cools below ambient temperature outdoors. The video covers the materials and how to apply the paint.
videos.w: HN points to it as an impressive, hands-on DIY demonstration of passive radiative cooling that works in practice.
videos.q: Great video about making home-made high reflectivity paint

videos.t: Amazing Invention- This Drone Will Change Everything
videos.s: Mark Rober visits Zipline and looks at its autonomous delivery drones, including medical and blood deliveries in Rwanda. He demonstrates how the drones' propeller design and cable-lowered delivery pod make them quiet and precise.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as the clearest look at Zipline's real-world drone operations, especially for medical delivery and the solved noise problem.
videos.q: They actually solved that. Watch Mark Robers video at 13m50s

videos.t: 31 Hamming, Learning to Learn: You and Your Research, 6 June 1995
videos.c: Hamming on Hamming: Learning to Learn
videos.s: The final lecture of Richard Hamming's Learning to Learn course, from 1995, based on his well-known talk 'You and Your Research'. It covers how to do important work and build a career.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as the capstone of Hamming's course and as career advice about working on important problems.
videos.q: It's the last lecture in a wonderful 31-lecture course

videos.t: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown's visual walkthrough of the attention mechanism inside transformers, covering self-attention, multiple heads and cross-attention. It is chapter 6 of his deep learning series.
videos.w: HN treats it as the go-to visual explanation of attention, recommended to people who find text-based transformer explainers hard to follow.
videos.q: what bade me finally understand the transformer architecture [0] and attention [1], are 3Blue1Brown's videos.

videos.t: How an Atomic Clock Really Works: Inside the HP 5061A Cesium Clock
videos.s: CuriousMarc powers up a vintage HP 5061A cesium beam clock and explains both the quantum principle and the HP implementation in detail. It is part of a longer atomic clock series.
videos.w: HN calls it one of the best explanations of how atomic clocks actually work.
videos.q: I've yet to see a description better than in CuriousMarc's HP 5061A series

videos.t: Crash Course - The SMIDSY
videos.s: A motorcycle safety video on the SMIDSY (sorry mate, I didn't see you) accident, explaining the perception and optical illusion that makes drivers fail to see riders, and how riders can spot the signs and avoid it.
videos.w: HN considers it an outstanding explanation of why drivers miss motorcycles and cyclists, linked in threads on visibility and junction crashes.
videos.q: This is an outstanding vid on the whole subject illustrating the problem and some avoidance methods.

videos.t: The Insane Battle To Sabotage a New Apartment Building Explains San Francisco's Housing Crisis
videos.s: ReasonTV tells the story of Bob Tillman, who spent nearly five years and $1.4 million trying to convert his San Francisco laundromat into apartments. It walks through the permitting, appeals and neighborhood opposition he faced.
videos.w: It is HN's go-to concrete example of how local regulation and NIMBYism block new housing in San Francisco and California.
videos.q: Here is a terrific video that everyone should watch that shows how insanely difficult it is to make affordable housing.

videos.t: The Truth about Hydrogen
videos.s: Real Engineering examines the efficiency of hydrogen as an energy carrier. It follows production, storage and fuel cell conversion losses and compares hydrogen cars with battery electric vehicles.
videos.w: HN links it in hydrogen threads as a clear breakdown of why compounded inefficiencies make hydrogen a poor fit for cars, though one commenter calls it outdated.
videos.q: This video gives a good breakdown on how the inefficiencies in hydrogen fuel cell based cars add up.

videos.t: Autonomous Testing and the Future of Software Development - Will Wilson
videos.s: Will Wilson explains autonomous testing: using deterministic simulation and fuzzing, building on FoundationDB's approach, to test software continuously. It sets out the ideas behind his later company Antithesis.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an excellent talk on generalizing deterministic simulation testing, and Antithesis hiring posts link it to explain the work.
videos.q: I would encourage you to listen to Will Wilson’s excellent talk on the subject of Autonomous Testing

videos.t: Richard Feynman talks about light
videos.s: A PBS clip in which Richard Feynman explains the strange nature of light and electromagnetic radiation. He conveys how little of it we actually see and how radio waves are present everywhere.
videos.w: Recommended as an entertaining, accessible way to get a feel for light and electric fields.
videos.q: I highly recommend you watch this video of Feynman explaining light

videos.t: Danny Carey | "Pneuma" by Tool (LIVE IN CONCERT)
videos.s: Drummer Danny Carey performs Tool's 'Pneuma' live in Boston, in a Vic Firth session with close views of his playing.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a showcase of astonishing drumming and music that gives chills.
videos.q: here's Danny Carey, quite possibly the greatest living drummer

videos.t: Emacs For Writers
videos.s: Science writer Jay Dixit explains how he uses Emacs as a non-programmer to write, edit and research more productively. He shows his plain-text writing workflow and what led him from tools like Scrivener to Emacs.
videos.w: Recommended as a favorite talk showing Emacs as a writing environment rather than just a programmer's editor.
videos.q: My favourite talk on this topic is "Emacs for writers

videos.t: "Finding bugs without running or even looking at code" by Jay Parlar
videos.s: Jay Parlar's Strange Loop talk shows how model checkers such as Alloy can find complex bugs in a system's design without running or reading any code. He walks through modeling architectures and checking every possible sequence of operations, including a real security bug and a UI feature-interaction bug.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as the best practical introduction to Alloy and to lightweight formal modeling.
videos.q: There is a talk that gives a good overview on Alloy and how useful using something like this is

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #606 - Randall Carlson
videos.s: A three-hour Joe Rogan podcast with Randall Carlson, builder and geomythologist, on catastrophic geological events, cosmic impacts and climate at the end of the last glacial period.
videos.w: Commenters in climate and impact-event threads send people to Carlson's Rogan appearances for his account of ancient cataclysms.
videos.q: he gives an enthralling account of the climate events at the time.

videos.t: How Do Nuclear Submarines Make Oxygen?- Smarter Every Day 251
videos.s: A Smarter Every Day episode from aboard a nuclear submarine on how the crew makes breathable air. It covers oxygen generation from seawater, oxygen candles and CO2 scrubbing with amine.
videos.w: Go-to link when oxygen candles, CO2 capture or submarine air quality come up.
videos.q: Smarter Every Day did an interesting series of videos about nuclear submarines.

videos.t: Fight of the Century: Keynes vs. Hayek - Economics Rap Battle Round Two
videos.s: A hip-hop music video from EconStories in which Keynes and Hayek rap-battle over how to handle recessions and government spending. It is the second round after the first rap battle.
videos.w: Offered as a quick, entertaining primer on Keynesian versus Austrian economics, especially for newcomers to Hayek.
videos.q: this throwback to the 2008 crisis is an easily consumed primer on Keynes vs Hayek

videos.t: The real story behind Wayland and X
videos.s: X.Org developer Daniel Stone explains the history and technical limits of the X Window System and why Wayland was created, debunking myths from forum comments. He covers topics such as network transparency and blocking calls.
videos.w: HN uses it as the go-to answer to claims that Wayland is unnecessary, from a developer who knew X's codebase well.
videos.q: It is quite fun and eye opening, he clearly knows his subject better than most of the comments.

videos.t: "We Really Don't Know How to Compute!" - Gerald Sussman (2011)
videos.s: Gerald Sussman's 2011 Strange Loop keynote argues we still do not know how to compute, comparing biological systems with how we program machines. It touches on propagators, constraint programming and robustness.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a mind-expanding talk on rethinking programming, and cite it in threads on propagators, constraints and brittleness.
videos.q: it made me question my views on what I think programming is

videos.t: CppCon 2015: Herb Sutter "Writing Good C++14... By Default"
videos.s: Herb Sutter's CppCon 2015 plenary on writing safe, modern C++ by default using the C++ Core Guidelines. It includes a demo of lifetime-checking static analysis tooling.
videos.w: HN cites it in C++ versus Rust safety debates for its lifetime profile demo, and recommends it as a modern C++ talk.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Take a look at Herb Sutter's CppCon talk this year

videos.t: John Cleese vs Extremism
videos.s: A two-minute John Cleese monologue showing the pathology of extremism, explaining why it feels good and how it drives out moderates.
videos.w: Shared in heated-discussion threads as a short, witty take on why extremism is appealing.
videos.q: is delightful and well worth the two minutes it takes to watch

videos.t: Golang UK Conf. 2016 - Liz Rice - What is a container, really? Let's write one in Go from scratch
videos.s: Liz Rice builds a container from scratch in about 100 lines of Go, showing that a container is not a lightweight VM but a set of Linux kernel features and flags.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible way to remove the magic from Docker and understand how containers work.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: have given talks on how to make containers from scratch that are very illuminating

videos.t: React.js Conf 2015 - Immutable Data and React
videos.s: Lee Byron of Facebook explains how persistent immutable data structures work and how to use them in React apps with Immutable.js. He covers memoization benefits and avoiding coupling through shared mutable state.
videos.w: HN points to it as a clear explanation of immutable data structures such as tries, and of the case for immutability with React and Flux.
videos.q: there's a great conference talk on this topic by Lee Byron from Facebook

videos.t: Why Russia is Invading Ukraine
videos.s: RealLifeLore explains with maps why Russia invaded Ukraine, focusing on energy resources, security buffers, Black Sea access and Crimea's strategic value.
videos.w: HN users shared it during the early 2022 invasion as a clear, map-driven overview of Russia's economic and strategic motives.
videos.q: is an excellent overview of the history that lead to this moment

videos.t: Replace Your Exploit-Ridden Firmware with Linux - Ronald Minnich, Google
videos.s: Ronald Minnich of Google explains how UEFI firmware is a large closed attack surface and describes Google's work replacing it with Linux-based boot firmware. It also touches on Intel ME and other security coprocessors.
videos.w: Recommended as the go-to talk on firmware security risks, Intel ME, and why replacing UEFI with Linux speeds up and hardens boot.
videos.q: Absolutely fantastic video from a google engineer

videos.t: Andrew Kelley: A Practical Guide to Applying Data Oriented Design (DoD)
videos.s: Andrew Kelley, creator of Zig, presents practical data-oriented design techniques for shrinking memory footprint and making programs cache friendly. He ends with a case study of how these ideas sped up the Zig compiler.
videos.w: HN cites it as one of the best talks on data-oriented design, applying struct-of-arrays and compact data layouts to a real compiler.
videos.q: A good introduction to SoA (for anyone curious) are the two most famous Data-Oriented Design talks

videos.t: BOLTR: DYSON HAIR DRYER. Is it WORTH the MONEY?
videos.s: AvE tears down a roughly $500 Dyson hair dryer, examining how its motor, airflow and electronics fit into a small body. He runs tests along the way and ultimately decides whether the engineering justifies the price.
videos.w: HN points to it as a favorite teardown, usually when discussing Dyson or how products are engineered and built, with some noting the host was impressed by the engineering.
videos.q: He was expecting to ridicule it but was instead blown away by the engineering

videos.t: i3wm: Jump Start (1/3)
videos.s: First of a three-part tutorial series on the i3 tiling window manager for Linux. It explains what i3 is, how to install it on Ubuntu, and how to use it.
videos.w: HN commenters call it the best i3 tutorial on YouTube and recommend it for getting started thoroughly.
videos.q: I highly recommend this 3-part video series from Code Cast

videos.t: Turning Earth Into a Telescope | The Terrascope
videos.s: David Kipping presents his proposed Terrascope, a telescope that uses Earth's atmosphere as a lens to achieve enormous magnification. He covers the history of telescopes and his path to the idea, plus Sol-scope and Jupiter-scope variants.
videos.w: HN people point to it as an excellent explanation of using Earth's atmosphere or gravity as a lens in astronomy threads.
videos.q: An excellent video on this

videos.t: re:publica 2015 - Aral Balkan: Beyond The Camera Panopticon
videos.s: Aral Balkan's re:publica 2015 talk argues that people are the product of surveillance-based business models. It makes an ethical case against data monopolies and for privacy as a human right.
videos.w: Recommended as a forceful statement of the privacy case, though some commenters found its tone elitist and politically charged.
videos.q: All in all, this is a great talk, I highly recommend you watch from start.

videos.t: Greg Young - CQRS and Event Sourcing - Code on the Beach 2014
videos.s: Greg Young's Code on the Beach 2014 talk on CQRS and event sourcing. He argues mature domains are built on facts that occurred rather than current state, and covers the business and technical benefits.
videos.w: HN developers recommend it as the talk that changed how they model systems, and as a clear intro to event sourcing's motivations.
videos.q: forever changed how I think about modeling systems, preserving history

videos.t: SQLite: The Database at the Edge of the Network with Dr. Richard Hipp
videos.s: SQLite creator Richard Hipp gives a history of SQLite and explains where it shines as a database at the edge of the network with no DBA. He covers long-term support, testing and how it is used in products.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an enthusiastic, funny talk straight from the creator, and cites it for facts like the name's pronunciation and Airbus support.
videos.q: I highly recommend to watch it, if only to get a sense of the smart and funny energy that Dr Richard Hipp puts off!

videos.t: Cassettes - better than you don't remember
videos.s: Techmoan's beginner introduction to the compact cassette, testing metal tapes and Dolby S noise reduction on a Sony TC-S1 deck. He checks whether a cassette can sound close to a CD when good tape and equipment are used.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever cassette quality comes up, as proof that cassettes sound good with decent gear, metal tape and Dolby noise reduction.
videos.q: They are more than capable of sounding great with the right tools.

videos.t: Worst Nuclear Accidents in History
videos.s: Kurzgesagt compares how many people nuclear accidents have killed against other energy sources. It walks through the worst nuclear accidents and puts their death tolls in context per unit of energy.
videos.w: HN uses it as a short, well-sourced overview showing that fossil fuels kill far more people than nuclear power.
videos.q: I really recommend watching this short video which gives a really excellent overview

videos.t: How To Be Alone
videos.s: An animated short film of Tanya Davis's spoken-word poem 'How To Be Alone', illustrated by Andrea Dorfman. It gently argues that being alone can be embraced and enjoyed.
videos.w: HN commenters point lonely people to it as a moving, comforting piece of art about getting comfortable with solitude.
videos.q: I think it nicely captures the sentiment of doing things alone.

videos.t: 7 Minutes of Terror: The Challenges of Getting to Mars
videos.s: NASA JPL engineers explain the final minutes of the Curiosity rover's entry, descent and landing on Mars, which combined aerobraking, a parachute and a skycrane. It lays out the tight sequence of events that all had to work automatically.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as an awe-inspiring example of engineering problem solving and the go-to explainer on how Mars landings work.
videos.q: If you have not watched the seven minutes of terror video produced by NASA, you absolutely must.

videos.t: The lamps you're not allowed to have.  Exploring the Dubai lamps
videos.s: Big Clive tears down the Dubai lamp, a Philips LED bulb developed with Dubai's ruler for maximum efficiency and long life. He examines its construction and circuitry, including underrun LEDs and many filament strips.
videos.w: HN points to it as proof that efficient, long-lived LED bulbs can be built and as an example of well-designed lamps.
videos.q: Check out the dubai lamp to see a lamp designed to be efficient and last

videos.t: 13TH | FULL FEATURE | Netflix
videos.s: Ava DuVernay's Oscar-nominated documentary on how the history of racial inequality in the US, from slavery through the 13th Amendment's exception clause, drives mass incarceration. It combines archival footage with testimony from activists and scholars.
videos.w: HN commenters strongly recommend it as a clear examination of structural racism in the criminal justice system and the war on drugs, and note it is free to watch.
videos.q: This documentary is an absolute must-watch

videos.t: Why Not Just: Think of AGI Like a Corporation?
videos.s: Robert Miles asks whether corporations can be thought of as artificial general superintelligences and how far the analogy holds. He argues the differences, such as being limited by employees' capabilities, matter for AI safety.
videos.w: HN points to it as an accessible rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just corporate risk.
videos.q: He presents the material in a very interesting and accessible way.

videos.t: Is SpaceX's Raptor engine the king of rocket engines?
videos.s: Everyday Astronaut explains the basic physics of rocket engines, the main engine cycles and fuel types, then compares SpaceX's methane-fueled full-flow staged combustion Raptor to other engines. It runs nearly 50 minutes with chapter markers.
videos.w: HN commenters send people here as the best accessible starting point for understanding why Raptor and fuel choice matter for Starship.
videos.q: A great place to start is this amazing video by The Everyday Astronaut

videos.t: Stuart Halloway - Narcissistic Design
videos.s: Stuart Halloway's satirical talk describes how to protect yourself from industry change by spreading complexity through systems while following idiomatic practice. It uses this inversion to catalog software design anti-patterns.
videos.w: HN commenters love it as a witty and insightful tour of design anti-patterns, applicable to DSLs, OOP and API design.
videos.q: a great talk by Stuart Halloway called Narcissistic Design.

videos.t: Electron transport chain
videos.s: A short Harvard Online animated lesson on how the mitochondrial electron transport chain works. It shows proton pumping and the machinery that drives ATP synthesis.
videos.w: HN commenters share it to show how cells work as nanoscale machines, which many find mind-blowing.
