videos.q: To get a flavour of the nanomachine aspect of it all, check out this video on electron transport across membranes

videos.t: GET LAMP: The Text Adventure Documentary
videos.s: Jason Scott discusses making his documentary GET LAMP at a Google Tech Talk and screens part of the film. It covers the history of text adventures and interactive fiction, with interviews of Infocom developers and others.
videos.w: HN recommends it to anyone interested in text adventures, Infocom, MUDs and early computer gaming history.
videos.q: Recommend watching “Get lamp” documentary to fans of MUDs, text adventures

videos.t: Preface | MIT Calculus Revisited: Single Variable Calculus
videos.s: The preface to Herb Gross's MIT OpenCourseWare 'Calculus Revisited: Single Variable Calculus', an older black-and-white lecture series. It introduces his approach to teaching calculus from the basics.
videos.w: HN recommends Herb Gross as an unusually clear teacher whose explanations make calculus click for people who struggled elsewhere.
videos.q: The way he explains things just clicked, after numerous failed attempts to learn from other sources.

videos.t: [AUDIO FIXED] The Truth Cannot be Sexist - Steven Pinker on the biology of sex differences
videos.s: An excerpt of the 2005 Harvard debate in which Steven Pinker gives his prepared case on biological sex differences and the under-representation of women in science. It covers cross-cultural patterns in preferences and abilities and the overlap between male and female distributions.
videos.w: Pointed to repeatedly in gender-in-tech threads, especially around the Google memo, as a science-based treatment of sex differences.
videos.q: I found it to be an excellent pre-existing discussion of the merits of the memo.

videos.t: Simon Peyton Jones: Data Parallel Haskell
videos.s: Simon Peyton Jones explains nested data parallelism and Data Parallel Haskell, an approach to exploiting multicore and distributed hardware while keeping a simple single-control-flow programming model.
videos.w: Recommended as a fascinating look at easy parallelism abstractions, though other commenters note the approach never beat sequential C by much.
videos.q: a promising language abstraction to do hard things with parallelism relatively easily

videos.t: A New Way to look at Networking
videos.s: Van Jacobson's 2006 Google Tech Talk on rethinking networking around named content instead of host-to-host conversations. He recounts packet-networking history and lays out the content-centric networking idea that later became NDN.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as an inspiring talk behind content-addressed designs like IPFS, Urbit and immutable URLs.
videos.q: amazing and inspiring Google Talk video from 2006

videos.t: The Map of Mathematics
videos.s: An animated 11-minute tour of the whole field of mathematics as a single map, showing how pure and applied math and their sub-fields relate to each other.
videos.w: Recommended to people asking how to self-learn math as a quick bird's-eye overview of the field.
videos.q: I suggest this "Map of mathematics" as a starting point that gives you a reasonable birds-eye view of the field.

videos.t: I Misunderstood the Greenhouse Effect. Here's How It Works.
videos.s: Sabine Hossenfelder explains how the greenhouse effect actually works, given that infrared is mostly absorbed low in the atmosphere already. She walks through why more CO2 still warms the surface.
videos.w: Recommended as an accessible, nuanced explanation of the mechanics of global warming, including the saturation puzzle.
videos.q: this video explains the mechanics of global warming in a way anybody can understand.

videos.t: Facebook Fraud
videos.s: Veritasium argues that Facebook's ad revenue relies partly on fake likes, after paying to promote his page and gaining tens of thousands of followers in developing countries who never engaged. He shares his experiment and cites other cases.
videos.w: Frequently cited as the source for claims about click farms and fake likes in Facebook advertising, though some argue its methodology was flawed.
videos.q: See a real live experiment someone did, to figure out the true reach and ROI on Facebook Advertizing.

videos.t: The Road to PS5
videos.s: PS5 lead system architect Mark Cerny gives a deep dive into the PS5's architecture, covering its SSD, I/O, audio and design goals. He explains how removing bottlenecks shapes future games.
videos.w: HN treats it as required viewing for understanding the PS5's SSD and architecture beyond raw specs.
videos.q: IMO required viewing for any dev to form a more informed opinion on the SSD tech.

videos.t: This Is Water by David Foster Wallace Full Speech
videos.s: David Foster Wallace's 2005 commencement speech at Kenyon College, about the default settings of the mind, choosing what to pay attention to, and what we end up worshipping.
videos.w: HN people point lost, lonely or burned-out readers to it as a short, humane piece of perspective on how to live.
videos.q: I highly recommend a 23 minute investment in David Foster Wallace's

videos.t: Civilizations at the End of Time: Iron Stars
videos.s: An Isaac Arthur episode on civilizations in the far future, past the Black Hole Era. It covers iron stars, Boltzmann brains, reversible computing and the idea of reversing entropy.
videos.w: HN recommends Isaac Arthur as an entry point for far-future and thermodynamic-endgame questions.
videos.q: My go-to entry point for exploring those kinds of questions was Isaac Arthur.

videos.t: Breaking The Creepy AI in Police Cameras
videos.s: Benn Jordan explains how Flock Safety's license plate cameras log and share vehicle locations, and explores how adversarial AI can defeat them. It covers weak security and the surveillance risks of private police-camera networks.
videos.w: HN treats it as the go-to overview of Flock's problems, and cites it in nearly every Flock thread.
videos.q: Benn Jordan did a great video on this.

videos.t: Linus Torvalds on why desktop Linux sucks
videos.s: Excerpts from Linus Torvalds's DebConf 14 talk on why desktop Linux struggles. He covers application distribution, distros breaking backwards compatibility, wasted package management effort and how Windows does app distribution better.
videos.w: Cited constantly in Flatpak, packaging and ABI-compatibility debates as Linus's blunt, insightful take on shipping software for Linux.
videos.q: Linus Torvalds explains it perfectly

videos.t: Why Tipping Should Be Banned - Adam Ruins Everything
videos.s: An Adam Ruins Everything segment arguing that tipping should be banned. It covers the history of tipping, its weak link to service quality, and why employers should pay a fair wage.
videos.w: Recommended in tipping threads as a fast, entertaining, sourced case against tipping culture.
videos.q: is worth watching if you are of the school of thought that tipping is bad

videos.t: The End of Suburbia - 52 minute documentary on peak oil
videos.s: A 52-minute short version of the documentary The End of Suburbia, about peak oil and the end of cheap energy. It argues that American suburbs depend on cheap oil and may become the slums of the future.
videos.w: Recommended in threads on suburbs, energy and urbanism as an entertaining, if biased, case for suburbia's dependence on cheap oil.
videos.q: It's entertaining and, IMO, well worth watching even if you disagree with some of the people they interview

videos.t: a better way to count
videos.s: jan Misali presents an humorous but earnest case for counting in base 6 (seximal) instead of base 10 or 12, comparing the arithmetic advantages of each.
videos.w: HN points to it as a funny, convincing take on number bases whenever dozenal or base 6 comes up.
videos.q: This video convinced me that base 6 would be even better for simple pen-and-paper math

videos.t: The Voting System That Gives You Two Votes
videos.s: CGP Grey explains Mixed-Member Proportional representation, the system used in New Zealand where voters get two votes. It covers how it differs from first-past-the-post.
videos.w: It is the go-to short explainer HN links when voting system alternatives, MMP or German-style elections come up.
videos.q: CGP Grey has a great video on it

videos.t: John Wiegley: Putting Lenses to Work
videos.s: John Wiegley's BayHac 2017 talk walks through Haskell lenses by example, showing many practical uses beyond simple record access. It is aimed at people who want to become productive with the lens library.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the fastest way to learn lenses by example, with far-out examples later on.
videos.q: you can learn enough lens to be productive in 1 hours with this talk without reading docs at all

videos.t: But what is a Fourier series?  From heat flow to drawing with circles | DE4
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown introduces Fourier series, from the heat equation to drawing arbitrary shapes with rotating circles. It builds a visual intuition for decomposing functions into sine waves.
videos.w: Recommended as the visual explanation that makes Fourier series and transforms click, even for laypeople.
videos.q: Helped click that there is a perfect visual analogy to the deconstruction of complex audio to sine waves.

videos.t: Twenty Minutes of Reasons to Use the RemedyBG Debugger
videos.s: Casey Muratori gives a fast tour of the RemedyBG debugger for Windows, which he uses daily. He shows its speed and features, especially the watch window.
videos.w: HN points to it as a demonstration of what fast, well-built developer tooling looks like and of why a debugger beats print statements.
videos.q: Here's Casey Muratori demonstrating all the way in which RemedyBG rocks.

videos.t: Learn music theory in half an hour.
videos.s: Andrew Huang teaches the basics of music theory in about half an hour, covering intervals, chords and patterns. He stresses understanding how music works over memorizing terminology.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a concise, approachable starting point for anyone asking how to learn music theory.
videos.q: I found this video to be an extremely helpful and concise explanation of music theory basics

videos.t: Introduction: The Chemical History of a Candle by Michael Faraday (1/6)
videos.s: Bill Hammack of engineerguy introduces his series on Michael Faraday's lectures on The Chemical History of a Candle. He describes the free companion book and the commentary and caption features that help modern viewers.
videos.w: Praised as a masterpiece of science education that recreates Faraday's demonstrations.
videos.q: is a masterpiece in science education.

videos.t: Ross's Game Dungeon: Deus Ex
videos.s: Ross Scott's Game Dungeon episode on Deus Ex, a long review of the game covering its narrative, politics and economic philosophy as well as its design.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a deeper look at Deus Ex's themes, and as the best essay on its politics and economics.
videos.q: For a deeper discussion, I can only recommend Ross Scott's review of the game

videos.t: Emacs Rocks! Episode 17: Magit
videos.s: A three-minute Emacs Rocks screencast demonstrating Magit, the Git interface inside Emacs, including staging and other everyday operations.
videos.w: HN users share it as the quick demo that shows what Magit can do, for people unfamiliar with it.
videos.q: I always share this demo with people to show off just a tiny portion of what it's capable of doing

videos.t: Clickbait is Unreasonably Effective
videos.s: Veritasium explains why clickbait titles and thumbnails work, how he tests them, and why educational creators feel pushed to use them. He classifies types of clickbait and discusses the trade-offs.
videos.w: HN cites it whenever YouTube titles and thumbnails come up, both to defend creators and to criticize the drift toward clickbait.
videos.q: Derek of Veritaseum made a video laying out why "clickbait-y" titles like that are necessary, and I feel like it makes a pretty good case.

videos.t: 4.5 Billion Years in 1 Hour
videos.s: Kurzgesagt's hour-long animated film that compresses Earth's 4.5 billion year history into one hour, roughly a million years per second. It follows the evolution of life through to humanity's tiny final stretch.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for the sense of perspective it gives on deep time and how brief human history is.
videos.q: This video puts things into perspective, mapping the whole of 4.5B years of Earth history to 1 hour

videos.t: The Golden Ratio (why it is so irrational) - Numberphile
videos.s: Numberphile's Ben Sparks shows why the golden ratio is the most irrational number, using seeds, continued fractions and rational approximations. He also explains why plants use it for spacing leaves and seeds.
videos.w: HN calls it illuminating for explaining why phi is the most irrational number, relevant to hashing, spirals and phyllotaxis.
videos.q: a mind-rewiring video by numberphile concerning the golden ratio [0] made sense of all the spiral overlay art

videos.t: Real Analysis, Lecture 1: Constructing the Rational Numbers
videos.s: The first lecture of Francis Su's Harvey Mudd real analysis course, covering the construction of the rational numbers. It begins a full lecture series that follows a standard analysis text.
videos.w: HN people recommend Su's lectures for building real analysis intuition, citing his phenomenal teaching style.
videos.q: his teaching style is phenomenal

videos.t: Triangle of Power
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown presents the Triangle of Power, an alternate notation that unifies powers, logarithms and roots in a single triangular symbol. The video shows how the inverse operations relate and how the notation could help.
videos.w: HN points to it in notation debates as a clean visual demonstration that exponents, logs and roots are three views of one relationship.
videos.q: My favorite new math notation is the triangle of power

videos.t: How Prince of Persia Defeated Apple II's Memory Limitations | War Stories | Ars Technica
videos.s: In an Ars Technica War Stories episode, Prince of Persia creator Jordan Mechner describes how he made the game on the Apple II, fighting hardware memory limits and the platform's decline. It covers the rotoscoped animation and the engineering tricks involved.
videos.w: Repeatedly called essential viewing for game development history and clever work under memory constraints.
videos.q: Essential viewing for anyone interested in game development history.

videos.t: "Clean" Code, Horrible Performance
videos.s: Casey Muratori shows how typical 'clean code' object-oriented patterns can cost large factors in performance. He benchmarks them against simpler data-oriented code.
videos.w: A frequent citation in debates about SOLID and Clean Code, representing the performance-first side of the argument.
videos.q: Look at Casey Murrey's Clean Code horrible performance youtube video

videos.t: Operation InfeKtion: How Russia Perfected the Art of War | NYT Opinion
videos.s: A New York Times Opinion documentary tracing Soviet and KGB disinformation, from the 1980s AIDS origin hoax to modern campaigns like Pizzagate. It features former KGB officers and the people who tried to counter the lies.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a clear explanation of how disinformation campaigns work and where today's tactics came from.
videos.q: This New York Times video explains it very well

videos.t: Doomed: The Embers of Amiga FPS
videos.s: A documentary by Stuart Brown (XboxAhoy) on the history of first-person shooters on the Amiga and how Doom's arrival affected the platform.
videos.w: Recommended as a well-researched piece of computing history on Amiga FPS games and Doom's impact.
videos.q: go watch Stuart Brown (aka XboxAhoy)'s excellent documentary on FPS on the Amiga

videos.t: DEF CON 19 - Moxie Marlinspike - SSL And The Future Of Authenticity
videos.s: Moxie Marlinspike's DEF CON 19 talk on the weaknesses of SSL and the certificate authority system. He explains how CA trust became a problem and proposes an alternative that removes the CA oligopoly without reducing security.
videos.w: HN points to it as the classic overview of why TLS certificate trust is flawed, and it resurfaces whenever CA or HTTPS security comes up.
videos.q: I've found Moxie Marlinspike's talk [1] to be a great overview of these sorts of issues.

videos.t: The Bell Curve
videos.s: Shaun's roughly 2.7-hour video essay on The Bell Curve. It covers intelligence, the g factor, IQ tests, IQ versus environment and the politics behind the book, with a critical reading of the sources.
videos.w: HN commenters most often cite it as a thorough, well-sourced debunking of The Bell Curve and of popular IQ claims.
videos.q: The video is well-researched; I've been a long-time fan of the creator for putting out quality stuff.

videos.t: Tearing Down the Model T of Our Time - Autoline After Hours 284
videos.s: An Autoline After Hours episode where Sandy Munro discusses his complete teardown of the BMW i3, along with automotive journalists. It covers the car's carbon fiber construction and manufacturing technology.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a fascinating look at the i3's revolutionary materials and production methods, and as a contrast point for Tesla.
videos.q: discussing the manufacturing tech within the i3; absolutely fascinating

videos.t: Renting vs. Buying a Home: The 5% Rule
videos.s: Ben Felix explains how to compare renting and buying a home by looking at unrecoverable costs, and distills it into the 5% rule of thumb. It is framed for a Canadian audience but broadly applicable.
videos.w: HN points to it for a clean first-order framework for the rent versus buy decision.
videos.q: This guy breaks down the analysis very cleanly to a first-order approximation, using 2019 figures

videos.t: Feynman: What things really are like FUN TO IMAGINE 1
videos.s: A clip from the 1983 BBC series Fun to Imagine in which Richard Feynman explains heat as the jiggling of atoms and how we perceive it as hot and cold.
videos.w: Recommended as a short, joyful example of Feynman's accessible way of explaining physics, which a transcript cannot capture.
videos.q: I really recommend them. You just can't capture his joy and passion with a transcript.

videos.t: How to Move the Sun: Stellar Engines
videos.s: Kurzgesagt explains stellar engines such as the Shkadov thruster and Caplan thruster, which could move the Sun and solar system across the galaxy over millions of years to avoid hazards and reach new regions.
videos.w: HN returns to it whenever moving the solar system, Kardashev civilizations or generation ships come up, with some calling it their favorite Kurzgesagt video.
videos.q: Out of every video Kurzgesagt has ever produced, my favorite is this one

videos.t: Design Patterns vs  Anti pattern in APL by Aaron W Hsu at FnConf17
videos.s: Aaron Hsu discusses design patterns and anti-patterns in APL and why the language is productive despite its write-only reputation. He argues that idioms matter more than libraries in array languages.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a terrific talk on APL readability and on the idea of idioms over libraries.
videos.q: On the readability of APL (terrific video)

videos.t: Dwarf Fortress Creator Explains its Complexity & Origins | Noclip Interview
videos.s: A /noclip interview with Tarn Adams of Bay 12 Games about Dwarf Fortress: where the ASCII simulation came from, how it works, and the plans for its Steam release. It includes his telling of the famous bug in which cats were poisoned by alcohol.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever Dwarf Fortress comes up, mainly for the alcohol-poisoned cats bug story and a developer's view of the game's depth.
videos.q: This interview with Tarn Adams (one of the creators of dwarf fortress) is amazing

videos.t: iPhone 1 - Steve Jobs MacWorld keynote in 2007 - Full Presentation, 80 mins
videos.s: The full 80-minute Macworld 2007 keynote in which Steve Jobs introduced the original iPhone. It includes the multitouch demos, visual voicemail and scrolling.
videos.w: Cited as a landmark tech presentation, especially for the audience's astonished reaction to touch scrolling and demo moments like visual voicemail.
videos.q: I consider AlphaGo - The Movie [1] to be a timeless classic that will never feel outdated.

videos.t: The mathematics of weight loss | Ruben Meerman | TEDxQUT (edited version)
videos.s: Ruben Meerman presents a TEDx talk on the stoichiometry of weight loss, showing with lab demonstrations where fat goes when it is lost. He argues that most of it is exhaled as carbon dioxide.
videos.w: HN regularly shares it in weight loss threads as a clear, precise explanation of the physics of weight loss.
videos.q: The mathematics of weight loss is laid out clearly in 20 minutes here

videos.t: How one tweet can ruin your life | Jon Ronson
videos.s: Jon Ronson's TED talk on public shaming on Twitter, centered on Justine Sacco and others whose lives were upended by online mobs. He argues we have become a baying crowd and should rethink how we treat each other online.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up in threads about online mobs and cancellation as a relevant talk by a journalist who interviewed shamed people.
videos.q: I'm reminded of this TED talk in these scenarios, by a journalist and author who interviewed many people who have been publicly shamed

videos.t: Dasher: information-efficient text entry
videos.s: David MacKay's 2007 Google Tech Talk presents Dasher, a text-entry system driven by continuous gestures and a language model, reaching about 35 words per minute with one finger and 25 hands-free. It explains the information-theory reasoning behind the design.
videos.w: Regarded as the seminal talk on Dasher, recommended in threads on accessible and alternative text input.
videos.q: Dasher is fantastic, because it's based on rock solid information theory, designed by the late David MacKay.

videos.t: Bitcoin - Unmasking Satoshi Nakamoto
videos.s: Barely Sociable presents a case that Bitcoin creator Satoshi Nakamoto is cryptographer Adam Back. It uses interview clips and circumstantial evidence, and also touches on the block size dispute.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a compelling, if not definitive, argument for Adam Back as Satoshi whenever the identity question comes up.
videos.q: painted quite a compelling story of why Adam Beck is Satoshi

videos.t: The A.I. Dilemma - March 9, 2023
videos.s: Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin of the Center for Humane Technology present why current AI capabilities pose catastrophic societal risks. They argue companies are racing to deploy without adequate safety, and that institutions must adapt. It was given before GPT-4's launch.
videos.w: Frequently recommended as the overview to get up to speed on AI risk, especially by people who valued The Social Dilemma.
videos.q: Here's a good overview to get up to speed

videos.t: Elm Europe 2017 - Evan Czaplicki - The life of a file
videos.s: Elm creator Evan Czaplicki's talk on how a file grows and when to split code up. He argues for keeping code in one file until it hurts and warns against premature extraction.
videos.w: Recommended as the argument for code colocation and delaying abstraction.
videos.q: Just stick everything in the same file until it actually hurts. This presentation[0] gets it right.

videos.t: Netflix JavaScript Talks - Async JavaScript with Reactive Extensions
videos.s: A Netflix JavaScript talk on using Reactive Extensions (Rx) for asynchronous UI code. It covers Observables, composing events such as drag and drop, and sequencing Ajax requests.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear, mind-changing introduction to observables and async programming from engineers using Rx in production.
videos.q: have a look at this presentation about Observables at Netflix as it's quite mind changing

videos.t: fr-08: .the .product by farbrausch | 64k intro (2000) (720p HQ demoscene demo)
videos.s: A recording of .the .product by Farbrausch, the first-place 64k intro at The Party 2000. It fits an 11-minute 3D demo with music into 64 kilobytes.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as the standard example of how much a tiny program can do, in contrast to bloated modern software.
videos.q: not very many 64Ks have reached the amazingness

videos.t: A NEW Trace! The FULL MH370 Story, so Far..
videos.s: Mentour Pilot's 56-minute account of the MH370 disappearance and what is now known, including the WSPR radio tracking technique and other sensing methods. It was made ahead of renewed search efforts.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a detailed, pilot's-eye summary of the whole MH370 story and the case for searching again.
videos.q: I highly recommend Mentour Pilots videos on the topic, for an indepth introduction to the whole story and the new search

videos.t: Marc Levoy - Lectures on Digital Photography - Lecture 1 (21mar16).mp4
videos.s: The first lecture in an 18-part series on digital photography from Marc Levoy's Stanford CS 178 course, recorded at Google in 2016. The series covers how digital cameras work and computational photography, with slides and assignments available on the course site.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a free, serious introduction to digital and computational photography from a professor who helped build the early Pixel cameras.
videos.q: It's short and fun, I recommend it to all HN readers.

videos.t: The Grille Trend that Kills 509 People per Year
videos.s: FortNine looks at the data on why newer pickup trucks with tall, blunt grilles kill so many pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists. It argues that lowering hood height would substantially cut fatalities.
videos.w: HN people cite it in threads on vehicle size and safety as a clear explanation tying grille height to deaths.
videos.q: This guy ties grill height directly to fatalities.

videos.t: End of Space – Creating a Prison for Humanity
videos.s: Kurzgesagt explains how accumulating space junk could trigger a collision cascade (Kessler syndrome) that makes launches too dangerous and traps humanity on Earth.
videos.w: The standard explainer HN links in satellite and debris threads for the collision-cascade risk.
videos.q: Kurzgesagt actually has a great video on the topic of space debris for anyone interested

videos.t: Immediate-Mode Graphical User Interfaces - 2005
videos.s: Casey Muratori's 2005 video introducing immediate-mode GUIs as an alternative to retained widget toolkits. He explains the motivation and shows minimal-state button logic.
videos.w: Seen as the origin of the IMGUI idea that inspired Dear ImGui, recommended to anyone curious about immediate-mode UI design.
videos.q: Check out this lecture/demo from nearly 20 years ago

videos.t: Bell's Theorem: The Quantum Venn Diagram Paradox
videos.s: MinutePhysics, with 3Blue1Brown, explains Bell's theorem using a Venn diagram paradox and polarizing filters. It shows why no local hidden variable theory can reproduce quantum correlations.
videos.w: Repeatedly recommended as the most accessible explanation of Bell's inequality, reducing it to a simple counting problem.
videos.q: did a two part collab that simplifies some of it down to a counting problem that'd be suitable for grade school.

videos.t: World's Roundest Object!
videos.s: Veritasium explains the effort to redefine the kilogram, which was still defined by a physical artifact, and how a near-perfect silicon sphere from the Avogadro project helps. It also covers the history of the unit's odd naming.
videos.w: Recommended in kilogram-redefinition threads as a clear, short explainer of the Avogadro and Planck approaches.
videos.q: this video is an imperative watch

videos.t: Nuclear 101: How Nuclear Bombs Work Part 1/2
videos.s: Harvard Belfer Center lecture by Matthew Bunn explaining how nuclear bombs work, including fission and fusion weapons and which parts of bomb-making are hard. It is part 1 of 2 in the Nuclear 101 series.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining, clear explanation of nuclear weapons basics from a policy expert.
videos.q: I highly recommend the "Nuclear 101: How Nuclear Bombs Work" lectures by Matthew Bunn

videos.t: Portable Air Conditioners - Why you shouldn't like them
videos.s: Technology Connections explains why single-hose portable air conditioners are inefficient and often a poor choice compared with window units. It details how the single hose pulls in warm outside air and wastes energy.
videos.w: The go-to recommendation to watch before buying a portable AC, cited in nearly every thread on cooling.
videos.q: If you are in the market for a portable AC I highly recommend you watch this video first

videos.t: A New Way to Achieve Nuclear Fusion: Helion
videos.s: Real Engineering's Brian McManus explains Helion's approach to nuclear fusion: colliding two plasma rings, compressing them magnetically, and capturing energy directly from the changing magnetic flux rather than boiling water. It covers why this pulsed design sidesteps problems of tokamaks and laser fusion.
videos.w: It is the go-to accessible explainer whenever HN discusses Helion or alternative fusion designs.
videos.q: I recommend you watch this excellent video by Real Engineering

videos.t: Datacenters Behaving Like Acoustic Weapons
videos.s: Benn Jordan investigates infrasound and low-frequency noise from data centers, including xAI's Colossus and a crypto mine, and reports his own experiments on the effects. The video covers the health and community impacts on nearby residents.
videos.w: Cited in data center siting debates as evidence that noise and infrasound can seriously affect people living nearby.
videos.q: an insightful, scary 30 min video covering the datacenter infrasound noise

videos.t: George Hotz: Hacking the Simulation & Learning to Drive with Neural Nets | Lex Fridman Podcast #132
videos.s: Lex Fridman interviews George Hotz, founder of Comma.ai, in a three-hour conversation. Topics include self-driving, Tesla and Waymo, crypto, GPT-3, immortality and book recommendations.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it as an entertaining, wide-ranging interview, and cite it for Hotz's views on end-to-end neural-net driving.
videos.q: Lots of topics covered: self-driving, immortality, UFOs, cryptocurrencies, Tesla/Waymo/OpenAI, GTP-3, AI, book recommendations.

videos.t: Stephen Wolfram's Introduction to the Wolfram Language
videos.s: Stephen Wolfram gives a 13-minute tour of the Wolfram Language, a symbolic, functional programming language with a built-in knowledgebase. He demos querying large datasets, interactivity and deployment.
videos.w: Commenters point to it as a compact, impressive demo of what the language can do.
videos.q: The demos are all pretty impressive

videos.t: It's Not About The Nail
videos.s: A two-minute comedy sketch in which a woman describes her problems while a visible nail sticks out of her head, and her partner keeps trying to fix it instead of listening. It dramatizes the gap between wanting empathy and being offered solutions.
videos.w: HN commenters link it as the quickest memorable illustration of listening versus problem-solving, and as shorthand in threads on empathy and support.
videos.q: This was the single most impactful thing I've ever been told to watch when it comes to 'solving' vs 'listening'.

videos.t: Animated Voting Methods
videos.s: An animated simulation comparing single-winner voting methods such as plurality, instant runoff and STAR. Colored regions show which candidate wins as a randomized electorate shifts across a two-dimensional political space, building on Ka-Ping Yee's earlier diagrams.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it in voting-reform threads as a visual argument that cardinal systems (STAR, approval) beat plurality and ranked-choice voting.
videos.q: I always recommend this pair of videos when discussing STAR voting vs other alternative systems.

videos.t: Dr. Satchin Panda on Time-Restricted Feeding and Its Effects on Obesity, Muscle Mass & Heart Health
videos.s: Rhonda Patrick interviews Salk Institute researcher Satchidananda Panda about circadian rhythms and the timing of food. They cover time-restricted feeding and its links to obesity, muscle mass, heart health, and light exposure.
videos.w: Recommended in threads on fasting and nutrition as a deep dive from the lead researcher on time-restricted eating.
videos.q: Dr. Panda goes into detail about fasting and coffee. Great podcast about fasting.

videos.t: Exposing Tether - Bitcoin's Biggest Secret
videos.s: Coffeezilla gives a comprehensive history of Tether, the stablecoin issued by a company controlled by the owners of Bitfinex. He lays out accusations that it is not fully backed.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the best single, entertaining overview of Tether's dubious history, and cite it when arguing Tether lacks real USD backing.
videos.q: one of the most comprehensive (and entertaining) takes on this

videos.t: Intrinsic Gravity by Still
videos.s: Intrinsic Gravity is a real-time demoscene production by Still, made with the Tooll tool for Under Construction 2014. It is a black-and-white op-art animation with a soundtrack by hoffman.
videos.w: HN people hold it up as a standout modern demo, praising its scene transitions and how it looks on 3D displays.
videos.q: It's lots of different scenes that transition beautifully from one to another

videos.t: How to crash an airplane – Nickolas Means | The Lead Developer UK 2016
videos.s: Nickolas Means tells the story of United Airlines Flight 232, which lost all flight control yet saved more than half its passengers. He draws lessons on teamwork, crew resource management and leadership for software teams.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a gripping case study whose lessons carry over to engineering management and safety.
videos.q: I watched a talk[1] by Nickolas Means recently that goes deeper into the events of that day and the lessons learned.

videos.t: introducing copyparty, the FOSS file server
videos.s: The author of copyparty introduces the FOSS file server he has built over five years, demoing its features such as resumable uploads, WebDAV and deduplication. The video itself is shown running on a demo server.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a model demo video and the quickest way to see how much one developer packed into a self-hosted file server.
videos.q: The launch video is well worth a quick watch

videos.t: Your Post Code Is the Directions, Not the Destination
videos.s: CGP Grey explains that postal codes are routing instructions for mail rather than geographic regions. He looks at the quirks and problems this causes.
videos.w: HN recommends it whenever zip codes, addresses or geospatial data come up, as a clear explanation of the hidden pattern in post codes.
videos.q: If you find this interesting and you haven't watched it, Go watch

videos.t: Best fan placement to move air through the house
videos.s: Matthias Wandel uses anemometer measurements to find where to place a fan to move the most air through a house at night. He finds that placing the fan some distance back from the window works better.
videos.w: Cited in cooling and fan-noise threads as a short video with actual data on fan placement.
videos.q: Matthias Wandel made a great video showing how it's better to place the fan a meter or two away from the window to get more air flow

videos.t: Flat Earth: A Measured Response
videos.s: hbomberguy investigates the modern flat earth movement and why people come to believe it. The video treats the community with a measured, humorous tone and looks at the social causes behind the belief.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an entertaining and thoughtful look at flat earthers that frames the belief as a distrust of failing institutions.
videos.q: I strongly recommend watching hbomberguy's video about flat earthers

videos.t: Domain Modeling Made Functional - Scott Wlaschin - KanDDDinsky 2019
videos.s: Scott Wlaschin shows how statically typed functional languages, using F# examples, can model a business domain so that invalid states cannot be represented. The type system acts almost like an instant unit test at compile time.
videos.w: HN treats it as the canonical, approachable example of domain-driven design with types and 'make invalid states unrepresentable'.
videos.q: this talk opened my eyes to the power of f# philosophy and type system

videos.t: .kkrieger - The FPS Game in 96KB (Full Gameplay)
videos.s: Full gameplay of .kkrieger, a first-person shooter by Farbrausch that fits into a 96KB executable by generating its textures, models and sounds procedurally.
videos.w: HN points to it as the standard example of procedural content generation and extreme size optimization in games.
videos.q: I suggest that you look at the result in awe

videos.t: Velocity 2012:  Richard Cook, "How Complex Systems Fail"
videos.s: Dr. Richard Cook, a physician and patient safety researcher, presents his ideas on how complex systems fail, at Velocity 2012. He argues for designing for resiliency rather than trying to exhaustively handle every failure mode.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as a must-watch for anyone running complex systems, and some rewatch it regularly to remember its principles.
videos.q: I would watch this talk every couple of months to remind myself of the principles.

videos.t: Ringing in Ears Tinnitus Treatment
videos.s: A short promotional video demonstrating a head-thumping technique that is claimed to relieve tinnitus. Covering the ears and tapping the back of the head is said to silence the ringing temporarily.
videos.w: Tinnitus sufferers share it as a free trick that briefly stops the ringing, though not as a cure.
videos.q: this trick helped me be in silence for the first time in decades.

videos.t: RSA ANIMATE: Language as a Window into Human Nature
videos.s: An RSA Animate in which Steven Pinker explains how the mind builds infinite meanings from finite language, and why people often speak indirectly. It covers ambiguity, politeness and mutual knowledge, including the emperor's new clothes example.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a short, clear explanation of why people avoid saying things explicitly and how common knowledge works socially and politically.
videos.q: this wonderful RSA Animate of Steve Pinker's discussion of how we use language

videos.t: Noam Chomsky: The five filters of the mass media machine | The Listening Post
videos.s: A short Al Jazeera animation narrated by Amy Goodman presenting Noam Chomsky's five filters of the mass media: ownership, advertising, media elite sourcing, flak and a common enemy. It is part of the MediaTheorised series.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a quick, accessible introduction to the propaganda model from Manufacturing Consent.
videos.q: Manufacturing Consent (there's a documentary form of it too) changed my entire outlook on media. Highly recommend.

videos.t: Super Pointy Sprint Missile - 0 to Mach 10 in 15 Seconds - 100Gs & 6000°F
videos.s: A short video on the US Sprint anti-ballistic missile, which accelerated to around Mach 10 in seconds under extreme g-forces and heat. It includes striking launch footage and a brief development history.
videos.w: Shared in hypersonic and missile threads as a compact, impressive overview of what Sprint achieved in the 1960s.
videos.q: It's a great overview of the development of the Sprint though, worth watching if it's of interest.

videos.t: Why is TV 29.97 frames per second?
videos.s: Matt Parker explains the history behind NTSC television running at 29.97 frames per second rather than 30, tracing it to the backward-compatible addition of color. He walks through the arithmetic behind the odd ratio.
videos.w: Go-to explanation whenever the strange 29.97 frame rate comes up, praised for its clarity and presenter.
videos.q: definitely go and watch Matt Parker's legendary explanation of why NTSC runs at 29.97fps

videos.t: Pop an ollie and innovate! | Rodney Mullen | TED
videos.s: Skateboarding pioneer Rodney Mullen talks about how the open skate community and its environments drive the invention of new tricks out of pure passion. He draws parallels to collaboration and open source.
videos.w: HN people share it as an inspiring talk linking skateboarding creativity to hacking and open-source knowledge sharing.
videos.q: talks a bit about the relationship between hacking and skateboarding in his TED talk

videos.t: Hilbert's Curve: Is infinite math useful?
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown explains space-filling curves and the Hilbert curve, and how infinite mathematical constructions connect to finite, practical approximations. It touches on mapping between dimensions and sensory ideas.
videos.w: Recommended as the best visual introduction to Hilbert curves, which come up in indexing, image layout and dimensionality mapping.
videos.q: This is a great video on the Hilbert curve

videos.t: The Infinite Pattern That Never Repeats
videos.s: Veritasium explains how Penrose tilings and quasicrystals overturned the belief that 5-fold symmetry and non-periodic crystals were impossible, including an interview with Paul Steinhardt.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a mind-bending, approachable explanation of aperiodic patterns, even enjoyable with kids.
videos.q: My kids and I geeked out over the Veritasium video on Penrose tiles

videos.t: Progressive Performance (Chrome Dev Summit 2016)
videos.s: Alex Russell's Chrome Dev Summit 2016 talk on building web experiences that work on slow, flaky networks and low-power devices. It argues developers should focus on the performance of real-world mobile hardware rather than desktop machines.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as the clearest case for why mobile devices are slow and why code-splitting and progressive web apps are needed.
videos.q: Take a look at this talk on why mobile devices are so much slower than desktop devices

videos.t: Anders Hejlsberg and Lars Bak: TypeScript, JavaScript, and Dart
videos.s: A Channel 9 conversation recorded at GOTO 2012 between Anders Hejlsberg (TypeScript) and Lars Bak (Dart). They discuss the two languages and different approaches to making JavaScript development safer, including runtime type checking.
videos.w: HN points to it as a rare side-by-side of the TypeScript and Dart designers, often to show how the two approaches to improving JavaScript differed.
videos.q: Debate (almost 10 years ago) TypeScript vs. Dart about the best way to improve JavaScript

videos.t: Jordan Walke - React to the Future
videos.s: Jordan Walke, creator of React, talks at ReasonConf 2019 about the ideas behind ReasonML and how it extends React's programming model with OCaml. He also discusses why familiar syntax matters.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the best introduction to Reason's motivations, straight from React's creator.
videos.q: I'd highly recommend Jordan Walke's (creator of React) talk on the ideas behind ReasonML

videos.t: How to Enjoy the End of the World
videos.s: A Virginia Tech presentation by Sid Smith about collapse, fossil fuels and overshoot, arguing that industrial civilization faces a decline and how one might live with that. It was later expanded into a video series.
videos.w: Recommended in collapse and energy threads as a sobering thermodynamic view of civilization, often with a warning that it is heavy.
videos.q: I recommend few videos for you. I must warn you ... it may hamper your ability to enjoy parties.

videos.t: The most feared song in jazz, explained
videos.s: Vox Earworm explains why John Coltrane's Giant Steps is so hard to improvise over: it is fast and moves through three keys. Musicians Braxton Cook and Adam Neely walk the host through the underlying music theory.
videos.w: Recommended as a well-produced, accessible explanation of Giant Steps and the harmonic ideas behind Coltrane's work.
videos.q: I highly recommend this Vox explainer on John Coltrane's

videos.t: World's Largest Batteries - (Pumped Storage)
videos.s: Practical Engineering explains pumped storage hydropower, which makes up most grid-scale electricity storage. It covers how it works and why it fits only certain geographies.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear explanation of pumped hydro and its limits in energy storage discussions.
videos.q: There's a good watch on pumped hydro, and how it is kinda sucky

videos.t: How I overcame alcoholism | Claudia Christian | TEDxLondonBusinessSchool
videos.s: Actress Claudia Christian tells how she overcame alcoholism using the Sinclair Method, which uses naltrexone to gradually reduce cravings. She discusses fresh perspectives on treating alcohol use disorder.
videos.w: HN commenters share it as the talk that introduced them to the Sinclair Method as an alternative approach to alcohol dependence.
videos.q: This TEDx talk was what convinced me to try it

videos.t: Brick Assembly
videos.s: A maker's time-lapse of building a working computer inside a LEGO-style brick, using a tiny 0.42-inch OLED screen, with a demo at the end.
videos.w: HN finds the miniaturization mind-blowing and cites it as a standout example of surreal hobbyist technology.
videos.q: This is a mind blowing level of miniaturization

videos.t: "Performance (Really) Matters" with Emery Berger
videos.s: Emery Berger argues that performance is hard to measure and deliver on modern systems, showing how code layout and link order can swamp optimization effects. He presents tools that evaluate performance more reliably.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever benchmarking pitfalls and layout effects come up, as an eye-opening talk on how unreliable naive measurements are.
videos.q: I highly recommend it. It's mind blowing, but also terrifying

videos.t: DropBox Demo
videos.s: The original five-minute Dropbox demo video, which presented the product's features before a finished product existed. It was aimed at technical early adopters and became famous as a launch strategy.
videos.w: HN cites it as the classic example of validating a product idea with a demo video, and many recall how compelling it was.
videos.q: I still remember seeing the original 5 minute demo (1). My jaw was on the floor, I instantly needed it.

videos.t: What People Get Wrong About Induced Demand
videos.s: Explains induced demand beyond roads, showing that it applies to transit, walking and cycling infrastructure too but with different consequences. It corrects common misunderstandings of the concept.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear treatment of induced demand across transport modes whenever threads debate road expansion versus transit.
videos.q: had a pretty good video on induced demand as it applies to both car transit and public transit

videos.t: EV Road Trips Suck Now (Except in a Tesla)
videos.s: Aging Wheels compares a road trip in a Polestar 2 with an identical drive in a Tesla, showing the charging problems of non-Tesla EVs. It argues that outside Tesla's network, EV road trips have become frustrating.
videos.w: HN cites it as a clear side-by-side showing the papercuts of non-Tesla fast charging in EV debates.
videos.q: Aging Wheels did an excellent video[1] on how frustrating the experience can be.

videos.t: Most People Don't Know How Bikes Work
videos.s: Veritasium explains why bicycles are stable, arguing that gyroscopic effects are not the answer. The video shows countersteering and an experiment where riders blocked from steering the opposite way cannot turn.
videos.w: HN links it in threads on bikes, countersteering and control systems as the clearest demonstration of how bikes actually steer and balance.
videos.q: It shows what happens if you prevent the rider from performing the countersteer before leaning into a turn [1].

videos.t: Slaughterbots
videos.s: Slaughterbots is a fictional short film, backed by Stuart Russell, depicting swarms of cheap autonomous drones that use facial recognition to assassinate targets. It was made to argue for banning autonomous weapons.
videos.w: HN invokes it as the standard reference whenever drone swarms, autonomous weapons or military AI come up in the news.
videos.q: see Stuart Russell's compelling short film

videos.t: Old Is the New New • Kevlin Henney • GOTO 2018
videos.s: Kevlin Henney's GOTO 2018 talk argues that much of what looks new in software is a recycling of concepts with long histories. It draws on history to show the slow, steady current beneath constant churn in frameworks and trends.
videos.w: HN recommends it for historical perspective on software ideas and for dispelling myths such as the origins of waterfall.
videos.q: There's a talk well worth watching by Kevlin Henney called 'Old Is the New New' [1]

videos.t: Hamming, Intro to The Art of Doing Science and Engineering: Learning to Learn (March 28, 1995)
videos.s: The introductory lecture of Richard Hamming's capstone course, The Art of Doing Science and Engineering: Learning to Learn. It focuses on style of thinking and on educating rather than training, using technical material only as illustration.
videos.w: HN regularly recommends Hamming's lecture series as a fascinating, wisdom-rich course on how to approach hard technical problems and a career, often preferred to the book.
videos.p: learning to learn and doing science
videos.q: I highly recommend Richard Hamming's wonderful course The Art of Doing Science and Engineering: Learning to Learn [1]

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #725 - Graham Hancock & Randall Carlson
videos.s: A three-hour Joe Rogan Experience conversation with Graham Hancock and Randall Carlson about lost civilizations, the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis and Earth's cataclysmic history.
videos.w: HN people point to it as an entry point to the Hancock and Carlson lost-civilization theories, while noting the ideas are controversial.
videos.q: Here's where to go to get on the Graham Hancock/Randall Carlson train

videos.t: Charlie Brooker's How to Report the News - Newswipe - BBC
videos.s: A short satirical segment from Charlie Brooker's Newswipe that lampoons the formulaic conventions of television news reporting, from stock shots to filler street interviews and news-speak.
videos.w: HN invokes it as the best spoof of how news is formulaically produced, often when discussing media quality or automated news.

videos.t: Neom - The Line - The Rise and Fall of Saudi Arabia's Linear City.
videos.s: Patrick Boyle's deadpan account of Saudi Arabia's Neom and The Line megaproject, a planned 170 km linear city that has been scaled back to a fraction of its size. He covers the feasibility problems and the financing.
videos.w: Recommended as the entertaining, skeptical overview of Neom whenever its progress comes up.
videos.q: is rather epic if you haven't seen it.

videos.t: Chinese Invisibility Cloak Hoax DESTROYED!!!
videos.s: Captain Disillusion debunks a viral Chinese invisibility cloak video while parodying popular educational channels. Along the way he explains chroma keying and green screen techniques.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining explanation of chroma keying, green screens and how cameras process color.
videos.q: My favorite video about green screens and chroma keying, from Captain Disillusion

videos.t: CRDTs and the Quest for Distributed Consistency
videos.s: Martin Kleppmann's QCon London 2018 talk on keeping data consistent in distributed systems without a central leader. It surveys CRDT algorithms for syncing devices and collaborative editing over peer-to-peer networks.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a clear, accessible survey of the CRDT landscape.
videos.q: I also highly recommend the talk

videos.t: 2. The Bronze Age Collapse - Mediterranean Apocalypse
videos.s: An episode of Fall of Civilizations on the Late Bronze Age Collapse around 1100 BC, when many Eastern Mediterranean societies were destroyed in a short span. It explores the Sea Peoples and the lessons for modern globalised societies.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an engaging, high-quality introduction to the Bronze Age Collapse and praise the channel generally.
videos.q: is also a great introduction

videos.t: The Thorium Molten-Salt Reactor: Why Didn't This Happen (and why is now the right time?)
videos.s: Kirk Sorensen's Google Tech Talk on thorium molten-salt reactors (LFTR). He covers why the technology was shelved after early development and argues that now is the right time to revisit it.
videos.w: Recommended as the go-to pitch for liquid fluoride thorium reactors whenever nuclear power comes up.
videos.q: Kirk Sorensen has been a major advocate of molten-salt reactors and gave a great Google tech talk on the subject.

videos.t: Mark Blyth ─ Global Trumpism
videos.c: Watson School of International and Public Affairs
videos.s: Mark Blyth's 2016 Brown University lecture on global Trumpism, explaining the rise of populism through economics, the decline of Western middle classes and revolt against technocracy.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a concise, chart-backed explanation of the economics behind anti-establishment politics.
videos.q: which concisely outlines the economics behind the decline of western middle classes

videos.t: MINIX 3: a Modular, Self-Healing POSIX-compatible Operating System
videos.s: Andrew Tanenbaum's FOSDEM 2010 talk on MINIX 3, a microkernel OS built for high reliability and security. It shows how the system detects and recovers from device driver crashes, and addresses microkernel performance concerns.
videos.w: HN points to it as an accessible explanation of microkernel isolation and fault-tolerant design, and as Tanenbaum's answer to performance objections.
videos.q: it's a very interesting but accessible talk for those interested in lower-level systems and fault-tolerant architectures.

videos.t: C++ Exceptions for Smaller Firmware - Khalil Estell - CppCon 2024
videos.s: Khalil Estell's CppCon 2024 talk argues C++ exceptions can reduce binary size in firmware. He digs into how exceptions work and how to shrink their code footprint on embedded platforms.
videos.w: Pointed to as the in-depth talk on exception mechanics and code size for embedded C++.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: In particular, his 2019 presentation [2] describes different error handling techniques

videos.t: The Alt-Right Playbook: Control the Conversation
videos.s: Innuendo Studios' video from the Alt-Right Playbook series on how bad-faith actors control the conversation through debate tactics and moving goalposts.
videos.w: HN recommends the series for explaining the tactics and mentality of bad-faith online arguments.
videos.q: I found it enormously helpful to understand the mentality and tactics of a group that kind of doesn't make any sense.

videos.t: The Houses that Can't be Built in America - The Missing Middle
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains missing middle housing, such as duplexes, townhouses and small apartment buildings. The video argues that zoning in the US and Canada has made these options almost illegal.
videos.w: Recommended as the standard short overview of missing middle housing and its link to zoning reform.
videos.q: you need to watch the NotJustBikes overview of the Missing Middle problem

videos.t: "A Political History of X" - Keith Packard (LCA 2020)
videos.s: Keith Packard traces the 35-year history of the X Window System at linux.conf.au 2020. He uses X to examine licensing, corporate interests and community dynamics in free software, including Unix workstation vendors and Stallman's influence.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the authoritative, firsthand account of how X came to be and why it isn't GPL.
videos.q: I invite anyone interested by the subject to watch Keith Packard's amazing presentation on this at LCA 2020

videos.t: How Imaginary Numbers Were Invented
videos.s: Veritasium tells the history of how imaginary numbers arose from the quest for a general solution to the cubic equation, including the duels and secrecy among Renaissance mathematicians. It argues math had to give up the requirement that it mirror reality.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a well-visualized, story-driven history of complex numbers, suitable for beginners; some quibble with its framing of algebra and geometry.
videos.q: I also highly recommend Veritasium's video[1] as an excellent explainer as well, especially regarding the roots of imaginary/complex numbers in geometry.

videos.t: Rich Hickey: Deconstructing the Database
videos.s: Rich Hickey, creator of Clojure and designer of Datomic, gives a JaxConf 2012 talk that takes apart traditional database architecture. He presents a different way to think about databases and explains the reasoning behind Datomic's fact-based design.
videos.w: HN points people to it as the clearest account of why Datomic is designed the way it is and of the problems with conventional database architecture.
videos.q: Rich Hickey's talk on the design of Datomic is also something every programmer should see at least once

videos.t: BBS The Documentary: Episode 1 of 8: BAUD (The Beginning)
videos.s: The first episode of Jason Scott's eight-part BBS documentary, covering the predecessors and beginnings of the dial-up bulletin board system. It includes interviews with pioneers such as Ward Christensen and Randy Suess, who created the first dial-up BBS in 1978.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend the series as the definitive history of BBS culture and its Fidonet roots, especially for nostalgia and the origins of the demoscene.
videos.q: He also gave us the brilliant BBS: The Documentary

videos.t: dotJS 2019 - James Long - CRDTs for Mortals
videos.s: James Long's dotJS 2019 talk on how CRDTs enable local-first apps and how simple they can be to implement. He shows how to use them to build robust offline-capable frontends.
videos.w: Recommended as an approachable introduction to CRDTs and the local-first idea behind apps like Actual.
videos.q: the same one who made a great talk on using CRDTs called CRDTs for Mortals

videos.t: React Today and Tomorrow and  90% Cleaner React With Hooks
videos.s: The first three talks from React Conf 2018, by Sophie Alpert, Dan Abramov and Ryan Florence. They introduce React Hooks and explain the problems with classes that hooks solve.
videos.w: It is the canonical introduction to hooks, given by the people who built them, and HN uses it to answer questions about why hooks exist.
videos.q: It's absolutely worth the watch, even if you're somewhat familiar with hooks.

videos.t: Edwin Brady - Idris 2 - Type-driven Development of Idris
videos.s: Edwin Brady, creator of Idris, presents Idris 2 and demonstrates type-driven development, where the compiler assists by filling holes and suggesting implementations from types.
videos.w: Recommended as the best demo of interactive, compiler-assisted dependently typed programming in action.
videos.q: Watch Edwin Brady's demo of Idris 2 [2] to see this form of interactive development in action.

videos.t: Depth-first search in APL
videos.s: John Scholes builds a depth-first tree-search operator step by step in a Dyalog APL session. It covers higher-order functions and runs the search on the N-Queens problem.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a beautiful, brilliant demonstration of APL's expressiveness and a model of clear narration.

videos.t: The Most Misunderstood Concept in Physics
videos.s: Veritasium's explainer on entropy, presented as one of physics' most important and least understood concepts. It uses examples such as heat engines and the sun's energy flowing through the Earth.
videos.w: HN commenters say it made entropy intuition click and point to it in threads on energy, heat and equilibrium.
videos.q: This veritasium video explained it in a way that finally clicked for me

videos.t: Infinity is bigger than you think - Numberphile
videos.s: Numberphile's James Grime explains Cantor's result that some infinities are bigger than others, including why the reals outnumber the integers. It is a short, accessible introduction to countable and uncountable infinity.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as a clear introduction to different sizes of infinity that non-mathematicians can follow.
videos.q: Numberphile did a pretty good introductory video to this if you want to learn more

videos.t: How Harley-Davidson Killed Itself
videos.s: FortNine explains how Harley-Davidson ended up in decline, from a narrow lifestyle niche and an aging customer base to the pandemic hitting a company already in trouble.
videos.w: Recommended as an entertaining overview of Harley's decline and as a case study in selling a lifestyle rather than a product.
videos.q: This very entertaining 11 minute video from Fortnine (still one of the best channels on YouTube)

videos.t: Making of "The Prodigy - Smack My Bitch Up" in Ableton by Jim Pavloff
videos.s: Jim Pavloff rebuilds the Prodigy track Smack My Bitch Up in Ableton, identifying the samples used and recreating the track by hand.
videos.w: Recommended as a fun, in-depth look at how sampling and music production work, and as proof that skilled humans can reconstruct tracks from scratch.
videos.q: I'm amazed at the level of musical knowledge needed to do this.

videos.t: How Myst Almost Couldn't Run on CD-ROM | War Stories | Ars Technica
videos.s: Myst co-creator Rand Miller recounts how the HyperCard-built game struggled to run on 1x CD-ROM drives. He and his brother Robyn compressed image and audio data heavily to get acceptable performance. Part of Ars Technica's War Stories series.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as the first-person story of how Myst grew out of HyperCard and fit on CD-ROM, especially in threads about HyperCard and retro game constraints.
videos.q: is actually more fascinating and entertaining in my opinion.

videos.t: Stephen Wolfram: Cellular Automata, Computation, and Physics | Lex Fridman Podcast #89
videos.s: Lex Fridman interviews Stephen Wolfram for about three hours on cellular automata, computation, the Wolfram Physics Project and his career with Mathematica and Wolfram Alpha.
videos.w: HN points to it as an accessible long-form introduction to Wolfram's ideas and a window into his passion, though some are critical of his claims.
videos.q: accessible intro

videos.t: Religions and babies | Hans Rosling
videos.s: Hans Rosling's TEDxSummit talk asks whether some religions have higher birth rates and how that affects population growth. He charts data across time and religions and reaches a surprising conclusion about fertility.
videos.w: Recommended whenever population growth comes up, as a data-driven correction to common assumptions.
videos.q: Then watch this video to understand the real trends in population growth.

videos.t: The Extreme Physics Pushing Moore’s Law to the Next Level
videos.s: Seeker's Focal Point short documentary on ASML's extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which make the most advanced chips. It shows how plasma-generated 13.5 nm light is used to push Moore's Law forward.
videos.w: HN links it in semiconductor threads as an accessible overview of why EUV lithography is so hard.
videos.q: Seeker released a very insightful feature about the ASML Extreme UV / soft X-ray (13.5 nanometers) photolithography system

videos.t: Intro to C on Windows - Day 1
videos.s: Day 1 of Handmade Hero's introduction to C on Windows, covering setting up Visual Studio, creating a Win32 project, the WinMain entry point and writing a first function. It is the starting point for Casey Muratori's from-scratch game series.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an approachable way into C and low-level programming that gets to something visible quickly.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: I think Handmade Hero's[0] intro to C is good

videos.t: Steve Jobs Insult Response
videos.s: A clip from Steve Jobs's 1997 WWDC session, in which he answers a hostile question from an audience member about Apple killing OpenDoc. He says to start with the customer experience and work back to the technology, and that saying no is part of focus.
videos.w: Commenters link it as a canonical statement of Jobs's product philosophy and as an example of handling an insult calmly and articulately.
videos.q: Watch Jobs in his prime a year later describing his philosophy

videos.t: Debugging with the Scientific Method - Stuart Halloway
videos.s: Stuart Halloway of Cognitect argues for debugging with the scientific method: form hypotheses, try to falsify them, and write everything down. The talk is given to the Clojure community but applies to any language.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a talk that changed how people debug, worth rewatching periodically.
videos.q: changed how I debug problems. I try to watch it once every year or two.

videos.t: Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem - Guy Steele Jr.
videos.s: Guy Steele presents a small geometric problem and compares four computational approaches: a classic sequential solution and three parallel-friendly ones. Each is illustrated pictorially and with working code, weighing total work against time to solution.
videos.w: HN points to it as a clear lesson that algebraic properties like associativity unlock parallelism, applicable in any language.
videos.q: watch Guy Steele's talks [1][2][3] if you are interested in data parallelism!

videos.t: Carl Sagan - Cosmos - Eratosthenes
videos.s: A short clip from Carl Sagan's Cosmos in which he explains how Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth using shadows in two Egyptian cities. It is a clear, visual account of an ancient scientific feat.
videos.w: HN commenters link it whenever the question of how the Earth's size was first measured comes up, calling it a wonderful explanation.
videos.q: Here is a wonderful video of Carl Sagan explaining it[0].

videos.t: You Need To Listen To This Leading COVID-19 Expert From South Korea | STAY CURIOUS #15
videos.s: Asian Boss interviews Professor Kim Woo-joo of Korea University Guro Hospital about COVID-19 in early 2020. He covers masks, testing, aerosol spread, and South Korea's response.
videos.w: In early pandemic threads, HN commenters pointed to it as an uninterrupted, practical expert view from Korea on masks, testing and airborne spread.
videos.q: The videos are excellent because the doctors are not interrupted with questions.

videos.t: Moral behavior in animals | Frans de Waal
videos.s: Frans de Waal's TED talk shows videos of behavioral experiments on primates and other mammals that reveal empathy, cooperation, fairness and reciprocity. He argues these moral traits are not uniquely human.
videos.w: Commenters call it a must-watch, funny and entertaining demonstration that morality has natural roots in animals.
videos.q: Here is one of his excellent must-watch Ted talks -

videos.t: Mars Helicopter (before it went to Mars)
videos.s: Veritasium's Derek Muller visits NASA JPL to see the Mars helicopter Ingenuity before it was mounted on the rover. He explains how it can fly in Mars's thin atmosphere with large, fast-spinning contra-rotating rotors and low mass, and covers power and cold.
videos.w: HN repeatedly recommends it as an excellent explanation of why flying on Mars is hard and how the helicopter was built.
videos.q: a really excellent video that answers all your questions

videos.t: Why Age? Should We End Aging Forever?
videos.s: Kurzgesagt's short animated video asks whether humanity should try to end aging, and argues the case for curing age-related disease. It is part one of a pair, with a second part by CGP Grey.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a compelling, concise argument for longevity research and a rebuttal to common objections to ending aging.
videos.q: A good counter-argument to commonly cited objections to biological immortality

videos.t: SYMBOLICS S-PACKAGES 3D GRAPHICS AND ANIMATION DEMO
videos.s: A demo of the Symbolics Graphics Division's S-Packages, a Lisp-based 3D color graphics and animation system from the 1980s. It was later used in developing for the Nintendo 64.
videos.w: HN cites it as a startling example of how advanced Lisp machine interactive graphics were, often in Lisp and REPL-driven development discussions.
videos.q: I really enjoyed the Symbolics graphics and animations demo[0] linked in the article.

videos.t: TiTAN - Overdrive 2 (RGB 50fps) - SEGA Mega Drive - Revision 2017 (1st Place)
videos.s: Overdrive 2 by TiTAN, a Sega Mega Drive demo that won first place in the Oldskool competition at Revision 2017. It shows effects and 3D graphics on the stock console.
videos.w: HN plugs it as a favorite example of what skilled demoscene coders can pull out of 30-year-old hardware.
videos.q: Overdrive 2 is my favorite example

videos.t: A quick tour of TeXmacs
videos.s: A four-minute tour of the TeXmacs scientific editor, showing math typing, figures, citations, a drawing tool, document styles, HTML export, presentations and animations.
videos.w: Recommended as the quickest way to see what TeXmacs can do, as a WYSIWYG alternative to LaTeX.
videos.q: See here a short video describing its features

videos.t: "CHASING ICE" captures largest glacier calving ever filmed - OFFICIAL VIDEO
videos.s: Footage from the Chasing Ice project of the largest glacier calving event ever filmed, at Greenland's Ilulissat Glacier in 2008. A 75-minute event is condensed to a few minutes of cameras watching ice collapse.
videos.w: Recommended whenever glaciers come up, as a stunning look at the scale of calving.
videos.q: If you have never seen a glacier calve before, check out these videos

videos.t: Ses 1: Introduction and Course Overview
videos.s: First session of MIT 15.401 Finance Theory I (Fall 2008) taught by Andrew Lo, giving a course overview and introducing core finance concepts. The course ran during the 2007-08 financial crisis.
videos.w: Recommended as a free, first-principles finance course for software engineers wanting to learn business and finance.
videos.q: The course is excellent.

videos.t: The Making of: ROM City Rampage (Retro City Rampage)
videos.s: Making-of video about ROM City Rampage, the NES version of Retro City Rampage, covering how the game's core was crunched to run on real 8-bit hardware and how NES games are made.
videos.w: Recommended as a fascinating look at fitting a modern game into NES constraints.
videos.q: There's also a fascinating video of him getting the core of the game to run on NES spec constraints

videos.t: How to Make an Attractive City
videos.s: The School of Life sets out principles for making attractive cities, arguing that the art has been lost in the modern world.
videos.w: Recommended in urban planning and housing threads as a concise summary of what makes cities livable and beautiful.
videos.q: This video is really informative in this regard and has changed my opinion on a few things

videos.t: The Milk-Industrial Complex: Why You Don't Need to Drink Milk
videos.s: A short Healthcare Triage episode by Aaron Carroll arguing that milk gets an undeserved pass in efforts to improve diets. It examines claims about calcium and bone strength and concludes you don't need to drink milk.
videos.w: Commenters link it as a concise evidence-based rebuttal to common beliefs about milk's health benefits.
videos.q: Here's a great video on the topic from one of the co-authors of this article

videos.t: Attention Is All You Need
videos.s: Yannic Kilcher walks through the Attention Is All You Need paper, which introduced the Transformer, a sequence model based solely on attention without recurrence or convolutions. He reviews the architecture and the paper's translation results.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible, clear walkthrough of the transformer paper for people with some AI background.
videos.q: The Yannic kilcher review is quite good.

videos.t: "Memories" - 256 byte MSDOS intro
videos.s: Memories is a 256-byte MS-DOS demo that packs eight effects and MIDI soundscapes into a tiny program. It won first place at Revision 2020.
videos.w: HN people share it as a mind-blowing example of demoscene craft and the reigning champion of 256-byte demos.
videos.q: producing stuff that is just as mindblowing as it was when it all began.

videos.t: The Mathematics of Quantum Computers | Infinite Series
videos.s: A PBS Infinite Series episode explaining the mathematics of quantum computers, including how qubits store complex numbers and how quantum computation differs from classical computation. Hosted by Kelsey Houston-Edwards.
videos.w: HN recommends it as one of the most accessible yet accurate introductions to quantum computing, and part of a wider series that covers Shor's algorithm.
videos.q: perhaps the most accessible and yet accurate explanations of quantum computing I have found so far.

videos.t: "Z2" - Upgraded Homemade Silicon Chips
videos.s: Sam Zeloof shows the upgraded second iteration of his homemade silicon integrated circuit fabrication process, producing chips with around a thousand transistors in his garage. It is a short overview of what the home fab can now do.
videos.w: HN uses it as the go-to proof that small-scale, hobbyist chip fabrication is real, and as an entry point to the topic.
videos.q: It's fantastic and I highly recommend watching it.

videos.t: Drone Delivery Was Supposed to be the Future. What Went Wrong?
videos.s: Wendover Productions explains why drone delivery has not become the future once promised. It covers no-fly zones, costs and the difficulty of the final drop-off.
videos.w: It is the standard answer when someone asks what happened to drone delivery.
videos.q: I think that Wendover has the best summary

videos.t: This is why we can't have nice things
videos.s: Veritasium explores planned obsolescence, from the Phoebus lightbulb cartel to printers and phones. It explains how companies deliberately shortened product lifetimes and why products aren't better.
videos.w: Commenters link it as the engaging go-to explainer on planned obsolescence and the lightbulb cartel.
videos.q: Veritasium made a video that reviews the history and presents the topic in an engaging way.

videos.t: Flying Dream
videos.s: Gary Garrett's stop-motion animation of his song Flying Dream, with notes arranged on a lattice of fifths and major thirds. It shows how harmony looks in just intonation, inspired by Harmonic Experience.
videos.w: Shared as a beautiful example of lattice-based harmony visualization.
videos.q: this beautiful song using it

videos.t: "Tree-sitter - a new parsing system for programming tools" by Max Brunsfeld
videos.s: Max Brunsfeld introduces Tree-sitter, a parsing system for developer tools that offers incremental parsing and robust error recovery through a uniform C API. The talk explains the design, based on LR extended to GLR parsing.
videos.w: HN points to it as the best explanation of tree-sitter's design choices and as an accessible introduction to parser generators.
videos.q: Highly recommend Max Brunsfield's strange loop talk if you want to learn more about the design choices behind tree-sitter

videos.t: CppCon 2016: Herb Sutter “Leak-Freedom in C++... By Default.”
videos.s: Herb Sutter's CppCon 2016 talk on lifetime safety in C++, aiming for code free of leaks and dangling pointers by default. It covers smart pointers, ownership, reference counting pitfalls and deferred reclamation resembling garbage collection.
videos.w: HN cites it in memory management debates for its treatment of reference counting problems, destructor stack overflows and deferred pointers.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Check all of Herb Sutter's CppCon videos from 2015-2016, especially this one

videos.t: The Vanishing of Flight 370
videos.s: LEMMiNO's 25-minute documentary on the 2014 disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. It walks through the official investigation's findings and the leading theories, including satellite data and hydrophone recordings.
videos.w: Regularly shared as the best well-made overview of the MH370 mystery, in threads on the search and ocean mapping.
videos.q: There is a really well put together video[1] by a YouTuber, who goes by the name of Lemmino

videos.t: Making Infrared Cooling Paint From Grocery Store Items (w/Novel CaCO₃ Microsphere Synthesis)
videos.s: NightHawkInLight shows how to make radiative sky cooling paint from grocery and hardware store materials, including a novel calcium carbonate microsphere synthesis. The paint can cool a surface below ambient air temperature in direct sunlight without electricity.
videos.w: It comes up whenever radiative cooling coatings are in the news, as a hands-on DIY guide that shows the approach working with household materials.
videos.q: Here is a frankly incredible video of how you could make such a paint

videos.t: How Time Becomes Space Inside a Black Hole | Space Time
videos.s: A PBS Space Time episode explaining how space and time swap roles inside a black hole's event horizon. It is part of the channel's black hole series.
videos.w: Recommended as the cleanest visual explanation of time and space switching roles past the horizon, and a gateway to the channel's black hole videos.
videos.q: I think this is the cleanest explanation with actual visual representation.

videos.t: Deskbound | Kelly Starrett | Talks at Google
videos.s: Kelly Starrett's Talks at Google presentation on staying healthy while desk bound, mixing anatomy and practical mobility advice. It shows how to set up a desk and sit and move to avoid pain.
videos.w: Often the first thing suggested to HN programmers asking about posture and back pain.
videos.q: my first recommended steps for you would be: 1. Watch the "Deskbound" Google Talk by Kelly Starett

videos.t: Build a Do-It-Yourself Air Purifier for About $40
videos.s: A University of Michigan Medicine demonstration of building a cheap DIY air purifier from a box fan and a HEPA or high-MERV filter using hardware-store parts. It explains why this helps against dust, smoke and viruses and ties it to local air quality readings.
videos.w: HN people link it during wildfire smoke and air quality threads as a practical, cheap fix, though a few doubt how rigorously its effectiveness was shown.
videos.q: Here's a video from the University of Michigan showing just how effective these cheap DIY air filters can be

videos.t: The US Has More Tribes Than the World Has Countries
videos.s: CGP Grey explains why "Indian" is often preferred over "Native American" in the United States, especially near reservations, and how many tribes exist in the US. He draws on conversations with people who identify as Indian.
videos.w: Cited again and again in terminology debates as a convincing source that many American Indians prefer the term Indian.
videos.q: CGP Grey made a very convincing video on the argument that at least in the US, unexpectedly enough, "Indian" is probably the most appropriate term

videos.t: SmoothLifeL
videos.s: Tim Hutton's demonstration of SmoothLifeL, a continuous version of Conway's Game of Life using floating point values. It shows gliders traveling in any direction, rotating pairs, and elastic cord-like structures, with config details to run it yourself.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever Game of Life or cellular automata come up, as the best visual example of a mesmerizing continuous-domain alternative.
videos.q: Must see evolution of GOL

videos.t: Bret Victor - Seeing Spaces
videos.s: Bret Victor's talk proposing a new kind of maker space built for seeing and understanding a project's behavior: inside it, across time and across possibilities. It argues for scientific understanding over recipes and rules of thumb.
videos.w: Listed alongside his other talks as foundational context for Dynamicland and visual-programming ideas, and he is the most frequently cited speaker on such threads.
videos.q: Highly recommend Bret's 2 talks for context
