videos.t: Doctor Dissects the Wim Hof Method - Cold Hard Science Analysis
videos.s: A cardiologist runs a detailed, skeptical review of the Wim Hof Method, covering the research on cold exposure and breathing techniques. It also teaches how to read scientific statistics critically.
videos.w: HN points people to it as a nuanced, medically informed take whenever Wim Hof breathing or cold plunges come up.
videos.q: Here is an amazing summary on the research of a sceptical doctor

videos.t: Valter Longo, Ph.D. on Fasting-Mimicking Diet & Fasting for Longevity, Cancer & Multiple Sclerosis
videos.s: Rhonda Patrick interviews USC gerontologist Valter Longo about fasting, the fasting-mimicking diet, and their effects on longevity, cancer, and multiple sclerosis. They discuss mechanisms such as IGF-1 and autophagy and clinical trials.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a deeper, more legitimate interview on fasting mechanics than typical diet content.
videos.q: For those interested in a deeper dive on the benefits of water-only fasting

videos.t: NOTCURSES III: THE SAGA CONTINUES (1080P)
videos.s: A seven-minute demo from the author of Notcurses, a C library for text user interfaces. It shows the 2.3.0 release, which adds Sixel and Kitty bitmap graphics integrated into its multiplane character-graphics model.
videos.w: HN people share it as a striking demonstration of how much graphics a modern terminal can do.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: the WTF effect that video had on me lasted quite a while.

videos.t: Geoffrey West on COMPLEXITY
videos.s: Physicist Geoffrey West speaks at an FQXi conference on time about complexity and scaling laws. He covers how metabolism, growth and lifespan scale across organisms and how the same mathematics applies to cities and companies.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an accessible introduction to scaling laws and to why cities keep growing while companies and organisms eventually die.
videos.q: For a great, accessible intro talk on this topic, check out Geoffrey West's

videos.t: DEF CON 18 - Moxie Marlinspike - Changing Threats To Privacy: From TIA to Google
videos.s: Moxie Marlinspike's DEF CON 18 talk argues that privacy threats have shifted from centralized state databases like TIA to corporate data collection by companies like Google, despite wins in strong cryptography and decentralization.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a formative talk on privacy, especially for its argument that voting with your feet fails as a privacy strategy.
videos.q: It was formative in my understanding of privacy and security.

videos.t: The Suburban Traffic Contradiction
videos.s: Oh The Urbanity! questions the framing that urban planning reforms like bike lanes and traffic calming wage war on suburbanites. It argues that suburban and urban residents alike want less traffic on their own streets.
videos.w: Cited in urbanism threads as a clear argument that car-dependent suburbs impose traffic on everyone.
videos.q: This video makes that point so crystal clear

videos.t: Depression is a disease of civilization: Stephen Ilardi at TEDxEmory
videos.s: Clinical psychologist Stephen Ilardi argues depression is a disease of modern civilization and presents a lifestyle-based program to treat it without drugs. Topics include exercise, sunlight, omega-3s and social connection.
videos.w: HN recommends it in depression threads as a practical, non-medication approach with concrete takeaways.
videos.q: Two points I remember clearly taking from this lecture

videos.t: War - Part Two: Anybody's Son Will Do (1 of 6)
videos.s: An episode of Gwynne Dyer's 1983 documentary series War, about how military basic training turns recruits into soldiers. It covers the psychological side of conditioning.
videos.w: Recommended as a classic documentary on military training and the psychology of going to war.
videos.q: This documentary explains in great detail the nature of military basic training and its psychological component

videos.t: How a transistor works
videos.s: Ben Eater gives a detailed look at how an NPN bipolar junction transistor works and what it does. It is an eleven-minute explanation aimed at building real understanding of the device.
videos.w: HN commenters prefer it over other transistor explanations as an enlightening starting point that leads into building logic gates and a CPU.
videos.q: I found Ben Eater's videos on how semiconductors work and how transistors work interesting and enlightening.

videos.t: A reality check on renewables - David MacKay
videos.s: David MacKay's TEDxWarwick talk uses basic arithmetic to show how much land and energy renewables would need to power a country like the UK. It explains the limits of sustainable options and why they should still be pursued.
videos.w: Cited in energy debates for its back-of-envelope scale of the transition and the land and storage limits of wind and solar.
videos.q: I found this ted talk on the feasibility of various renewable energy sources quite eye opening

videos.t: Why Koko (Probably) Couldn't Talk (Sorry) | The Deep Dive
videos.s: A long video essay arguing that Koko the gorilla probably could not actually use sign language. It examines the cherry-picked data and the lack of transparency behind the claims, drawing on published critiques.
videos.w: Recommended as a thorough debunking of Koko's supposed language ability in threads about animal communication.
videos.q: While this video is long, it explains the controversy very well

videos.t: [1299] Unpickable Locks From Stuff Made Here
videos.s: The Lock Picking Lawyer tests the supposedly unpickable lock designs built by the Stuff Made Here channel. He looks for bypasses and weaknesses in the novel anti-picking mechanisms.
videos.w: HN points to it in lock-security threads as a good example of engineering meeting real-world exploitation, where flaws unrelated to the headline mechanism get found.
videos.q: The interaction of engineering and "use" by the Lock Picking Lawyer

videos.t: Timothy Snyder Speaks, ep. 14: Politics of Eternity, Politics of Inevitability
videos.s: Historian Timothy Snyder explains the politics of inevitability and the politics of eternity, two ways of thinking about time that frame his books On Tyranny and The Road to Unfreedom.
videos.w: Recommended as a short, clear introduction to these two concepts for making sense of current politics.
videos.q: You will love this video (12m)

videos.t: The world depends on a collection of strange items. They're not cheap
videos.s: Veritasium visits NIST to explain Standard Reference Materials, the carefully characterized items such as peanut butter used to calibrate instruments and keep measurements consistent. It covers why they exist and why they are expensive.
videos.w: Whenever NIST's pricey peanut butter or reference materials come up, commenters point to this as the clear explanation of why they exist.
videos.q: Veritasium [1] did a video of exactly this and explains why it exists

videos.t: Microsoft Re-Designs the iPod Packaging
videos.s: A 2006 parody made by a Microsoft team that shows how the company would redesign iPod packaging, with a box piled with feature claims, logos and clutter in contrast to Apple's clean design.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up whenever Microsoft product naming, branding or marketing is confusing, pointing to it as a long-running self-aware critique.
videos.q: brutal but hilarious commentary on Microsoft's inherent dysfunction when it comes to product naming and packaging

videos.t: Lecture: Biblical Series I: Introduction to the Idea of God
videos.s: Jordan Peterson's first lecture in his Biblical Series examines the idea of God as sovereignty and power abstracted from any individual ruler, and as the pattern inherent in human dominance hierarchies.
videos.w: HN fans say it offers value even to atheists by interpreting Bible stories as psychological and evolutionary archetypes, and some credit it with helping them through depression.
videos.q: You can be a hardline atheist and still get tons of value out of these lectures.

videos.t: Look Around You: Season 1 Pilot - Calcium
videos.s: The pilot of the British comedy series Look Around You, a deadpan parody of 1970s and 80s school science programmes, in which the scientists examine calcium.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a surreal, perfectly observed parody of old educational films, and quote it in jokes.
videos.q: a lot of HN readers might love it. It's a surreal but perfectly observed parody

videos.t: The Zipf Mystery
videos.s: Vsauce's explainer on Zipf's law, the pattern in which the frequency of a word is inversely related to its rank. It shows the pattern across many domains and discusses why it remains unexplained.
videos.w: Linked as an entertaining introduction to Zipf's law and power-law distributions.
videos.q: It's actually a very deep question, called the Zipf mystery

videos.t: "Agile Methods The Good, the Hype and the Ugly," Bertrand Meyer
videos.s: Bertrand Meyer's ACM webcast giving a critical look at agile methods, separating good ideas from hype and from practices he thinks damage projects. It is based on his book on the same subject.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a sober critique of agile, though one commenter found it mixed.
videos.q: Agile!: The Good, the Hype and the Ugly by Bertrand Meyer is a must read.

videos.t: Gabriella Gonzalez – How to market Haskell to a mainstream programmer
videos.s: Gabriella Gonzalez argues that developers misunderstand marketing as deception or hype, and applies the technology-adoption ideas of Crossing the Chasm to Haskell. She looks at what keeps Haskell from reaching mainstream programmers and what a community can do about it.
videos.w: Commenters point to it as a clear take on why functional languages stall outside niches, and its lessons are seen as applying to any technology trying to go mainstream.
videos.q: although aimed at haskell programmers, is really about any technology looking to grow into the mainstream

videos.t: Computer Scientist Explains One Concept in 5 Levels of Difficulty | WIRED
videos.s: WIRED has UCLA professor Amit Sahai explain zero-knowledge proofs to a child, a teen, a college student, a grad student and an expert. Each round goes deeper into the cryptography and why it matters.
videos.w: It is the go-to accessible explanation of zero-knowledge proofs, linked whenever a thread needs an intuitive introduction.
videos.q: This is the best explanation I have seen

videos.t: CD / Color
videos.s: Captain Disillusion's comedic, fast-paced explainer on how color works in cameras, displays and video. It covers the biology of color perception and what it means for screens.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it as a dense but entertaining primer on color theory and color in video systems.
videos.q: I went looking for an understanding of how color works in video systems, and ran across this gem from Captain Disillusion

videos.t: Why Trains are so Expensive
videos.s: A Wendover Productions explainer on why train tickets, especially Amtrak in the US, cost so much compared with flying. It breaks down staffing, speed and the cost components behind a ticket.
videos.w: HN links it in rail-versus-air threads as a clear cost breakdown of American passenger rail.
videos.q: There's a good video that breaks down the costs that make up your train ticket

videos.t: How To Terraform Venus (Quickly)
videos.s: Kurzgesagt lays out a speculative plan to terraform Venus, covering its hostile atmosphere and how it might be made Earth-like, with a sources page linked.
videos.w: Offered as a readable explainer whenever Venus terraforming or alternatives to Mars colonization come up.
videos.q: There is a decent kurzgesagt video explaining what transforming a new planet would look like

videos.t: Leading Questions - Yes Prime Minister
videos.s: A clip from Yes Prime Minister in which Sir Humphrey shows how leading questions can make a survey support or oppose national service. It is a short satirical scene.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up whenever a poll or survey result looks suspect, as the classic illustration of biased question framing.
videos.q: An excellent illustration of this

videos.t: Colossus - The Greatest Secret in the History of Computing
videos.s: Chris Shore of the Centre for Computing History explains how Colossus was built, how it worked, and how it affected the course of World War II. It is an hour-long museum lecture on the codebreaking computer.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an excellent deep dive on the real Colossus, full of stories about unsung engineers.
videos.q: It was very worth the watch, lots of fascinating tidbits including some stories of unsung heroes / geniuses.

videos.t: 60 Minutes - Luxottica. Do you know who makes your glasses?
videos.s: A 60 Minutes segment on Luxottica, the company that owns most major eyewear brands and retailers and dominates the market. It shows how consolidation of brands and manufacturing affects glasses prices.
videos.w: HN repeatedly cites it in any thread on why glasses are expensive, as the eye-opening explanation of Luxottica's monopoly.
videos.q: See this eye-opening 60 Minutes story on Luxottica

videos.t: Testing 432 Hz Frequencies (and temperaments)
videos.s: Adam Neely tests the claims for tuning to A=432 Hz by trying the unusual tuning systems that its proponents' numerology requires. He compares how they sound against standard tuning and temperaments.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever the 432 Hz versus 440 Hz debate or tuning systems come up, and as an accessible entry point to music theory for non-musicians.
videos.q: As someone who hasn't taken any musical theory or similar, it was quite interesting to hear.

videos.t: Why SpaceX is Making Starlink
videos.s: Real Engineering explains why SpaceX is building Starlink, including the economics of satellite internet. It covers the latency advantage of light in vacuum over fiber for long-distance links.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear explanation of Starlink's purpose and the case that it can beat fiber on latency for long routes.
videos.q: the whole video is worth watching

videos.t: Should We Colonize Venus Instead of Mars?
videos.s: A PBS Space Time episode asking whether Venus would be a better colonization target than Mars. It covers Venus's habitable altitudes, floating balloon habitats, and the term surfacism.
videos.w: HN links it in Mars-colonization threads as a concise case for Venus.
videos.q: Don't miss the PBS Space Time episode suggesting we should colonize Venus instead of Mars which gives some good arguments and goes through the basics.

videos.t: Salman Khan TED Talk 2011 (from ted.com)
videos.s: Salman Khan's TED 2011 talk on Khan Academy. He shows that it goes beyond video lectures to self-paced practice and analytics for teachers, and argues for filling gaps in understanding.
videos.w: HN recommends it to show Khan Academy's real model of mastery learning and teacher tools, often as a rebuttal to critics.
videos.q: If you watch his (excellent) TED talk [1], you'll see that his organization isn't just about video lectures

videos.t: The surprising pattern behind color names around the world
videos.s: Vox explains the Berlin and Kay research showing that languages around the world tend to invent color words in the same order. It walks through the hierarchy and the debate around it.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a clear, well-made summary of the linguistics of color naming and how culture shapes it.
videos.q: there is a pretty well done video by Vox on how color names are influenced by culture

videos.t: The True Nature of Matter and Mass | Space Time | PBS Digital Studios
videos.s: A PBS Space Time episode asking what matter, mass, and energy really are, starting with inertial versus gravitational mass and what mass-energy equivalence means.
videos.w: HN recommends it, and the whole channel, as a clear and deeper-than-usual physics explainer.
videos.q: The YouTube channel PBS SpaceTime gives an excellent overview of these same ideas.

videos.t: Bytebeat: Experimental music from very short C programs
videos.s: Viznut demonstrates bytebeat, experimental music generated by extremely short C programs. It is the first of a series of videos on the technique.
videos.w: HN calls it the video that started the one-line-code music trend and recommends exploring the demoscene author's channel.
videos.q: The video that started it all

videos.t: Call Between Alexey Navalny and FSB Officer Konstantin Kudryavtsev [English Subtitles]
videos.s: Bellingcat's publication of the recorded call in which Alexey Navalny, posing as a security aide, gets FSB officer Konstantin Kudryavtsev to describe the operation to poison him. It has English subtitles.
videos.w: HN cites it as a striking confession obtained through caller ID spoofing and social engineering.
videos.q: But the best part is how he did it: caller ID spoof + social engineering.

videos.t: 7 Minutes of Terror: Curiosity Rover's Risky Mars Landing | Video
videos.s: NASA's animated explanation of the Curiosity rover's Mars landing, which relied on a complex automated sequence taking about seven minutes. It features NASA engineers discussing the risks before the 2012 landing.
videos.w: Recommended as a gripping look at how hard Mars entry, descent and landing is.
videos.q: Here's a video that blows my mind every time I watch it.

videos.t: California's Renewable Energy Problem
videos.s: Real Engineering looks at the numbers for running California on renewables, focusing on the large energy storage needed. It argues about the cost of batteries and the role of other sources.
videos.w: Offered in energy and nuclear debates as a numbers-based walkthrough of renewable storage costs, though one commenter disliked its tone.
videos.q: Walks through the numbers on what it would take to run California on renewables + storage alone.

videos.t: Homeless man talks openly about being addicted to heroin. We have an opioid crisis in America.
videos.s: A short street interview from Invisible People with Keith, a homeless man in Los Angeles who lost his housing-industry job in the crash and moved from painkillers to heroin because it was cheaper. He talks candidly about the grip of addiction.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it in threads on homelessness and drug policy as a short, honest firsthand account from an articulate addict.
videos.q: Extremely powerful 5 minute interview with an obviously intelligent homeless person addicted to heroin: Terrifying

videos.t: Keynote: Embedded Ethics by Patricia Aas
videos.s: Patricia Aas's EuroBSDCon keynote is about ethics for people who build software, covering how the tech industry got to its current state and what engineers can do about it. It steps back from technical detail to the bigger picture.
videos.w: HN commenters strongly recommend it as a thoughtful talk on tech worker ethics that has not aged.
videos.q: Hasn't aged one bit. If anything Patricia is spot on pretty much everything.

videos.t: DEF CON 23 - Chris Domas - Repsych: Psychological Warfare in Reverse Engineering
videos.s: Chris Domas's DEF CON 23 talk on psychological warfare against reverse engineers. He builds code whose disassembly and control flow graphs mislead, intimidate and demoralize anyone analyzing it.
videos.w: Recommended as an entertaining and well-explained talk on anti-reverse-engineering tricks.
videos.q: Christopher Domas is one of my absolute favorite all-time hackers. He does such a fantastic job of explaining his work.

videos.t: Social Physics: How Good Ideas Spread | Sandy Pentland | Talks at Google
videos.s: Sandy Pentland of MIT presents his book on social physics, which uses big-data studies of how people interact to explain how ideas spread. He describes findings on collective intelligence and social influence.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for the finding that idea exchange and connectivity drive productivity and wealth, which they apply to cities, offices and online communities.
videos.q: There's a great Authors at Google talk by Sandy Pentland

videos.t: Xanadu Basics 1a - VISIBLE CONNECTION
videos.s: Ted Nelson explains the original Xanadu hypertext idea of visible connection, the notion that links between documents should be shown and preserved. He argues that the Web and current document standards lost this concept.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as the author's own short explanation of Xanadu's core ideas, usually in threads on hypertext, linking and decentralizing the web.
videos.q: Ted Nelson recently did a series of videos on the important ideas in Xanadu. Start here

videos.t: Keynote - JSON Graph: Reactive REST at Netflix
videos.s: Jafar Husain's ACM keynote presents Netflix's JSON Graph and Falcor, which let web developers treat all cloud data as one virtual JSON model. It combines reactive programming with REST principles.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as an alternative take on the data-fetching problem GraphQL addresses, and as a clear argument for when RPC or graph models beat plain REST.
videos.q: gives a very nice summary of when and how you might prefer RPC to REST

videos.t: Surface-Stable Fractal Dithering Explained
videos.s: Rune Skovbo Johansen explains Surface-Stable Fractal Dithering, a technique he invented and released as open source. It makes dithering stick to 3D surfaces and covers the experiments and shortcomings along the way, inspired by Return of the Obra Dinn.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the original explainer for a clever dithering technique and the go-to video in dithering threads.
videos.q: a 4-days old video related to dithering which is really worth watching.

videos.t: Small Planes Over Big Oceans (ETOPS Explained)
videos.s: A short Wendover Productions explainer on ETOPS, the rules that let twin-engine jets fly long routes over oceans. It covers the economics that favored twinjets like the 787 over four-engine aircraft like the A380 and 747.
videos.w: HN recommends it whenever threads touch twin-engine ocean flights, diversions, or why the 747 and A380 are being retired.
videos.q: did a fanatastic video about this, really recommend it

videos.t: 36C3 -  Open Source is Insufficient to Solve Trust Problems in Hardware
videos.s: A 36C3 talk by Bunnie Huang arguing that open source is necessary but not sufficient for trustworthy hardware, because verifying hardware is destructive and so creates a time-of-check/time-of-use gap. It surveys supply chain security and classes of hardware attacks, and presents the Betrusted approach to narrowing tha…
videos.w: HN commenters point to it whenever the question is how far hardware can be trusted, including FPGAs, supply chain attacks and firmware TPMs.
videos.p: hardware trust and supply chain security
videos.q: Here's an excellent talk that addresses your question

videos.t: This giant model stopped a terrible plan
videos.s: Tom Scott tells how John Reber's plan to dam San Francisco Bay was disproved by the Army Corps of Engineers' giant hydraulic Bay Model in Sausalito. The model showed the plan would have been dangerously wrong.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a short, fascinating story of a scale model preventing a terrible engineering decision.
videos.q: I learned of this plan via this short Tom Scott video. Fascinating.

videos.t: Я позвонил своему убийце. Он признался
videos.s: Alexei Navalny phones an FSB chemical-weapons specialist, posing as a senior official, and gets him to describe the 2020 Novichok poisoning and its cover-up. The video is in Russian; HN commenters point to English subtitles.
videos.w: Praised as a remarkable piece of social engineering, spoofed caller ID plus pretexting, that produced direct evidence of the poisoning.
videos.q: But the best part is how he did it: caller ID spoof + social engineering.

videos.t: Backpropagation, intuitively | Deep Learning Chapter 3
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown's third deep learning chapter gives a visual, intuitive account of backpropagation and what happens to a neural network as it learns. A follow-up video covers the underlying calculus.
videos.w: Recommended as the most accessible introduction to backprop for people who struggle with the pure math.
videos.q: I found the explainations by 3Brown1Blue to be very intuitive when it comes to neural networks

videos.t: Learning from dirty jobs | Mike Rowe
videos.s: Mike Rowe, host of Dirty Jobs, shares stories from messy real-world jobs in this TED talk. He argues that hard work has been unjustly degraded in society.
videos.w: It comes up in threads on career choice, trades, handiness and the 'follow your passion' advice.
videos.q: This guy is a big proponent of more down to earth careers and I agree with everything he says

videos.t: Virtual Barber Shop (Audio...use headphones, close ur eyes)
videos.s: A binaural audio demo, the 'Virtual Barber Shop', that places a barber moving around your head. It works best with headphones and closed eyes.
videos.w: It is the classic demo HN people point to for showing positional 3D audio working on ordinary headphones.
videos.q: try this 3d demo. And don't forget to close your eyes.

videos.t: Why Hershey bars taste like vomit (and I love them)
videos.s: Adam Ragusea explores why Hershey's chocolate tastes the way it does to many non-Americans, tracing it to butyric acid and Hershey's history, and why familiarity makes Americans love it. He compares it with British Cadbury.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a fascinating explanation of how taste is cultural and why American chocolate tastes distinctive.
videos.q: Adam Ragusea has an excellent video on this very topic

videos.t: The Part of History You've Always Skipped | Neoslavery
videos.s: A long documentary-style video arguing that slavery in the US effectively continued through convict leasing and the prison system until around 1942. It covers the constitutional carveout and the history of neoslavery.
videos.w: Recommended in threads on prison labor and American history as a thorough account of the post-Civil War period.
videos.q: presented a compelling case that US slavery truly ended in 1942

videos.t: Head Tracking for Desktop VR Displays using the WiiRemote
videos.s: Johnny Lee demonstrates head tracking with a Wii remote and a head-mounted pair of IR LEDs, so a screen acts like a window into a 3D scene as your head moves.
videos.w: It is the classic reference for head-tracked parallax displays, cited whenever new 3D or holographic display tech appears.
videos.q: Can confirm, the 3D effect is 100% spot on

videos.t: Why do competitors open their stores next to one another? - Jac de Haan
videos.s: A short animated TED-Ed lesson in which two competing ice cream vendors on a beach illustrate why rival shops cluster together. It introduces game theory and the Nash equilibrium through the Hotelling model.
videos.w: HN people use it as a clear, quick explanation of Nash equilibrium and why competitors cluster.
videos.q: this is the best explanation i've found so far on Nash's Equilibrium

videos.t: The US electrical system is not 120V
videos.s: Technology Connections explains that US household power is split-phase, with two 120V legs that combine to 240V for large appliances. It covers the breaker panel and how the system works.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it to correct misconceptions about US voltage and to explain 240V availability in American homes.
videos.q: There's a lot of misconceptions about US electricity. This video does a nice job at pointing out the good and the bad.

videos.t: DEF CON 26  - Christopher Domas - GOD MODE UNLOCKED Hardware Backdoors in redacted x86
videos.s: Christopher Domas presents research at DEF CON 26 showing a hidden alternate instruction set and undocumented hardware backdoor in some x86 processors, found on a third-party CPU. He uses it to ask how feasible wider hardware backdoors are.
videos.w: HN regulars treat Domas as a favorite hacker and bring this talk up in any discussion of CPU backdoors, hidden instruction sets or processor security.
videos.q: Christopher Domas is one of my absolute favorite all-time hackers. He does such a fantastic job of explaining his work.

videos.t: "Why do you lock your door?" - RVASec 2012
videos.s: Locksport historian Schuyler Towne's RVASec 2012 talk on why people lock their doors, tracing the history of locks and the assumptions about security behind them.
videos.w: HN commenters call it a passionate and educational history of locks and physical security, and a good starting point for the subject.
videos.p: history of locks and physical security
videos.q: It's a great place to start.

videos.t: Why is Ukraine the West's Fault? Featuring John Mearsheimer
videos.s: University of Chicago lecture in which John Mearsheimer argues the West, through NATO and EU expansion, bears primary responsibility for the Ukraine crisis. He also discusses how to end it and its consequences.
videos.w: During 2022 HN threads, commenters shared it as the realist counter-perspective to understand the Russian position, though others dispute his record.
videos.q: I find his viewpoint helpful as it’s very much Machiavellian and not focused on demonizing the Other.

videos.t: Is AI Safety a Pascal's Mugging?
videos.s: Robert Miles examines whether the case for AI safety is a Pascal's mugging, a tiny probability of an enormous payoff. He argues it is not, because AI risk does not depend on vanishingly small probabilities.
videos.w: HN points to it as a reasoned rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just Pascal's wager.
videos.q: the main point of the video is that kind of situation happens when the probability involved is vanishingly small

videos.t: How our voting system (and IRV) betrays your favourite candidate
videos.s: The Center for Election Science explains favorite betrayal in instant-runoff voting: in some elections, ranking your favorite first can cause your least favorite to win. It contrasts this with plurality voting's spoiler problem.
videos.w: The standard link in ranked-choice voting threads to show IRV does not eliminate the spoiler effect.
videos.q: here's a video explaining the strategic voting issue

videos.t: Perhaps the weakest link in the US electrical system
videos.s: Technology Connections explains weaknesses in the US electrical system, centering on how cord and circuit ratings can mismatch and cause fires. It covers extension cords, power strips and plug history in about 25 minutes.
videos.w: HN points to it as a clear explanation of why under-rated extension cords and daisy-chained power strips are dangerous.
videos.q: here's a 25 minute mini-documentary of the US electrical system's history and problems

videos.t: Welcome to the Internet - Bo Burnham (from "Inside" -- ALBUM OUT NOW)
videos.s: Bo Burnham's song from his special Inside, a satirical take on internet culture, attention and extremism.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up in threads about the internet, attention economy and smartphones, mostly as a favorite, with a few dissenters.
videos.q: This is one of my favourite songs now

videos.t: Lec 1 | MIT 6.00 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming, Fall 2008
videos.s: First lecture of MIT 6.00, an introductory computer science course taught in Python by Eric Grimson and John Guttag. It covers the goals of the course, what computation is, and data types, operators and variables.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a simple, direct entry point for beginners who want to learn computer science, not just programming.
videos.q: Professor keeps everything simple and direct because this class is designed for beginners with no or little programming experience.

videos.t: Space Oddity
videos.s: Commander Chris Hadfield performs a revised version of David Bowie's Space Oddity, recorded aboard the International Space Station. It was released as a music video in 2013.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it for the sense of wonder and chills it gives, and bring it up in threads about Bowie, space and astronauts.
videos.p: space oddity cover from the iss
videos.q: It gives me chills every time I listen to it.

videos.t: The Moon's Orbit is WEIRD
videos.s: A minutephysics explainer showing that the Moon's path around the Sun is not a spiral but closer to a 12-sided polygon with curved corners. It argues the Moon arguably orbits the Sun rather than the Earth.
videos.w: HN links it whenever the Moon's orbit comes up, as a concise explanation of why the Moon always curves toward the Sun.
videos.q: I can't explain better than minute physics, highly recommend

videos.t: How Gamers Killed Ultima Online's Virtual Ecology | War Stories | Ars Technica
videos.s: An Ars Technica War Stories episode in which Richard Garriott and Starr Long describe Ultima Online's planned virtual ecology and how players wrecked it. Players slaughtered the animals and also broke the in-game economy.
videos.w: HN uses it as a canonical anecdote that designers badly predicted player behavior, and in threads about UO and sharding.
videos.q: Instead the players indiscriminately killed both the carnivores and the herbivores, because the players were human.

videos.t: Christophe Pettus - PostgreSQL Proficiency for Python People - PyCon 2016
videos.s: A three-hour PyCon 2016 tutorial by Christophe Pettus that orients Python developers to PostgreSQL. It covers installation, administration, and use, including vacuuming, MVCC, replication and backups.
videos.w: HN readers recommend it as a thorough, practical introduction to Postgres fundamentals and optimization for application developers.
videos.q: I found this to be great introductory that touches on all the major points to keep in mind with Postgres.

videos.t: CppCon 2016: Nicholas Ormrod “The strange details of std::string at Facebook"
videos.s: Nicholas Ormrod's CppCon 2016 talk on how Facebook optimizes std::string with its open-source replacement fbstring. It covers storage layout tradeoffs, small string optimization and memory allocation behavior.
videos.w: HN returns to it as the go-to talk on string internals, small string packing and why small percentage optimizations matter at scale.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: it's still definitely worth a watch

videos.t: 15 Sorting Algorithms in 6 Minutes
videos.s: A visualization and sonification of 15 sorting algorithms, from selection sort to bogo sort, run on shuffled integers in six minutes. Each algorithm gets a size and speed scaled to its complexity.
videos.w: A classic that HN points to for seeing how sorting algorithms behave, valued for how satisfying it is to watch and hear.
videos.q: just want to quickly share an IMHO interesting sorting algorithm visualization video

videos.t: The Fall of The Simpsons: How it Happened
videos.s: Super Eyepatch Wolf analyzes why The Simpsons declined after its golden age, pointing to changes in the writers' room and a shift in the style and complexity of its comedy.
videos.w: HN treats it as the definitive explanation of the Simpsons decline, recommended in every thread asking when the golden age ended.
videos.q: For an actual exploration of what happened, I highly recommend this video.

videos.t: DEFCON 17: That Awesome Time I Was Sued For Two Billion Dollars
videos.s: Jason Scott of textfiles.com tells the story at DEFCON 17 of being sued for two billion dollars by a scammer who plagued him and others for over a decade. The talk is tragic and funny, covering what he learned about misleading schemes.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a great, hilarious talk about legal threats and cease and desist letters.
videos.q: Watch his talk on the matter, it is really great

videos.t: YouTubers have to declare ads. Why doesn't anyone else?
videos.s: Tom Scott examines why YouTubers must declare paid endorsements while TV, film and other media face no such rule, comparing regulations in the UK and US.
videos.w: HN cites it as a clear explainer on sponsorship and ad disclosure rules and their inconsistency across media.
videos.q: Tom Scott has a great video on the inconsistency that online influencers and youtubers have to declare ads/product-placements while traditional media does not.

videos.t: Tesla Battery Day
videos.s: Tesla's 2020 Battery Day event, with a company update and a keynote on new cell design, manufacturing, vertical integration and cheaper lithium and materials. It ends with the Plaid Model S and a Q&A.
videos.w: Treated as the essential primary source for Tesla's battery and cost-reduction plans, and a feast for engineering nerds.
videos.q: for anyone even remotely interested in this space and this topic, I think it is an essential watch.

videos.t: Ubuntu Slaughters Kittens | BSD Now 103
videos.s: A BSD Now episode featuring a long interview with Joyent CTO Bryan Cantrill on dtrace, ZFS, pkgsrc, containers and more. It includes his rant on why Linux epoll is flawed and stories from Sun.
videos.w: HN links it for Cantrill's entertaining epoll versus kqueue rant and his stories, such as bricking a machine with rm -rf.
videos.q: There's a good (and wildly entertaining) discussion/rant about it in this BSD Now episode

videos.t: My old BBC Micro system
videos.s: Mike of mikeselectricstuff shows his heavily modified old BBC Micro system in a 28-minute tour of 8-bit hardware archaeology.
videos.w: Recommended as an entry point to a favorite electronics channel, valued for deep knowledge and no showy bravado.
videos.q: Recommended - this guy knows his stuff, and unlike certain other youtube channels in this genre there is no annoying bravado.

videos.t: Game Critics
videos.s: A videogamedunkey video essay on video game critics. It argues that a critic's taste and integrity matter as much as their score, and tries to explain why major outlets give such inflated ratings.
videos.w: Recommended as an amusing but thoughtful take on review inflation and game journalism, in threads about reviews and ratings.
videos.q: Dunkey presented a fairly well-argued idea why major publications tend to give 9+/10 reviews to games

videos.t: Inside a Huge PCB Factory
videos.s: Strange Parts tours JLCPCB's large PCB factory in Huizhou, China, walking through the printed circuit board manufacturing process step by step. It shows the machinery, quality checks and scale behind cheap prototype boards.
videos.w: Recommended as the best look inside a modern PCB fab, cited in threads on hobby PCB vendors, manufacturing in China and automation.
videos.q: It's a tour of JLCPCB's factory, where they go through all the PCB manufacturing steps.

videos.t: The Daily Show - Burn Noticed
videos.s: A Daily Show with Jon Stewart segment from 2014 covering the People's Climate March in New York and a House science committee struggling with basic global warming facts. It mixes satire with an argument against climate denial.
videos.w: Commenters call it a favorite Daily Show clip and link it as a ready answer to climate-skeptic arguments.
videos.q: my all time favorite Daily Show clip, Burn Notice

videos.t: OK Go - Upside Down & Inside Out
videos.s: OK Go's music video for Upside Down & Inside Out, filmed during parabolic flights so the band and performers are weightless in the plane.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it as a creative music video shot entirely in zero gravity, citing it in threads about parabolic flights and space.
videos.q: One of my preferred video clip ever was filmed entirely during a parabolic flight

videos.t: Blender Motion Tracking - Room Transformation!
videos.s: Ian Hubert shows how to use Blender's motion tracking to turn ordinary footage of a room into a stylized digital environment for an indie film. It is a quick, practical walkthrough in his loose, lazy-tutorial style.
videos.w: Recommended as an eye-opening, fast introduction to what Blender can do and a model of a productive workflow.
videos.q: This video of his really opened my eyes to what Blender can do

videos.t: Wendelstein 7-X – from concept to reality
videos.s: A CAD-based animation from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics showing how the Wendelstein 7-X stellarator is configured and what its fusion research aims to achieve. It runs about 11 minutes.
videos.w: HN links it in stellarator and fusion threads as an understandable look at the design and engineering challenges.
videos.q: This video explains the elements quite in an understandable way

videos.t: RAT POISON AND BRANDY: THE 1904 ST. LOUIS OLYMPIC MARATHON.
videos.s: Jon Bois tells the story of the 1904 St. Louis Olympic marathon, a chaotic race involving fraud, rat poison, brandy, feral dogs and near-deaths. It is an episode of his show Pretty Good.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a funny, well-told retelling of one of the strangest sporting events ever.
videos.q: He has a video on the marathon that's very worth the 21 minutes

videos.t: "Stop Rate Limiting! Capacity Management Done Right" by Jon Moore
videos.s: Jon Moore's Strange Loop 2017 talk argues that rate limiting is the wrong tool for protecting services from noisy clients. He proposes concurrency-based capacity management and quotas instead.
videos.w: HN engineers recommend it for its core insight that limiting concurrency naturally yields request-rate limits, and for its link to queueing theory.
videos.q: The basic premise is not do do req/s limiting but rather concurrency limiting which results in req/s limiting by itself.

videos.t: Who is Yahweh - How a Warrior-Storm God became the God of the Israelites and World Monotheism
videos.s: An ESOTERICA episode tracing Yahweh from a warrior-storm god near Mt Seir to the god of the Israelites in the Judean highlands. It examines how Yahwism absorbed and contended with Canaanite religion.
videos.w: HN users recommend it as an impressively well-sourced, academic look at the origins of the Abrahamic religions.
videos.q: it was one of the few videos I’ve seen recently that really impressed me

videos.t: The Backwards Brain Bicycle - Smarter Every Day 133
videos.s: Destin of Smarter Every Day learns to ride a bicycle whose steering is reversed, taking about eight months, and compares it with how his young son learned much faster. It illustrates knowledge versus understanding and brain plasticity in adults versus children.
videos.w: HN cites it widely in discussions of tacit knowledge, habit, unlearning and adult versus child learning.
videos.q: There is an absolutely fascinating video about plasticity of learning between adults and children that I'd highly recommend watching [1].

videos.t: How to Cure Aging – During Your Lifetime?
videos.s: A Kurzgesagt animated explainer on whether aging could be cured within our lifetimes, made with Lifespan.io and the LEAF foundation. It introduces the idea of treating aging as a medical problem.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to longevity research that changed some commenters' views.
videos.q: Yes this is a great introduction into the topic.

videos.t: Edwin Brady - Idris 2: Type-driven development of Idris | Code Mesh LDN 18
videos.s: Edwin Brady presents Idris 2, a rewrite of the Idris dependently typed language, and shows type-driven development in practice. The demos show the compiler filling in whole functions from their types.
videos.w: HN points to it as a good introduction to Idris 2 and a striking demonstration of what dependent types enable.
videos.q: this looks like a good introduction

videos.t: China is erasing its border with Hong Kong
videos.s: A Vox Borders episode with Johnny Harris explaining how China is gradually erasing the line between mainland China and Hong Kong since the 1997 handover. It describes the one country, two systems arrangement and its expiration date.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a concise, captivating introduction to the Hong Kong conflict during the 2019 extradition-law protests.
videos.q: At 15 minutes, it's a captivating introduction to the conflict.

videos.t: ★ Cab ride 🇨🇭St. Moritz - 🇮🇹Tirano (Bernina pass), Switzerland to Italy [10.2019]
videos.s: A two-hour driver's-eye cab ride along the Bernina railway from St. Moritz in Switzerland to Tirano in Italy. The UNESCO-listed line crosses the Alps at high altitude with steep adhesion gradients.
videos.w: Recommended as relaxing slow-TV, a long scenic video to unwind with.
videos.q: Some of my favorite long ones. They are incredibly relaxing.

videos.t: Writing a Wayland Compositor in Zig - Isaac Freund
videos.s: Isaac Freund, author of the River Wayland compositor, talks about writing a Wayland compositor in Zig. He covers why he chose Zig over C and Rust and how Zig can wrap a hairy C library.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a phenomenal talk on Zig's C interop and on choosing between C, Rust and Zig for systems work.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: I loved his Zig+Wayland screencast [1], where he explained very engagingly how Zig is able to embrace and extend a pretty hairy C library

videos.t: Emily Shea - "Perl Out Loud"
videos.c: The Perl and Raku Conference - Greenville, SC 2026
videos.s: Emily Shea, a Fastly engineer with repetitive strain injury, describes using voice dictation as her main way of programming. She covers homophones, custom vocabulary and building her own voice commands to write Perl.
videos.w: HN treats it as a phenomenal demonstration that voice-driven development is viable and as an eye-opener on accessibility-unfriendly coding habits.
videos.q: This video from the article is a phenomenal demonstration of dictation coding

videos.t: Why renewables can’t save the planet | Michael Shellenberger | TEDxDanubia
videos.s: Michael Shellenberger argues in a TEDx talk that solar and wind need huge amounts of land and mining, and says nuclear power is a better path to protecting both the climate and nature.
videos.w: HN commenters credit it with changing their minds on nuclear power and cite it for the downsides of renewables.
videos.q: it's what changed my mind and therefore in my opinion the best delivery of the argument I'm aware of.

videos.t: Pi hiding in prime regularities
videos.s: 3Blue1Brown shows how pi emerges from prime numbers via complex numbers and sums of squares, culminating in a formula for approximating pi.
videos.w: Praised as a beautiful, understandable proof and a favorite among 3Blue1Brown videos.
videos.q: This is a really beautiful proof that connects complex numbers and primes to derive a formula for calculating pi.

videos.t: Vintage Electronics - The Tefifon
videos.s: Techmoan demonstrates the Tefifon, a vintage German audio player that combines elements of record and tape with a grooved elastic loop. He shows how it works and plays it.
videos.w: HN fans use it as the gateway to the Techmoan channel and praise it as one of the most fascinating obscure audio formats.
videos.q: My gateway video was the one on the Tefifon

videos.t: Pepin Debone Chicken.flv
videos.s: Jacques Pepin demonstrates deboning a whole chicken, quickly and with complete control. It is a short, wordless-feeling technique demo that shows a skill most cooks never learn.
videos.w: HN calls it the single best cooking video on the internet and suggests it as a skill worth practicing for an hour.
videos.q: Pepin's chicken deboning video is the best cooking video that has ever or will ever be put on the Internet

videos.t: I'm Allowed to Rob You!
videos.s: A short anarchist-leaning video by Larken Rose arguing that the Constitution and similar documents cannot legitimately grant anyone the right to take other people's property. It uses a rhetorical 'paper that lets me rob you' setup to challenge belief in political authority.
videos.w: Libertarian-minded commenters post it in surveillance, government and constitution threads as a red-pill argument that political authority is illusory.
videos.q: Here's all you need to know about the Constitution

videos.t: Blender 3.0 Beginner Tutorial - Part 1
videos.s: Blender Guru's beginner tutorial series, in which you model, light, texture and render a donut while learning Blender's core features. This is Part 1 of the Blender 3.0 version.
videos.w: Called a rite of passage for new Blender users and the standard first recommendation for learning the program.
videos.q: the Donut tutorial is great.

videos.t: Did Nintendo really forget to Optimize Super Mario 64 ? | MVG
videos.s: Modern Vintage Gamer examines the claim from the Super Mario 64 decompilation project that the game shipped unoptimized, and puts it in the context of 1996 N64 development.
videos.w: Recommended as a well-researched rebuttal of the idea that Nintendo simply forgot an optimization flag.
videos.q: ModernVintageGamer did a video discussing the topic that's pretty well-researched

videos.t: The Most Underrated Algorithm
videos.s: Veritasium tells the story of the Fast Fourier Transform, from its use in detecting nuclear tests to Cold War politics, and how it could have changed the arms race. It includes a short, intuitive explanation of what the Fourier transform does.
videos.w: HN points people to it as the explanation that finally made Fourier transforms and the FFT click, with a good historical story.
videos.q: The 2-minute brute-force explanation of Fourier transforms in a recent Veritasium video

videos.t: Andres Duany Lecture. Suburban Sprawl.
videos.s: A recording of Andres Duany's 1991 'San Antonio By Design' seminar on suburban sprawl. He lays out how codes, zoning and policy produce sprawl and makes the case for new urbanism.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a comprehensive, still-accurate and often funny account of how zoning and policy force suburban sprawl.
videos.q: His talk from 30 years ago is still so eerily precise and comprehensive

videos.t: Festo - SmartBird
videos.s: Festo's promo video of SmartBird, an ultralight bionic flying model inspired by the herring gull that flaps and twists its wings to fly. It shows the robot in flight.
videos.w: Recommended as a spectacular example of bio-inspired robotics, and a pointer to Festo's other work.
videos.q: Their Smart Bird is spectacular.[2]

videos.t: Construction of the 10000 year clock - Alexander Rose (SETI Talks)
videos.s: Alexander Rose of the Long Now Foundation describes the design and construction of the 10,000 year clock conceived by Danny Hillis. He covers the project's history, methods, and how different cultures built things to last millennia.
videos.w: Recommended in threads about long-lasting structures and passing knowledge across generations, as a long but fascinating talk.
videos.q: this very long but fascinating video discusses it

videos.t: Single particle creates interference after double slit - Wave particle duality at the workshop
videos.s: A short demo of a walking droplet on a vibrating silicone oil bath passing through a double slit and producing interference, a macro-scale analogue of pilot-wave behavior.
videos.w: HN users share it to build intuition about wave-particle duality and pilot-wave ideas in quantum mechanics threads.
videos.q: If you want to develop intuition, look at this video

videos.t: Louis CK Everything Is Amazing And Nobody Is Happy
videos.s: A clip of Louis CK on Conan riffing that everything is amazing and nobody is happy, about people complaining over airplane wifi and taking modern technology for granted.
videos.w: HN invokes it whenever people grumble about convenience, technology or AI that would have seemed miraculous not long ago.
videos.q: here is a good Conan clip, with a great title

videos.t: 2012 Burnett Lecture Part 1 Keynote Speaker: Russell A. Barkley, Ph.D.
videos.s: Russell Barkley gives the keynote at UNC's 2012 Burnett Seminar on ADHD. He presents it as an executive function disorder and discusses its effects and how to help.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a rigorous clinical look at ADHD, including the view that it has no benefits and that external prompts help.
videos.q: Educate yourself by watching this

videos.t: TUN: Un-Ruining the MMO
videos.s: MrBtongue argues that modern theme-park MMOs lost what made earlier sandbox online games compelling, and that MMOs could be saved by returning to sandbox design.
videos.w: Commenters call it one of the best, most insightful explanations of sandbox versus theme-park MMO design.
videos.q: it's one of the best videos explaining this concept.

videos.t: FreeCAD 0.20 For Beginners | 1 | Setup , preferences and navigation | Easy Tutorial for Learning CAD
videos.s: The first lesson of MangoJelly's FreeCAD 0.20 beginner course, covering setup, preferences and navigation. The series teaches fundamentals through complete workflows such as sketching, Part Design and STL export.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an excellent beginner series that fills FreeCAD's gap in learning material.
videos.q: MangoJelly does an excellent work on that.

videos.t: Taipei 101 Damper movement on 12 May 08
videos.s: Tourist footage of the 660-ton tuned mass damper in Taipei 101 swaying during tremors from the 2008 Sichuan earthquake. The damper hangs from the 92nd floor.
videos.w: Recommended whenever skyscraper dampers come up, since it shows how huge the moving mass is.
videos.q: There's a good video of it moving that gives you an idea of just how colossal these things are

videos.t: Sci-Fi Short Film “Slaughterbots” | DUST
videos.s: Slaughterbots is a short sci-fi film in which swarms of cheap autonomous drones are programmed to kill targets by profile. It was made as arms-control advocacy against autonomous weapons.
videos.w: HN keeps citing it whenever drone swarms, autonomous weapons or AI warfare come up, as a believable depiction of where this leads.
videos.q: which depicts exactly this in harrowing detail

videos.t: Steve Jobs Insult Response - Highest Quality
videos.s: A clean-audio clip from Apple's 1997 WWDC where Steve Jobs answers a hostile question from a developer about OpenDoc. He argues you must start with the customer experience and work backwards to the technology.
videos.w: Quoted constantly as the canonical statement of product-first thinking over technology-first thinking, and as a model of handling a heckler.
videos.q: Steve Job's response is brilliant here, frankly quite timeless and ultimately (in my view) apropos.

videos.t: RailsConf 2015 - Nothing is Something
videos.s: Sandi Metz argues that hidden assumptions in code are missing concepts, and shows how to name and expose them so code is easier to understand and change. It covers null objects and messages in Ruby.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a funny, smart and well-constructed talk on abstraction, duplication and object-oriented design.
videos.q: as a talk it is fantastic - funny, smart, well put together.

videos.t: How We're Redefining the kg
videos.s: Veritasium explains why the kilogram is being redefined in terms of Planck's constant rather than a physical metal artifact. It visits NIST to show the Kibble balance and why measuring mass precisely is hard.
videos.w: Praised as an excellent, accessible account of why the kilogram's definition changed, in redefinition threads.
videos.q: I found the Veritasium video to be a bit more interesting for the "why" aspect of this change

videos.t: How The Auto Industry Carjacked The American Dream | Climate Town
videos.s: A Climate Town video on how the auto industry reshaped American cities and culture through advertising, lobbying and campaigns like the 1939 World's Fair. It is snarky in tone but backed by a published source document.
videos.w: Recommended in urbanism threads as a well-sourced account of how car dependency was manufactured.
videos.q: Climate town videos are all well researched and provide an enormous amount of follow-up content from their sources.

videos.t: Lecture 19: Dynamic Programming I: Fibonacci, Shortest Paths
videos.s: Erik Demaine's MIT 6.006 lecture introducing dynamic programming through Fibonacci numbers and shortest paths. It covers memoization, subproblems and optimal substructure.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear introduction to dynamic programming from a well-regarded instructor.
videos.q: Please watch this MIT intro

videos.t: Tabs Outliner Overview
videos.s: A short overview of Tabs Outliner, a Chrome extension that shows browser tabs and windows as a nestable tree. It demonstrates organizing, saving and restoring tabs.
videos.w: Commenters who struggle with tab overload use it to show what tree-based tab management looks like and recommend the extension.
videos.q: Tabs Outliner puts every tab as a leaf in a tree, and you can nest leaves

videos.t: Bret Victor - Media for Thinking the Unthinkable
videos.s: Bret Victor's 2013 MIT Media Lab talk argues that the media we think with determine which thoughts are possible. He demos new representations for scientific papers, circuits, filters and signal processing.
videos.w: HN treats it as one of the canonical Bret Victor talks, cited whenever discussion turns to better tools and interfaces for thinking.
videos.q: Tools let us think previously unthinkable thoughts.

videos.t: How To Sharpen A Knife In About 5 Minutes With ONE Stone | EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW FAST! 2023
videos.s: A beginner-focused tutorial on freehand knife sharpening with a single stone, aiming for a shaving-sharp edge in about five minutes.
videos.w: Recommended by commenters who say its practical, scientific explanations finally taught them how and why sharpening works.
videos.q: he's pragmatic, approachable, and scientific, and now I actually understand how to sharpen a knife and why it works.

videos.t: Thoth's Pill - an Animated History of Writing
videos.s: NativLang's 47-minute animated documentary traces the birth and evolution of writing, from early cave marks to modern scripts. It presents the history of the world's writing systems as a story.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a fun, amazing overview of writing systems whenever the alphabet or cuneiform comes up.
videos.q: I also recommend Thoth's Pill, an amazing historical overview of writing systems

videos.t: Slavoj Žižek + Paul Holdengräber "Surveillance and whistleblowers" - International Authors' Stage
videos.s: Slavoj Zizek and Paul Holdengraber discuss surveillance and whistleblowers at the International Authors' Stage, ranging over Snowden, Assange, Pussy Riot and humor.
videos.w: HN commenters call it an entertaining, complementary philosophical take on surveillance, with a funny story about jamming secret police.
videos.q: I think Slavoj Žižek and Paul Holdengräber on "Surveillance and whistleblowers" is worth a watch.

videos.t: Plastic Recycling is an Actual Scam | Climate Town
videos.s: Climate Town gives a comedic, fast-paced account of how the plastics industry promoted recycling, including the resin-code recycling symbol, while knowing most plastic could not be economically recycled. It points viewers to the Frontline documentary Plastic Wars for a deeper treatment.
videos.w: Commenters send it as a short, entertaining explanation of why people believe plastic is recyclable and how industry PR created that belief.
videos.q: This video is under 10mins and features a lot of the PR adverts.

videos.t: How technology loses out in companies, countries & continents and what to do about it
videos.s: A conference presentation by Bert Hubert on how companies lose their technological edge and become outsourcing hubs. It argues the same dynamic applies to whole countries and continents, and ends with suggestions for reversing it.
videos.w: HN points to it as a sharper explanation of why outsourcing and specialization erode deep expertise, in threads on Intel, Boeing and software decline.
videos.q: this excellent video talks about the problems with outsourcing everything

videos.t: Lecture 1 | Programming Paradigms (Stanford)
videos.s: The first lecture of Stanford's CS107 Programming Paradigms, taught by Jerry Cain, giving an overview of the course. The course goes from C and assembly through C++, concurrency, Scheme and Python.
videos.w: Commenters rate the whole playlist as high-quality, clear teaching that builds foundations from memory and machine instructions up to different paradigms.
videos.q: The presentation is clear and it simplifies in just the right places to give you the foundations.

videos.t: Training AI Without Writing A Reward Function, with Reward Modelling
videos.s: Robert Miles explains reward modelling, in which an AI learns what humans want from their preference comparisons instead of a hand-written reward function. He walks through the 2017 paper on deep reinforcement learning from human preferences.
videos.w: Seen as the clearest introduction to the idea behind RLHF, and also borrowed by commenters as a metaphor for human motivation.
videos.q: I find this video by Rob Miles still the best presentation of the ingenious original 2017(!) paper

videos.t: Verbatim: What Is a Photocopier? | Op-Docs
videos.s: A New York Times Op-Docs short in which actors perform a real legal deposition transcript. A lawyer gets tangled in an absurd argument with a county employee about what counts as a photocopier, in a dispute over fees for public records.
videos.w: Commenters share it as a funny, memorable example of evasive depositions and of obstruction over public records requests.
videos.q: The New York Times did an amazing reenactment from transcripts of the legal deposition

videos.t: Paul Graham at Startup School 08
videos.s: Paul Graham speaks at Startup School 2008 about how to create a successful startup. His talk emphasizes being good, not just avoiding being evil, as a strategic advantage.
videos.w: HN points to it as a staple pg talk, and it appears in lists of the best startup videos and tech talks.
videos.q: He outlines many ways why it's not merely ethically appropriate to be good

videos.t: Times Tables, Mandelbrot and the Heart of Mathematics
videos.s: Mathologer shows how times table diagrams on a circle produce cardioids and other curves connected to the Mandelbrot set. He explains the patterns and links to a tool for making your own diagrams.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the clearest explanation of the patterns behind modular multiplication diagrams and times table art.
videos.q: This YouTube video explains the algo behind what you're seeing.

videos.t: Ali Rahimi's talk at NIPS(NIPS 2017 Test-of-time award presentation)
videos.s: Ali Rahimi's NIPS 2017 Test-of-Time award talk, in which he argues that modern machine learning has become alchemy, working without being rigorously understood. He calls for more rigor and understanding in the field.
videos.w: HN points to it as the sharpest, most-quoted critique of deep learning practice, and cites it whenever ML reliability or understanding is debated.
videos.q: For a more cutting and insightful critique, watch Ali Rahimi's short talk at NIPS 2017

videos.t: Eben Moglen - Freedom in The Cloud
videos.s: Eben Moglen speaks at NYU in 2010 about freedom in the cloud, arguing that centralized services and handing over personal data and server logs erode privacy and freedom. The talk lays out the motivation for FreedomBox, a personal server for your own data.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the foundational talk behind FreedomBox and the case against centralized web services.
videos.q: It's worth the watch/listen to get the idea in full.

videos.t: The Future of War, and How It Affects YOU (Multi-Domain Operations) - Smarter Every Day 211
videos.s: Destin Sandlin of Smarter Every Day explains Multi-Domain Operations through footage from his last mission at RIMPAC 2018. He covers missile and torpedo testing and interviews military leaders about the cyber and information domains.
videos.w: HN cites it for an insider's look at defense work and at how the military thinks about information operations and cyberspace.
videos.q: It's an insightful how-and-why explanation for those wondering why there aren't more conscientious objectors

videos.t: Why you DON'T want Perfect Pitch
videos.s: Adam Neely explains what perfect (absolute) pitch is, how it differs from relative and quasi-absolute pitch, and why he would not want it. He covers its drawbacks, including drift with age.
videos.w: HN links it in threads on absolute pitch as a musician's useful summary of its downsides and age-related decline.
videos.q: This video by Adam Neely was helpful

videos.t: Anagrams, but where you can break apart letters: "Anagraphs"
videos.s: Tom Scott-style exploration by suckerpinch (Tom7) of generalized anagrams where letters can be broken into pieces, called anagraphs, with a whimsical computational approach.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a typical example of Tom7's technically astounding and playful videos.
videos.q: Definitely give it a watch.

videos.t: "Data Driven UIs, Incrementally" by Yaron Minsky
videos.s: Yaron Minsky of Jane Street shows how the OCaml Incremental library lets trading UIs express data transformations that are easy to read and efficient on streaming data. It includes a live table demo.
videos.w: Recommended in incremental computation and reactive UI threads as the best conceptual overview of Incremental and incr_dom.
videos.q: Any discussion about incremental UI should include Yaron Minsky's talk about Jane Street's OCaml framework, incr_dom from 2016

videos.t: Moishe Lettvin - What I Learned Doing 250 Interviews at Google
videos.s: Moishe Lettvin, a former Google engineer, shares lessons from 250 interviews and his time on the hiring committee. He tells how the committee given anonymized packets, including its own, would hire almost none of them.
videos.w: Linked often in hiring-process threads for the anecdote about Google's committee refusing to hire itself, as evidence interviews are noisy.
videos.q: The one I found very enlightening is from Moishe Lettvin given at Etsy

videos.t: Why Cars Rarely Crash into Buildings in the Netherlands
videos.s: Not Just Bikes explains why cars rarely crash into buildings in the Netherlands, attributing it to street design that forgives mistakes and to systematic crash investigation. It contrasts this with North American acceptance of such crashes.
videos.w: HN cites it for the systems-over-blame view of road safety and for Dutch infrastructure design.
videos.q: tl;dw: because they actually do what you suggest, and they incorporate their findings into better road designs.

videos.t: The Fermi Paradox Compendium
videos.s: Isaac Arthur surveys the popular proposed solutions to the Fermi Paradox in a 71-minute compendium. He weighs the strengths and weaknesses of each argument.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend Arthur's Fermi Paradox videos as a thorough, clear treatment of the subject.
videos.q: He describes the Fermi Paradox and related concepts 100x better than anyone else.

videos.t: The Dumbest Excuse for Bad Cities
videos.s: Not Just Bikes takes on the common excuse that a country is simply too big or spread out for good transit and walkable cities. The video argues that city density and short everyday trips matter, not national size or overall population density.
videos.w: HN users cite it as the standard rebuttal whenever someone says that America is too big for rail or good urban design.
videos.q: For a video describing how wrong it is, refer to Not Just Bikes

videos.t: The Gambler - Fuck You
videos.s: A short clip from the film The Gambler in which John Goodman's character gives a monologue about the 'position of fuck you': building enough financial security that you owe nobody anything. The scene is a compact statement of financial independence as freedom.
videos.w: HN points to it as the source and best distillation of 'fuck you money', in threads about FIRE, windfalls, layoffs and financial literacy.
videos.q: this scene really distills a lot of good stuff into a few minutes

videos.t: Pilot Wave Theory and Quantum Realism | Space Time | PBS Digital Studios
videos.s: A PBS Space Time episode introducing de Broglie-Bohm pilot wave theory, an interpretation of quantum mechanics that avoids much of the strangeness of the mainstream views. It is aimed at curious lay viewers.
videos.w: HN commenters regularly send people to it as an accessible, friendly introduction whenever pilot wave theory comes up.
videos.q: Here's another great video from PBS Spacetime on this topic

videos.t: Pink Floyd Echoes & 2001 A Space Odyssey HD
videos.s: Pink Floyd's Echoes played in sync with the final Jupiter and Beyond the Infinite segment of Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey. The song's length closely matches the sequence.
videos.w: HN commenters share it as a favorite audiovisual experience, with some calling the sync the best thing they have seen.
videos.q: the sync of Echoes and 2001 is the BEST thing I have ever seen in my life

videos.t: The Delayed Choice Quantum Eraser, Debunked
videos.s: Sabine Hossenfelder explains the delayed choice quantum eraser and argues it does not rewrite the past, as popular accounts claim. She walks through what the experiment actually shows.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear debunking of the retrocausality interpretation of the quantum eraser.
videos.q: Later Sabine Hossenfelder did a video debunking the proposition that DCQE somehow showed that the past was being rewritten.

videos.t: Don't Say Velcro
videos.s: Velcro Brand's legal team makes a short, humorous ad asking people not to use "velcro" as a noun or verb and to say hook and loop instead. It is a tongue-in-cheek lesson in defending a trademark against genericization.
videos.w: HN cites it as the go-to example of a company defending its trademark, and many also find it funny.
videos.q: it's hilarious and worth watching

videos.t: Segmented Displays
videos.s: Posy explores segmented displays, from the seven-segment display to alternative designs with fewer or more segments, with patents and history.
videos.w: Recommended as a meditative, geeky tour of alternative display designs.
videos.q: here is a meditative video on alternative segmented displays.

videos.t: Hans Rosling: Debunking third-world myths with the best stats you've ever seen
videos.s: In this TED talk, Hans Rosling uses animated statistics to debunk myths about the developing world, showing how health and income have improved across countries.
videos.w: Cited as the classic data-driven argument that the first-world versus third-world split is outdated and the world is improving.
videos.q: There is a great TED talk by Hans Rosling showing the same improving global condition through different metrics.

videos.t: Wild Tricks for Greenscreen in Blender
videos.s: Ian Hubert shows quick, unconventional tricks for greenscreen compositing in Blender, as a follow-up to his motion tracking video.
videos.w: Recommended as a favorite among practical Blender guides from a hugely productive solo artist.
videos.q: My favourite guides of his are not in the Lazy Tutorials playlist, though.

videos.t: Stephen Fry on the Joys of Swearing
videos.s: A short clip of Stephen Fry defending swearing as a rich and essential part of the English language and rejecting the idea that it is unnecessary.
videos.w: HN commenters post it in swearing and profanity debates as the best statement against taking offense at profanity.
videos.q: Stephen Fry says it best

videos.t: Cgroups, namespaces, and beyond: what are containers made from?
videos.s: Jérôme Petazzoni explains how Linux containers are built from kernel features like cgroups, namespaces and SELinux. He demonstrates putting the pieces together by hand to make a container and compares runtimes and approaches like jails and zones.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a talk that makes containers click, showing that containerization is not virtualization and demystifying what Docker does.
videos.q: I watched this talk couple of years ago that made docker/containers finally click for me.

videos.t: Blockchain vs. Bullshit: Thoughts on the Future of Money [Classic Bitcoin & Open Blockchain  Talk]
videos.s: Andreas Antonopoulos explains how to tell Bitcoin-style blockchains from corporate blockchain hype. He argues the goal should be de-banking everyone rather than banking the unbanked.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a corrective to enterprise blockchain marketing and as an explanation of what makes Bitcoin distinctive.
videos.q: Just watch Blockchain vs. Bullshit

videos.t: Telescope Building with John Dobson
videos.s: A roughly 90-minute film of John Dobson building a Dobsonian telescope step by step, including hand-grinding the mirror.
videos.w: Recommended to anyone interested in telescope making as a guide from Dobson himself.
videos.q: Here's a 90 minute youtube video on how to build one, with John Dobson himself

videos.t: Baz Luhrmann - Everybody's Free To Wear Sunscreen
videos.s: The original music video for Everybody's Free to Wear Sunscreen, a spoken-word piece built on Mary Schmich's 1997 column of life advice, produced by Baz Luhrmann.
videos.w: Posted as timeless, comforting life advice in threads about careers, aging, and uncertainty.
videos.q: A lot of wisdom in a 5min song

videos.t: Mad Men - The Carousel (Higher Quality)
videos.s: The Kodak Carousel pitch scene from the Mad Men season finale, in which Don Draper sells nostalgia through a slide projector. It runs about three minutes.
videos.w: HN holds it up as one of the best pitches ever, an example of selling feeling and nostalgia rather than features.
videos.q: Mad Men's Kodak presentation in season one is one of the best pitches I've seen.

videos.t: CppCon 2015: Sean Parent "Better Code: Data Structures"
videos.s: Sean Parent's CppCon 2015 talk on better use of standard containers and the goal of having no incidental data structures. It argues that proper containers can greatly simplify code.
videos.w: Commenters say it changes how you think about types and the STL, and makes a case for simple modern C++.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: this one really made me aware of what just might be the best way to think about it.

videos.t: Basic Beginners FreeCAD v1.0 : Introduction to Course
videos.s: The introduction to MangoJelly's beginner course for FreeCAD 1.0. The course teaches solid modeling with the Part Design, Sketcher and Part workbenches.
videos.w: HN users recommend MangoJelly's thorough tutorials as the best way to learn FreeCAD properly, since trial and error doesn't work.
videos.q: MangoJelly has done an amazing job in churning out high quality tutorials for FreeCAD

videos.t: "An approach to computing and sustainability inspired from permaculture" by Devine Lu Linvega
videos.s: Devine Lu Linvega of Hundred Rabbits talks about low-power, offline computing, esoteric languages and the Uxn virtual machine, informed by years of sailing the Pacific. The talk frames computing sustainability through a permaculture lens.
videos.w: Praised as a standout, non-standard Strange Loop talk explaining the reasoning behind Uxn and resilient computing.
videos.q: Devine had a great talk about the "why" of Uxn at Strange Loop last year

videos.t: Shouting in the Datacenter
videos.s: A two-minute 2008 clip from Sun's Fishworks team in which Brendan Gregg uses DTrace to show disk latency spiking while he shouts at a rack of drives. Bryan Cantrill narrates the demonstration.
videos.w: It is the go-to viral demo whenever HN discusses vibration, acoustic attacks, or sound affecting hard drives.
videos.q: this entertaining YouTube video from 2009, in which someone demonstrates the effect by literally shouting at a rack of servers

videos.t: The Energy Project | Tony Schwartz | Talks at Google
videos.s: Tony Schwartz of The Energy Project speaks at Google about managing energy rather than time. He draws on The Power of Full Engagement and his work on stamina and sustained performance.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it in discussions of shorter workweeks and productivity, arguing that rest and energy matter more than hours.
videos.q: It's worth watching this talk from the Leading @ Google series -

videos.t: Randomness is Random - Numberphile
videos.s: Numberphile with Simon Pampena on how humans misunderstand randomness, including coin-flip sequences, run lengths and the gambler's fallacy.
videos.w: Recommended as an accessible demonstration that people are bad at producing or judging random sequences.
videos.q: Here's a great video demonstrating how people tend to misunderstand randomness

videos.t: Interview with Larry Summers, Former Secretary of the Treasury | The Problem with Jon Stewart
videos.s: A short excerpt of Jon Stewart interviewing former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers about the causes of inflation and whether workers or corporate profits are to blame. It comes from an episode of The Problem With Jon Stewart.
videos.w: HN commenters link it in threads on greedflation and corporate pricing power as an accessible exchange of opposing views.
videos.q: It's a real good exchange of viewpoints on the matter -- better than you'd get with most other commentary.

videos.t: Flight of the Navigator | VFXcool
videos.s: Captain Disillusion's VFXcool episode, led by Alan Melikdjanian, takes a 41-minute nostalgic look at how the visual effects of Flight of the Navigator were made. It covers early computers, motion control, in-camera effects and practical crafts.
videos.w: Strongly recommended as a detailed, entertaining history of 1980s CGI and film techniques, including the role of the Foonly F1.
videos.q: I highly recommend this video on the making of Flight of the Navigator.

videos.t: Playing a Neural Network's version of GTA V: GAN Theft Auto
videos.s: Sentdex demonstrates GAN Theft Auto, a GameGAN-based neural network that recreates GTA V so the network itself is the playable environment. He shows the results and releases the code.
videos.w: Cited as an early, striking demo of neural networks acting as game engines and world models.
videos.q: This YouTube video, to me, shows the promise of things to come.

videos.t: Walls, Floors, & Ceilings
videos.s: Pannenkoek explains how Super Mario 64 handles wall, floor and ceiling collisions, including triangles, normal vectors, quarter steps and out of bounds. It is a detailed 37-minute technical walkthrough of the game's physics.
videos.w: Praised as an engrossing, in-depth look at SM64 mechanics that is surprisingly compelling to watch.
videos.q: each longer than half an hour (and both of them extremely interesting)

videos.t: Building a Marsbase is a Horrible Idea: Let’s do it!
videos.s: A Kurzgesagt animation walking through how a Mars base could be built and why it would be punishing, covering radiation, temperature extremes, toxic dust and the need for shielding.
videos.w: Recommended as a sobering, accessible overview of the practical challenges of living on Mars.
videos.q: sobering run down of the realities when living on mars

videos.t: Space Station 13 Review | AHELP: Clown Grief Pls Ban He™
videos.s: SsethTzeentach reviews Space Station 13, the chaotic multiplayer game, by recounting absurd stories of singularities, malfunctioning AIs and plasma fires.
videos.w: HN considers it the go-to link for conveying the chaos of Space Station 13 in any related discussion.
videos.q: No SS13 discussion is complete without linking to SsethTzeentach's infamous absurd-sounding review

videos.t: Richard Feynman Lecture -- "Los Alamos From Below"
videos.s: A 78-minute Richard Feynman lecture of anecdotes about working at Los Alamos on the Manhattan Project, followed by about ten minutes of audience Q&A in which he tells three safe-cracking stories.
videos.w: Strongly recommended for its funny, human account of Los Alamos, which one commenter calls almost a stand-up act.
