videos.s: Bjarne Stroustrup's CppCon 2015 keynote on using C++14 to write better code, not just different code. It introduces the C++ Core Guidelines and the machine-checkable rules and GSL library behind them.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as the starting point for modern C++ and for the language's safety story.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: If you want to start with modern c++ watch this

videos.t: The Trolley Problem in Real Life
videos.s: Vsauce's Michael Stevens stages a realistic version of the trolley problem with unsuspecting subjects who believe they must decide a life-or-death outcome. The Mind Field episode compares what people say they would do with what they actually do.
videos.w: Recommended as a worthwhile real-world experiment whenever trolley problems or moral dilemmas come up.
videos.q: The video is well worth a watch

videos.t: Life is easy. Why do we make it so hard? | Jon Jandai | TEDxDoiSuthep
videos.s: Thai farmer Jon Jandai talks about leaving Bangkok to farm and build his own house, arguing that food, shelter, clothing and medicine are easy to provide and that modern life is made needlessly complicated. He founded the Pun Pun Center for Self-reliance.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a thoughtful counterpoint to the pursuit of complicated, consumption-driven lives.
videos.q: He self-reports being much much happier, whether you believe it or not.

videos.t: TWO Unpickable (?) Locks for Lock Picking Lawyer!
videos.s: Engineer Stuff Made Here builds two new supposedly unpickable locks with different designs and sends them to the Lock Picking Lawyer to see whether they can be defeated. The video covers the novel anti-picking mechanisms.
videos.w: HN people recommend it, along with the Lock Picking Lawyer's response, as an engaging look at lock design and how clever mechanisms get bypassed.
videos.q: Together they give a whole new understanding of lock design and picking methods.

videos.t: Weird webcam mod that enables eye-contact conversation
videos.s: DIY Perks builds a webcam mod using a two-way mirror in a box so the camera sits behind the screen image. This allows real eye contact on video calls.
videos.w: Whenever eye contact in video calls comes up, commenters point to this as the cheap homemade teleprompter-style solution.
videos.q: it's a really interesting DIY solution to ensuring eye contact when video conferencing.

videos.t: Razor1911
videos.s: Razor 1911's eponymous demo celebrating 40 years of the group, which won first place at the Revision 2026 demo competition and the public's choice award. It is a retrospective of keygen and warez scene culture with chiptune music.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as an impressive showpiece of the demoscene and a nostalgic career retrospective of a legendary group.
videos.q: This Razor1911 career retrospective demo from Revision was pretty impressive

videos.t: Bed Bugs- What You've Been Told is Totally False
videos.s: Mark Rober digs into bed bugs, testing popular beliefs about where they come from and how to get rid of them. It mixes entertaining experiments with research-based advice on what works and what does not.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a fun, research-grounded explainer whenever bed bug threads come up.
videos.q: mark rober did a good entertaining video on this

videos.t: Backspin Basketball Flies Off Dam
videos.s: A short Veritasium video showing how far a backspinning basketball would travel dropped off a dam. It demonstrates the Magnus effect and links to Flettner rotor ships and aircraft.
videos.w: HN uses it as a quick, clear demonstration of the Magnus effect behind spinning-cylinder ships and planes.
videos.q: There's a great Veritasium video explaining the Magnus effect and the Flettner rotor here

videos.t: Permaculture Greening the Desert - Geoff Lawton
videos.s: Geoff Lawton documents a permaculture project that turned barren Jordanian desert into green, productive land. It covers the techniques he used.
videos.w: Cited in climate and carbon-removal threads as an inspiring example of re-greening deserts.
videos.q: Geoff Lawtons work in Jordan is inspiring

videos.t: Defcon 21 - The Secret Life of SIM Cards
videos.s: A DEF CON 21 talk by Karl Koscher and Eric Butler on how SIM cards work, including Java Card applets, the SIM toolkit and the OS running on the card. It shows how much control the network and the card have independent of the phone.
videos.w: HN cites it as the go-to overview of what SIM cards can run and do, usually in threads about Java Card, SIM attacks or phone security.
videos.q: This video from defcon gives a good overview of what Java Card applets is

videos.t: Origins of Go Concurrency style by Rob Pike
videos.s: Rob Pike's 2010 talk at OSCON's Emerging Languages Camp on where Go's concurrency style comes from. It traces the idea from Hoare's CSP through Squeak, Newsqueak and Limbo to Go.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the clearest account of the CSP lineage behind Go's goroutines and channels.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Check out this video by Pike

videos.t: The Loudness War
videos.s: A two-minute demonstration of the loudness war, showing how heavy dynamic range compression in CD mastering makes music louder while degrading sound quality. It uses audio examples so you can hear the distortion.
videos.w: HN keeps linking it as the shortest clear explanation of over-compression and brickwalled mastering.
videos.q: this video which gave a very succinct answer to my question

videos.t: ClojureScript in the Age of TypeScript — David Nolen
videos.s: David Nolen explains how ClojureScript is used at Vouch.io to build mobile and web software with a single language and REPL-driven workflow. The talk includes a live coding demo of React Native development.
videos.w: Pointed to as a concrete demonstration of REPL-driven development and ClojureScript with React Native.
videos.q: David Nolen gave a relevant talk[0] about the workflow they use to integrate Clojure and React Native for mobile and web development

videos.t: 17. Succinct Structures I
videos.s: Erik Demaine's MIT 6.851 Advanced Data Structures lecture introducing succinct data structures, covering rank, select and tries. It is part of the Spring 2012 course.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear, high-quality introduction to succinct data structures from a leading authority.
videos.q: Erik Demaine [1] gave two good lectures on succinct data structures [2] in the 2012 MIT 6.851 Advanced Data Structures course

videos.t: Gender Neutral Pronouns: They're Here, Get Used To Them
videos.s: Tom Scott argues that grammatical gender is a silly concept and that the singular 'they' is an established gender-neutral pronoun. The description carries later corrections and reflections he added in 2019.
videos.w: HN commenters link it as a short, friendly explanation of singular they and grammatical gender in discussions of pronoun usage.
videos.q: Tom Scott has a great video on grammatical gender that is worth a watch

videos.t: CppCon 2017: Herb Sutter “Meta: Thoughts on generative C++”
videos.s: At CppCon 2017 Herb Sutter presents his work on evolving C++ through compile-time code generation, including metaclasses and reflection. The aim is to make the language both more powerful and simpler by letting programmers express intent directly.
videos.w: Praised as the best talk of CppCon 2017 and the key introduction to metaclasses and generative C++.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Herb Sutter's talk about it is by far the best talk I've seen from from CppCon17.

videos.t: "The Clean Code Talks  -- Inheritance, Polymorphism, & Testing"
videos.s: Misko Hevery's Clean Code Talk shows how to use object-oriented techniques such as polymorphism to remove repeated if and switch statements. The result is code that is easier to test, understand and maintain.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a thorough treatment of replacing conditionals with polymorphism and why flags and deep ifs can be code smells.
videos.q: This talk gives a great overview of why boolean flags (rather, if-statements) can be a code smell

videos.t: ASPLOS Keynote: The Golden Age of Compiler Design in an Era of HW/SW Co-design by Dr. Chris Lattner
videos.s: Chris Lattner's ASPLOS 2021 keynote on the golden age of compiler design in an era of hardware and software co-design, covering compiler infrastructure for accelerators and unifying hardware IRs.
videos.w: Recommended for explaining where the compiler ecosystem lacks standardization for accelerators and why efforts like MLIR and CIRCT matter.
videos.q: I watched Chris Lattner's ASPLOS talk and it finally clicked.

videos.t: Rant: Entity systems and the Rust borrow checker ... or something.
videos.s: Jonathan Blow's hour-long livestreamed response to a RustConf 2018 closing keynote about entity systems in Rust. He argues that index-based entity systems amount to manual memory management that sidesteps the borrow checker, and he talks about friction for game developers.
videos.w: It is the standard citation in HN arguments over Rust for game development, the borrow checker and ECS designs, as a skeptical view from an experienced game developer.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: A more detailed description of his opinions are laid out here where he goes into much more detail

videos.t: The Alt-Right Playbook: Introduction
videos.s: The introduction to Innuendo Studios' video essay series on the rhetorical tactics of the alt-right. It examines how bad-faith debate and harassment work online.
videos.w: Recommended as a primer on recognising trolling and dog-whistle tactics in online discussion.
videos.q: I recommend the YouTube series The Alt-Right Playbook for an overview of these tactics

videos.t: The Search for the Perfect Door - Deviant Ollam
videos.s: Deviant Ollam shows that most physical attacks on doors bypass the lock, with photo and video examples of how doors, frames and hardware get defeated. It is a physical security talk from Shakacon.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an interesting talk on how weak real-world door security is, and cites it for the stories of bad doors.
videos.q: Heard it recently and thought it was really interesting.

videos.t: Vertical Bifacial Solar Panel Performance Results Part 1
videos.s: A hobbyist compares vertical bifacial solar panels against south-facing angled panels using winter production results. It tests whether the usual mounting approach is actually best.
videos.w: HN points to it as real-world, side-by-side data on vertical versus angled panel orientation.
videos.q: this person did a side by side experiment on their property with both angled and vertical bifacial with some interesting results.

videos.t: Defcon 20 - Dan Tentler - Drinking from the caffeine firehose we know as shodan
videos.s: Dan Tentler's DEF CON 20 talk on odd things he found on the internet through Shodan, such as stoplights, power systems and other non-computer devices exposed online. It highlights how many devices need no credentials.
videos.w: HN points to it when discussing exposed IoT and industrial devices, as an eye-opening look at how much is reachable online.
videos.q: Warning - watching this may readjust your faith in humanity.

videos.t: SHIPBREAKERS | Would you risk your life dismantling the world’s largest ships just to survive? | NFB
videos.s: An NFB documentary about the shipbreaking yards of Alang, India, where about 40,000 people dismantle huge ships by hand in dangerous conditions.
videos.w: HN recommends it for an up-close look at the shipbreaking industry.
videos.q: Both mortifying and fascinating to see this industry up close.

videos.t: OSCON 2010:  Rob Pike, "Public Static Void"
videos.s: A 13-minute OSCON 2010 talk in which Rob Pike argues about what is wrong with mainstream languages like C++, Java and C#, and presents Go as a response. He discusses verbosity and what lightness means in a language.
videos.w: HN uses it as a concise statement of the thinking behind Go's design.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: gave this short speech at OSCON 2010 about what's wrong with programming languages, their thinking, and their recent direction

videos.t: miniKanren - Dan Friedman and William Byrd
videos.s: Dan Friedman and William Byrd demonstrate miniKanren, a logic programming system for Scheme, in an unconference talk. It includes generating programs by running relations in reverse.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a mind-blowing and fun introduction to logic programming for working programmers.
videos.q: I highly recommend watching Dan Friedman and William Byrd give their miniKanren conference talk

videos.t: Peter Rizun, Andrew Stone -- 1 GB Block Tests -- Scaling Bitcoin Stanford.
videos.s: Peter Rizun and Andrew Stone present results of tests running 1 GB blocks on a Bitcoin test network at Scaling Bitcoin Stanford. The talk argues for big-block scaling and discusses its consequences.
videos.w: Cited by big-block advocates as evidence that Bitcoin could handle far higher throughput.
videos.q: A good talk about really big blocks on bitcoin and what the ramifications are;

videos.t: Which key is the saddest?
videos.s: Musician Adam Neely examines whether certain keys sound sadder than others, looking at the history of tuning systems and temperaments and at how instrument timbre shapes the emotional character we hear. It draws on historical aesthetics writing and audio examples.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for its historical context on tuning systems and for how instruments influence what music gets composed.
videos.q: lots of historical context about tuning systems, but also raising the issue of timbre of specific instruments

videos.t: Carbon Offsets: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: A Last Week Tonight segment explaining carbon offsets, what they claim to do, and how they may worsen climate change. It looks at perverse incentives and questionable projects.
videos.w: HN points to it as an informative explainer on why many carbon offset schemes are not genuine.
videos.q: John Oliver with a quite informative video about why many carbon offsets/carbon credits schemes are most likely not genuine

videos.t: CSS Grid Changes EVERYTHING - Amazing Presentation
videos.s: Morten Rand-Hendriksen's WordCamp Europe 2017 talk presents CSS Grid Layout as a native two-dimensional layout system that changes how web pages are structured, including responsive layouts independent of source order. It was given as browsers began shipping support.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an inspiring demonstration of how powerful CSS Grid is and how it repairs the relationship between HTML and CSS.
videos.q: The speaker is good but I think I like it just because it fixes the relationship between HTML and CSS.

videos.t: Dr. Jason Fung: Fasting as a Therapeutic Option for Weight Loss
videos.s: Dr. Jason Fung's talk at the 2018 CrossFit Health Conference on therapeutic fasting for weight loss. He explains why long-term weight loss is hard and tackles common myths.
videos.w: HN people point to Fung as the best resource for understanding fasting and weight loss.
videos.q: The best resource for weight loss via fasting is Dr. Jason Fung

videos.t: How Kodak Exposed Nuclear Testing
videos.s: Veritasium tells how Kodak film was fogged by radioactive fallout from the first atomic tests, letting the company detect nuclear testing before anyone announced it. The video also covers the deal to keep it quiet and how fallout contaminated packaging.
videos.w: HN commenters bring it up as a good related watch in any thread about fallout, nuclear tests or detecting hidden events through indirect evidence.
videos.q: Veritasium did an eye opening vid on how fallout blew across the country and was ruining Kodak's film on the East Coast.

videos.t: Laws that choke creativity | Larry Lessig
videos.s: Larry Lessig's TED talk argues that copyright law chokes creativity, drawing on John Philip Sousa, celestial copyrights and the ASCAP cartel to make the case for reviving remix culture.
videos.w: Recommended in copyright, patent and SOPA threads as a clear case for copyright reform.
videos.q: Here is some sound reasoning on the topic from Larry Lessig

videos.t: Susan Crawford on Captive Audience: The Telecom Industry & Monopoly Power in the New Gilded Age
videos.c: Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society
videos.s: Susan Crawford talks at Harvard's Berkman Klein Center about her book Captive Audience. She argues that deregulation and consolidation left a few telecom companies in control of American internet access, so people pay too much for slow service.
videos.w: Recommended in broadband and net neutrality threads as an overview of the US telecom monopoly problem.
videos.q: It goes over the telecom industry, how it's not competitive and the current day incentives/problems.

videos.t: The Secret Chinese War for Your Opinion!
videos.s: Serpentza, a Westerner living in China, describes Chinese influence efforts abroad and the cultural conflict between Shen Yun and Confucius Institutes. It is a commentary from his personal perspective.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an interesting on-the-ground perspective on Confucius Institutes and Chinese influence operations.
videos.q: This was an interesting video by a westerner who is in China (often)

videos.t: The Classroom Only Works for One Kid in the Room
videos.s: CGP Grey argues that a classroom works well only for the one student pitched at the average level, and sketches a future of personalized instruction. It introduces the idea of a Digital Aristotle, a tutor for every learner.
videos.w: Brought up in nearly every discussion of AI tutors and the future of schooling as the original Digital Aristotle idea.
videos.q: I keep coming back to CGP Grey's take[0] on the issue

videos.t: You Can Win the Presidency With 22% of the Vote
videos.s: A short CGP Grey animation showing how the US electoral college lets a candidate win the presidency with as little as about 22 percent of the popular vote. It lays out the arithmetic of winning states by narrow margins.
videos.w: Linked in electoral-system discussions as a quick, clear argument against the electoral college.
videos.q: you can effectively become president if you can get the right 22% of the USA to vote for you.

videos.t: Meaningful Play: Getting Gamification Right
videos.s: A Google Tech Talk by Sebastian Deterding on gamification. It looks at what points and badges get wrong and what lessons game design offers for non-game applications.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a thoughtful take on doing gamification and game design well.
videos.q: getting it right can make really powerful games

videos.t: Craig Ferguson Speaks From The Heart
videos.s: A clip of Craig Ferguson's late-night monologue in which he talks about his past as an alcoholic. He explains why he will not mock Britney Spears over her breakdown.
videos.w: HN users share it in threads on drinking and addiction as an honest account of alcoholism and sobriety.
videos.q: Craig Ferguson's comments on alcoholism are worth listening to

videos.t: My Gift To Climate Alarmists
videos.s: Tony Heller presents a short video arguing that climate science relies on data truncation, cherry-picking and selective presentation of statistics. It is a one-sided polemic against mainstream climate claims.
videos.w: Shared by climate-skeptic commenters as a counter-argument to alarmist statistics, a contested source rather than consensus.

videos.t: Johnny Cash - Hurt
videos.s: The official music video for Johnny Cash's cover of Nine Inch Nails' Hurt, from his American Recordings era, filmed late in his life. It is a stark, emotional performance of the song.
videos.w: HN commenters hold it up as one of the greatest cover versions ever, so powerful that Trent Reznor said the song was no longer his.
videos.q: It's one the greatest rock and roll covers ever

videos.t: Sequelitis - Mega Man Classic vs. Mega Man X
videos.s: Egoraptor's Sequelitis compares Mega Man Classic and Mega Man X, analyzing how the games teach players through level design without explicit tutorials. It mixes comedy with design analysis.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as the standard example of invisible onboarding and good game design, praising it as funny and insightful.
videos.q: it does make some very very good points about video game design

videos.t: New Voxel Engine Reveal - Crystal Islands Experiment
videos.s: John Lin reveals a rewritten voxel engine demonstrated in a Crystal Islands scene, with much finer voxel detail, fast collision, fracture and path-traced global illumination.
videos.w: HN cites it as a showcase of one of the best voxel engines, impressive for its detail and smoothness.
videos.q: Crystal Island looks amazingly detailed and smooth.

videos.t: George Hotz | Programming | we do coronavirus science aka hacking nature #lockdown part1 | COVID-19
videos.s: A long George Hotz livestream in which he explores the coronavirus genome and molecular biology from scratch using a browser and Python, hacking on the science in real time.
videos.w: HN suggests it for coders curious how an outsider approaches coronavirus biology, though it is described as unscientific.
videos.q: Interesting for coders/hackers

videos.t: A Million Dollars vs A Billion Dollars, Visualized: A Road Trip
videos.s: Tom Scott makes the difference between a million and a billion dollars tangible by using distance on a road trip instead of volume. The drive makes the scale of a billion intuitively felt.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever discussion turns to billionaire wealth or the human difficulty of grasping very large numbers.
videos.q: Tom Scott has a great video on it

videos.t: How A Blind Developer Uses Visual Studio
videos.s: Saqib Shaikh, a blind developer, shows how he writes and debugs code in Visual Studio 2017 using a screen reader. The short demo shows an expert doing ordinary developer tasks.
videos.w: HN recommends it, especially to developers losing their sight, as a concrete demonstration of coding with text-to-speech.
videos.q: I think it is a good demonstration of an expert doing typical developer activities.

videos.t: Samsung SSD Awesomeness
videos.s: A Samsung-backed viral demo that builds a fast computer from 24 256GB MLC SSDs in a RAID 0 array and shows the throughput results.
videos.w: HN passed it around in 2009 as a funny, impressive demo of SSD speed despite its marketing origin.
videos.q: Samsung has a funny and impressive "viral" ad video showing 24 SSD drives in a RAID array.

videos.t: The Long, Twisted And Slightly Ridiculous Story of Avgas Part 1
videos.s: AVweb's Paul Bertorelli explains why general aviation has failed to replace leaded avgas, blaming industry inertia, bureaucratic delay and an exemption that removes the incentive. This is part one of two.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as an insightful, humorous account of why unleaded aviation fuel is so hard to approve.
videos.q: here are a few insightful videos that summarize the story

videos.t: How did consciousness evolve? - with Nicholas Humphrey
videos.s: A Royal Institution lecture in which Nicholas Humphrey presents his theory of phenomenal consciousness and its evolution. He draws on the book Sentience and discusses evidence for animal sentience.
videos.w: Recommended as a good high-level view of Humphrey's book and his argument on how consciousness evolved.
videos.q: His recent RI lecture was great and a good high level view of the book.

videos.t: Ron Vale (UCSF, HHMI) 1: Molecular Motor Proteins
videos.s: Ron Vale of UCSF and HHMI gives an introductory lecture on kinesin, dynein and myosin motor proteins. He covers their roles in cells and how they turn ATP hydrolysis into directed motion and force.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it to show how strange and mechanical cellular machinery is, and to explain how kinesin walks along microtubules.
videos.q: This shows how they look.

videos.t: 1. Introduction, Finite Automata, Regular Expressions
videos.s: The first lecture of Michael Sipser's MIT 18.404J Theory of Computation course, covering course mechanics, finite automata, regular languages and regular expressions. It proves closure of regular languages under union and begins concatenation.
videos.w: HN recommends Sipser's free lectures as the companion to the standard theory of computation textbook and a path to understanding how computers fundamentally work.
videos.q: Sipser also has corresponding lectures that are available for free on YouTube here

videos.t: 電磁祭囃子 in NEO TOKYO 🏮
videos.s: A short music video by the Japanese group Electronicos Fantasticos, led by Ei Wada, playing festival-style music on repurposed old electronics. Instruments include CRT TVs, a barcode reader, an electric fan harp and TV taiko drums.
videos.w: HN users share it as a delightful example of people making real music from obsolete electronics and self-built instruments.
videos.q: It's this band from Japan who make incredible music with instruments they made themselves.

videos.t: Howard Payne & Deviant Ollam  - This Key is Your Key, This Key is My Key
videos.s: A HOPE conference talk by Howard Payne and Deviant Ollam on common keys, such as elevator and fire service keys, that open many buildings. It covers physical security weaknesses from shared key standards.
videos.w: Brought up in threads on elevators and locks as an engaging talk on common keys.
videos.q: I have to also mention another video of theirs

videos.t: Miniatur Wunderland *** official video *** largest model railway / railroad of the world
videos.s: The official tour video of Miniatur Wunderland in Hamburg, the world's largest model railway. It shows the 1,300 square meter layout with trains, aircraft, cars and ships moving around.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an absorbing look at the most elaborate model railroad ever built.
videos.q: You can watch a short tour of it at

videos.t: Low Latency Routing in Space
videos.s: A short visualization from HotNets researchers of routing and latency over SpaceX's proposed Starlink constellation, based on its FCC filings. It shows orbital shells, link topology and how inter-satellite routes could beat terrestrial fiber on long distances.
videos.w: It is the go-to visual for how Starlink's constellation and laser links could cut global latency, linked in many satellite internet threads.
videos.q: This video goes a bit into the probable topology of the links and gives a good look at how the eventual constellation would look.

videos.t: Forget big change, start with a tiny habit: BJ Fogg at TEDxFremont
videos.s: BJ Fogg of Stanford's Persuasive Tech Lab argues that lasting change comes from tiny habits, such as flossing one tooth or doing one pushup, anchored to things you already do.
videos.w: Recommended in habit and motivation threads for its simple anchor-then-tiny-action recipe.
videos.q: After I X, I will do Y. X must be sure, Y must be small.

videos.t: Free software, free society: Richard Stallman at TEDxGeneva 2014
videos.s: Richard Stallman's TEDxGeneva 2014 talk describing how nonfree programs give companies control over users and what users can do to regain control. It introduces the free software movement and the four freedoms.
videos.w: HN uses it constantly as the reference for the argument that either the user controls the software or the software controls the user, and it is recommended as a basic introduction.
videos.q: I'd recommend this[1] talk by Richard Stallman, it's pretty basic, but it gets the idea across well.

videos.t: HBO Intro - Behind the Scenes
videos.s: A 1983 behind-the-scenes film about making the HBO 'Feature Presentation' starship logo sequence. It shows the handcrafted miniature city, motion-control cameras and practical effects.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a look at pre-CGI effects work that looks like CGI but was entirely physical.
videos.q: looks CGI but is entirely physical models, motion controlled cameras, and clever compositing

videos.t: The Insane Engineering of James Webb Telescope
videos.s: Real Engineering explains the engineering behind the James Webb Space Telescope, including its folding mirror, sunshield, orbit and cooling systems, and why deployment was so difficult.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible in-depth explanation of how Webb works and why its deployment was remarkable.
videos.q: For some context around what makes this deployment so remarkable, watch this[0] video

videos.t: How government programs drive up college tuitions
videos.s: Peter Schiff, during his 2010 Senate campaign, argues that government loan programs and subsidies push college tuition up.
videos.w: Cited in tuition-cost threads for the argument that easy government-backed loans enable high prices.
videos.q: Here's a solid video on the topic where Peter Schiff explains why college tuition is so high

videos.t: Why Life Seems to Speed Up as We Age
videos.s: Veritasium explores why time seems to speed up as we age, covering chronoception and several competing explanations beyond the common proportional-theory argument.
videos.w: Cited in threads about perceived time as a good, detailed explanation of the effect.
videos.q: Veritasium explores this and IMO the alternative arguments are more compelling

videos.t: #NSDR (Non-Sleep Deep Rest) with Dr. Andrew Huberman
videos.s: A roughly 10-minute guided Non-Sleep Deep Rest session voiced by neuroscientist Andrew Huberman. It is meant to reduce daytime fatigue, improve focus and aid sleep.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a short, practical guided rest session to use during a midday break or nap.
videos.q: I like this guided NSDR session with Andrew Huberman.

videos.t: How does a whip break the sound barrier? (Slow Motion Shockwave formation) - Smarter Every Day 207
videos.s: Smarter Every Day uses high-speed and Schlieren photography to show how a whip crack is a supersonic shockwave formed at the tip. It references academic papers on whip physics.
videos.w: Recommended as the clearest footage of a whip tip going supersonic, and cited in shockwave discussions.
videos.q: I highly recommend it.

videos.t: Chess Fundamentals #1: Undefended Pieces
videos.s: First video in John Bartholomew's Chess Fundamentals series, focused on spotting undefended pieces. He teaches habits for scanning your own and your opponent's position to avoid hanging pieces.
videos.w: HN chess improvers recommend Bartholomew's beginner playlist as a clear, approachable path to getting better.
videos.q: I'd recommend these youtube videos [1] by John Bartholomew.

videos.t: Stanford Seminar: Beyond Floating Point: Next Generation Computer Arithmetic
videos.s: John Gustafson presents posits, a proposed drop-in replacement for IEEE 754 floats that is simpler in hardware and more flexible in precision. The seminar includes a live demo and machine learning results.
videos.w: Cited in floating-point threads as the main introduction to posits and unums as an alternative to IEEE floats.
videos.q: Here's a nice introductory presentation

videos.t: Jared Mauch - Getting Fiber To My Town (NLNOG Live! September 2020)
videos.s: Jared Mauch tells how he got fed up with poor internet options in rural Michigan and built his own fiber network to his town. The talk was given at NLNOG Live in September 2020.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever community or DIY fiber ISPs come up, as a first-hand account of how an individual built one.
videos.q: At this year's (virtual) NLNOG there was presentation from a fellow who was fed up with slow Internet options in his rural Michigan county

videos.t: KiCad 6 STM32 PCB Design Full Tutorial - Phil's Lab #65
videos.s: A 100-minute tutorial from Phil's Lab on designing an STM32-based 'black pill' PCB in KiCad 6. It covers schematic capture, two-layer layout and routing, USB, and sending the board for manufacture and assembly.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a practical way to learn KiCad and PCB design by following one full project.
videos.q: The Youtube channel Phil's Lab has a really good series

videos.t: The Boring Company Information Session
videos.s: A long information session where The Boring Company presents its vision for Loop, an underground high-speed transit system, and the traffic problems it aims to solve. It includes discussion of faster tunnel boring and electrification.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as the primary source for what the company is actually proposing, in threads skeptical of the project.
videos.q: It's worth watching to see what they are proposing.

videos.t: Why We Sleep: Science of Sleep & Dreams | Matthew Walker | Talks at Google
videos.s: Berkeley sleep scientist Matthew Walker presents the science of sleep and dreams and how sleep affects health and lifespan, based on his book Why We Sleep.
videos.w: HN suggests it as an easy alternative to the book for people who want Walker's sleep findings.
videos.q: that I recommend watching if you're not a book person

videos.t: The Best (and Worst) Ways to Shuffle Cards - Numberphile
videos.s: Persi Diaconis explains on Numberphile the mathematics of card shuffling, including why seven riffle shuffles are needed to randomize a deck and how different shuffles compare.
videos.w: HN points to it as a good, anecdote-filled introduction to the math of shuffling from the expert himself.
videos.q: It gives a lot of insight and anectdotes in addition to the central theorem

videos.t: Pentagon Wars - Bradley Fighting Vehicle Evolution
videos.s: A roughly ten-minute scene from the movie The Pentagon Wars showing how the Bradley Fighting Vehicle's requirements ballooned through committee demands into a compromised design. It is a satirical dramatization of military procurement.
videos.w: Linked in nearly every F-35 or procurement thread as the classic illustration of feature creep and design by stakeholder committee, including in software.
videos.q: It's a great example of how trying to design a product that works well for every stakeholder in every scenario leads to a Frankenstein of a product

videos.t: harvard & aliens & crackpots: a disambiguation of Avi Loeb
videos.s: Physicist Angela Collier gives an hour-long critique of Avi Loeb's alien claims and reputation, placing them within the broader topic of physics crackpots. The Loeb discussion starts around the 24 minute mark.
videos.w: Frequently linked as an in-depth, well-presented skeptical take whenever Loeb's alien claims come up.
videos.q: I was surprised about myself that I watched the entire thing and I guess it's because of the high quality of the presentation

videos.t: The Kilimanjaro Darkjazz Ensemble - Here Be Dragons (Full Album)
videos.s: A full-length album by The Kilimanjaro Darkjazz Ensemble, a dark, cinematic electronic jazz group. It runs about 55 minutes across nine tracks.
videos.w: HN commenters suggest it as atmospheric, near-ambient music for programming and focus.
videos.q: still in the spirit of heavy, nearly ambient

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #1191 - Peter Boghossian & James Lindsay
videos.s: Joe Rogan interviews Peter Boghossian and James Lindsay, who describe their hoax papers submitted to academic journals in grievance studies. The conversation runs about two hours and covers academic publishing, ideology and victimhood culture.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an entertaining account of how easily fake papers get published and of problems in academic peer review.
videos.q: If you have not watched Peter Boghossian and James Lindsay on the Joe Rogan show you should.

videos.t: Monads and Gonads
videos.s: Douglas Crockford's Google Tech Talk explains monads without category theory or Haskell, implementing them in JavaScript and tying them to Ajax and promises. He also touches on odd asides such as coloring code by scope.
videos.w: Often recommended as a demystifying monad talk in plain JavaScript, though some find it light on definitions.
videos.q: what I thought to be one of DC's greatest talks

videos.t: EEVblog #186 - Soldering Tutorial Part 3 - Surface Mount
videos.s: Dave Jones of EEVblog shows hand soldering of surface-mount parts, including drag soldering and tack-and-reflow of 0.5mm fine-pitch ICs, with solder paste and hot air.
videos.w: Recommended as a good introduction to SMD soldering techniques for beginners.
videos.q: Check out Dave Jones' multi-part videos on soldering

videos.t: Why Starting A Rocket Engine Is So Hard!
videos.s: Tim Dodd's hour-long deep dive on how rocket engines start, from solid motors to liquid engines. It covers thermal conditioning, spin-up, ignition methods, starting in space, and a step-by-step RS-25 startup.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the best explanation of why engine start is hard and what can go wrong.
videos.q: Here's a 1hr video from the Everyday Astronaut explaining the process and everything that can go wrong.

videos.t: Meeting my hero! Sailing legend Sven Yrvind
videos.s: Sam Holmes Sailing visits sailing legend Sven Yrvind and tours his boat, covering the man and his small-boat design philosophy.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to Yrvind and his minimalist boat ideas.
videos.q: I watched this video [1] to get an idea about the man and his boat design philosophy and it's very cool.

videos.t: Lecture 1: Introduction to Information Theory
videos.s: The first lecture of David MacKay's Cambridge course on information theory, pattern recognition and neural networks. It introduces the core ideas of his book Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms.
videos.w: Recommended as an enjoyable, clear introduction to information theory that pairs well with MacKay's free textbook.
videos.q: It was very enjoyable for me to learn the material from his lectures.

videos.t: Timeshares: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on timeshares covers how people get sold into them, why they are so hard to leave, and the exit-company scams that target owners trying to get out.
videos.w: Cited in threads about hard-to-cancel subscriptions and timeshare scams as an informative overview of the sketchy exit industry.
videos.q: I think this Last Week Tonight episode is very informative on the topic

videos.t: Tesla Is Lightyears Ahead Of... Tesla
videos.s: SuperfastMatt looks at how the Tesla Model S retracting door handles were redesigned over time, from many parts to a motor plus sensor, with a focus on engineering and reliability.
videos.w: Recommended whenever door handles or car reliability engineering come up, as an enjoyable look at design iteration.
videos.q: This is a great video by SuperfastMatt on the engineering behind and evolution of the Tesla door handle.

videos.t: Why lockdowns are the wrong policy: Swedish expert Prof. Johan Giesecke
videos.s: UnHerd interview with Swedish epidemiologist Johan Giesecke, who explains why he thinks lockdowns are the wrong policy and describes Sweden's approach during the spring 2020 pandemic.
videos.w: Commenters point to it for the Swedish insider perspective on lockdowns, with some later calling its statements prescient.
videos.q: Here's an interesting interview with a senior epidemiologist partly responsible for Sweden's unconventional strategy

videos.t: Freeman Dyson on the Global Warming Hysteria April, 2015
videos.s: A 2015 interview in which physicist Freeman Dyson, then 91, argues that global warming concerns are exaggerated, that CO2 is beneficial and that climate models oversimplify complex systems. It is posted on a channel that opposes climate consensus.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a prominent physicist's skeptical counter-view, usually when someone asks for dissenting opinions.
videos.q: He explains his position quite coherently

videos.t: In full: Rowan Atkinson on free speech
videos.s: Rowan Atkinson's speech at the launch of the Reform Section 5 campaign in Parliament in 2012. He argues against criminalizing insulting words and for answering speech with more speech.
videos.w: Recommended as an eloquent defense of free speech against laws on offensive or insulting speech.
videos.q: Rowan Atkinson made an excellent speech on the matter back then [2]

videos.t: Why It's Rude to Suck at Warcraft
videos.s: Folding Ideas' long essay on why playing poorly in World of Warcraft feels rude. It traces how raiding culture shifted from relaxed fun to optimization, theorycrafting and wikis.
videos.w: Recommended as a thoughtful, research-heavy dive into game culture and the social pressure of competitive play.
videos.q: is worth the watch

videos.t: Why CG Sucks (Except It Doesn't)
videos.s: RocketJump Film School argues that we only notice bad CG while great CG is invisible, so CG seems to be everywhere ruining movies when it often is not.
videos.w: Used as a counterpoint whenever commenters claim CGI always looks fake.
videos.q: This video from a few years ago is a great counterpoint

videos.t: CppCon 2015: Timur Doumler “C++ in the Audio Industry”
videos.s: Timur Doumler's CppCon 2015 talk on how C++ is used in the audio industry. It covers the patterns and tools audio developers rely on, including handling real-time constraints.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an introduction to real-time and low-latency programming in C++ for people getting into audio.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: he goes through real time strategies to keep the response time under around 30ms IIRC

videos.t: High Performance Web Sites and YSlow
videos.s: A Google Tech Talk on Yahoo's 14 rules for faster web pages and the YSlow tool. It covers front-end practices like avoiding @import and fixing ETags, with live analysis of popular sites.
videos.w: Praised as solid, research-backed advice on front-end web performance.
videos.q: Everything they produce about the subject (and I don't just mean the plugin) is solid gold.

videos.t: The REAL reason behind the housing crisis
videos.s: Gary's Economics argues that the UK housing crisis stems from wealth inequality, treating housing as an asset like shares that rich people bid up. He contends that simply building more housing won't fix affordability.
videos.w: HN commenters share it as a counterargument to the YIMBY build-more-housing view, linking wealth concentration to asset prices.
videos.q: It feels to me like a good faith counterargument to the YIMBY build more housing line of thought, so might be an interesting perspective

videos.t: How Not to Land an Orbital Rocket Booster
videos.s: SpaceX's own compilation of failed orbital booster landing attempts, set to sound, showing the crashes before landings succeeded.
videos.w: HN uses it as evidence that SpaceX iterated through visible failures and is open and humorous about them.
videos.q: you might enjoy this official SpaceX Blooper reel from 2017 that shows the numerous spectacular failures that they worked through.

videos.t: Black Hat USA 2013 - OPSEC failures of spies
videos.s: Journalist Matthew Cole's Black Hat 2013 talk on the CIA's operational security failures in the 2003 Milan kidnapping. Phone and location metadata exposed the team and led to arrest warrants.
videos.w: Recommended as a non-technical, concrete case study of how metadata and phone records expose covert operations.
videos.q: The whole talk is worth watching.

videos.t: Erlang: The Movie (Fixed Audio)
videos.s: A 12-minute film in which Erlang's creators demonstrate the language's fault tolerance and live-system features, including phoning each other to show it working. This version has fixed audio.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a charming, concise demonstration of what makes Erlang special, from the people who built it.
videos.q: the most glorious 11 minutes of some programmers explaining how their creation works you will ever see

videos.t: "Compacting the Uncompactable" by Bobby Powers
videos.s: Bobby Powers presents Mesh, a drop-in malloc replacement that eliminates memory fragmentation in unmodified C/C++ programs by compacting memory. The talk covers how it works despite C's fixed object addresses, and its benefits for programs like Redis.
videos.w: Recommended as a great talk on solving fragmentation for C/C++ and runtimes like Ruby and Python without code changes.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: There was a great talk at Strange Loop about a drop-in malloc replacement which compacts.

videos.t: Michael Seibel - Building Product
videos.s: Y Combinator CEO Michael Seibel lectures at Startup School on building a product people want: identifying the problem, the customer, an MVP and which customers to pursue first.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as practical YC advice on iterating on a product and talking to users.
videos.q: Watched this lecture by Michael Seibel to YC in 2018 and thought it was useful.

videos.t: Classic Game Postmortem: Alone in the Dark
videos.s: Frederick Raynal gives a GDC postmortem of Alone in the Dark, the game that helped create the survival horror genre. He covers how the team built it and shows some of the old tools used.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a firsthand account from the creator, including the old tooling.
videos.q: There is a very nice presentation [1] in which Raynal shows some of the old tools that were used to create Alone in the Dark.

videos.t: (Sponsored) KiCad STM32 + USB + Buck Converter PCB Design and JLCPCB Assembly - Phil's Lab #11
videos.s: A roughly three-hour screen recording of designing a barebones STM32F4 board in KiCad, covering schematic, four-layer layout and routing, USB and a buck converter. It ends with ordering manufacture and assembly through JLCPCB.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as a real, end-to-end PCB design walkthrough that beginners successfully imitated to learn KiCad.
videos.q: successfully imitated this guy's tutorials

videos.t: Infinite fractions and the most irrational number
videos.s: Mathologer uses continued fractions to show why the golden ratio is the most irrational number, comparing it with root 2, e and pi and pointing to where this shows up in nature.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear, visual explanation of continued fractions and why phi is hardest to approximate by fractions.
videos.q: Pretty good Mathologer video about continued fractions

videos.t: WLW's 500,000 Watt Transmitter
videos.s: A tour of the historic WLW transmitter facility in Mason, Ohio, recorded at Hamvention 2013. It shows the surviving equipment from the 500,000 watt AM era, when WLW was the only US station at that power, and explains the history.
videos.w: Recommended as the definitive visual walkthrough of the WLW 500 kW transmitter, with detailed equipment views and lots of history.
videos.q: You get to see the high power equipment in detail accompanied by lots of history about the facility.

videos.t: Are Crows the Ultimate Problem Solvers? | Inside the Animal Mind | BBC Earth
videos.s: A BBC Earth clip from Inside the Animal Mind in which a crow named 007 solves an eight-step puzzle to get a reward. It showcases crow problem-solving.
videos.w: Shared in crow-intelligence threads as a striking demonstration that changes how people see crows.
videos.q: This one impressed me so much, I never looked at Crows again the same way

videos.t: Climate Change Debate: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: A short Last Week Tonight segment where John Oliver stages a statistically representative climate debate, with Bill Nye facing a crowd of dissenters. It satirizes false balance in media coverage.
videos.w: Cited to illustrate false balance and the trouble with giving all sides equal weight.
videos.q: There is a nice visual example of this made by John Oliver on his show

videos.t: The 5 Most Dangerous Chemicals on Earth
videos.s: A SciShow episode in which Hank Green introduces five of the most dangerous chemicals, from lethal toxins to substances that explode on contact. It is an entertaining overview of extreme chemical hazards.
videos.w: Recommended as a fun companion to threads about hazardous chemistry, such as hydrofluoric acid and reactive substances.
videos.q: This is a fun video to watch

videos.t: Veritasium: A Story of YouTube Propaganda
videos.s: Tom Nicholas critiques Veritasium's sponsored video on driverless cars, using it to examine YouTube sponsorships, science-channel credibility and how statistics and misinformation can be used in branded content.
videos.w: HN cites it in discussions of sponsored science content and Veritasium's credibility, usually as the go-to critique.
videos.q: Tom Nicholas did a good job breaking down the problems with it

videos.t: I sent robot forgeries to a handwriting expert
videos.s: Stuff Made Here builds a handwriting robot and sends its output to a handwriting expert to see whether it can pass as forgery. It walks through the engineering trials and errors along the way.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as the physical-machine take on replicating handwriting, with plenty of explained iteration.
videos.q: really cool video by Stuff Made Here explaining how he tried to make 'realistic' handwritten forgeries with a pen plotter

videos.t: Unlocking UAP Mysteries: Economics, Aliens, and The Great Filter | Merged EP0109
videos.s: A 146-minute Merged Podcast episode in which UAP researcher Ryan Graves talks with economist Robin Hanson about UFOs. Topics include the Great Filter, Hanson's grabby aliens model, and the push for more inquiry into UAPs.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it for Hanson's grabby aliens reasoning as an unusual framework for thinking about UFO behavior and intelligent life in the cosmos.
videos.q: Grabby Aliens concept by Robin Hanson is an interesting new take on UFOs.

videos.t: Joe Rogan Experience #1245 - Andrew Yang
videos.s: Joe Rogan's long interview with Andrew Yang during his 2020 presidential run. They discuss universal basic income, automation and his policy proposals.
videos.w: Suggested as a starting point for understanding Yang's capitalist case for UBI, though some note it is long and dated.
videos.q: The Joe Rogan interview is a good place to start

videos.t: Why does light slow down in water?
videos.s: Fermilab's Don Lincoln explains why light travels slower in water and glass. He knocks down common wrong explanations such as absorption and re-emission, then gives the wave-mechanics reason tied to refractive index.
videos.w: HN commenters link it to correct the widespread misconception about why light slows in a medium.
videos.q: See this video for an explanation of why light travels slower through a medium with an index of refraction greater than one.

videos.t: DEFCON 20: Hacker + Airplanes = No Good Can Come Of This
videos.s: A DEF CON 20 talk by RenderMan on the security weaknesses of ADS-B, the unencrypted, unauthenticated aircraft tracking broadcast. It shows how easily the data can be spoofed and what that means for security designed in too late.
videos.w: Cited whenever aviation or vehicle communication security comes up, as the standard demonstration that ADS-B is naively designed and trivially spoofable.
videos.q: Good watch if you wanna see how naively designed the whole thing is.

videos.t: Does Vienna Have the World's Best Council Housing? Swimming Pools, Private TV Channels & More
videos.s: Channel 4's George Clarke visits a council estate in Vienna and is surprised by amenities such as swimming pools and private TV channels. It showcases Vienna's high-quality social housing.
videos.w: HN points to it as proof that government-provided housing can be attractive, in housing and homelessness threads.
videos.q: See this video for what government provided housing could be.

videos.t: A walk through of installing Synapse+Riot+Jitsi from scratch on Debian
videos.s: A walkthrough of installing Synapse, Riot and Jitsi from scratch on Debian to run your own Matrix communication service. The description warns it is now quite outdated and links to updated material.
videos.w: Recommended as a practical demonstration that self-hosting a Matrix server is fairly easy, even on a small droplet.
videos.q: I found this video to be super helpful

videos.t: Infinite Mario AI - Long Level
videos.s: A bot built by Robin Baumgarten plays Infinite Mario using A* path-finding, shown as a red planned path that updates as new obstacles appear. It won the Mario AI competitions and uses only on-screen information.
videos.w: HN points to it as a vivid demo that plain A* search can beat fancier machine-learning approaches in game AI.
videos.q: It's pretty interesting, a lot of people wrote/are writing high falutin' machine learning algorithms

videos.t: The UK's Failed Experiment in Rail Privatization
videos.s: Wendover Productions explains how UK rail privatization worked and why it failed. It covers the fragmented operator and infrastructure structure and why market forces apply poorly to rail.
videos.w: Recommended in privatization and rail threads as a clear, well-sourced explanation of the UK rail mess.
videos.q: the people on the Wendover YouTube channel did a video on this back in March which explained the issue really well.

videos.t: The Fallen of World War II
videos.s: Neil Halloran's animated, data-driven documentary visualizes the human cost of World War II and compares it with other wars and the trend toward fewer war deaths in recent decades.
videos.w: HN cites it for a sense of the scale of WWII casualties by country and the long decline in violence.
videos.q: does a great job of giving a sense of what the proportions are of relative tragedies in terms of loss of life.

videos.t: I Have Delivered Value... But At What Cost?
videos.s: A short KRAZAM comedy sketch satirizing corporate tech life, where a worker reckons with having delivered value at the cost of his soul, complete with Slack chimes.
videos.w: Praised as painfully accurate office satire, with the channel's sketches called genius.
videos.q: The videos on that channel are so good that they're painful to watch

videos.t: How Many Holes Does a Human Have?
videos.s: Vsauce asks how many holes a human has and uses topology to show the answer depends on what counts as a hole, with animations and expert input.
videos.w: Pointed to as a fun, light introduction to topology and to answer the human-holes question.
videos.q: If you'd like a fun, light, video introduction to this topic, this Vsauce video is worth a watch

videos.t: Bret Victor - Inventing on Principle
videos.s: Bret Victor's talk from Dropbox's DBX conference about living by a guiding principle, in his case that creators need an immediate connection to what they are making. He shows live-coding and time-manipulation demos that let ideas take form at the speed of thought.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as the best demonstration of why instant feedback matters in programming tools.
videos.q: Bret Victor's Inventing on Principle is probably the best demonstration of why this matters

videos.t: Why are we changing maps?  (from The West Wing)
videos.s: A short clip from The West Wing in which staffers meet a group advocating the Peters projection and challenge the Mercator map. It was shown as geography humor at a Salt Lake GIS user group meeting.
videos.w: HN links it in any thread on map projections and the Mercator distortion of country sizes, often calling it a favorite scene.
videos.q: my favorite scene from The West Wing

videos.t: Hyperbolica: A Non-Euclidean Adventure [Old Trailer]
videos.s: The old announcement trailer for Hyperbolica, CodeParade's Unity game set in hyperbolic and spherical space. The creator has since posted devlog videos on building it.
videos.w: Pointed to when non-Euclidean geometry or games in hyperbolic space come up, along with the creator's well-liked devlog.
videos.q: CodeParade has been working on hyperbolica for a while now and doing fantastic videos on the process.

videos.t: Jailbreaking the Simulation with George Hotz | SXSW 2019
videos.s: George Hotz gives a SXSW 2019 talk on the idea that we live in a simulation and asks what actions would be available from inside it. He takes a hacker's view of whether it could be escaped.
videos.w: Shared in simulation-argument threads as an entertaining, hacker-minded take, though some commenters criticize Hotz himself.
videos.q: He's taking the hacker's perspective and exploring if the simulation would be hackable from inside.

videos.t: Khan Academy and the Effectiveness of Science Videos
videos.s: Veritasium examines research suggesting science explainer videos like Khan Academy's make students feel they understand while tests show they have not learned, because misconceptions go unaddressed. It suggests how to partly fix this.
videos.w: HN uses it in debates on video-based teaching and how confronting misconceptions helps learning, though some find its Khan Academy critique flawed.
videos.q: please watch the whole video because it explains one massive problem with video science lessons and how to partially fix the problem.

videos.t: Dance p 3 Mar09
videos.s: Geoff Cumming uses a simulation to show how wildly the p value varies from one replication to the next because of sampling variability. He argues for estimation and confidence intervals over null hypothesis significance testing.
videos.w: Recommended as a vivid visual demonstration of how unreliable p-values are.
videos.q: absolutely fantastic and well worth watching

videos.t: Why 50 Million Chinese Homes are Empty
videos.s: PolyMatter explains China's housing bubble and why around 50 million homes sit empty. It covers cultural and economic reasons behind the overbuilding and the government's bind.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear, compact explainer on China's empty homes, ghost cities and property troubles.
videos.q: it explains clearly (for a complex situation) what's been going on in China's real estate, the 'ghost cities' and the demolitions.

videos.t: Bryan Cantrill on ARC: A Self-Tuning, Low Overhead Replacement Cache [PWL SF] 10/2017
videos.s: Bryan Cantrill presents the ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) paper by Megiddo and Modha at Papers We Love. He opens with a survey of caching strategies before digging into the self-tuning LRU/MFU design.
videos.w: Recommended in cache-algorithm threads as a fun, informative walk through caching strategies and ARC.
videos.q: Bryan Cantrill does a pretty good survey of caching strategies in the intro

videos.t: The Origins of Russian Authoritarianism
videos.s: Kraut traces centuries of political development, from Mongol rule and the Orthodox church to Muscovite autocracy, that shaped Russia's authoritarian state. It uses countryball animation and compares Russia with Europe and China.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a good introduction to Russian authoritarianism, though some commenters say it is flawed or wrong on many points.
videos.q: this video gives a good introduction to the origins of Russian Authoritarianism

videos.t: The Longest Year in Human History (46 B.C.E.)
videos.s: Historia Civilis tells the story of 46 BCE, the 445-day year in which Julius Caesar reformed the Roman calendar. It covers the political context, including the civil war, Cato and Cicero.
videos.w: Recommended as an entertaining and well-explained account of why our calendar looks the way it does.
videos.q: Historia Civilis has a great video explaining how Caeser used the longest year to his advantage in war

videos.t: America's Nerve Gas Arsenal
videos.s: A 1973 NBC News documentary on the US nerve gas arsenal, covering leaks in Okinawa, a Utah test that killed thousands of sheep, and the long-term hazards of storage sites. It won an Emmy.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a fascinating, Emmy-winning look at US chemical weapons stockpiles and their dangers.
videos.q: If you're interested in this type of stuff this documentary is incredible and apparently won an Emmy.

videos.t: Making Badass Developers - Kathy Sierra (Serious Pony) keynote
videos.s: Kathy Sierra's Fluent 2015 keynote on the one metaskill for developers: the ability to come up to speed quickly and stay there. She covers how people learn, cognitive resources versus willpower, and building skill.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it when asked how to learn better or keep improving.
videos.q: Kathy Sierra gave an informative talk on the topic of learning at the 2015 O'Reilly Fluent conference.

videos.t: TWiST #46 with David Heinemeier Hansson
videos.s: An episode of This Week in Startups in which Jason Calacanis interviews Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson. They discuss startups, bootstrapping and 37signals' approach to business.
videos.w: Recommended as an entertaining look at DHH's views and what the 37signals founders stand for.
videos.q: People, please watch these few videos to genuinely understand what 37Signal guys (David and Jason) stand for

videos.t: Disney's Practical Guide to Path Tracing
videos.s: Walt Disney Animation Studios' short introduction to path tracing, showing how rays are traced and bounced through a virtual scene to simulate light. It explains how this approach is used in animated films.
videos.w: Recommended as an approachable intro to path tracing in ray tracing and rendering threads.
videos.q: here's a great Disney video introducing path tracing

videos.t: First Follower: Leadership Lessons from Dancing Guy
videos.s: Derek Sivers annotates a short clip of a lone dancer at a festival, showing how a first follower turns a ridiculous act into a movement. He draws out lessons about leadership and making it easy to follow.
videos.w: A go-to short explanation of how movements start and why early followers matter.
videos.q: Watch this 2 minute to see how this works, you may have seen this before

videos.t: Star Wars: The Phantom Menace Review (Part 1 of 7)
videos.s: The first of seven parts of RedLetterMedia's long review of Star Wars: The Phantom Menace. It argues that the film's central flaw is its characters and the lack of audience connection.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as sharp film criticism and a lesson in filmmaking, and cite it when arguing the prequels failed on basics.
videos.q: thanks to them I have learned a lot about movies, actors, directors and movie making in general.

videos.t: Sam Aaron live coding an ambient electro set w/ Sonic Pi
videos.s: Sam Aaron live codes an ambient electronic set using Sonic Pi, the music programming environment he created. The performance shows code driving music in real time.
videos.w: Offered as an example of live-coded music and a fun entry point to Sonic Pi.
videos.q: Sam Aaron is the guy behind the project, he does a lot of ambient type stuff

videos.t: Jim Keller: The Future of Computing, AI, Life, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #162
videos.s: Lex Fridman interviews chip architect Jim Keller about the future of computing, AI, life and consciousness. Topics include CPU design, branch prediction and why imperfect designs often win.
videos.w: Recommended as a stellar long-form interview with someone both very smart and wise, mined for CPU design insights.
videos.q: Investing time to listen to the guy seems to be not worse.

videos.t: Twitter and Visual Studio Rant
videos.s: Casey Muratori responds on-stream to a dismissive Twitter post by demonstrating how slow Visual Studio's startup and debugger watch window are, comparing it to much older software and machines. It is a long rant about software performance and bloat.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as the canonical concrete demonstration that modern developer tools got slower despite vastly faster hardware.
videos.q: Casey Muratori has some great YouTube videos (a.k.a.: rants)

videos.t: Why Spotify Will Ultimately Fail
videos.s: Benn Jordan argues that Spotify's business model undermines the music it sells, using streaming payout figures and the economics for artists and labels.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it as an artist's informed explanation of streaming economics and why Spotify pays so little compared with alternatives like Bandcamp.
videos.q: I find this artist's explanation of the situation helpful

videos.t: OODA Loop & Evolutionary Epistemology of John Boyd by Chuck Spinney
videos.s: Chuck Spinney, a long-time associate of John Boyd, presents Boyd's thinking on the OODA loop and evolutionary epistemology. The talk runs about two and a half hours and includes Q&A.
videos.w: HN readers recommend it as the way to learn what Boyd actually meant by OODA, straight from a collaborator, rather than from the popularized loop diagram.
videos.q: It shows the thinking method behind the OODA Loop--Evolutionary Epistemology

videos.t: RAAIS 2017 - Simon Knowles, Co-Founder and CTO of Graphcore
videos.c: The Research and Applied AI Summit - RAAIS
videos.s: Simon Knowles, co-founder and CTO of Graphcore, talks about "intelligence processors", chips designed specifically for machine learning. The talk was given at the RAAIS 2017 summit and covers Graphcore's architecture.
videos.w: HN points to it as a technical talk from a chip designer on why AI hardware should put memory close to compute and use async data transfers.
videos.q: Here's a nice technical talk from Graphcore's CTO about that

videos.t: Richard Hipp - Git: Just Say No
videos.s: SQLite author Richard Hipp's talk at SouthEast LinuxFest criticizing Git's workflow and introducing Fossil as an alternative. He lists Git enhancements and argues for keeping history intact.
videos.w: Recommended for the SQLite author's reasoned case for a different approach to version control, and as an introduction to Fossil.
videos.q: If the author of SQLite advances some arguments around the proper way of doing version management, I would advise to error on the side of caution and listen at least a second time.

videos.t: I thought this rotating house was impossible.
videos.s: Tom Scott visits a rotating house near San Diego and explains how electricity, gas and water keep working on the rotating part. It includes a 3D render of the utility connection system.
videos.w: HN likes the clear animation of how slip rings and piping let a house rotate.
videos.q: Tom Scott did a video last year that has a great 3D render of the system

videos.t: The call to learn | Clifford Stoll
videos.s: Clifford Stoll's energetic TED talk, a wandering mix of anecdotes, a science experiment and thoughts on curiosity, education and technology. He is the author of The Cuckoo's Egg.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for Stoll's infectious enthusiasm and his case for teaching kids science, and often mention it in threads about him and his Klein bottles.
videos.q: He's brilliant, bonkers, and wonderful company.

videos.t: Noam Chomsky on Propaganda - The Big Idea - Interview with Andrew Marr
videos.s: A 1996 BBC interview in which Noam Chomsky explains his propaganda model of the media to Andrew Marr, including how filters shape what journalists report and the role of self-censorship.
videos.w: Recommended and quoted in threads on media bias, press and power, and self-censorship.
videos.q: The 30 minute episode[1] is well worth a watch

videos.t: CUFP 2013: Julien Verlaguet, Facebook: Analyzing PHP statically
videos.s: Julien Verlaguet of Facebook describes applying static analysis and type inference to a very large PHP codebase, using OCaml. The work led to the Hack language.
videos.w: Pointed to as the origin story of Hack and a real-world example of OCaml in production.
videos.q: Another cool one from CUFP this year is how Facebook is using OCaml to add incremental type inference to their vast PHP code base.

videos.t: Gil Scott-Heron - Whitey On the Moon (Official Audio)
videos.s: Gil Scott-Heron's 1970 spoken-word piece, in an official audio upload. It contrasts the Apollo moon program with poverty and neglect at home.
videos.w: Posted in space-spending threads as a classic critique of priorities, usually with a quip.
videos.q: Only two minutes, worth a listen

videos.t: Shakespeare: Original pronunciation (The Open University)
videos.s: David and Ben Crystal introduce the Original Pronunciation production of Shakespeare and show what it reveals about the history of English, including puns and rhymes lost in modern speech.
videos.w: Frequently linked as a short, accessible demonstration of how Shakespeare actually sounded.
videos.q: I very much enjoyed this quick introduction to Shakespeare in Original Pronunciation

videos.t: Etching small patterns in Glass
videos.s: Huygens Optics experiments with etching tiny patterns in glass, covering hydrofluoric acid risks, buffered oxide etch, photoresist and chromium masks, and laser-induced etching. It ends with attempts at microscopic Tesla valves.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a highly informative look at micro-etching glass and the smallest Tesla valves.
videos.q: The video on micro etching glass with HF is highly informative on this post...

videos.t: Hauntology, Lost Futures and 80s Nostalgia
videos.s: A video essay explaining hauntology, Mark Fisher's idea of lost futures, and 80s nostalgia. It uses the Fallout games and other media as examples of a retro-futurism that mourns futures that never arrived.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear introduction to hauntology and lost futures in discussions of Mark Fisher and cyberpunk.
videos.q: I think this guy does a great job of explaining it through the analogy of the Fallout videogame series

videos.t: Emojli: Behind the Scenes and Why You Should Never Build An App
videos.s: Tom Scott and Matt Gray talk at Electromagnetic Field about making Emojli, an emoji-only messenger that began as a joke, how it was built and why they never want to do it again.
videos.w: Recommended as an entertaining story of a joke side project growing out of hand, brought up in threads on emoji and side projects.
videos.q: There is a wonderful talk by the founders of emoj.li about how it was all a joke which got out of hand.

videos.t: Retirement Plans: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
videos.s: A Last Week Tonight segment on retirement plans, high fees and bad financial advice, with comedic sketches. It explains how fees eat into retirement savings and favors low-cost passive investing.
videos.w: HN links it in personal finance threads as an entertaining explanation of how fees erode retirement savings.
videos.q: John Oliver had a great bit on retirement plans [1] if you're interested in passive investing.

videos.t: Leonard Cohen - Everybody Knows (Official Audio)
videos.s: The official audio of Leonard Cohen's 'Everybody Knows' from the album I'm Your Man.
videos.w: Commenters name it among their favourite Cohen songs, especially in threads after his death.
videos.q: I don't know what it is about that song that keeps me coming back.

videos.t: Pandora's Box, E1: The Engineers' Plot
videos.s: The first episode of Adam Curtis's 1992 BBC series Pandora's Box, on the engineers' plot, examining communism in the Soviet Union and the rise and limits of technocratic central planning.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a fun, well-made documentary on Soviet planning, Gosplan, and why central control failed.
videos.q: I recommend watching Pandora's Box documentary. It is fun and pretty well made

videos.t: Is the EU Democratic? Does Your Vote Matter?
videos.s: Kurzgesagt explains how the European Union is governed, how its officials are elected or appointed, and whether a citizen's vote actually matters.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a quick factual primer on EU institutions when threads get into EU politics and policy.
videos.q: Here is a quick video explaining how it works

videos.t: "Uptime 15,364 days - The Computers of Voyager" by Aaron Cummings
videos.s: A Strange Loop 2019 talk by Aaron Cummings on the computing systems aboard Voyager 1 and 2, which control the spacecraft and record and return data decades after launch in 1977.
videos.w: HN recommends it in Voyager threads as a good talk on how these old computers have proved durable and adaptable.
videos.q: this talk was really good

videos.t: You've (Likely) Been Playing The Game Of Life Wrong
videos.s: Veritasium explains why many real-world systems follow power laws rather than normal distributions. It covers self-organized criticality, with simulations of sandpiles, magnetism and forest fires.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for changing how they think about distributions and for showing how criticality shows up across earthquakes, wildfires and other fields.
videos.q: Before I watched this I would default to thinking about most distributions as normal.

videos.t: Mike Arrington at Startup School 08
videos.s: Mike Arrington of TechCrunch speaks at Startup School 2008 about how to get press coverage for a startup and how to respond to it.
videos.w: HN recommends it as practical advice on dealing with tech press, whenever someone asks how to pitch TechCrunch and similar outlets.
videos.q: Mike Arrington's talk from startup school on dealing with press is quite good

videos.t: ADHD & How Anyone Can Improve Their Focus
videos.s: Andrew Huberman discusses ADHD, its biology and myths, behavioral and pharmacologic treatments, and training protocols to improve focus for people with or without ADHD. It covers dopamine and the coordination of brain networks.
videos.w: HN people offer it as practical focus and ADHD advice from a credentialed neuroscientist, though some treat it as only a reference.
videos.q: He's pretty well credentialed though, so I trust on average the advice is good

videos.t: What It Really Takes to Convert an Office Building to Apartments | Odd Lots
videos.s: An Odd Lots podcast episode on why converting empty office buildings into apartments is hard. A managing director at Vanbarton Group walks through the zoning, financing and construction obstacles, mostly in New York.
videos.w: HN links it whenever office-to-residential conversion comes up, as a good deep dive into why the idea is not simple.
videos.q: a good deep dive into why this is not a simple proposition.

videos.t: Category Theory in Life - Eugenia Cheng
videos.s: Eugenia Cheng gives the opening keynote at Lambda World 2017, presenting category theory as very abstract algebra whose abstraction gives it broad applicability. She applies it to everyday questions including privilege and prejudice.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible, gentle introduction that makes category theory feel approachable and shows its analogy-making power.
videos.q: To get a flavor of and gentle introduction to the analogy-making power of category theory, I recommend this talk by Eugenia Cheng

videos.t: How Does Kodak Make Film? (Kodak Factory Tour Part 1 of 3) - Smarter Every Day 271
videos.s: Destin Sandlin of Smarter Every Day tours a Kodak factory to show how photographic film is manufactured. This is part one of a three-part series covering the large-scale coating and production process.
videos.w: HN viewers find the film manufacturing process and the engineering behind it fascinating, especially the continuous roll changes.
videos.q: it’s a fascinating look at the process of film manufacturing

videos.t: Making R run Fast - Jan Vitek
videos.s: Jan Vitek of Northeastern University gives a meetup talk on the challenges of making the R language run fast. He explains what in R's semantics makes it hard to optimize and to build a JIT compiler for.
videos.w: HN points to it as the best explanation of why R is so hard to optimize, often paired with talks on Python and used to explain what makes Julia fast.
videos.q: Another talk on the difficulty of optimising R is this fantastic one by Jan Vitek

videos.t: 3D Gaussian Splatting - Why Graphics Will Never Be The Same
videos.s: A two-minute explainer of 3D Gaussian Splatting, the rendering technique from a 2023 research paper. It outlines why it could change how 3D graphics are made.
videos.w: HN uses it as a quick, non-expert primer whenever Gaussian splatting comes up.
videos.q: I really enjoyed this succinct YouTube video on the topic, for those interested in a primer

videos.t: Consciousness is Not a Computation (Roger Penrose) | AI Podcast Clips
videos.s: Clip from Lex Fridman's podcast with Roger Penrose in which Penrose argues that consciousness is not a computation. He discusses Godel-style arguments and the possible role of quantum effects in microtubules.
videos.w: Pointed to in consciousness and AI threads as the best-known statement of Penrose's view, which commenters find interesting even when they disagree.
videos.q: I don't take Roger's view about consciousness for granted but it is very interesting nevertheless.

videos.t: High-performance Tree Wrangling, the APL Way // Aaron Hsu // Dyalog '18
videos.s: Aaron Hsu shows how to manipulate and transform tree data in APL using arrays and inverted tables instead of pointers. He claims much smaller code, better performance and easier parallelisation.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a striking example of high-performance tree handling with array programming.
videos.q: He has one talk (available on YouTube) about his approach to using arrays to working with tree structures in a high-performance way in APL

videos.t: The Joy of Programming in Jai - Part 1: Hello World
videos.s: The first part of a series on programming in Jai, Jonathan Blow's in-development language. It covers compiling, writing hello world and using code from other files.
videos.w: Jai had no public release, so commenters point to this beta user's videos as a way to see what the language is actually like.
videos.q: One of the beta testers has published some more up to date videos with his language introduction and initial experience

videos.t: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets | Lex Fridman Podcast #309
videos.s: A five-hour Lex Fridman interview with John Carmack covering Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, programming, games and rockets.
videos.w: HN mines it for Carmack's views on AGI, debuggers, tooling and the metaverse, and recommends it as worth the full length.
videos.q: The entire video is worth viewing, an impressive 5:15h!

videos.t: "Building a Toolkit for Design" by Matthew Griffith
videos.s: Matthew Griffith, creator of elm-ui, presents a toolkit for designing layouts in Elm as an alternative to CSS. He explains the opinionated approach to layout and styling.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a fresh perspective on layout and styling in CSS discussions.
videos.q: For those who want a fresh perspective on CSS, layout and styling, check out this talk by Matthew Griffith

videos.t: Birth of The Transistor: A video history of Japan's electronic industry. (Part 1)
videos.s: First part of a four-part video history of Japan's electronics industry, covering the birth of the transistor and the rise of Japanese semiconductors. It appears to draw on NHK documentary material.
videos.w: Recommended in documentary and semiconductor-history threads as a detailed look at Japan's chip industry.
videos.q: There is a four-part documentary I saw on YouTube that went into much more (fascinating) detail.

videos.t: 26. Chernobyl — How It Happened
videos.s: MIT 22.01 lecture by Michael Short explaining the Chernobyl accident technically, including RBMK reactor positive feedback, xenon poisoning and the cascade of human errors during the test.
videos.w: Recommended as the detailed technical account of exactly what happened at Chernobyl.
videos.q: This is a presentation to students by an MIT professor that goes over exactly what happened, the sequence of events, mistakes made, and so on.
