videos.t: BSidesLV 2013   3 2 7 Sixteen Colors Archiving the Evolution of ANSI and ASCII Art   Doug Moore Bren
videos.s: A BSidesLV 2013 talk from the Sixteen Colors project on archiving the ANSI and ASCII art scene. It traces the scene's evolution from BBSs to the NFO and IRC era.
videos.w: Commenters recommend it as the best introduction to the history of the ANSI and ASCII art scene.
videos.q: If you want to watch a cool talk about the evolution of NFO and ascii (color) art scene and processes, I recommend watching

videos.t: Understanding the rise of China | Martin Jacques
videos.s: Economist Martin Jacques offers three building blocks for understanding China's rise, including seeing China as a civilization-state rather than a nation-state. He also covers how Chinese people view the state.
videos.w: HN recommends it in discussions of China's surveillance and social-credit systems for explaining Chinese attitudes toward the state.
videos.q: I highly recommend Martin Jacques' Ted talk [0] on this very subject from over 7 years ago.

videos.t: Bach, Toccata and Fugue in D minor, organ
videos.s: Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor on organ, shown with a Music Animation Machine bar-graph score instead of traditional notation.
videos.w: Recommended as a music visualization that makes the structure easier to follow than sheet music.
videos.q: videos are eye-opening

videos.t: Jake Vanderplas - Statistics for Hackers - PyCon 2016.mp4
videos.s: Jake Vanderplas's PyCon 2016 talk shows how sampling-based methods such as simulation, shuffling and bootstrapping make statistics intuitive. His pitch is that if you can write a for-loop, you can do statistics.
videos.w: It is recommended to programmers who want to learn statistics through simulation rather than memorized formulas.
videos.q: The presenters advocate using simulation/bootstrapping/shuffling methods instead of memorizing formulas.

videos.t: How to Get Good at Small Talk, and Even Enjoy It
videos.s: A Harvard Business Review video with tactics for getting better at small talk and enjoying it, such as setting goals, allowing pauses, and starting and ending conversations.
videos.w: HN commenters share it as a short, practical resource for people who struggle with small talk.
videos.q: If you need some small talk tips, see this short video.

videos.t: Peter Thiel on “The Straussian Moment”
videos.s: Peter Robinson interviews Peter Thiel at the Hoover Institution about Thiel's essay The Straussian Moment. Thiel discusses how people trust the will more than the intellect and reason, and how the question of human nature has been abandoned.
videos.w: HN points to it as a primer on Thiel's thinking and as an example of Peter Robinson's skill as an interviewer.
videos.q: There is a Peter Robinson interview about the essay that can serve as a good primer[1].

videos.t: Microtonal Guitar (Fixed Fret) - Tolgahan Çoğulu
videos.s: Tolgahan Cogulu demonstrates a fixed-fret microtonal guitar, playing music that uses notes between the usual twelve semitones. The channel is dedicated to his microtonal guitar designs.
videos.w: Linked in music theory and tuning threads as a listenable example of microtonal guitar that sounds good.
videos.q: Tolgahan Çoğulu and his awesome microtonal guitar creations

videos.t: I, Pencil: The Movie
videos.s: A short film from the Competitive Enterprise Institute adapting Leonard Read's 1958 essay I, Pencil, showing how no one person knows how to make a pencil and how many people cooperate without central planning.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a quick video version of the classic essay on specialization and economic interdependence.
videos.q: It's really about specialization and the interdependency of everything in the economy

videos.t: NeXTSTEP Release 3 Demo
videos.s: Steve Jobs demos NeXTSTEP Release 3, showing the object-oriented development environment and UI that later became the basis of Mac OS X. Midway through he builds a database-backed GUI app with Interface Builder and Enterprise Objects Framework with almost no code.
videos.w: HN uses it as the classic example of rapid visual app building and of a polished early Jobs presentation, often with timestamps pointing to the database demo.
videos.q: There's a video of steve jobs building a fairly complex DB app without a single line of code, including joins.

videos.t: How American Fire Departments are Getting People Killed
videos.s: Not Just Bikes argues that oversized American fire trucks and fire department requirements push cities toward wide roads and dangerous street design. He compares this with the Dutch approach to emergency response.
videos.w: HN people link it in threads on big vehicles and road safety as a comparison of US and Dutch fire department approaches.
videos.q: shows quite well the major difference in approach between fire departments in the USA vs the Netherlands

videos.t: Renting vs. Buying a Home: What People Get Wrong
videos.s: Ben Felix argues that common beliefs about renting versus buying are wrong: homes are not great investments, mortgages are not a wealth hack, and ownership does not reliably bring happiness.
videos.w: Recommended as detailed math on rent versus buy, showing the choice is often roughly a wash.

videos.t: Orbital Data Centers Yes or No
videos.s: Eager Space examines the practicality of putting data centers in orbit, walking through three scenarios with cost calculations and the launch cost reductions that would be required.
videos.w: Recommended in orbital data center threads as a thorough, numbers-based assessment.
videos.q: Goes into great detail with extensive calculations (for a YT video at least).

videos.t: Pachelbel Rant
videos.s: Comedian and cellist Rob Paravonian rants about having to play Pachelbel's Canon in D, and shows how many pop songs reuse its chord progression. It was recorded live at Penn State.
videos.w: Brought up in threads about chord progressions and musical copyright as the funny canonical version of the idea.
videos.q: There was a relevant and entertaining stand-up bit about this

videos.t: Classic Game Postmortem - Another World
videos.s: Eric Chahi's GDC 2011 postmortem of Another World (Out of This World), describing how he built the game. He shows his polygon art approach, rotoscoping and animation tools.
videos.w: HN points to it whenever Another World comes up, as one of the better GDC talks by the game's creator.
videos.q: it's one of the better GDC talks

videos.t: Pulling Clear Images Directly Off Satellites | GOES-15,16,17 and Himawari 8 HRIT
videos.s: The Thought Emporium shows how to receive clear images directly from GOES-15, 16 and 17 and Himawari 8 geostationary weather satellites with software-defined radio. It covers the extra effort needed to receive GOES data.
videos.w: HN commenters credit it for inspiring their own satellite-reception hobby and praise the channel's high-quality content.
videos.q: The Thought Emporium makes really high quality content.

videos.t: Denmark's Forest Kindergartens
videos.s: An SBS Dateline short documentary on Danish forest kindergartens, where children play freely outdoors, climb trees and use knives with little adult intervention.
videos.w: Recommended as a concise look at the culture behind outdoor kindergartens in threads on parenting and education.
videos.q: This is a very concise (11:32) video that goes over some of the culture and thinking around outdoor kindergartens.

videos.t: How to Survive in Gamedev for Eleven Years Without a Hit
videos.s: Jake Birkett of Grey Alien Games explains at GDC 2016 how an indie developer survived eleven years without a hit by building a long tail of games and redefining success.
videos.w: Recommended in indie and solo game development threads as a grounded account of making a living in games.
videos.q: you can redefine your idea of "success" a little and make a comfortable living

videos.t: I tried using AI. It scared me.
videos.s: Tom Scott describes trying ChatGPT to fix his Gmail labels and being unsettled by how capable it was. He argues that we cannot know where we are on the technology curve, comparing it to Napster.
videos.w: HN cites it for the argument that we cannot tell whether AI is early or late on its sigmoid curve until hindsight.
videos.q: Tom Scott's video[0] makes a very good argument: we don't know where we are on the technology curve.

videos.t: Transport Tycoon 2014 Soundtrack (remaster with real instrument from original creator)
videos.s: A complete remastered soundtrack for the Transport Tycoon 2014 mobile game, re-recorded with real instruments rather than the original MIDI. The music was composed by John Broomhall for the classic Transport Tycoon.
videos.w: Fans of Transport Tycoon and OpenTTD point to it as a nostalgic, live-instrument version of the game's music.
videos.q: The composer performed it with real instruments sometime in the past few years and it really brought on those nostalgic feelings

videos.t: Jordan Peterson - Controversial Facts about IQ
videos.s: A clip of psychologist Jordan Peterson lecturing on intelligence and IQ, covering how it is defined and its correlation with academic and work success.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as supporting material in arguments about IQ and the g-factor view of intelligence.
videos.q: IQ has an amazingly high correlation with academic success and work success

videos.t: DEFCON 19: Steal Everything, Kill Everyone, Cause Total Financial Ruin! (w speaker)
videos.s: Jayson E. Street's DEF CON 19 talk shows photos from real security engagements where he was already inside client facilities, illustrating how social engineering and physical intrusion can cause huge losses. For each attack he also explains what defenses would have stopped him.
videos.w: It is a repeat pick in 'favorite tech talk' threads as a funny, eye-opening look at how easily physical security and people can be bypassed.
videos.q: The absolute funniest tech talk I've seen

videos.t: Former fusion scientist on why we won't have fusion power by 2040
videos.s: A former fusion scientist argues why fusion power by 2040 is unrealistic, covering the physics challenges, neutron issues and optimistic company claims, with a brief note of good news.
videos.w: Praised as the best crash course on fusion reactor design nuances from an insider, used to temper fusion hype.
videos.q: I find it's the best crash course on the nuances of reactor design that I've seen.

videos.t: Bob Nystrom - Is There More to Game Architecture than ECS?
videos.s: Bob Nystrom, author of Game Programming Patterns, gives a Roguelike Celebration 2018 talk questioning whether entity component systems are the only way to structure a game. He walks through alternative architectures drawn from roguelike development.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as a level-headed counterpoint to ECS zealotry and a good intro to game architecture beyond ECS.
videos.q: Bob Nystrom has an excellent talk on roguelike architecture [0]

videos.t: Risking My Life To Settle A Physics Debate
videos.s: Veritasium investigates whether a wind-powered vehicle can travel directly downwind faster than the wind, driving the Blackbird craft himself. The video explains the physics behind a claim some physics professors dispute.
videos.w: Frequently linked whenever wind-powered vehicles come up, as the clearest visual explanation of how the craft works.
videos.q: The visual that made it click for me was at 18:54 in the original video

videos.t: The Secrets Of Cornwall - Part 1 - Communications
videos.s: A documentary on how Cornwall became a hub for the world's communications, from the first transatlantic radio signal to modern undersea fibre cables. It describes how cable landing stations and the systems are put together.
videos.w: Recommended as a rare look at the unmarked buildings and infrastructure where undersea cables come ashore.
videos.q: Documentary about the cable landing stations: The Secrets of Cornwall

videos.t: Black Wednesday (BBC 1997)
videos.s: A 1997 BBC documentary on Black Wednesday in 1992, when sterling was forced out of the Exchange Rate Mechanism. It covers the crisis from the British government side, including George Soros's trade and political mistakes.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a detailed documentary on the Soros-versus-Bank-of-England episode.
videos.q: This wonderful BBC documentary explains everything on detail.

videos.t: Find your primal posture and sit without back pain: Esther Gokhale at TEDxStanford
videos.s: Esther Gokhale's short TEDx talk argues that the natural human spine is curved rather than straight and teaches a 'primal posture' for sitting without back pain.
videos.w: Recommended in back pain and posture threads as a short, practical idea that helped some commenters.
videos.q: I found this Ted talk helped me with some lower back and leg issues.

videos.t: What I Wish I Had Known Before Scaling Uber to 1000 Services • Matt Ranney • GOTO 2016
videos.s: Matt Ranney of Uber talks at GOTO Chicago 2016 about what Uber learned from growing past 1,000 production microservices. He covers regrets, sprawl and organizational effects.
videos.w: Often brought up as an honest account of microservice sprawl, including the fact that nobody at Uber knew exactly how many services existed.
videos.q: I enjoyed that video

videos.t: Computers for Cynics 0 - The Myth of Technology
videos.s: The opening episode of Ted Nelson's Computers for Cynics series, in which he casts doubt on conventional accounts of computer basics. He argues that conventions and packaging are mistaken for technology.
videos.w: HN likes it for Nelson's habit of reframing computing history so that past decisions look arbitrary.
videos.q: Ted has a knack for reframing things in ways that make the arbitrariness of certain historical decisions clear

videos.t: The Secret Life of Machines - Vacuum Cleaners  1/2
videos.s: Part 1 of an episode of the British educational TV series The Secret Life of Machines, about how vacuum cleaners work and their history. It mixes humor with explanation of household technology.
videos.w: HN recommends the series as an entertaining way to learn how everyday machines work, enough to start debugging them.
videos.q: These overviews give you just enough knowledge to start debugging a broken household machine.

videos.t: C++ and Beyond 2012: Herb Sutter - atomic Weapons 2 of 2
videos.s: Part two of Herb Sutter's C++ and Beyond 2012 session on atomic weapons, a deep dive into the C++ memory model, atomics, memory ordering, and hardware behavior. It ends with the modern meaning of volatile.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an in-depth, practical introduction to atomics and weak versus strong memory ordering, relevant to ARM and Rust as well as C++.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: For a more in depth introduction to the topic with a lot of practical code examples, I highly recommend

videos.t: Who Killed Captain Alex: Uganda's First Action Movie (English Subtitles & Video Joker) - Wakaliwood
videos.s: Who Killed Captain Alex is Uganda's first action movie, made for under $200 by Nabwana IGG in Wakaliga. This version has English subtitles and a video joker (VJ Emmie) providing running commentary.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a fun, surprisingly entertaining low-budget film made better by the live-style commentary.
videos.q: Despite the very low budget, the movie is surprisingly entertaining, and the commentary makes it even better.

videos.t: Shader Basics, Blending & Textures • Shaders for Game Devs [Part 1]
videos.s: The first part of Freya Holmer's three-part, nearly four-hour lecture on shader coding for game devs in Unity. It covers what shaders are, vertex and fragment shaders, interpolators, data types, blending and textures.
videos.w: Recommended as a good first-steps shader tutorial that also teaches broad graphics knowledge.
videos.q: I liked this tutorial series as a "first steps" by Freya Holmér

videos.t: GopherCon 2016: The Design of the Go Assembler - Rob Pike
videos.s: Rob Pike's GopherCon 2016 talk on the design of the Go assembler, explaining why Go uses a common assembly language translated to each architecture.
videos.w: HN points to it for background on how the Go toolchain targets many architectures and why its assembler is designed that way.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Its Rob Pike talking about the go assembler and he answers a few of your questions.

videos.t: The Higgs Mechanism Explained | Space Time | PBS Digital Studios
videos.s: PBS Space Time explains the Higgs field and how the Higgs mechanism gives particles mass within quantum field theory. It is a ten-minute overview for a lay audience.
videos.w: Recommended as a clear explanation of how electrons gain mass, and the channel itself gets binge-watch praise.
videos.q: I think this video does a good job explaining it, much better than I could

videos.t: Sam Aaron live coding a DJ set with Sonic Pi
videos.s: A long live-coded DJ set in which Sam Aaron creates all the music in real time by writing code in his Sonic Pi system. It demonstrates algorithmic electronic music performance.
videos.w: HN people recommend it as the most impressive demonstration of live coding music, especially to those curious about programmable music.
videos.q: The most impressive thing you can do with it is live coding

videos.t: The Holographic Universe Explained
videos.s: A PBS Space Time episode explaining the holographic principle: the idea that our 3+1 dimensional universe may be described by information on a lower-dimensional boundary. It walks through black hole entropy and the AdS/CFT correspondence.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as an accessible way to get a grip on AdS/CFT and the holographic principle whenever black holes or information physics come up.
videos.q: Here's a video that made me feel like I almost half-way understood one of the main underlying principles (AdS/CFT correspondence)

videos.t: Adam Ruins Everything - The Truth About the McDonald's Coffee Lawsuit
videos.s: An Adam Ruins Everything segment on the real facts of the McDonald's hot coffee lawsuit, covering the severity of the burns and the corporate PR campaign that painted it as frivolous.
videos.w: HN cites it as a quick, entertaining explainer to correct the myth of the frivolous coffee lawsuit.

videos.t: Lec 1 | MIT 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science, Fall 2010
videos.s: The first lecture of MIT 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science, taught by Tom Leighton, introducing mathematical proofs. It covers propositions, implication and basic proof methods.
videos.w: HN users recommend it as a good discrete math course for programmers, praising Leighton's relatable stories that motivate new concepts.
videos.q: the professor tells relatable stories to motivate the new concepts

videos.t: There is No Algorithm for Truth - with Tom Scott
videos.s: Tom Scott's Royal Institution discourse on science communication in the age of social media, how recommendation algorithms shape popularity, and why view counts can matter more than truth. It includes a segment on parasocial relationships.
videos.w: HN returns to it in discussions of algorithmic feeds, misinformation and parasocial relationships, as a clear and thoughtful talk.
videos.q: did a really good segment on the parasocial relationship as part of his talk to the Royal Institution

videos.t: 8/28/2006 Peter Schiff On Kudlow & Co: Predicts The US Economic Collapse
videos.s: A 2006 television appearance in which Peter Schiff warns on Kudlow & Co about the housing bubble and an approaching US economic collapse.
videos.w: Offered as an example of someone who publicly predicted the financial crisis ahead of time, in arguments about economic forecasting.
videos.q: There have been people like Peter Schiff warning about the recession and specifically saying when it will happen and how long it will last

videos.t: Introducing a Memory-Safe Successor Language in Large C++ Code Bases - John McCall - CppNow 2023
videos.s: John McCall of Apple's Swift team presents at CppNow 2023 on introducing a memory-safe successor language into large C++ code bases. He argues incremental improvement of C++ hits hard limits and explains Swift's C++ interoperability for gradual migration.
videos.w: Used as the primary source for Apple's stated plan to make Swift its successor to C++ and for how interop supports gradual transition.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: Finaly a recent gem from CppNow 2023

videos.t: How to Fix America's Corrupt Political System
videos.s: A short RepresentUs explainer on how money corrupts American politics and what an anti-corruption act could do about it. It covers lobbying, super PACs and campaign finance, and pitches the group's proposed reforms. The video was later superseded by an updated version.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it as a brief summary of the problem and the proposed Anti-Corruption Act solution when arguing for getting money out of politics.
videos.q: I find these videos to be helpful in briefly understanding the problem and their proposed solution

videos.t: No, The Tank Is Not Dead.
videos.s: Armor expert The Chieftain explains why tanks still have a place on the modern battlefield despite drones and guided weapons. He responds to the 'tank is dead' debate, noting that tanks have been declared dead repeatedly since 1919.
videos.w: Pointed to as an authoritative answer, from a former Abrams commander and tank historian, to claims that tanks are obsolete.
videos.q: I'd recommend this video by a former Abrams commander and tank historian who presents this argument far better than I can.

videos.t: The Art of the Bodge: How I Made The Emoji Keyboard
videos.s: Tom Scott explains how he built his emoji keyboard, which turned out to be a series of bodged-together tools including AutoHotkey and LuaMacros. He tells stories about the value of quick-and-dirty solutions.
videos.w: HN links it as a charming defense of bodging and of AutoHotkey, and as the go-to example when custom keyboards or hotkey hacks come up.
videos.q: I saw a good talk on it from Tom Scott some time ago[0] which I think is relevant.

videos.t: Joscha: From Computation to Consciousness (31c3)
videos.s: Joscha Bach's 31c3 talk argues that the mind should be understood as an information-processing system and that even the physical universe can be seen as computational. It tours the philosophy underlying artificial intelligence and cognitive science.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an inspiring summary of a computational model of mind and a first lecture in a series on the brain as a computer.
videos.q: stuff like talks by Joscha Bach on C3

videos.t: Large Language Models from scratch
videos.s: A short cartoon explaining how language models like ChatGPT work, from autocomplete and conditional probabilities to neural networks, gradient descent and backpropagation. It shows how networks act as universal function approximators.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a quick, non-dumbed-down way to get up to speed on how LLMs are built.
videos.q: I highly recommend this video by Steve Seitz

videos.t: Animation Bootcamp: An Indie Approach to Procedural Animation
videos.s: David Rosen of Wolfire Games explains how simple procedural techniques can produce fluid, interactive character animation from very few keyframes. Examples come from Overgrowth, Receiver and Black Shades, from his 2014 GDC session.
videos.w: HN points to it as a concrete case of procedural animation that keeps characters responsive, often in threads about Overgrowth and game feel.
videos.q: Here's a video I've enjoyed of David Rosen giving a presentation at Game Developers Conference 2014

videos.t: The Hyperbolic Geometry of DMT Experiences (@Harvard Science of Psychedelics Club)
videos.s: Andres Gomez Emilsson of the Qualia Research Institute presents a model of DMT experiences using hyperbolic geometry and dynamical systems theory. He describes how different intoxication levels correspond to changing curvature and information content of experience.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as an interesting lecture related to psychedelics, brain geometry and hyperbolic space, with a good intro to hyperbolic geometry.
videos.q: has a good intro in the beginning.

videos.t: Algorithmic Redistricting: Elections made-to-order
videos.s: AlphaPhoenix uses Monte Carlo simulation and annealing-style methods to draw North Carolina congressional district maps, both gerrymandered and fair. He focuses on the fascinating computational problem rather than the politics.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining demonstration of how powerful algorithmic gerrymandering can be.
videos.q: For a great (and entertaining!) look into how you can use simulations to generate these types of maps

videos.t: Turning the Sun Into a Giant Telescope with Dr. Slava Turyshev
videos.s: Fraser Cain interviews JPL physicist Slava Turyshev about using the Sun's gravity as a lens to image distant exoplanets. They cover how the lens works, how a spacecraft would align with it, and mission design.
videos.w: HN points to it as the best accessible explanation of the solar gravitational lens mission plan.
videos.q: It is the most interesting interview that I have seen in years, possibly ever.

videos.t: Why is it so Easy to be Thin in Japan?
videos.s: Joseph Everett compares the food environment of the US, with roughly 30% obesity, to Japan's, around 3.5%. He argues that what is available and normal to eat explains much of the gap.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as an accurate account of everyday Japanese eating and of why the US food environment is so much worse.
videos.q: This youtube video goes into more detail about the US problem compared to japan

videos.t: A Third of America Belongs to America
videos.s: CGP Grey explains what it means that a third of the United States is federally owned land. It describes the agencies that manage it and why so much of it is in the western states.
videos.w: Offered as the quick, clear explainer on US federal land ownership whenever land use in the West comes up.
videos.q: You might enjoy CGP Grey's "What is federal land?" [0].

videos.t: Salad Mug - DYNAMO DREAM, Ep1
videos.s: The first episode of Ian Hubert's Dynamo Dream series, a one-person sci-fi short made in Blender with a gritty futuristic city setting. It was made with help from friends and Patreon supporters over about three years.
videos.w: HN holds it up as an impressive example of what a tiny team can achieve with Blender.
videos.q: I always post this link when Blender is discussed because it's so impressive.

videos.t: 50TH ANNIVERSARY OF THE COMPUTER SCIENCE DEPARTMENT AT THE UNIVERSITY OF UTAH
videos.s: A full-day recording of the University of Utah computer science department's 50th anniversary event with panels, keynotes and talks by alumni and pioneers. It includes Ivan Sutherland's presentation on single flux quantum electronics.
videos.w: HN points to specific segments, especially Sutherland's SFQ talk and graphics pioneers, rather than the full seven hours.
videos.q: It's a very interesting presentation, from the history to the mechanics of how it works, to the possibilities.

videos.t: How Quantum Computers Break Encryption | Shor's Algorithm Explained
videos.s: MinutePhysics explains Shor's algorithm, showing how a quantum computer factors large integers by finding the period of a number modulo N. It walks through the modular arithmetic and number theory that give the exponential speedup over classical factoring, and why this threatens encryption.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a clear, approachable explanation of Shor's algorithm and what quantum computers actually do.
videos.q: Minute Physics has a really good explanation of Shor's algorithm, and by proxy, Quantum computing.

videos.t: "Liberating the Smalltalk lurking in C and Unix" by Stephen Kell
videos.s: Stephen Kell's Strange Loop talk argues that C and Unix already contain Smalltalk-like dynamism and introspection that can be exposed. He presents his liballocs research on bridging dynamic and compiled languages.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it in Smalltalk and Unix threads as a demonstration of runtime dynamism hiding in native binaries and shared libraries.
videos.p: dynamic features in c and unix
videos.q: there's a great video of one of his talks

videos.t: MIT Godel Escher Bach Lecture 1
videos.s: The first lecture of an MIT course on Douglas Hofstadter's Godel, Escher, Bach, covering themes like self-reference, recursion and incompleteness. The full lecture series is on YouTube.
videos.w: Recommended as a companion to reading the dense book.
videos.q: They’re great to watch as you work through the book

videos.t: How The Immune System ACTUALLY Works – IMMUNE
videos.s: A Kurzgesagt animation giving a big-picture tour of the human immune system, its organs, transport network, and the cells it produces every day. It accompanies their IMMUNE book.
videos.w: HN commenters suggest it as a simple, well-made introduction to how immune responses work when discussing infection, T cells or chronic illness.
videos.q: I like the series that Kurzgesagt made on the immune system as a way to explain this complexity a little more simply.

videos.t: Lichess founder Thibault Duplessis lectures on Lichess (2017)
videos.s: Lichess founder Thibault Duplessis talks at Big Techday 10 in Munich about how Lichess works and how he built it. He covers the project's origins and technical challenges including cheating detection.
videos.w: HN commenters point to it as a good talk on how one person built a major free, open-source chess server with few resources, and on the cheating problem.
videos.q: He has a good talk about how he did it here

videos.t: Design Your Own Keyboard!
videos.s: Ben Vallack walks through designing a custom keyboard PCB from scratch using Ergogen and KiCad, ending with a gerber file ready to order from a PCB fabricator. The example is a split keyboard.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a thorough, general walkthrough of the steps in designing your own keyboard.
videos.q: It's targeting a split keyboard, but I think it details the general steps involved pretty well.

videos.t: Using ground relays with Starlink
videos.s: Mark Handley of UCL explains, with simulation visualizations, how early Starlink satellites without inter-satellite links could still give low-latency wide-area communication by hopping via ground relays. He shows it can beat fibre on many long paths.
videos.w: Cited in Starlink latency debates as a clear visual analysis showing sub-100ms latency is plausible even without inter-satellite links.
videos.q: as Mark Handley has elegantly pointed out in his incredible video

videos.t: Avi Bryant demos Dabble db
videos.s: Avi Bryant demos Dabble DB, a web-based spreadsheet-like database for building apps without code. It shows how users can model and relate data through a smooth interface.
videos.w: HN points to it as a lost example of intuitive low-code tooling, and as inspiration for newer products.
videos.q: The UI was very intuitive, and it did a better job with things like table relations than it's competitors.

videos.t: Yanis Varoufakis: The Global Minotaur: America, Europe and the Future of the Global Economy
videos.s: Yanis Varoufakis talks at a festival in Zagreb about his book The Global Minotaur. He argues the postwar global economy and the 2008 crisis stem from deeper structural causes than greed or weak regulation.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a narrative of a century of political economy and the geopolitics behind the 2008 crash.
videos.q: a nice narrative of the last 100 years of the political economy

videos.t: Francis Bacon: A Brush with Violence (2017)
videos.s: A BBC documentary on Francis Bacon, the loud, hard-drinking British painter, drawing on people who knew him. It explores the haunted man behind the Roaring Boy persona.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it as a well-made, interesting and sad documentary on Bacon's troubled life.
videos.q: Pretty interesting and sad at the same time. It's worth a watch, IMO.

videos.t: Speed Up Your JavaScript
videos.s: A 2009 Google Tech Talk by Nicholas Zakas on the hidden performance pitfalls of JavaScript. It covers what is fast and slow in the language and how to avoid common bottlenecks.
videos.w: Recommended as a classic JavaScript performance talk whose fundamentals about reflow and efficient code still apply.
videos.q: the fundamental ideas are still the same.

videos.t: Automatic Bullseye, MOVING Dartboard
videos.s: Mark Rober shows an automatic bullseye dartboard that tracks a thrown dart with motion capture and moves in real time so it always hits the center. He spent over three years on the project.
videos.w: HN calls it a great, impressive engineering project involving real-time trajectory calculation.
videos.q: Another great video is his automatic bulls eye dartboard [2].

videos.t: David Heinemeier Hansson-Unlearn Your MBA (Entire talk)
videos.s: David Heinemeier Hansson, creator of Ruby on Rails and partner at 37signals, argues that planning is guessing and startups should focus on today. He says constraints are an advantage and that startups can bootstrap profitably in sizable markets.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the classic counterpoint to Silicon Valley growth-at-all-costs startup thinking.
videos.q: His talk "How to unlearn your MBA" in particular was fantastic in providing a counterpoint to Silicon-valley style Startups

videos.t: Diablo: Original Game Development
videos.s: David Brevik's GDC 2016 post-mortem of the original Diablo, covering how it evolved from a turn-based claymation DOS game into the genre-defining action RPG. It includes development anecdotes and lessons learned.
videos.w: HN considers it one of the best GDC post-mortems, with funny anecdotes (such as turning down Hotmail equity) and multiplayer insights.
videos.q: GDC post mortems are amazing, especially the ones on Diablo[0] and Fallout[1].

videos.t: Attenborough: the amazing Lyre Bird sings like a chainsaw! Now in high quality | BBC Earth
videos.s: A short BBC Earth clip from David Attenborough's Life of Birds showing a lyrebird imitating sounds, including a chainsaw and camera shutter, so accurately it is hard to tell from the real thing.
videos.w: Shared whenever birds mimic sounds come up, as a mind-blowing example of vocal mimicry.
videos.q: Here's the one that blows my mind

videos.t: Aalto Talk with Linus Torvalds [Full-length]
videos.s: Linus Torvalds is interviewed at Aalto University in 2012, followed by an audience Q&A. He talks about Linux, kernel development and the desktop, and about Nvidia support. The Q&A has a well-known moment where he is blunt about Nvidia.
videos.w: HN links it for individual clips: the Nvidia moment, his views on C and his blunt communication style. Some commenters say the whole talk is worth watching.
videos.q: the whole talk by itself is very recommendable

videos.t: Speaking Piano - Now with (somewhat decent) captions!
videos.s: A player piano is made to reproduce human speech, here reciting a European Environmental Criminal Court proclamation in German at the 2009 World Venice Forum. This upload adds subtitles so the words become understandable.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the canonical talking-piano example, uncanny and impressive once you read the captions.
videos.q: This is a other great example

videos.t: The Long, Twisted and Slightly Ridiculous Story of Avgas Part 2
videos.s: AVweb's Paul Bertorelli explains in part two of a series why general aviation has not replaced leaded avgas. He covers industry inertia, bureaucratic delays and the exemption that lets the industry keep using lead.
videos.w: HN recommends the series for explaining why unleaded avgas has been so hard to approve, usually in threads about FAA and EPA fuel decisions.
videos.q: AVWeb made 2 videos on the subject of leaded avgas and on how hard it is to get it approved.

videos.t: Special Lecture: F-22 Flight Controls
videos.s: A special lecture from MIT's Private Pilot Ground School in which Lt. Col. Randy Gordon, a fighter and test pilot, describes F-22 flight controls. Topics include thrust vectoring, the pilot command system and how software handles failures.
videos.w: Recommended as a fascinating insider account of how the F-22's software makes it easier to fly than a Cessna.
videos.q: the talk is that good!

videos.t: Put Your Name on Your Game, a Talk by Bennett Foddy and Zach Gage
videos.s: At GDC 2019, Bennett Foddy and Zach Gage ask why game developers rarely sign their work. They argue that indie developers could benefit from putting their names on their games.
videos.w: HN recommends it when people ask why games aren't marketed by creator like films, and for the value of attaching your name to your work.
videos.q: Great talk on that from the GettingOverIt/QWOP dev

videos.t: I wrote a Raytracer for DOS, 16 VGA colors
videos.s: Bisqwit writes a raytracer from scratch in C++ for DOS, rendering in the 16-color VGA palette at 640x480. The video also covers color quantization and ordered dithering.
videos.w: HN fans praise Bisqwit as a favorite programming YouTuber and this video as an excellent look at dithering.
videos.q: Bisqwit's discussion of dithering is outstanding

videos.t: JSON Parser 100% From Scratch in Haskell (only 111 lines)
videos.s: Tsoding live-codes a JSON parser from scratch in Haskell in about 111 lines, using only the standard library. It is an edited Twitch stream that explains the intuition behind parser combinators, functors, applicatives and monads.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a hands-on way to understand Haskell and parser combinators by watching a parser get built live.
videos.q: this guy writes a json parser live, giving his intuition along the way. It's helped me immensely.

videos.s: An hour-long absurdist Lasagna Cat video in which John Blyth Barrymore muses philosophically on a single Garfield strip. It is set to the full score of Philip Glass's Kundun.
videos.w: HN cites it as the prime example of going absurdly deep on a tiny subject, and as a favorite among long YouTube videos.
videos.q: I love this deep absurd analysis of a single Garfield comic.

videos.t: Exclusive: Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition Analysis - The First Triple-A Game Built Around Ray Tracing
videos.s: Digital Foundry's Alex Battaglia analyzes Metro Exodus Enhanced Edition, the first AAA game built around ray tracing. It covers the new global illumination, emissive lighting, DLSS and performance on AMD and Nvidia hardware.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a good overview of what ray-traced lighting changes for developers and players.
videos.q: is a good overview of why this is such a huge leap forward for developers and players alike.

videos.t: Andreas Antonopoulos - 51% Bitcoin Attack
videos.s: A two-minute clip of Andreas Antonopoulos explaining why a 51% attack on Bitcoin would not destroy it and what such an attack would cost. It is a succinct take on mining security.
videos.w: HN commenters link it as a short, favorite explanation of Bitcoin's security and the sustainability of a 51% attack.
videos.q: Andreas Antonopoulos has a good take on this for Bitcoin

videos.t: Procedural World Generation of Ubisoft’s Far Cry 5 | Etienne Carrier | Houdini HIVE Utrecht
videos.s: Ubisoft procedural technical artist Etienne Carrier explains the Houdini-based tools used to build Far Cry 5's roughly 100 square km open world. It covers generating biomes, texturing terrain, freshwater networks, cliff rocks and vegetation placement.
videos.w: HN points people to it as a rare, concrete look at how a AAA studio uses procedural tools to fill huge worlds with natural-looking environments.
videos.q: You may enjoy this talk, the devs for Far Cry 5 procedurally generated quite a lot of their world

videos.t: DIY mass spectrometer measures potassium in dietary salt substitute
videos.s: Ben Krasnow of Applied Science builds and operates a simple mass spectrometer, using it to measure potassium isotopes in a salt substitute. He explains the design choices and the theory behind it.
videos.w: Recommended as an expert-made DIY build that explains why the apparatus is designed as it is, though one commenter notes a missing baseline run.
videos.q: he tries to explain why it's built the way it is and give you a good basis of the theory of operation.

videos.t: Carbon Capture Isn't Real
videos.s: Adam Something gives a short, sarcastic argument that carbon capture does not live up to its promises. He says the energy it uses would be better spent replacing fossil sources directly.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it to argue carbon capture is a distraction from stopping emissions at the source.
videos.q: 100 times out of 100, you would rather just stop the emissions at the source by making the emitter use the green energy.

videos.t: Netanel Rubin: The Perl Jam: Exploiting a 20 Year-old Vulnerability
videos.s: Netanel Rubin's 31C3 talk chains Perl's syntax quirks into a powerful remote code execution attack, taking down popular Perl-based projects.
videos.w: Recommended as a funny, engaging look at how Perl's quirks create real security vulnerabilities.
videos.q: try this great Perl presentation from Netanel Rubin

videos.t: (405) Choosing a High Security Lock
videos.s: Lock-picking YouTuber Bill Johnson (BosnianBill) explains how to choose a high-security lock and why, showing examples and comparing designs. It covers what makes some padlocks more pick-resistant than others.
videos.w: HN users recommend it as an amusing, practical overview of padlocks from cheap to high security.
videos.q: Here's an amusing overview of available padlocks, starting with crap Master Locks and moving upward.

videos.t: Netdev 0x16 - Keynote: It's Time to Replace TCP in the Datacenter
videos.s: John Ousterhout's Netdev 0x16 keynote arguing that nearly every aspect of TCP is wrong for the datacenter, from connections and streams to reliable delivery and congestion control. He presents the case for a replacement protocol.
videos.w: Recommended as the thorough case for replacing TCP in datacenters and for Ousterhout's Homa protocol.
videos.q: The Netdev talk I've linked below is really good

videos.t: What if Current Foundations of Mathematics are Inconsistent? | Vladimir Voevodsky
videos.s: Vladimir Voevodsky's IAS lecture starts from Godel's second incompleteness theorem to explore whether first-order arithmetic could be inconsistent. It motivates his vision of univalent foundations and computer-checked proofs.
videos.w: Recommended as a thought-provoking lecture from a Fields medalist on the foundations of mathematics and formal proof verification.
videos.q: I recommend this video

videos.t: Category Theory by Tom LaGatta
videos.s: Tom LaGatta's talk on category theory at a 2014 LispNYC meetup, covering objects, morphisms and the basic ideas in an informal, conversational style. It runs about 97 minutes.
videos.w: Recommended as a more approachable introduction to category theory than the more formal lecture series people often start with.
videos.q: Milewski's YouTube lectures gets mentioned a lot, but I couldn't make much sense of them before watching Tom LaGatta's more informal and conversational presentation

videos.t: Leonard Susskind | "ER = EPR" or "What's Behind the Horizons of Black Holes?" - 1 of 2
videos.s: Stanford physicist Leonard Susskind gives the first of two mini-lectures on "ER = EPR", the idea that quantum entanglement and wormholes are related. It covers what lies behind black hole horizons.
videos.w: HN people point to it as the more detailed follow-up when articles touch on entanglement, holography and black holes.
videos.q: I found these lectures by Leonard Susskind very insightful

videos.t: A Crash Course in Modern Hardware by Cliff Click
videos.s: Cliff Click walks through a small performance example on a modern out-of-order CPU. He covers pipelining, ILP, CISC vs RISC, multicore, and why cache misses and the memory subsystem dominate performance.
videos.w: Recommended as an accessible refresher on how modern hardware and caches affect software performance.
videos.q: it's a really accessible refresher if you're a bit outdated on how all these caches work and interact

videos.t: Brian Warner - Magic Wormhole- Simple Secure File Transfer - PyCon 2016.mp4
videos.s: Brian Warner, author of magic-wormhole, presents the tool at PyCon 2016. He explains how a few secret words let two computers securely transfer files, covering the cryptography (NaCl, SPAKE2) and library use.
videos.w: Recommended as the author's own explanation of the design and security of magic-wormhole.
videos.q: Author has a very good video on it at pycon-2016

videos.t: VFX Artists React to DUNE Bad & Great CGi
videos.s: Corridor Crew VFX artists react to the visual effects of the 2021 Dune and compare them with David Lynch's 1984 version. They discuss which effects were practical and which were CGI.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it in debates about practical effects versus CGI, as a fun comparison of old and new Dune.
videos.q: a really good example of this is this comparison between the old and new Dune movies

videos.t: Why Japan's Conviction Rate is 99% (Actually Explained)
videos.s: Yuta explains what Japan's 99% conviction rate actually means, noting that prosecutors drop cases unless confidence is very high. He argues that the number is widely misunderstood and cites his sources.
videos.w: Recommended as a sourced, nuanced corrective whenever the Japanese justice system's conviction rate is raised.
videos.q: I've seen this Japanese person explaining the situation informally but thoroughly.

videos.t: Get Ready to Rock with Sonic Pi - The Live Coding Music Synth for Everyone • Sam Aaron • GOTO 2018
videos.s: Sam Aaron, creator of Sonic Pi, gives a demo-heavy GOTO Chicago 2018 talk on live coding music. He covers the history of Sonic Pi, how it evolved, and what it can do for education and professional musicians.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the best talk from Sonic Pi's creator, with live-coding examples and technical and teaching insights.
videos.q: There's also a _great_ talk from the creator (Sam Aaron) on Sonic Pi

videos.t: LibreSSL: The first 30 days, and what the Future Holds
videos.s: Bob Beck of OpenBSD gives a BSDCan 2014 talk on the first month of LibreSSL, the OpenSSL fork. He explains why they forked, what they removed, and examples of the problems found in the OpenSSL code base.
videos.w: Recommended as a funny, fascinating tour of how bad the OpenSSL code was and what cleanup looks like.
videos.q: There is a fascinating and funny talk by Bob Beck from OpenBSD on the first 30 days after forking OpenSSL.

videos.t: 4 Chords | Music Videos | The Axis Of Awesome
videos.s: A comedy-music medley from the Australian band The Axis of Awesome showing that dozens of famous pop songs use the same four-chord progression. The performers cycle through a long list of hits over the same chords.
videos.w: HN commenters use it as the canonical demonstration that popular songs reuse one chord progression, especially in threads on music analysis and AI-generated music.
videos.q: the "4 Chords" medley by Axis of Awesome is a great demonstration of its ubiquity

videos.t: Why I Cook With Induction
videos.s: Chef Jon Kung explains why he cooks almost exclusively on induction, citing fast heating, cleanliness and precise temperature control. He shows a rounded induction wok burner.
videos.w: HN points to it in gas-versus-induction threads as a professional chef making the positive case, including for wok cooking.
videos.q: Jon Kung makes the positive case for an induction wok better than I can

videos.t: Tea Consent
videos.s: A three-minute animated video that explains sexual consent through the analogy of offering someone a cup of tea. It is based on a blog post by Emmeline May.
videos.w: Used as the classic analogy for consent, applied to opt-out data collection and privacy practices.
videos.q: Here’s a very educational video on how giving consent works

videos.t: Roger Penrose: Physics of Consciousness and the Infinite Universe | Lex Fridman Podcast #85
videos.s: Lex Fridman interviews physicist Roger Penrose on consciousness, the limits of computation, quantum mechanics and his cyclic cosmology. It covers his views on AI and the big bang.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an accessible walkthrough of Penrose's ideas on consciousness and cosmology, interesting even if debatable.
videos.q: Penrose delivered a very accessible walkthrough of his historical and current thoughts on the topic.

videos.t: The psychology of evil | Philip Zimbardo
videos.s: Psychologist Philip Zimbardo explains how ordinary people can be pushed into doing evil by situations and systems. He draws on the Stanford prison experiment and unseen Abu Ghraib photos, then turns to the opposite case: how ordinary people can become heroes.
videos.w: HN uses it to argue that systems rather than bad apples drive cruelty, and for its section on how anonymity changes behavior.
videos.q: Here's Zimbardo's TED talk on what makes people do evil

videos.t: RacketCon 2013: Dan Liebgold - Racket on the Playstation 3? It's Not What you Think!
videos.s: Dan Liebgold of Naughty Dog gives a RacketCon 2013 keynote on using Racket in PlayStation 3 game development. He explains the Racket-based DSLs used for game data and scripting, which replaced the studio's earlier GOAL-based toolchain.
videos.w: HN cites it whenever Lisp in games, Naughty Dog or Racket in production comes up, as the main first-hand account.
videos.q: There's a talk by one of the engine devs at RacketCon from a few years ago on youtube about how they use these DSLs

videos.t: Intel - Anti-Competitive, Anti-Consumer, Anti-Technology.
videos.s: AdoredTV's history of Intel's monopolistic behavior over three decades, covering its dealings with AMD and its anti-consumer practices.
videos.w: Recommended as an overview of Intel's anti-competitive past and why it kept dominating despite AMD's competitive products.
videos.q: This is a very good overview of bad anti-consumer practices Intel has done throughout the last 30 years

videos.t: Windows "SUCKS": How I'd Fix it by a retired Microsoft Windows engineer
videos.s: Dave Plummer, a retired Microsoft engineer who wrote Task Manager, responds to the claim that Windows sucks. He describes how he would fix common annoyances, in what he calls a love letter to Windows wrapped in a rant.
videos.w: HN people share it in Windows 11 backlash threads as an even-handed insider's view of what is wrong with Windows.
videos.q: I find this take (from the guy who wrote the Windows task manager while at Microsoft) to be evenhanded.

videos.t: CS480/680 Lecture 19: Attention and Transformer Networks
videos.s: A university lecture from CS480/680 by Pascal Poupart on attention mechanisms and transformer networks, worked through on a chalkboard.
videos.w: HN recommends it to newcomers as a clear explanation of attention, including the query/key/value intuition.
videos.q: I would also recommend Pascal Poupart's talk [1] on Attention and Transformers.

videos.t: Satoshi Kon - Editing Space & Time
videos.s: A video essay from Every Frame a Painting on animator Satoshi Kon and his editing style, which distorts and warps space and time. It draws on his four features and one TV series.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the best short introduction to Kon's editing before watching his films.
videos.q: Watch Every Frame a Painting’s video[1] and pick any movie.

videos.t: The complete FUN TO IMAGINE with Richard Feynman
videos.s: All six episodes of the 1983 BBC series Fun to Imagine, in which Richard Feynman muses on jiggling atoms, fire, rubber bands, magnets, electricity and more. He explains how to think about nature and why imagination is fun.
videos.w: HN recommends it for Feynman's intuitive explanations and his joy in understanding how things work.
videos.q: Pondering these questions and learning about them gives joy, excitement, peace of mind and is my great hobby.

videos.t: Princes of the Yen | The Hidden Power of Central Banks
videos.s: Michael Oswald's documentary, based on Richard Werner's book, argues that Japan's 1990s crash was engineered by the central bank and powerful interests. It focuses on the Bank of Japan's hidden influence over the economy.
videos.w: HN commenters recommend it for a more cynical view of central bank power, though some caveat it as conspiracy-leaning.
videos.q: did a good job of illustrating the dangers of having such high powered unaccountable cabals

videos.t: The spelled-out intro to language modeling: building makemore
videos.s: Andrej Karpathy builds a bigram character-level language model from scratch, introducing torch.Tensor and the framework of training, sampling and loss evaluation. It is the first step toward a GPT-style Transformer in his makemore series.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a long but worthwhile way to demystify how language models work technically.
videos.q: It's long (2h), but well worth the time if anyone is curious about the technical workings of LLMs.

videos.t: Ira Glass on the Creative Process (www.getoutthebox.org)
videos.s: A two-minute video of Ira Glass on the creative process, describing the gap between taste and skill when starting out and urging you to keep producing until your work matches your taste.
videos.w: Shared as encouragement for beginners learning design or craft, on persisting through the taste-skill gap.
videos.q: You learn how to differentiate between good and bad much faster than you learn how to create good.

videos.t: Chris Lattner: Future of Programming and AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #381
videos.s: Lex Fridman's long podcast conversation with Chris Lattner, creator of Swift, LLVM and MLIR and co-founder of Modular. Topics include the Mojo language, the future of programming and AI, and hardware.
videos.w: HN points to it as the main place to hear Lattner's motivations and design ideas for Mojo, often in Mojo threads.
videos.q: further emboldened my stance that if Mojo can succeed, Lattner is one of the best-positioned engineers to see it through

videos.t: I Built a COMPUTER in Magic: The Gathering
videos.s: Kyle Hill of Because Science explains and demonstrates, using real cards, how Magic: The Gathering can be used to build a Turing machine, a computer inside the card game.
videos.w: HN links it as the accessible, hands-on demo behind the claim that Magic is Turing complete.
videos.q: Because Science did a thorough breakdown and demonstration, using actual cards

videos.t: Charlie Brooker's Newswipe 25/03/09
videos.s: A clip from Charlie Brooker's Newswipe in which a forensic psychiatrist argues that intense news coverage of school shooters encourages copycat attacks, alongside Brooker's satire of formulaic news reporting.
videos.w: HN cites it in discussions about how media should report mass shootings, as an expert-backed argument for not glorifying perpetrators.
videos.q: Basically at the end the forensic psychiatrist says that giving this intense superficial coverage about the gunman only encourages more copycat killers.

videos.t: The KGB, the Computer, and Me.
videos.s: A WGBH/NOVA re-enactment of Clifford Stoll's hunt for KGB-linked hacker Markus Hess, based on his book The Cuckoo's Egg. It starts from a 75-cent accounting discrepancy at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory.
videos.w: Mentioned alongside The Cuckoo's Egg as the screen version of an early computer-security detective story.
videos.q: Then check out the old Nova documentary about the story

videos.t: El Sendero Luminoso ft. Alex Honnold | The North Face
videos.s: A short film of Alex Honnold free soloing El Sendero Luminoso, a 2,500-foot route in El Potrero Chico, Mexico, in a little over three hours with no rope. It was made by The North Face with climbing footage and music.
videos.w: It is linked whenever Honnold or free soloing comes up, as a gripping and frightening example of extreme climbing.
videos.q: one of the most frightening videos I have ever seen

videos.t: The Constitution of Athens
videos.s: Historia Civilis explains the constitution of ancient Athens, including its assembly, offices and use of sortition to choose leaders. It draws on Aristotle and Plutarch.
videos.w: Recommended in governance threads for showing how randomness and short terms prevented power concentration.
videos.q: This is a good video on this

videos.t: The Original Skunk Works – Nickolas Means | The Lead Developer UK 2017
videos.s: Nickolas Means tells the story of Lockheed's Skunk Works and how its engineers built the U-2, SR-71 and F-117 under tight deadlines and budgets. He draws lessons for modern software teams.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a well-done history of Skunk Works, popping up in SR-71 threads.
videos.q: I would also recommend this conference talk on the subject by Nickolas Means, it was very well done

videos.t: How Music Works 1 - Melody - Part 1
videos.s: The first part of a four-part Channel 4 (UK) documentary series presented by Howard Goodall, this episode covers melody and why tunes affect us so deeply. It explains how melody works in Western music with historical background and music theory.
videos.w: HN people recommend the series as a good, approachable introduction to music theory with historical context.
videos.q: There's also a great TV series from England called 'How Music Works' which gives more of a historical background.

videos.t: Why city flags may be the worst-designed thing you've never noticed | Roman Mars
videos.s: Roman Mars gives a funny TED talk on vexillology, laying out five basic principles of good flag design and why many city flags fail them.
videos.w: The canonical reference on flag and logo design principles, cited in branding and design threads.
videos.q: one must watch the short talk on state and country flags

videos.t: Should Knowledge Be Free?
videos.s: Medlife Crisis asks whether academic research should sit behind paywalls, covering publisher profit margins, unpaid reviewers, Sci-Hub and Aaron Swartz. It includes an interview with Sci-Hub founder Alexandra Elbakyan.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an informative review of the academic publishing business and its monopoly-like structure.
videos.q: I found this discussion really informative

videos.t: Code Bubbles: Rethinking the User Interface Paradigm of Integrated Development Environments
videos.s: A short demo of Code Bubbles, an IDE interface built around editable code fragments in bubbles instead of files. It was a research prototype for Java development.
videos.w: HN keeps returning to it as the most convincing example of moving past file-based code editing, even though it never left prototype stage.
videos.q: Code Bubbles (from 2010) is the most convincing code visualization tool that I can recall

videos.t: Does "land area" assume a country is perfectly flat?
videos.s: Matt Parker of Stand-up Maths asks whether a country's reported land area accounts for hills and mountains, working through how surface area depends on the resolution of elevation data. It follows up on a question from a viewer and work by researchers who measured it.
videos.w: HN recommends it in map projection and coastline threads as a fun look at how measurement choices change area figures.
videos.q: Matt Parker from Standup Maths made a great video on exactly this subject

videos.t: A4 Paper Is Too Perfect
videos.s: CGP Grey explains the elegant ratio of A4 and the metric paper sizes, then zooms out across scales from the Planck length to the observable universe.
videos.w: Loved for its zoom-out tour of physical scales and recommended alongside other paper-size and scale-of-the-universe discussions.
videos.q: the most psychedelic experience one can have without doing drugs

videos.t: Lecture 1 | Modern Physics: Classical Mechanics (Stanford)
videos.s: The first lecture of Leonard Susskind's Stanford Continuing Studies course on modern physics, beginning with classical mechanics. It is the start of a six-quarter sequence on the theoretical foundations of physics.
videos.w: HN recommends Susskind as a very good explainer who uses real math at an accessible level, and links this lecture series for self-learners.
videos.q: He is a very good explainer.

videos.t: James Kunstler: How bad architecture wrecked cities
videos.s: James Howard Kunstler's TED talk argues that American public spaces and architecture have become unworthy of care, damaging civic life. He presents suburban sprawl and car-first design as failures of the common good.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an engaging introduction to the critique of car-centric design and bad architecture.
videos.q: Here's a far more engaging critique of car-first design by James Kunstler

videos.t: Peter McCullough, MD testifies to Texas Senate HHS Committee
videos.s: Testimony by Peter McCullough, MD, to the Texas Senate Health and Human Services Committee on March 10, 2021, about COVID-19 outpatient treatment. It was posted by the AAPS.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it in pandemic-era threads about early treatments and ivermectin, though the claims are contested.

videos.t: "NTFS really isn't that bad" - Robert Collins (LCA 2020)
videos.s: Robert Collins explains why rustup installs were painfully slow on Windows and how changes to rustup and Windows cut install time from 3m30s to 14s. The talk covers NTFS, small files and the cost of antivirus hooks on file close.
videos.w: The go-to reference for why file operations are slow on Windows and how antivirus filters, not NTFS itself, are the cause.
videos.q: This is a great talk on the topic

videos.t: Tom Lehrer - Wernher von Braun
videos.s: Tom Lehrer's satirical song about Wernher von Braun, the German rocket scientist who went from the Nazi missile program to the US space program. It includes the famous line about not caring where the rockets come down.
videos.w: HN quotes it constantly, mostly as a joke or reference, whenever rocketry, engineers' ethics or skill-versus-morality comes up.
videos.q: Tom Lehrer is indeed a national treasure, and his satire is top shelf.

videos.t: Was Roman Concrete Better?
videos.s: Practical Engineering compares modern concrete with that of the Roman Empire, covering modern techniques like roller compacted concrete and water-reducing admixtures. It explains the tradeoffs of Roman construction versus reinforced concrete.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a clear, balanced answer to claims that Roman concrete was better than ours.
videos.q: Here's a good video on the use and tradeoffs of Roman concrete engineering

videos.t: Console Hacking 2016 (33c3)
videos.s: A 33c3 talk by marcan on reverse engineering the PS4 hardware to run Linux with 3D acceleration. It covers how the console differs from a PC and includes a story about tunneling PCIe over RS-232.
videos.w: Recommended as an approachable, detailed look at console hardware architecture, FreeBSD in the PS4 and console hacking.
videos.q: This is a good watch, it goes into detail on the architecture of the PS4

videos.t: The US-Canada Border Is 5,500 Miles of Pure Nonsense
videos.s: CGP Grey walks through the odd history and quirks of the US-Canada border, including how it was surveyed and its irregularities such as exclaves.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an entertaining overview in any thread about border oddities.
videos.q: There's a great CGP Grey video on the Canada-US border well worth watching if this interests you

videos.t: Modern C and What We Can Learn From It - Luca Sas [ ACCU 2021 ]
videos.s: Luca Sas's ACCU 2021 talk on Modern C, a style of C and C-like C++ aligned with data-oriented design. It covers centralized memory management, zero-is-initialization, error handling and API design.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a good overview of modern C patterns, including in threads about learning C.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: This video gives a good overview of some modern patterns in C

videos.t: The One Tiny Law That Keeps Amtrak Terrible
videos.s: Wendover Productions explains why Amtrak trains run late: most Amtrak routes run on freight-owned track, and the law giving passenger trains priority is rarely enforced. The video covers rail ownership versus control and how freight carriers hold the leverage.
videos.w: HN commenters cite it whenever passenger rail delays or expansion come up, as the clearest explanation of freight priority over Amtrak.
videos.q: Wendover Productions made a great video [0] explaining this situation.

videos.t: that dark matter video aged like milk
videos.s: Angela Collier, a physicist, revisits her earlier dark matter video, explaining dark matter as a set of observations rather than a theory and discussing MOND comments.
videos.w: HN points to her videos as a counterpoint to popular dark matter discussion, framing it as the discrepancy that needs explaining.
videos.q: these YouTube videos are a nice counterpoint to a lot of popular communication and discussion on dark matter

videos.t: Daniel Henry Holmes Ingalls Jr.: The Live Web. Drag 'n drop in the cloud
videos.s: Smalltalk pioneer Dan Ingalls presents the Lively Kernel at JSConf US 2012, a live, direct-manipulation programming environment running in the browser. He shows drag-and-drop building of live objects on the web.
videos.w: Commenters link it as a demo of what a live, inspectable, Smalltalk-style environment in the browser can be, in threads about Alan Kay, Smalltalk and web limitations.
videos.q: Dan Ingalls himself presenting his continued work in the browser at JSConf US 2012

videos.t: #NoEstimates (Allen Holub)
videos.s: Allen Holub's keynote arguing that estimation is harmful, particularly in Agile, and presenting planning approaches based on data and flow instead. It covers the distinction between estimation and data-driven prediction.
videos.w: Recommended in estimation and sprint debates as a well-reasoned account of where waste is and isn't in agile.
videos.q: If you want a well-reasoned discussion of where the waste is and isn't, I highly recommend Allen Holub's talk #NoEstimates

videos.t: Ptolemy and Homer (Simpson)
videos.s: A short animation reconstructing a planet's looping orbit using Ptolemy's epicycles and deferents, with the epicycles tracing out the face of Homer Simpson. It shows how enough circles can reproduce nearly any shape.
videos.w: HN uses it as a vivid demonstration that Fourier series and epicycles can fit anything, and as a warning about models with too much wiggle room.
videos.q: This is my favourite visualisation of this fact

videos.t: Why Japan Arrests Foreigners
videos.s: Paolo fromTOKYO explains why foreign tourists get arrested in Japan, covering strict laws and the justice system's very high conviction rate.
videos.w: Commenters mostly use it as a lead-in to recommending interviews with Japanese lawyers about detention and the justice system, and one says they learned from it.
videos.q: I enjoyed learning from this video years ago

videos.t: The UK Election Results Were the Worst in History
videos.s: CGP Grey explains how the 2015 UK general election showed the flaws of first-past-the-post voting, with parties like UKIP winning many votes but few seats.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a short, clear illustration of how first-past-the-post misrepresents voters.
videos.q: Great CGP Grey video on the 2015 General Election in the UK

videos.t: Gridfinity: Your Ultimate Modular Workshop is FREE!
videos.s: Zack Freedman introduces Gridfinity, his free, open-source modular workshop storage system of 3D-printable bins and baseplates. The video walks through the design, the parametric templates and the many module types that fit parts, tools and accessories.
videos.w: HN points people to it as the original explanation of what Gridfinity is and why it exists, in threads about the project and its catalogs.
videos.q: Watching Zack's original video on the concept really helps to cement why this exists.

videos.t: Crust of Rust: Lifetime Annotations
videos.s: In this first Crust of Rust episode, Jon Gjengset live-codes an example that needs multiple explicit lifetime annotations. Along the way he covers string types and generics over a custom trait.
videos.w: Recommended as a slow-paced, detailed live-coding session that makes lifetimes click once you are past Rust basics.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: each one is actually writing carefully chosen code that runs and talking through what's going on

videos.t: Edsger W. Dijkstra on Dutch TV
videos.s: A 2001 VPRO Noorderlicht documentary episode, filmed in Austin in 2000, visiting Edsger Dijkstra and his views on thinking as a discipline. It is in Dutch with English subtitles.
videos.w: Recommended as a short documentary that shows the human side of Dijkstra.
videos.q: For anyone interested in seeing the human side of Dijkstra, I recommend this documentary

videos.t: Lotus Improv for NeXT 1990
videos.s: A 1990 Lotus sales demo of Improv, a spreadsheet built for the NeXT computer that rethought the grid with named categories and multiple views. The uploader, who tested it at Price Waterhouse, presents it as an early, innovative vision of the spreadsheet.
videos.w: HN links it in spreadsheet-reinvention threads as the clearest look at what Improv did differently, with a distinctive NeXTstep aesthetic.
videos.q: for anyone who hasn't seen Lotus Improv before and is both curious about what it did differently

videos.t: Software Art Thou: Glenn Vanderburg - Real Software Engineering
videos.s: Glenn Vanderburg asks whether software development can be real engineering, surveying other engineering disciplines and decades of programming experience. He envisions what a software engineering worthy of the name might look like.
videos.w: HN recommends it in debates about software engineering rigor, agile, and formal methods.
videos.q: he explores the question of whether "software engineering" is or can really be engineering.

videos.t: How I Upgraded My iPhone Memory 800% - in Shenzhen, China
videos.s: Scotty Allen of Strange Parts travels through Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei markets and learns to upgrade an iPhone 6s from 16GB to 128GB by swapping its flash chip. It is part 3 of his custom iPhone series and shows the difficulty of the hands-on repair work.
videos.w: HN people recommend it for its vivid look at Shenzhen's repair culture and for the flash chip upgrade, and cite it in discussions of hardware modding.
videos.q: it gives such a cool sense of Shenzhen as a place to make and modify things

videos.t: Computer Science - A Guide for the Perplexed • Joe Armstrong • GOTO 2018
videos.s: Joe Armstrong's GOTO 2018 talk contrasts the problems computer scientists study with the problems users have. He revisits forgotten great ideas such as tuple spaces, flow-based programming, Xanadu and Unix pipes, with anecdotes.
videos.w: HN calls it a superb, funny and engaging talk, and links it often after Armstrong's death as one of his best.
videos.q: One of my favorite talks by Joe Armstrong

videos.t: Slow Motion Flipping Cat Physics | Smarter Every Day 58
videos.s: Destin of Smarter Every Day films a cat falling in high-speed slow motion to show how cats right themselves in midair, and introduces the physics behind it.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a good visual explanation of how cats land on their feet.
videos.q: This video has a good explanation of the process

videos.t: AI Language Models & Transformers - Computerphile
videos.s: Rob Miles explains on Computerphile how language models generate plausible text and how transformers improved on recurrent networks, with a look at what comes next.
videos.w: Pointed to as an accessible early explanation of transformers and attention for newcomers.
videos.q: You can check-out his other videos on NLP as well they are all excellent.

videos.t: Hans Zimmer - Time (Inception)
videos.s: Hans Zimmer's 'Time', the closing piece from the Inception soundtrack, set to a static image.
videos.w: Recommended as powerful soundtrack music, including for listening while coding.
videos.q: Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard are also great

videos.t: Cracking Enigma in 2021 - Computerphile
videos.s: Dr Mike Pound of Computerphile shows how a modern laptop can crack Enigma, using a ciphertext-only attack based on an older paper. He compares it with the tooling in CrypTool.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a good starting point on practical Enigma cryptanalysis with modern hardware.
videos.q: would be a good place to start.

videos.t: Erik Satie - Gymnopédie No.1
videos.s: A recording of Erik Satie's Gymnopedie No. 1, one of the best-known pieces of minimalist piano music by the French composer.
videos.w: Recommended as an accessible entry to Satie and calm ambient classical music, and mentioned as a famous influence on game soundtracks.
videos.q: perhaps putting a name to it will give you some appreciation for why his work is valued

videos.t: The Smartphone CPU Review You NEED to Watch!
videos.s: Geekerwan reviews smartphone CPUs by power efficiency rather than benchmark scores, with test methodology and chapters on Qualcomm, Apple, Samsung and Google chips. It explains why high benchmark scores can coexist with heat and poor battery life.
videos.w: HN people cite it as detailed data on mobile SoC efficiency, sustained performance and ARM core efficiency curves.
videos.q: explores the power efficiency graphs and that's probably what most phone users really want

videos.t: Differential Synchronization
videos.s: Neil Fraser of Google presents Differential Synchronization, the algorithm behind MobWrite, for keeping multiple copies of a document in sync in real time. The talk argues the approach is robust, convergent and efficient.
videos.w: HN points to it as a simple diff-and-patch alternative to operational transforms and CRDTs for collaborative editing.
videos.q: The really nice bits, though, are that it is a simple algorithm

videos.t: What's It Really like Working at Valve?
videos.s: People Make Games interviewed 16 current and former Valve employees to examine how the company's no-bosses, no-titles structure works in practice, and where it falls short.
videos.w: Recommended as well-researched, interview-based coverage of the Valve model and its failures, often linked in threads about Valve and flat organizations.
videos.q: People Make Games made an enlightening documentary on the Valve model and where it fails

videos.t: Jacob Appelbaum (Part 2/2) Digital Anti-Repression Workshop - April 26 2012
videos.s: Part 2 of a Q&A workshop with security researcher Jacob Appelbaum from April 2012, covering mobile phone security, cellphone forensics, state repression and surveillance. Topics include booting Tails from USB and surveillance self-defense resources.
videos.w: Recommended as a practical talk on privacy and anonymity options, including diskless laptops running Tails.
videos.q: Worth listening to Jake Appelbaum's 'digital anti repression workshop' [1].

videos.t: Ryan Dahl - History of Node.js
videos.s: Ryan Dahl tells the history of Node.js and why he created it at a Phoenix meetup. He explains the push for non-blocking IO on a clean slate rather than extending an existing ecosystem.
videos.w: HN recommends it as the creator's own account of why Node was built and how he thinks about humility.
videos.q: He didn't want to use an ecosystem that had existing blocking code.

videos.t: Farbrausch & Neuro - Masagin (HD Stereo)
videos.s: Masagin is a realtime demoscene production by Farbrausch and Neuro with music by paniq, using animated recursive SVG graphics made in Inkscape. It is a psychedelic, nested-dials audiovisual piece.
videos.w: HN recommends it as a showcase of what the demoscene can do, with high-res antialiased vector graphics and motion blur.
videos.q: features animated, recursive SVGs with antialiasing and motion blur at high rez and high frame rate.

videos.t: The Unix Chainsaw - Gary Bernhardt
videos.s: Gary Bernhardt's Cascadia Ruby Conference 2011 talk on using the Unix shell for practical problem solving. He builds pipelines interactively by iterative refinement, using small tools as levers.
videos.w: Recommended as a brilliant demonstration of how to think in Unix pipelines.
videos.q: gave a great talk about practical problem solving with the unix shell

videos.t: How big is a visible photon?
videos.s: Huygens Optics shows through a laser interference experiment that the question of a photon's size is really about coherence length. It argues that photons exist as energy exchanges between radiation and matter, not as little particles in free space.
videos.w: HN recommends it as an approachable, intuitive explanation of why visible photons can be surprisingly large, from a channel known for practical optics.
videos.q: I like this one for the approachable and intuitive explanation

videos.t: w
videos.s: jan Misali traces the history of the letter W, including why it is called double u. The video is part of a series of deep dives into individual letters.
videos.w: Recommended for readers who enjoy fascinating deep dives into the history of odd letters and the alphabet.
videos.q: If you're interested in fascinating deep dives into the history of a few odd letters

videos.t: Arithmetic, Population and Energy - FULL LENGTH
videos.s: Physicist Albert Bartlett's full-length lecture on how steady exponential growth in population and energy use collides with finite resources. It uses examples like bacteria in a bottle and covers peak oil.
videos.w: HN repeatedly quotes its thesis that humanity's greatest shortcoming is failing to understand the exponential function.
videos.q: it shows a common blindspot in a way that is both clear, enlightening and frightening.

videos.t: Homochirality: Why Nature Never Makes Mirror Molecules
videos.s: Steve Mould explains homochirality: why biological molecules like sugars and amino acids come in only one handedness. He covers ideas about how this asymmetry might have arisen, touching on meteorite samples and RNA.
videos.w: Cited as a clear, accessible explanation of why life uses only one version of chiral molecules.
videos.q: Here is a video talking about molecular chirality and how nature really only produces one version of molecules

videos.t: RustConf 2016 - A Modern Editor Built in Rust by Raph Levien
videos.s: Raph Levien presents Xi editor at RustConf 2016, a high-performance text editor built in Rust. The talk goes into technical details, building polished GUI apps, and running a community-focused open source project.
videos.w: HN lists it among good resources on building text editors and as a recommended lunch-and-learn talk.
videos.cn: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
videos.q: So far I've found and enjoyed reading/watching the resources below

videos.t: The Non-capitalist Solution to the Housing Crisis
videos.s: About Here looks at the housing crisis and argues for non-market solutions such as co-op and social housing, drawing on Vancouver's situation. It discusses how public supply can hold down rents.
videos.w: Recommended in housing threads as a decent dive into the problem and possible long-term solutions.
videos.q: I found this video [0] a decent dive into issues and possible long term solutions.

videos.t: The ascent of Alex Honnold
videos.s: A CBS News (60 Minutes) profile of free solo climber Alex Honnold, who scales sheer rock faces without ropes. Lara Logan reports on his climbing and his apparent lack of fear, including his Half Dome ascent.
